\displaystyle {\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s,
$$ where $C$ is the path along the polar curve $r=4\operatorname{sec}⁡\theta $ for $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{4}.$" :question/worked-solution "The line integral of unity with respect to arc length over $C$ is equal to the arc length $L$ of $C,$ i.e.,

$$
{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s=L.
$$

In polar coordinates, the arc length element $\text{d}s$ is given by

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }\right)}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

So, for a polar curve defined as $r=r(\theta )$ for ${\theta }_{1}\le \theta \le {\theta }_{2},$ we have

$$
L={\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }\right)}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r=4\operatorname{sec}⁡\theta ,$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }=4\operatorname{sec}⁡\theta \operatorname{tan}⁡\theta .
$$

Therefore, we evaluate our line integral as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }\right)}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\sqrt{{(4\operatorname{sec}⁡\theta )}^{2}+{(4\operatorname{sec}⁡\theta \operatorname{tan}⁡\theta )}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\sqrt{16{\sec }^{2}⁡\theta +16{\sec }^{2}⁡\theta {\tan }^{2}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\sqrt{16{\sec }^{2}⁡\theta (1+{\tan }^{2}⁡\theta )}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\sqrt{16{\sec }^{4}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =4{\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}{\sec }^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =4\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta \,{|}_{0}^{\pi /4} \\  & =4[\operatorname{tan}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right)-\operatorname{tan}⁡(0)] \\  & =4.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186447156 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "92d7287d-2c86-57db-807a-ce851e800dbe" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\pi }{2}" :db/id 17592186447122} {:answer/id #uuid "ad21357d-24c8-5905-9453-f8cf49c4c786" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\pi " :db/id 17592186447130} {:answer/id #uuid "bfd8c063-a572-53c2-b4ce-461228304503" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2\pi " :db/id 17592186447134} {:answer/id #uuid "c9ae75cb-ec9f-5d2a-90c0-9d53665a6116" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2\sqrt{2}" :db/id 17592186447136} {:answer/id #uuid "cf8e5566-d63d-5c74-aea1-6e226a17823d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\pi }{\sqrt{2}}" :db/id 17592186447137}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186447137} :answer-field/id #uuid "f262cbb1-b41b-5a16-a002-abeb999c9afc" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186447149}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "6947d1ad-4cd9-585a-b94f-f141875b9f2d" :question/math-academy-id "q-123581" :question/problem "![](images/36/36008a9155a01a07136cee263ce0a89239719227541536e8c2f8ea358d43e6df.png)

Calculate $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s,
$$ where $C$ is the path along the polar curve $r=\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,$ for $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2},$ shown above." :question/worked-solution "The line integral of unity with respect to arc length over $C$ is equal to the arc length $L$ of $C,$ i.e.,

$$
{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s=L.
$$

In polar coordinates, the arc length element $\text{d}s$ is given by

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }\right)}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

So, for a polar curve defined as $r=r(\theta )$ for ${\theta }_{1}\le \theta \le {\theta }_{2},$ we have

$$
L={\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }\right)}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r=\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,$ we have 

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }=\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .
$$

Therefore, we evaluate our line integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }\right)}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{{(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )}^{2}+{(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{{\sin }^{2}⁡\theta +2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +{\cos }^{2}⁡\theta +{\cos }^{2}⁡\theta -2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +{\sin }^{2}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{{\sin }^{2}⁡\theta +\cancel{2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }+{\cos }^{2}⁡\theta +{\cos }^{2}⁡\theta -\cancel{2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }+{\sin }^{2}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{2({\sin }^{2}⁡\theta +{\cos }^{2}⁡\theta )}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\sqrt{2}(\frac{\pi }{2}-0) \\  & =\frac{\pi }{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186447157 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "36dfca93-7965-545e-ae64-ea4e15350f14" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2{\int }_{0}^{3\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{\theta }{3}\right)\,\text{d}\theta " :db/id 17592186447102} {:answer/id #uuid "6b63604b-d8a6-599a-838b-2b74c3f0610a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\sqrt{2}{\int }_{0}^{3\pi }{\sin }^{2}⁡\left(\frac{\theta }{3}\right)\,\text{d}\theta " :db/id 17592186447112} {:answer/id #uuid "76d06d75-8601-5c9f-931a-e187e9f7e576" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2{\int }_{0}^{3\pi }{\cos }^{2}⁡\left(\frac{\theta }{3}\right)\,\text{d}\theta " :db/id 17592186447113} {:answer/id #uuid "8e346b38-71c5-5bc3-bda7-aa1f806c4b1f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{\int }_{0}^{3\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{\theta }{3}\right)\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{\theta }{3}\right)\,\text{d}\theta " :db/id 17592186447120} {:answer/id #uuid "b38cf43c-b624-53ab-921c-a21f0a6ea62f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{\int }_{0}^{3\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{\theta }{3}\right)\,\text{d}\theta " :db/id 17592186447131}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186447113} :answer-field/id #uuid "c16bafac-0287-5357-8266-d49db38ec2b3" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186447147}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "70661cc4-274a-5311-99fc-fa9cf5ff480d" :question/math-academy-id "q-123426" :question/problem "Which of the following is equivalent to $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s,
$$ where $C$ is the path along the polar curve $r=2{\cos }^{3}⁡\left(\frac{\theta }{3}\right)\,$ for $0\le \theta \le 3\pi $ ?" :question/worked-solution "The line integral of unity with respect to arc length over $C$ is equal to the arc length $L$ of $C,$ i.e.,

$$
{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s=L.
$$

In polar coordinates, the arc length element $\text{d}s$ is given by

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }\right)}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

So, for a polar curve defined as $r=r(\theta )$ for ${\theta }_{1}\le \theta \le {\theta }_{2},$ we have

$$
L={\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }\right)}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r=2{\cos }^{3}⁡\left(\frac{\theta }{3}\right)\,$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }=-2{\cos }^{2}⁡\left(\frac{\theta }{3}\right)\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{\theta }{3}\right).
$$

Therefore, the expression for our line integral is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }\right)}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3\pi }\sqrt{{(2{\cos }^{3}⁡\left(\frac{\theta }{3}\right))}^{2}+{(-2{\cos }^{2}⁡\left(\frac{\theta }{3}\right)\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{\theta }{3}\right))}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2{\int }_{0}^{3\pi }\sqrt{{\cos }^{6}⁡\left(\frac{\theta }{3}\right)+{\cos }^{4}⁡\left(\frac{\theta }{3}\right){\sin }^{2}⁡\left(\frac{\theta }{3}\right)}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2{\int }_{0}^{3\pi }{\cos }^{2}⁡\left(\frac{\theta }{3}\right)\sqrt{{\cos }^{2}⁡\left(\frac{\theta }{3}\right)+{\sin }^{2}⁡\left(\frac{\theta }{3}\right)}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2{\int }_{0}^{3\pi }{\cos }^{2}⁡\left(\frac{\theta }{3}\right)\,\text{d}\theta \,.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186447206 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "04c30f5a-bf33-559a-b8a4-5e69bbf5720d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2.923" :db/id 17592186447175} {:answer/id #uuid "3ff7dee6-d555-52cc-9d52-dea07a26c3b1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1.732" :db/id 17592186447180} {:answer/id #uuid "50c8789a-ed1d-5026-941b-7b2b50d0c177" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1.702" :db/id 17592186447184} {:answer/id #uuid "7b195181-6ca7-5730-8661-e95dd7cb57ac" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2.023" :db/id 17592186447189} {:answer/id #uuid "bec1fd83-dfc0-5da0-b29c-9bbb9be7c789" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1.903" :db/id 17592186447195}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186447180} :answer-field/id #uuid "e27dc486-028e-5b85-8121-cb4f3fc8a15b" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186447204}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "47805108-6203-5bb3-98d1-dea670ffc279" :question/math-academy-id "q-84763" :question/problem "A fair $8$-sided die with numbers $1$ through $8$ is rolled $12$ times. What is the standard deviation of the number of times we get an even number? Round your answer to $3$ decimal places." :question/worked-solution "Let the random variable $X$ be equal to the number of times we get an even number.

Here, we have the following information:

- there are $n=12$ rolls of the die

- the probability of getting an even number (i.e., a $2,$ $4,$ $6,$ or $8$) on any roll of the die is

$$
p=\frac{4}{8}=\frac{1}{2}.
$$

So, $X$ follows a binomial distribution, where $X∼B(12,\frac{1}{2}).$

For a binomial random variable $X,$ the standard deviation is given by

$$
\text{SD}[X]=\sqrt{\text{Var}[X]}=\sqrt{np(1-p)},
$$

where $n$ is the number of experiments, and $p$ is the probability of success on each experiment.

So, the standard deviation of the number of times we get an even number is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{SD}[X] & =\sqrt{np(1-p)} \\  & =\sqrt{12\cdot \frac{1}{2}\cdot (1-\frac{1}{2})} \\  & =\sqrt{3} \\  & =1.732\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $3$ decimal places."} {:db/id 17592186447295 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "5a58cff2-1268-5a47-8339-f8986d6b3b53" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{dy}{dt}=3-y" :db/id 17592186447265} {:answer/id #uuid "899816c6-722e-5949-9ce4-1a89698b454a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{dy}{dt}=y-3{y}^{2}" :db/id 17592186447269} {:answer/id #uuid "9d888226-313c-58ec-b603-27ecf200a67a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{dy}{dt}=4+y" :db/id 17592186447271} {:answer/id #uuid "e86aa13e-6c97-5b82-b6ff-679f462956c1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{dy}{dt}=y+3{y}^{2}" :db/id 17592186447285} {:answer/id #uuid "fff1f2be-796e-56e8-9751-6260916e4506" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{dy}{dt}=9-{y}^{2}" :db/id 17592186447287}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186447269} :answer-field/id #uuid "a6064b7d-2ce9-5405-a285-35f32d2b4760" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186447293}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "337615da-7bae-5da8-aef5-ed48be968edc" :question/math-academy-id "q-83852" :question/problem "Which of the following differential equations is a logistic growth equation?" :question/worked-solution "A logistic growth equation has the form

$$
\frac{dy}{dt}=ky(a-y),
$$

where $k>0$ is a constant of proportionality, and $a>y$ is the carrying capacity.

From the given options, the only logistic growth equation is

$$
\frac{dy}{dt}=y-3{y}^{2}.
$$

To see this, let's factor the right-hand side of the equation. This gives,

$$
\frac{dy}{dt}=3y(\frac{1}{3}-y).
$$

From here, we see that the constant of proportionality is $k=3,$ and the carrying capacity is $a=\frac{1}{3}.$"} {:answer/id #uuid "be9a2db1-529d-5628-9061-7052c51aa8d2" :answer/type {:db/id $x{y}^{2}=3-2y$ is the tangent vector to the curve perpendicular to the vector $\mathbf{i}?$" :question/worked-solution "First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}x{y}^{2} & =3-2y \\ x{y}^{2}+2y & =3\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y)=x{y}^{2}+2y,$ our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=3.$ 

A tangent vector to the level curve can be computed as follows:

$$
t(x,y)={f}_{y}(x,y)\,i-{f}_{x}(x,y)\,j
$$

So, we calculate $t(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}t(x,y) & ={f}_{y}(x,y)\,i-{f}_{x}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(x{y}^{2}+2y)\,i-\frac{∂}{∂x}(x{y}^{2}+2y)\,j \\  & =(2xy+2)\,i-{y}^{2}\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Since our tangent vector needs to be perpendicular to $i,$ we must have $t\cdot i=0.$

$$
\begin{aligned}t(x,y)\cdot i & =0 \\ ((2xy+2)\,i-{y}^{2}\,j)\cdot i & =0 \\ 2xy+2 & =0 \\ xy+1 & =0 \\ y & =-\frac{1}{x}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $y=-\frac{1}{x}$ into the equation of our curve gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x{y}^{2} & =3-2y \\ x{\left(-\frac{1}{x}\right)}^{2} & =3-2\left(-\frac{1}{x}\right) \\ \frac{1}{x} & =3+\frac{2}{x} \\ \frac{1}{x} & =-3 \\ x & =-\frac{1}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, for $x=-\frac{1}{3},$ we get $y=3,$ and the corresponding point is $(-\frac{1}{3},3).$"} {:answer/id #uuid "009695df-eb16-5bf9-8f7d-15e791cfc73f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} Substituting $a=⟨1,1,2⟩$ and $b=⟨2,4,4⟩$ into the above expression, we get

$$

Computing $∇f$ and evaluating at $c=⟨{c}_{1},{c}_{2},{c}_{3}⟩,$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f & =⟨4y,4x,-4z⟩ \\ ∇f(c) & =⟨4{c}_{2},4{c}_{1},-4{c}_{3}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}4 & =∇f(c)\cdot ⟨1,3,2⟩ \\ 4 & =⟨4{c}_{2},4{c}_{1},-4{c}_{3}⟩\cdot ⟨1,3,2⟩ \\ 4 & =4{c}_{2}+12{c}_{1}-8{c}_{3} \\ 1 & =3{c}_{1}+{c}_{2}-2{c}_{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

Parametrizing the line, we get

$$

$$

Since $c=⟨{c}_{1},{c}_{2},{c}_{3}⟩$ satisfies the equation of the line, we have

$$
{c}_{1}=t+1,\,{c}_{2}=3t+1,\,{c}_{3}=2t+2.
$$

Substituting the above in the equation $3{c}_{1}+{c}_{2}-2{c}_{3}=1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}3(t+1)+(3t+1)-2(2t+2) & =1 \\ 3t+3+3t+1-4t-4 & =1 \\ 2t & =1 \\ t & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}

We can now find the values of ${c}_{1},$ ${c}_{2},$ and ${c}_{3}.$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{c}_{1} & =\frac{1}{2}+1=\frac{3}{2}, \\ {c}_{2} & =3\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)+1=\frac{5}{2}, \\ {c}_{3} & =2\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)+2=3.\end{aligned}
$$

\begin{aligned}∇f & =⟨-z,3{y}^{2},-x⟩ \\ ∇f(c) & =⟨-{c}_{3},3{c}_{2}^{2},-{c}_{1}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}0 & =∇f(c)\cdot ⟨1,-1,-1⟩ \\ 0 & =⟨-{c}_{3},3{c}_{2}^{2},-{c}_{1}⟩\cdot ⟨1,-1,-1⟩ \\ 0 & =-{c}_{3}-3{c}_{2}^{2}+{c}_{1}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the fact that $C$ lies on $\overset{―}{AB}.$ So, let's first find the equation of the line.

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-0}{1} & =\frac{y-0}{(-1)}=\frac{z-0}{(-1)} \\ x & =-y=-z\end{aligned}
$$

Parametrizing the line, we get

$$
x=t\,\,y=-t,\,z=-t,\,0\le t\le 1.
$$

Since $c=⟨{c}_{1},{c}_{2},{c}_{3}⟩$ satisfies the equation of the line, we have

$$
{c}_{1}=t\,\,{c}_{2}=-t,\,{c}_{3}=-t.
$$

Substituting the above in the equation $-{c}_{3}-3{c}_{2}^{2}+{c}_{1}=0,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}-(-t)-3(-t)^{2}+t & =0 \\ t-3{t}^{2}+t & =0 \\ 2t-3{t}^{2} & =0 \\ t(2-3t) & =0 \\ t & =0,\,\frac{2}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now we proceed to find the coordinates of the points that satisfy the mean value theorem.

- For $t=0,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{c}_{1} & ={c}_{2}={c}_{3}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the coordinates of the first point $C$ are $(0,0,0).$

- For $t=\frac{2}{3},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{c}_{1} & =\frac{2}{3}, \\ {c}_{2} & =-\frac{2}{3}, \\ {c}_{3} & =-\frac{2}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
f(b)-f(a)=∇f(c)·(b-a).
$$

 

Notice that the function $f(x,y)={x}^{3}-xy+1$ is differentiable at each point on the line segment $\overset{―}{AB}.$ So, we can apply the mean value theorem.

Substituting $a=⟨0,1⟩$ and $b=⟨1,3⟩$ into the above expression, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(1,3)-f(0,1) & =∇f(c)\cdot (⟨1,3⟩-⟨0,1⟩) \\ -1-1 & =∇f(c)\cdot ⟨1,2⟩ \\ -2 & =∇f(c)\cdot ⟨1,2⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing $∇f$ and evaluating at $c=⟨{c}_{1},{c}_{2}⟩,$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f & =⟨3{x}^{2}-y,-x⟩, \\ ∇f(c) & =⟨3{{c}_{1}}^{2}-{c}_{2},-{c}_{1}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}-2 & =∇f⟨c⟩\cdot ⟨1,2⟩ \\ -2 & =⟨3{{c}_{1}}^{2}-{c}_{2},-{c}_{1}⟩\cdot ⟨1,2⟩ \\ -2 & =3{{c}_{1}}^{2}-{c}_{2}-2{c}_{1}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the fact that $C$ lies on $\overset{―}{AB}.$ So, let's first find the equation of the line.

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{y-{y}_{a}}{{y}_{b}-{y}_{a}} & =\frac{x-{x}_{a}}{{x}_{b}-{x}_{a}} \\ \frac{y-1}{3-1} & =\frac{x-0}{1-0} \\ \frac{y-1}{2} & =x \\ y & =2x+1.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $c=⟨{c}_{1},{c}_{2}⟩$ satisfies the equation of the line, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{c}_{2} & =2{c}_{1}+1.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the equation $3{{c}_{1}}^{2}-{c}_{2}-2{c}_{1}=-2$, we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}3{{c}_{1}}^{2}-(2{c}_{1}+1)-2{c}_{1} & =-2 \\ 3{{c}_{1}}^{2}-4{c}_{1}+1 & =0 \\ (3{c}_{1}-1)({c}_{1}-1) & =0 \\ {c}_{1} & =\frac{1}{3},\,1.\end{aligned}
$$

Now we proceed to find the coordinates of the points that satisfy the mean value theorem.

- For ${c}_{1}=\frac{1}{3},$ we obtain

$$
{c}_{2}=2\left(\frac{1}{3}\right)+1=\frac{5}{3}.
$$

Therefore, the coordinates of the first point are $(\frac{1}{3},\frac{5}{3}).$

- For ${c}_{1}=1,$ we obtain

$$
{c}_{2}=2(1)+1=3.
$$

Therefore, the coordinates of the second point are $(1,3).$

Finally we can conclude that the coordinates of the points that satisfy the mean value theorem are $(\frac{1}{3},\frac{5}{3})$ and $(1,3).$"} {:db/id 17592186447640 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0222ab38-0a5d-5644-b548-b49f314a6f5e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(\frac{5}{2},\frac{7}{2})" :db/id 17592186447480} {:answer/id #uuid "6f049334-5ef6-5847-8455-946eb960be10" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(2,\frac{7}{2})" :db/id 17592186447534} {:answer/id #uuid "9718bb12-ffd6-5092-abb0-5cf104f4bf17" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(\frac{8}{3},\frac{11}{3})" :db/id 17592186447560} {:answer/id #uuid "a6a5f9b0-a9d6-5235-859a-a70242d8865e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(\frac{3}{2},\frac{7}{2})" :db/id 17592186447567} {:answer/id #uuid "df2c5b96-7e46-538a-b432-978f7151418c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(\frac{7}{5},\frac{19}{5})" :db/id 17592186447587}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186447567} :answer-field/id #uuid "301da0d6-3394-5ca9-822c-794b43878a03" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186447603}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "cde771f2-0ae1-5186-919d-63d0f22b095d" :question/math-academy-id "q-36826" :question/problem "Find a point that satisfies the mean value theorem for $f(x,y)=3{y}^{2}+xy+2{x}^{2}$ on the line segment $\overset{―}{AB},$ where the position vectors of $A$ and $B$ are $a=⟨0,3⟩$ and $b=⟨3,4⟩,$ respectively." :question/worked-solution "The mean value theorem states that if $f(x,y)$ is differentiable at each point on the line segment $\overset{―}{AB},$ then there exists a point $C\in \overset{―}{AB}$ with position vector $c$ such that

$$
f(b)-f(a)=∇f(c)·(b-a).
$$

Notice that the function $f(x,y)=3{y}^{2}+xy+2{x}^{2}$ is differentiable at each point on the line segment $\overset{―}{AB}.$ So, we can apply the mean value theorem.

Substituting $a=⟨0,3⟩$ and $b=⟨3,4⟩$ into the above expression, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(3,4)-f(0,3) & =∇f(c)\cdot (⟨3,4⟩-⟨0,3⟩) \\ 3(4)^{2}+3(4)+2(3)^{2}-(3(3)^{2}+0(3)+2(0)^{2}) & =∇f(c)\cdot ⟨3,1⟩ \\ 51 & =∇f(c)\cdot ⟨3,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing $∇f$ and evaluating at $c=⟨{c}_{1},{c}_{2}⟩,$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f & =⟨4x+y,x+6y⟩, \\ ∇f(c) & =⟨4{c}_{1}+{c}_{2},{c}_{1}+6{c}_{2}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}51 & =∇f⟨c⟩\cdot ⟨3,1⟩ \\ 51 & =⟨4{c}_{1}+{c}_{2},{c}_{1}+6{c}_{2}⟩\cdot ⟨3,1⟩ \\ 51 & =12{c}_{1}+3{c}_{2}+{c}_{1}+6{c}_{2} \\ 51 & =13{c}_{1}+9{c}_{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the fact that $C$ lies on $\overset{―}{AB}.$ So, let's first find the equation of the line.

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{y-{y}_{a}}{{y}_{b}-{y}_{a}} & =\frac{x-{x}_{a}}{{x}_{b}-{x}_{a}} \\ \frac{y-3}{4-3} & =\frac{x-0}{3-0} \\ y-3 & =\frac{x}{3} \\ y & =\frac{x}{3}+3.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $c=⟨{c}_{1},{c}_{2}⟩$ satisfies the equation of the line, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{c}_{2} & =\frac{{c}_{1}}{3}+3.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the equation $13{c}_{1}+9{c}_{2}=51,$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}13{c}_{1}+9(\frac{{c}_{1}}{3}+3) & =51 \\ 13{c}_{1}+3{c}_{1}+27 & =51 \\ 16{c}_{1} & =24 \\ {c}_{1} & =\frac{3}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we find $$
\displaystyle {c}_{2}=\frac{{c}_{1}}{3}+3=\frac{7}{2}.
$$ So, the point $C$ that satisfies the mean value theorem is $(\frac{3}{2},\frac{7}{2}).$"} {:db/id 17592186447641 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "102ed920-ce8d-56fe-b777-875c7526e3cc" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(0,0,0)" :db/id 17592186447486} {:answer/id #uuid "5bd61385-d886-5f5b-99fd-e976df1a87a2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}},\frac{4}{\sqrt{3}},\frac{5}{\sqrt{3}})" :db/id 17592186447522} {:answer/id #uuid "5d9cb7a3-ee66-57e2-b4d2-ed1892ce5fbf" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(1,2,\frac{5}{2})" :db/id 17592186447523} {:answer/id #uuid "6aaf3b28-e8a1-5430-9157-532cf5a5a3a9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(2,4,5)" :db/id 17592186447533} {:answer/id #uuid "7e59e230-39cc-5cb0-843b-3ae813f2f120" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}},\frac{4}{\sqrt{5}},\sqrt{5})" :db/id 17592186447544}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186447522} :answer-field/id #uuid "e986ee90-2a8a-564a-b524-a14859996d35" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186447623}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "db61b5b3-00ff-5d08-ac35-b46068ec6075" :question/math-academy-id "q-106860" :question/problem "Find a point that satisfies the mean value theorem for $f(x,y,z)=xyz$ on the line segment $\overset{―}{AB},$ where the position vectors of $A$ and $B$ are $a=⟨0,0,0⟩$ and $b=⟨2,4,5⟩,$ respectively." :question/worked-solution "The mean value theorem states that if $f(x,y,z)$ is differentiable at each point on the line segment $\overset{―}{AB},$ then there exists a point $C\in \overset{―}{AB}$ with position vector $c$ such that

$$

Notice that $f(x,y,z)=xyz$ is differentiable at each point on the line segment $\overset{―}{AB}.$ So, we can apply the mean value theorem.

Substituting $a=⟨0,0,0⟩$ and $b=⟨2,4,5⟩$ into the above expression, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(2,4,5)-f(0,0,0) & =∇f(c)\cdot (⟨2,4,5⟩-⟨0,0,0⟩) \\ 40-0 & =∇f(c)\cdot ⟨2,4,5⟩ \\ 40 & =∇f(c)\cdot ⟨2,4,5⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing $∇f$ and evaluating at $c=⟨{c}_{1},{c}_{2},{c}_{3}⟩,$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f & =⟨yz,xz,xy⟩ \\ ∇f(c) & =⟨{c}_{2}{c}_{3},{c}_{1}{c}_{3},{c}_{1}{c}_{2}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}40 & =∇f(c)\cdot ⟨2,4,5⟩ \\ 40 & =⟨{c}_{2}{c}_{3},{c}_{1}{c}_{3},{c}_{1}{c}_{2}⟩\cdot ⟨2,4,5⟩ \\ 40 & =2{c}_{2}{c}_{3}+4{c}_{1}{c}_{3}+5{c}_{1}{c}_{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the fact that $C$ lies on $\overset{―}{AB}.$ So, let's first find the equation of the line.

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-0}{2} & =\frac{y-0}{4}=\frac{z-0}{5} \\ \frac{x}{2} & =\frac{y}{4}=\frac{z}{5}\end{aligned}
$$

Parametrizing the line, we get

$$
x=2t,\,\,y=4t,\,z=5t,\,0\le t\le 1.
$$

Since $c=⟨{c}_{1},{c}_{2},{c}_{3}⟩$ satisfies the equation of the line, we have

$$
{c}_{1}=2t\,\,{c}_{2}=4t,\,{c}_{3}=5t.
$$

Substituting the above in the equation $2{c}_{2}{c}_{3}+4{c}_{1}{c}_{3}+5{c}_{1}{c}_{2}=40,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}2(4t)(5t)+4(2t)(5t)+5(2t)(4t) & =40 \\ 40{t}^{2}+40{t}^{2}+40{t}^{2} & =40 \\ 120{t}^{2} & =40 \\ {t}^{2} & =\frac{1}{3} \\ t & =\pm \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $-\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}<0<1,$ it's clear that $t=-\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$ corresponds to a point that does not lie on $\overset{―}{AB}.$ Therefore, we can ignore it. Thus, $t=\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}.$

For $t=\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}},$ we can now find the values of ${c}_{1},$ ${c}_{2},$ and ${c}_{3}.$  This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{c}_{1} & =2\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\right)=\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}, \\ {c}_{2} & =4\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\right)=\frac{4}{\sqrt{3}}, \\ {c}_{3} & =5\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\right)=\frac{5}{\sqrt{3}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the coordinates of $C$ are $$
\displaystyle (\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}},\frac{4}{\sqrt{3}},\frac{5}{\sqrt{3}}).

"3ed7acf8-9750-5997-81ee-fb6a8cd2e910" :question/math-academy-id "q-76685" :question/problem "Evaluate the integral $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{C}(x-y)\,\text{d}s,
$$ where the curve $C$ is given in polar form by $r=\sqrt{\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta }\,$ for $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{4}.$" :question/worked-solution "In polar coordinates, the formula for the line integral is given by

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }\right)}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

 

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =\sqrt{\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta }\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \sqrt{\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta }, \\ y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =\sqrt{\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta }\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \sqrt{\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta }.\end{aligned}
$$

So, along our curve, we have $x=\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \sqrt{\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta }$ and $y=\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \sqrt{\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta }$, where $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{4}.$

Now, if $f(x,y)=x-y$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \sqrt{\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta }-\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \sqrt{\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta } \\  & =(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\sqrt{\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta }.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(\theta ) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta }(\sqrt{\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta }) \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta }}\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta )\cdot 2 \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta }{\sqrt{\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta }}\end{aligned}
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }\right)}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  & =\sqrt{\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta +\frac{{\cos }^{2}⁡2\theta }{\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta }} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{{\sin }^{2}⁡2\theta +{\cos }^{2}⁡2\theta }{\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta }} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta }} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta }}.\end{aligned}
$$

   

Finally, we now evaluate the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}(x-y)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }\right)}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\sqrt{\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta }\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta }}\cdot \text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )\,{|}_{0}^{\pi /4} \\  & =(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}+\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2})-(0+1) \\  & =\sqrt{2}-1\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186455447 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1b7d45a6-b7b5-5b6e-a82c-a1748d83e603" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-9\pi " :db/id 17592186454946} {:answer/id #uuid "7e4f36c3-2d0c-50c9-a36d-272fd914e84a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3\pi " :db/id 17592186455133} {:answer/id #uuid "c26f1bdf-26e0-5acd-bbc9-1a8e6be78f5f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-3\pi " :db/id 17592186455239} {:answer/id #uuid "c3275529-012a-5a31-82a4-2f28fcd1acb1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0" :db/id 17592186455240} {:answer/id #uuid "ff6f64d6-184a-5394-8a28-a8c004572db7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "9\pi " :db/id 17592186455340}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186455240} :answer-field/id #uuid "bbf611c1-7a64-56ff-a8ce-599f171848cc" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186455404}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "442b3fed-648b-5cc8-977b-6700ae26738b" :question/math-academy-id "q-125482" :question/problem "Calculate the circulation $Γ$ of the vector field $\mathbf{F}(x,y)=\frac{1}{y}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\frac{1}{x}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}$ along the circle $C$ with equation ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=9$ oriented counterclockwise." :question/worked-solution "The closed curve $C$ is the circle of radius $3$ centered at the origin. It can be parameterized in the counterclockwise direction as

$$
r(t)=3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j,\,0\le t\le 2\pi .
$$

The circulation $Γ$ measures the total work done by a force $F$ in moving a particle along a *closed* curve $C.$
It is given by the formula

$$
Γ={∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=3\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=3\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

So,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =\frac{1}{y}\,i+\frac{1}{x}\,j \\  & =\frac{1}{3\operatorname{sin}⁡t}\,i+\frac{1}{3\operatorname{cos}⁡t}\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,j \\  & =-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =(\frac{1}{3\operatorname{sin}⁡t}\,i+\frac{1}{3\operatorname{cos}⁡t}\,j)\cdot (-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j) \\  & =\frac{1}{3\operatorname{sin}⁡t}\cdot (-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)+\frac{1}{3\operatorname{cos}⁡t}\cdot 3\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\  & =-1+1 \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, we conclude that:

$$
\begin{aligned}Γ={∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t=0\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186455449 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "89a99bb2-59a1-56e7-886a-f86b8515a140" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "6e^{8-4x}" :db/id 17592186455153}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186455153} :answer-field/id #uuid "a6f760f5-5d84-52a0-b935-56a6e8048378" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186455395}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "45c14947-ce9d-54ff-a45e-efd6339354f3" :question/math-academy-id "q-343941" :question/problem "Consider the initial value problem

$$
{y}^{′}+4y=f(x),\,y(2)=6
$$

where $f(x)$ is a $3$-periodic function. Fill in the missing part in the solution of the IVP, where the infinite sum on the right-hand side below represents a particular solution ${y}_{p}$ of the differential equation.

*Hint: In this specific problem, the forcing function $f(x)$ is chosen such that the particular solution ${y}_{p}$ satisfies ${y}_{p}(2)=0.$*

The solution is 

$y(x)∼$   
{{field-1}} 
$$
\displaystyle +{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }({a}_{n}\cos \,(\frac{2\pi n}{3}x)+{b}_{n}\sin \,(\frac{2\pi n}{3}x))
$$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that the general solution of a linear differential equation of the form ${y}^{′}+P(x)y=f(x)$ is given by

$$
y={y}_{c}+{y}_{p},
$$

where ${y}_{c}$ is the general solution of the corresponding homogeneous equation, and ${y}_{p}$ is a particular solution.

First, we find the homogeneous solution. The general solution of ${y}^{′}+4y=0$ is 

$$
{y}_{c}=A{e}^{-4x},
$$

where $A$ is an arbitrary constant.

Next, we identify the form of the general solution. Because the operator ${y}^{′}+4y$ involves a first derivative, a periodic forcing function $f(x)$ results in a particular solution containing both sine and cosine terms:

$$
y(x)∼A{e}^{-4x}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }({a}_{n}\cos \,(\frac{2\pi n}{3}x)+{b}_{n}\sin \,(\frac{2\pi n}{3}x))
$$

Now, we apply the initial condition $y(2)=6.$ Using the hint that the particular solution part evaluates to zero at $x=2,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}y(2) & =A{e}^{-4(2)}+{y}_{p}(2) \\ 6 & =A{e}^{-8}+0 \\ A & =6{e}^{8}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute $A$ back into the homogeneous part:

$$
{y}_{c}=(6{e}^{8}){e}^{-4x}=6{e}^{8-4x}
$$

Therefore, the solution is

$$
y(x)∼6{e}^{8-4x}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }({a}_{n}\cos \,(\frac{2\pi n}{3}x)+{b}_{n}\sin \,(\frac{2\pi n}{3}x)).
$$"} {:db/id 17592186455453 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "4b297024-5803-5e1f-806e-e9147fe90127" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{2+\pi }{4}" :db/id 17592186455031} {:answer/id #uuid "77014ac8-9188-566a-ab76-fd0f1159cb28" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1+2\pi }{4}" :db/id 17592186455121} {:answer/id #uuid "a33f9d01-31ec-5113-88f0-e574bdf8e345" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1+2\pi }{2}" :db/id 17592186455192} {:answer/id #uuid "cf548da9-86b9-58e8-bfb8-e84b31a042ef" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{4+\pi }{4}" :db/id 17592186455267} {:answer/id #uuid "f822b4a7-0b96-5267-a032-717ecb4736cb" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1+\pi }{4}" :db/id 17592186455328}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186455031} :answer-field/id #uuid "cfa59a1c-e79f-5e55-9bec-480e8a735e4d" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186455411}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "50bd506e-5f91-5da4-a6e7-565dbeb70122" :question/math-academy-id "q-165416" :question/problem "Evaluate the integral $$

$$

So, along our curve, we have $x=\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \sqrt[3]{\operatorname{sin}⁡3\theta }$ and $y=\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \sqrt[3]{\operatorname{sin}⁡3\theta }$, where $$
\displaystyle \frac{\pi }{4}\le \theta \le \frac{3\pi }{4}.
$$

Now, if $f(x,y)={y}^{2}$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & =(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \sqrt[3]{\operatorname{sin}⁡3\theta })^{2} \\  & ={\sin }^{2}⁡\theta \sqrt[3]{{\sin }^{2}⁡3\theta }.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta } & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta }(\sqrt[3]{\operatorname{sin}⁡3\theta }) \\  & =3\cdot \frac{1}{3\sqrt[3]{{\sin }^{2}⁡3\theta }}\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡3\theta  \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡3\theta }{\sqrt[3]{{\sin }^{2}⁡3\theta }}\end{aligned}
$$

$$" :question/worked-solution "In polar coordinates, the formula for the line integral is given by

$$

$$

 

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =\sqrt[3]{\operatorname{cos}⁡3\theta }\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \sqrt[3]{\operatorname{cos}⁡3\theta }, \\ y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =\sqrt[3]{\operatorname{cos}⁡3\theta }\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \sqrt[3]{\operatorname{cos}⁡3\theta }.\end{aligned}
$$

So, along our curve, we have $x=\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \sqrt[3]{\operatorname{cos}⁡3\theta }$ and $y=\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \sqrt[3]{\operatorname{cos}⁡3\theta }$, where $$
\displaystyle -\frac{\pi }{4}\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{4}.
$$

Now, if $f(x,y)={x}^{2}$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & =(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \sqrt[3]{\operatorname{cos}⁡3\theta })^{2} \\  & ={\cos }^{2}⁡\theta \sqrt[3]{{\cos }^{2}⁡3\theta }.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta } & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta }(\sqrt[3]{\operatorname{cos}⁡3\theta }) \\  & =3\cdot \frac{1}{3\sqrt[3]{{\cos }^{2}⁡3\theta }}\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡3\theta ) \\  & =-\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡3\theta }{\sqrt[3]{{\cos }^{2}⁡3\theta }}\end{aligned}
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }\right)}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  & =\sqrt{(\sqrt[3]{\operatorname{cos}⁡3\theta })^{2}+{\left(-\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡3\theta }{\sqrt[3]{{\cos }^{2}⁡3\theta }}\right)}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{\sqrt[3]{{\cos }^{2}⁡3\theta }+\frac{{\sin }^{2}⁡3\theta }{\sqrt[3]{{\cos }^{4}⁡3\theta }}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{{\cos }^{2}⁡3\theta +{\sin }^{2}⁡3\theta }{\sqrt[3]{{\cos }^{4}⁡3\theta }}} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt[3]{{\cos }^{2}⁡3\theta }}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we now evaluate the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}{x}^{2}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{-\pi /4}^{\pi /4}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }\right)}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /4}^{\pi /4}{\cos }^{2}⁡\theta \sqrt[3]{{\cos }^{2}⁡3\theta }\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt[3]{{\cos }^{2}⁡3\theta }}\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /4}^{\pi /4}{\cos }^{2}⁡\theta \text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{-\pi /4}^{\pi /4}(1+\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta )\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{[\theta +\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta ]}_{-\pi /4}^{\pi /4} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\frac{\pi }{4}+\frac{1}{2}-(-\frac{\pi }{4}-\frac{1}{2})) \\  & =\frac{2+\pi }{4}\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186455480 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0810bb3f-c2fa-58b5-b891-5c4514181eb0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{2}x)({\sum }_{n=0}^{\infty }{a}_{n}+4)" :db/id 17592186454923} {:answer/id #uuid "3a590d58-adcd-5aee-ba5f-885b57614221" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{2}x)(-4-{\sum }_{n=0}^{\infty }{a}_{n})" :db/id 17592186454998} {:answer/id #uuid "6ef76db9-b5c3-5953-bc60-e1853032b616" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{2}x)(-4-{\sum }_{n=0}^{\infty }{a}_{n})" :db/id 17592186455108} {:answer/id #uuid "a4e1e40b-afb1-57b5-bd98-93d521a6c0e6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{2}x)(-4+{\sum }_{n=0}^{\infty }{a}_{n})" :db/id 17592186455193}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186455108} :answer-field/id #uuid "69a096f9-2884-52fa-b0ef-ba88ca249a75" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045494} :db/id 17592186455371}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "96918677-d74f-5a11-bcee-c80ebc5a3b95" :question/math-academy-id "q-344035" :question/problem "$$
{y}^{″}+2y=f(x),\,y(0)=-4,\,{y}^{′}(0)=0
$$

Consider the initial value problem above, where $f(x)$ is an even, $4$-periodic function. Select the missing part in the solution of the IVP, where the second infinite sum on the right-hand side below represents a particular solution of the differential equation.

$$
y(x)∼{{field-1}}+{\sum }_{n=0}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\cos \,(\frac{n\pi }{2}x)
$$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that the general solution of a linear differential equation of the form ${y}^{″}+{\omega }^{2}y=f(x)$ is given by $y={y}_{c}+{y}_{p},$ where ${y}_{c}$ is the solution to the homogeneous equation and ${y}_{p}$ is a particular solution.

First, we address the particular solution ${y}_{p}.$ Since $f(x)$ is an even function and the differential operator contains no ${y}^{′}$ (damping) term, the particular solution inherits the symmetry and is also an even function consisting only of cosine terms. This is represented by the term

$$
{y}_{p}(x)={\sum }_{n=0}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\cos \,(\frac{n\pi }{2}x).
$$

Next, we find the homogeneous solution. The characteristic equation ${\lambda }^{2}+2=0$ gives roots $\lambda =\pm \sqrt{2}\text{i}.$ So, we have

$$
{y}_{c}=A\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{2}x)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{2}x).
$$

To find the unknown constants, we apply the initial conditions. Differentiating the total solution gives

$$
{y}^{′}(x)∼-A\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{2}x)+B\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{2}x)-{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{n\pi }{2}{a}_{n}\sin \,(\frac{n\pi }{2}x).
$$

Using the derivative condition ${y}^{′}(0)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(0) & =-A\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(0)+B\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)-{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{n\pi }{2}{a}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(0) \\ 0 & =0+B\sqrt{2}-0 \\ B & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Note that because the total solution is an even function, its derivative is an odd function, which must vanish at $x=0.$

Next, we use the condition $y(0)=-4.$ With $B=0,$ the total solution is

$$
y(x)∼A\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{2}x)+{\sum }_{n=0}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\cos \,(\frac{n\pi }{2}x).
$$

Applying $y(0)=-4$ and noting that $\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)=1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}-4 & =A+{\sum }_{n=0}^{\infty }{a}_{n} \\ A & =-4-{\sum }_{n=0}^{\infty }{a}_{n}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $A$ back into ${y}_{c}=A\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{2}x),$ we find the missing part:

$$
y(x)∼\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{2}x)(-4-{\sum }_{n=0}^{\infty }{a}_{n})+{\sum }_{n=0}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\cos \,(\frac{n\pi }{2}x)
$$"} {:db/id 17592186455509 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "30e86b23-ab58-5191-ad26-f69ae3689883" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{81}{64}" :db/id 17592186454977} {:answer/id #uuid "436fc72b-b372-56c4-8b22-e7ad0b501850" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{27}{32}" :db/id 17592186455016} {:answer/id #uuid "669bf703-838e-5938-ae0d-38fb979f2c88" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{27}{128}" :db/id 17592186455090} {:answer/id #uuid "79e64d1a-8928-56a0-b539-e3221053a6ad" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{27}{64}" :db/id 17592186455127} {:answer/id #uuid "fb8a62c2-9594-5471-887e-0b239c4e7aad" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{9}{128}" :db/id 17592186455336}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186455090} :answer-field/id #uuid "d0754811-61f8-5b43-b64d-d1916d6e8f79" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186455412}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "eec86b54-2bc2-5f46-8f9a-0f8c56be4962" :question/math-academy-id "q-76769" :question/problem "Evaluate the integral $$

{{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "Applying the average value formula, we find that the average value of the function is

Consider the path $C$ shown above. Which of the following is equivalent to the line integral 

$$
{∮}_{C}({y}^{2}-\operatorname{ln}(1+{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}x))\hspace{0.167em}\mathrm{d}x+({x}^{2}+3xy)\hspace{0.167em}\mathrm{d}y\hspace{0.167em}?
$$" :question/worked-solution "Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

In our case, the region $D$ and its boundary $C$ satisfy the conditions of Green's theorem:

![](images/48/4822bfa926feccb0a12c14580ac325f4f10a0e4f815d0247b2231bf08b8c2326.png)

Since $P(x,y)={y}^{2}-\operatorname{ln}(1+{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}x)$ and $Q(x,y)={x}^{2}+3xy,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}=2y,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=2x+3y.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}({y}^{2}-\operatorname{ln}(1+{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}x))\hspace{0.167em}\mathrm{d}x+({x}^{2}+3xy)\hspace{0.167em}\mathrm{d}y & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(2x+3y-2y)\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(2x+y)\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that the region $D$ can be represented in polar coordinates as

$$
Δ=\{(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 2,\,\frac{\pi }{2}\le \theta \le \pi \}.
$$

The change of variables formula for plane polar coordinates states that 

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

Therefore, we can write our double integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}(2x+y)\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}(2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }\,{\int }_{0}^{2}{r}^{2}(2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,dr\,d\theta .\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186459214 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "32fd1c99-c75a-5e72-bdbc-62e3df1f62af" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "⟨3,\,5,\,4⟩" :db/id 17592186458725} {:answer/id #uuid "3ab1590d-78ce-55f3-b79e-b8a03c6af2c8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "⟨5,\,4,\,3⟩" :db/id 17592186458740} {:answer/id #uuid "41c7b8fc-82a3-509f-bd64-4222260a2212" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "⟨4,\,3,\,5⟩" :db/id 17592186458749} {:answer/id #uuid "5585ea1a-956a-530b-bd90-d0d4394646d5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "⟨4,\,5,\,3⟩" :db/id 17592186458775} {:answer/id #uuid "ef5d7403-6a5c-5a33-afde-3d0beaeb0501" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "⟨0,\,3,\,7⟩" :db/id 17592186459052}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186458775} :answer-field/id #uuid "5d3e9841-7ba0-53f6-959d-76e8dffb6e00" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186459125}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "1b76a888-c386-580d-abe0-7db8002d6871" :question/math-academy-id "q-98163" :question/problem "Calculate $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{0}^{1}[\frac{2}{3}f(t)+\frac{1}{2}g(t)]\,\text{d}t
$$ given that $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{0}^{1}f(t)\,\text{d}t=⟨3,\,6,\,-3⟩

\displaystyle {\int }_{0}^{1}g(t)\,\text{d}t=⟨4,\,2,\,10⟩.
$$" :question/worked-solution "From the vector addition and scalar multiplication rules, we have

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}f(c)(b-a) & ={\int }_{a}^{b}f(x)\,\text{d}x \\ f(c) & =\frac{1}{b-a}{\int }_{a}^{b}f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{4-(-2)}{\int }_{-2}^{4}2{x}^{2}+10\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\frac{1}{6}\cdot (\frac{2{x}^{3}}{3}+10x)|}_{-2}^{4} \\  & =\frac{1}{6}[(\frac{2\cdot {4}^{3}}{3}+10\cdot 4)-(\frac{2\cdot (-2)^{3}}{3}+10\cdot (-2))] \\  & =\frac{1}{6}\cdot 108 \\  & =18.\end{aligned}

$$"} {:db/id 17592186459219 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "244c1d8b-d2e8-5d24-8f75-383e240735c7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{3\sqrt{3}}{4\pi }" :db/id 17592186458700}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186458700} :answer-field/id #uuid "d8b7040b-1c28-5651-827d-d9a23db3b9d8" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186459185}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "280ecae1-be4d-57a7-89a2-e0f1aff5f58a" :question/math-academy-id "q-344694" :question/problem "Find the average value ${f}_{\text{avg}}$ of the function $f(x)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)$ on the interval $[0,\frac{\pi }{3}].$ Do not round the answer.

$$

Now, since

 we have that

$$

Applying Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}({e}^{x}-8{x}^{2}y)dx+({y}^{7}+8x{y}^{2})\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(8{y}^{2}-(-8{x}^{2}))\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}8({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that the region $D$ can be represented in polar coordinates as

$$

$$

The change of variables formula for plane polar coordinates states that

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .

Finally, we can calculate our double integral, as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}8({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}8({r}^{2}{\cos }^{2}⁡\theta +{r}^{2}{\sin }^{2}⁡\theta )\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{0}{\int }_{0}^{2}8{r}^{3}({\cos }^{2}⁡\theta +{\sin }^{2}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{0}{\int }_{0}^{2}8{r}^{3}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{0}[2{r}^{4}]_{0}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{0}32\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =32[\theta ]_{-\pi /2}^{0} \\  & =32\cdot \frac{\pi }{2} \\  & =16\pi .\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186459225 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "2117bd03-1c6f-5cad-b477-24bd9e729cc6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2\pi +1" :db/id 17592186458694} {:answer/id #uuid "23985b75-b87d-5b4e-ad83-43ea19508d98" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2\pi " :db/id 17592186458698} {:answer/id #uuid "70d83f85-c4ae-51b5-a84d-afc0738bd70a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\pi -1" :db/id 17592186458825} {:answer/id #uuid "a749ad1d-665b-5427-9988-ca625952b300" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\pi " :db/id 17592186458928} {:answer/id #uuid "ed479c26-ff80-5972-bd9a-95bf483b94d8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3-\pi " :db/id 17592186459048}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186458928} :answer-field/id #uuid "bc27ed2e-bc72-50af-9261-a3b5d2e0cb7f" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186459167}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "3643194d-d38f-5e28-b2ac-1e1d3a327966" :question/math-academy-id "q-129290" :question/problem "Find $$

$b$" :question/worked-solution "First, we apply the distributive law:

$$
\begin{aligned}2a+8(\frac{5a}{2}-\frac{b}{4}) &= 2a+8\left(\frac{5a}{2}\right)-8\left(\frac{b}{4}\right) \\ &= 2a+\frac{40a}{2}-\frac{8b}{4} \\ &= 2a+20a-2b\end{aligned}

Then, we collect and combine the like terms, simplifying the coefficients as much as possible:

$$
{∮}_{C}(x+y)\hspace{0.167em}\mathrm{d}x-{x}^{2}y\hspace{0.167em}\mathrm{d}y={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\hspace{-0.167em}{\int }_{0}^{5}\enclose{box}{\phantom{AAAAAAAA}}\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}r\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}\theta ,
$$

where $C$ is the circle ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=25$ oriented counterclockwise, what is the missing part of the equation?" :question/worked-solution "Green's theorem states that 

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

In our case, the region $D$ and its boundary $C$ satisfy the conditions of Green's theorem:

![](images/04/0470588a034222b183694b087d417e8ead0d2fd72357e796373794d00523708f.png)

Since $P(x,y)=x+y$ and $Q(x,y)=-{x}^{2}y,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}=1,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=-2xy.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}(x+y)\,dx-{x}^{2}y\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-2xy-1)\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that the region $D$ can be represented in polar coordinates as

$$
Δ=\{(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 5,\,0\le \theta \le 2\pi \}.
$$

The change of variables formula for plane polar coordinates states that 

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

Therefore, we can write our double integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}(-2xy-1)\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}(-2\cdot r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -1)\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}(-2{r}^{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -r)\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,{\int }_{0}^{5}-{r}^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )-r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186459237 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "5bd28227-284a-5a33-8f08-23296c53f5df" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "⟨\frac{3}{4},\,-3,\,-14⟩" :db/id 17592186458781} {:answer/id #uuid "69245a2b-24ad-57f6-b7b2-9025bc32aa3a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "⟨-1,\,0,\,-2⟩" :db/id 17592186458812} {:answer/id #uuid "89b404f6-abb3-55f4-987d-b91201cfbab7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "⟨4,\,1,\,\frac{1}{3}⟩" :db/id 17592186458870} {:answer/id #uuid "90811072-dc3c-55b9-bba4-9fd3bbbf2d7e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "⟨0,\,\frac{3}{2},\,-5⟩" :db/id 17592186458881} {:answer/id #uuid "c27ac7a2-3ca9-59a9-a856-170e1f39ded5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "⟨-3,\,-3,\,-14⟩" :db/id 17592186458978}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186458978} :answer-field/id #uuid "0bd20933-4707-5b47-8e83-30dc4abf3031" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186459090}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "502c15a4-2b20-54ef-9a03-875448a388c3" :question/math-academy-id "q-129152" :question/problem "Calculate $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{1}^{3}[4f(t)-3g(t)]\,\text{d}t

\displaystyle {\int }_{1}^{3}g(t)\,\text{d}t=⟨\frac{2}{3},\,-1,\,2⟩.

$$

Therefore,

$$

$$

and 
$$

Consider the path $C$ shown above. Given that $\mathbf{F}(x,y)=⟨y+\frac{2}{3}{y}^{3},\hspace{0.222em}\operatorname{ln}({y}^{2}+10)+2x⟩,$ which of the following is equivalent to $$
{∮}_{C}\mathbf{F}\cdot \mathrm{d}\mathbf{r}\hspace{0.167em}?
$$" :question/worked-solution "First, notice that we can rewrite our integral as 

$$
{∮}_{C}\mathbf{F}\cdot \mathrm{d}\mathbf{r}={∮}_{C}(y+\frac{2}{3}{y}^{3})\hspace{0.222em}\mathrm{d}x+(\operatorname{ln}({y}^{2}+10)+2x)\hspace{0.222em}\mathrm{d}y.
$$

Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

In our case, the region $D$ and its boundary $C$ satisfy the conditions of Green's theorem:

![](images/93/93a1c20377ddd0731c6190712d9d6d77551124fa33001334e84f52049bb6b800.png)

Since $P(x,y)=y+\frac{2}{3}{y}^{3}$ and $Q(x,y)=\operatorname{ln}⁡({y}^{2}+10)+2x,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}=1+2{y}^{2},\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=2.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}(y+\frac{2}{3}{y}^{3})\,dx+(\operatorname{ln}⁡({y}^{2}+10)+2x)\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(2-(1+2{y}^{2}))\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(1-2{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that the region $D$ can be represented in polar coordinates as

$$
Δ=\{(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 9,\,0\le \theta \le \frac{3\pi }{2}\}.
$$

The change of variables formula for plane polar coordinates states that 

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

Therefore, we can write our double integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}(1-3{y}^{2})\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}A & ={∬}_{\mathrm{Δ}}(1-2\cdot {r}^{2}{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}\theta )\hspace{0.222em}r\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3\pi /2}\hspace{0.222em}{\int }_{0}^{9}(1-2{r}^{2}{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}\theta )r\hspace{0.222em}\mathrm{d}r\hspace{0.222em}\mathrm{d}\theta .\end{aligned}

Evaluate $$
\displaystyle {∮}_{C}({x}^{2}-x{y}^{2})dx+(\sqrt{{y}^{7}+3}+{x}^{2}y)\,dy,
$$ where the path $C$ is shown above." :question/worked-solution "Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

In our case, the region $D$ and its boundary $C$ satisfy the conditions of Green's theorem:

![](images/d8/d816d9153e22dd109e20e3e387f6a0028e3f6a9eaf1d284dfae8b5fdf54cfc6e.png)

Now, since 

$$
P(x,y)={x}^{2}-x{y}^{2},\,Q(x,y)=\sqrt{{y}^{7}+3}+{x}^{2}y,
$$

 we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}=-2xy,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=2xy.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}(\sqrt{x}-x{y}^{2})dx+(\sqrt{{y}^{7}+3}+{x}^{2}y)\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(2xy-(-2xy))\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}4xy\,\text{d}A\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that the region $D$ can be represented in polar coordinates as

$$
Δ=\{(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 2,\,0\le \theta \le \frac{3\pi }{2}\}.
$$

The change of variables formula for plane polar coordinates states that

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

Finally, we can calculate our double integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}4xy\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}4(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{2}2{r}^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta ){\int }_{0}^{2}2{r}^{3}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta ){[\frac{{r}^{4}}{2}]}_{0}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3\pi /2}8\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =4[-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )]_{0}^{3\pi /2} \\  & =4[-\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\pi )+\operatorname{cos}⁡0] \\  & =8.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186459273 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "515b197f-4673-5a1c-a567-0bc1fa171663" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-3" :db/id 17592186458772}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186458772} :answer-field/id #uuid "388db07d-138b-5e93-8934-380434a72117" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186459113} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "c05ccb32-8966-53e4-9d10-3d74a13d9dc2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1" :db/id 17592186458975}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186458975} :answer-field/id #uuid "ee7a1c58-5c7d-5c74-9e8e-4e4a9faebb3c" :answer-field/key "field-2" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186459194}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "b16fe381-16d5-5d5d-acea-e99a321f7b25" :question/math-academy-id "q-316284" :question/problem "In **ascending order**, the **exact** values of $c$ that satisfy the mean value theorem for integrals for  $f(x)={x}^{2}+2x$ on the interval $[-3,3]$ are

$$
\begin{aligned}f(c)(b-a) & ={\int }_{a}^{b}f(x)\,\text{d}x \\ f(c) & =\frac{1}{b-a}{\int }_{a}^{b}f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{3-(-3)}{\int }_{-3}^{3}{x}^{2}+2x\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\frac{1}{6}\cdot (\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}+{x}^{2})|}_{-3}^{3} \\  & =\frac{1}{6}[(\frac{{3}^{3}}{3}+{3}^{2})-(\frac{(-3)^{3}}{3}+(-3)^{2})] \\  & =\frac{1}{6}\cdot [(9+9)-(-9+9)] \\  & =\frac{1}{6}\cdot 18 \\  & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the expression for $f(x)$ to solve for the value of $c:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(c) & =3 \\ {c}^{2}+2c & =3 \\ {c}^{2}+2c-3 & =0 \\ (c+1)^{2}-4 & =0 \\ c+1 & =\pm 2 \\ c & =-3,\,1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, in ascending order, the values of $c$ that satisfy the mean value theorem on the interval $[-3,3]$ are 

$$
c=-3,\,\text{and}\,c=1.

\displaystyle {\int }_{1}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡y}y{e}^{x}\,dx\,dy=
$$" :question/worked-solution "The integral is defined over a type II region.

First, we evaluate the inner integral by integrating with respect to $x$, treating $y$ as a constant:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡y}y{e}^{x}\,dx\,dy & ={\int }_{1}^{2}[{\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡y}y{e}^{x}\,dx]dy \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}[y{e}^{x}]_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡y}\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}(y{e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡y}-y{e}^{0})\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}({y}^{2}-y)\,dy\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate with respect to $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{2}({y}^{2}-y)\,dy & ={[\frac{1}{3}{y}^{3}-\frac{1}{2}{y}^{2}]}_{1}^{2} \\  & =(\frac{8}{3}-2)-(\frac{1}{3}-\frac{1}{2}) \\  & =\frac{2}{3}+\frac{1}{6} \\  & =\frac{5}{6}\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186475934 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "06ddc08d-d22f-5193-bf06-38fb8c7ba7c7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4" :db/id 17592186475455} {:answer/id #uuid "0af3f2c2-59c9-5249-a2d8-811877a6ca18" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-1" :db/id 17592186475461} {:answer/id #uuid "19987fb0-bc40-51ba-b84d-d8cb0087f00a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{4}{\pi }" :db/id 17592186475476} {:answer/id #uuid "226d0641-c568-50b8-93be-58d7db8760ad" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\pi " :db/id 17592186475487} {:answer/id #uuid "87b7e1f6-b074-5206-8b9b-5827ab7b73bd" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{4}{{\pi }^{2}}" :db/id 17592186475648}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186475461} :answer-field/id #uuid "32ad6879-6146-512a-b9ce-7b997929ffe5" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186475843}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "480ef21f-535f-5e73-9903-6cc50742dda8" :question/math-academy-id "q-102713" :question/problem "Consider the surface $z\operatorname{cos}⁡(x+y)-xyz=2+\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{2}.$ Given that $n=⟨a,b,c⟩$ is a non-zero normal vector to the surface at the point $(\frac{\pi }{2},-\frac{\pi }{2},2),$ what is the value of $\frac{a}{b}?$" :question/worked-solution "Let's define  $f(x,y,z)=z\operatorname{cos}⁡(x+y)-xyz.$ Then, our surface can be viewed as the level surface $f(x,y,z)=2+\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{2}.$  

Now, we find the gradient of $f(x,y,z)$ and evaluate it at $(\frac{\pi }{2},-\frac{\pi }{2},2):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\,j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\,k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(z\operatorname{cos}⁡(x+y)-xyz)i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(z\operatorname{cos}⁡(x+y)-xyz)j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(z\operatorname{cos}⁡(x+y)-xyz)k \\  & =(-z\operatorname{sin}⁡(x+y)-yz)i+(-z\operatorname{sin}⁡(x+y)-xz)j+(\operatorname{cos}⁡(x+y)-xy)k \\ ∇f(\frac{\pi }{2},-\frac{\pi }{2},2) & =(-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}-\frac{\pi }{2})-2\left(-\frac{\pi }{2}\right))\text{ }i+(-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}-\frac{\pi }{2})-2\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right))\text{ }j+(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}-\frac{\pi }{2})-\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right)\left(-\frac{\pi }{2}\right))\text{ }k \\  & =\pi \text{ }i-\pi \text{ }j+(1+\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{4})\text{ }k \\  & =⟨\pi ,\,-\pi ,\,1+\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{4}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our normal vector is $n=⟨a,b,c⟩=⟨\pi ,\,-\pi ,\,\frac{{\pi }^{2}+4}{4}⟩.$

Finally, $\frac{a}{b}=\frac{\pi }{-\pi }=-1.$"} {:db/id 17592186475984 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0de413f9-cd7a-535a-8ffa-46d5c7da302d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1" :db/id 17592186475463} {:answer/id #uuid "2a020e56-2589-5e05-8a71-55eaf678b2b0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-2" :db/id 17592186475498} {:answer/id #uuid "5d0e7c8f-f911-5f64-b0c6-19e7a9add138" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\frac{1}{2}" :db/id 17592186475578} {:answer/id #uuid "720df5c2-6cd7-54e9-a9af-ea4b64405c63" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{3}{2}" :db/id 17592186475604} {:answer/id #uuid "7c27cb5a-7606-5667-9a19-07de7ad9160b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3" :db/id 17592186475621}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186475463} :answer-field/id #uuid "2652e0ca-544c-51d5-827f-9347b3d96ac0" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186475840}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "fd38a4fc-c1e2-5044-998c-eee65f3245ff" :question/math-academy-id "q-162559" :question/problem "![](images/80/804976bf326ed561ff8e7b4f5a6c65361039a686a4449edfdf8e6f497ee5cbda.png)

Consider the vector field $F(x,y,z)=⟨0,\,xy-z,\,0⟩$ and the surface $S$ defined by the bounding region of the rectangular solid shown above in the first octant. Calculate the flux of $F$ through $S.$" :question/worked-solution "If $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $n,$ and $F$ is continuous vector field, then the flux of $F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $n$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S.
$$

Notice that only the $y$-component of $F=⟨0,\,xy-z,\,0⟩$ is non-zero. Since the lateral sides of $S$ are parallel to the $y$-axis, the flux of $F$ through $S$ will be non-zero only at the right and left sides. 

![](images/de/de9eb8381df05d2d5e6222a51b0ccbc5729e522df94a4aace570881d1226a1ca.png)

 

Let's consider the flux of $F$ through these two sides.

- Let ${S}_{1}$ denote the right surface. On this surface, we have $y=1$ for $0\le x\le 1$ and $0\le z\le 2.$ The outward-pointing unit normal vector to ${S}_{1}$ is

$$
{n}_{1}=⟨0,\,1,\,0⟩.
$$

Using the fact that $y=1$ on ${S}_{1},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot {n}_{1} & =⟨0,\,xy-z,\,0⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,1,\,0⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,x-z,\,0⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,1,\,0⟩ \\  & =x-z.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $F$ across ${S}_{1}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}x-z\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}x-z\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}x-z\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}z \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{[\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}-xz]}_{x=0}^{x=1}\,\text{d}z \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{1}{2}-z\,\text{d}z \\  & ={[\frac{1}{2}z-\frac{1}{2}{z}^{2}]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =1-2 \\  & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

- Let ${S}_{2}$ denote the left surface. On this surface, we have $y=0$ for $0\le x\le 1$ and $0\le z\le 2.$ The outward-pointing unit normal vector to ${S}_{2}$ is

$$
{n}_{2}=⟨0,\,-1,\,0⟩.
$$

Using the fact that $y=0$ on ${S}_{2},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot {n}_{2} & =⟨0,\,xy-z,\,0⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,-1,\,0⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,-z,\,0⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,-1,\,0⟩ \\  & =z.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $F$ across ${S}_{2}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{2}}z\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}z\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}z\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}z \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\,\text{d}x{\int }_{0}^{2}z\,\text{d}z \\  & =[x]_{0}^{1}\cdot {[\frac{{z}^{2}}{2}]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =1\cdot 2 \\  & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S+{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & =(-1)+2 \\  & =1.\end{aligned}

$$
f(x,y)=\left\{\begin{aligned}2y, & 0\le x\le 1,\,0\le y\le 1, \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

The marginal CDF ${F}_{X}(x)$ of $X$ is given by

$$
{F}_{X}(x)=\left\{\begin{aligned}0, & x<0 \\ g(x), & 0\le x\le 1 \\ 1 & x>1.\end{aligned}\right.
