where $t$ is the time, in years, since the observations began. According to this model, what is the maximum possible number of homes that will adopt clean energy?

The maximum possible number of homes that will adopt clean energy is
{{field-1}}." :question/worked-solution "A logistic growth equation has the form

$$
{y}^{′}=ky(a-y),
$$

where $k>0$ is a constant of proportionality, and $a>y$ is the carrying capacity. 

The carrying capacity $a$ represents the maximum possible number of clean-energy-adopting homes in the city. A diagram showing a typical logistic growth curve is shown below.

![](images/d8/d8133f1c4203903bac606bbae61c73717e2ba2dc15a97a77f48eaaeaf4736d06.png)

First, let's rewrite the right-hand side of the given equation so that it matches the form above:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =3y(20-\frac{y}{125}) \\  & =3y\left(\frac{2\,500-y}{125}\right) \\  & =\frac{3y}{125}(2\,500-y) \\  & =0.024y(2\,500-y)\end{aligned}
$$

$$

Then, the series converges for all $x\in R.$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{p}\,q & =\frac{p\cdot q}{p\cdot p}p \\  & =\frac{{p}_{x}{q}_{x}+{p}_{y}{q}_{y}+{p}_{z}{q}_{z}}{{p}_{x}^{2}+{p}_{y}^{2}+{p}_{z}^{2}}p \\  & =\frac{3\cdot 6+2\cdot (-1)+(-1)\cdot 8}{{3}^{2}+{2}^{2}+(-1)^{2}}p \\  & =\frac{8}{14}⟨3,2,-1⟩ \\  & =\frac{4}{7}⟨3,2,-1⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{12}{7},\frac{8}{7},-\frac{4}{7}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186480697 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "081d2611-c9d5-5ff8-acf0-23903af25f7a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1\,200" :db/id 17592186480126} {:answer/id #uuid "2cb6f314-795c-5293-badb-a09dd380b034" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0" :db/id 17592186480182} {:answer/id #uuid "4004a3d0-2cbf-51cf-a3c3-743093b7b616" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\infty " :db/id 17592186480215} {:answer/id #uuid "7ac27f65-90ba-5e1a-903c-2209418975d4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "900" :db/id 17592186480313} {:answer/id #uuid "a7813003-46c8-549a-951a-80403b679f4e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "600" :db/id 17592186480390}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186480126} :answer-field/id #uuid "c9c885db-a51b-565f-802d-b5e3e3429fb9" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186480601}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "da1f1140-0b6f-5e8e-98c1-c5bc7c260a47" :question/math-academy-id "q-118587" :question/problem "Consider the following differential equation for the function $y=y(t):$

$$
{y}^{′}=9y(1-\frac{y}{1\,200}),\,y(0)=200
$$

What is $\lim_{t\to \infty }y(t)?$" :question/worked-solution "A logistic growth equation has the form

$$
{y}^{′}=ky(a-y),
$$

where $k>0$ is a constant of proportionality, and $a>y$ is the carrying capacity.

A diagram showing a typical logistic growth curve is shown below.

![](images/57/57f4b604c546daed4f1cb3895191fae0ccac33b5c17aac705f203f0a837c7e69.png)

First, let's rewrite the right-hand side of the given equation so that it matches the form above:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =9y(1-\frac{y}{1\,200}) \\  & =9y\left(\frac{1\,200-y}{1\,200}\right) \\  & =\frac{9y}{1\,200}(1\,200-y) \\  & =\frac{3y}{400}(1\,200-y)\end{aligned}
$$

From here, we see that $a=1\,200.$ Hence, the carrying capacity is $1\,200.$

For a given logistic growth model, $y\to a$ as $t\to \infty .$ Therefore,

$$
\lim_{t\to \infty }y(t)=1\,200.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186481343 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "30fd4f57-3f0a-5ebc-aa07-bb84afb9cc7a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\operatorname{ln}⁡2" :db/id 17592186480833} {:answer/id #uuid "3f270f12-02ec-5549-8988-b03e5d2eae95" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{6}" :db/id 17592186480861} {:answer/id #uuid "cc1e541a-a0b5-50e1-8a46-d0f83df1d6c4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{6}" :db/id 17592186481124} {:answer/id #uuid "e902cbe7-031f-5540-a22a-6e30754fbd91" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3\operatorname{ln}⁡2" :db/id 17592186481184} {:answer/id #uuid "fbe6534a-9156-5f3a-a3f4-adabfe81028f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186481226}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186480861} :answer-field/id #uuid "149fcd69-9998-58e5-a043-dbc9ef09dd8b" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186481248}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "03e70789-b720-5486-ac24-d7c0b4013554" :question/math-academy-id "q-160937" :question/problem "Use a change of variables to evaluate the double integral 

$$
{∬}_{D}\frac{x+3y}{x}\,dxdy,
$$

where $D$ is the quadrilateral region with vertices $(1,-\frac{1}{3}),$  $(2,-\frac{2}{3}),$  $(2,-\frac{1}{3}),$ and $(1,0).$" :question/worked-solution "Let's define a transformation $T$ as follows:

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}⟶\begin{bmatrix}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{bmatrix}
$$

This transformation maps some region $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane to our region $D$ in the $xy$-plane.

To compute the required integral, we can use the change of variables formula

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dxdy={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(x(u,v),y(u,v))\,|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\text{ }dudv
$$

where $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T.$

To compute the required integral, we proceed as follows:

**Step 1**: Find a suitable change of variables.

The integrand

$$
f(x,y)=\frac{x+3y}{x}
$$

suggests that we use the change of variables 

$$
u=x,\,v=x+3y.
$$

This change of variables gives us the *inverse* function ${T}^{-1},$ that is

$$
{T}^{-1}:\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}u(x,y) \\ v(x,y)\end{bmatrix}.
$$

**Step 2**: Find $Δ,$ which is the image of $D$ under the action of ${T}^{-1}.$ 

The vertices of our domain $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane are as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{T}^{-1}(1,-\frac{1}{3}) & =(1,1+3\left(-\frac{1}{3}\right)) \\  & =(1,0) \\ {T}^{-1}(2,-\frac{2}{3}) & =(2,2+3\left(-\frac{2}{3}\right)) \\  & =(2,0) \\ {T}^{-1}(2,-\frac{1}{3}) & =(2,2+3\left(-\frac{1}{3}\right)) \\  & =(2,1) \\ {T}^{-1}(1,0) & =(1,1+3(0)) \\  & =(1,1)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our domain in the $uv$-plane is the following rectangle:

$$
Δ=\{(u,v)\,:\,1\le u\le 2,\,0\le v\le 1\}
$$

![](images/33/33a7fa05505942d0729e5a5be2bd691a49c242937fdb9de18f6a6f97b5799424.png)

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 1 & 3\end{vmatrix} \\  & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 4**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T:$

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}={\left(\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)}\right)}^{-1}=\frac{1}{3}
$$

Note that $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}\ne 0$ everywhere inside $Δ.$ In other words, $T$ has no critical points inside $Δ.$

**Step 5**: Perform the change of variables, and evaluate the integral:

Performing the change of variables, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\frac{x+3y}{x}\,\text{d}x\text{d}y & ={∬}_{Δ}\frac{v}{u}\,|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}\frac{v}{u}\,|\frac{1}{3}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{1}^{2}\frac{v}{u}\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{\int }_{0}^{1}v\,\text{d}v{\int }_{1}^{2}\frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\cdot {[\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}]}_{0}^{1}\cdot [\operatorname{ln}⁡u]_{1}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\cdot \frac{1}{2}\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡2 \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{6}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186481353 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "ff37ba3f-b657-5468-a046-c7a885ae86ed" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{17}{16}" :db/id 17592186481235}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186481235} :answer-field/id #uuid "c9a275f8-e12f-531b-9ed6-2c3eda31cf0e" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186481313}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "2dbc86c1-eb39-5436-87d8-eb16a5d4d270" :question/math-academy-id "q-179401" :question/problem "$$
\displaystyle (7-5)^{-4}+{(\frac{3}{5}-\frac{1}{2})}^{0}=
$${{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "To evaluate the given expression, we use PEMDAS. 

First, we compute the expression inside the parentheses:

$$
\begin{aligned}(7-5)^{-4}+{(\frac{3}{5}-\frac{1}{2})}^{0} &= {2}^{-4}+{(\frac{6}{10}-\frac{5}{10})}^{0} \\ &= {2}^{-4}+{\left(\frac{1}{10}\right)}^{0}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, notice that ${\left(\frac{1}{10}\right)}^{0}=1.$ So, we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}{2}^{-4}+{\left(\frac{1}{10}\right)}^{0} &= {2}^{-4}+1\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, notice that $$
\displaystyle {2}^{-4}=\frac{1}{{2}^{4}}=\frac{1}{16}.
$$ So, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{2}^{-4}+1 &= \frac{1}{16}+1 \\ &= \frac{1+16}{16} \\ &= \frac{17}{16}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186481355 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "031fe889-8bcf-55b6-9e2c-5bc76ff27045" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{7}" :db/id 17592186480742} {:answer/id #uuid "18283892-3eb2-55cd-b35f-59a9010c6395" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{7}{3}" :db/id 17592186480785} {:answer/id #uuid "2e9c3feb-96eb-537a-af4e-a8b745ab09c2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{2}{3}" :db/id 17592186480824} {:answer/id #uuid "43f5d7d0-17b2-565d-a98f-1e82335af6f5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{3}" :db/id 17592186480869} {:answer/id #uuid "f9d07389-9d7e-558b-836a-ab159ef21592" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{3}{7}" :db/id 17592186481224}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186480869} :answer-field/id #uuid "aed2c6d7-4afd-5487-8b46-d9d9acb8c258" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186481301}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "372dbe69-5a97-5673-bcbc-f7d304887030" :question/math-academy-id "q-100293" :question/problem "${7}^{-1}\times (2+\frac{1}{3})=$" :question/worked-solution "To evaluate the given expression, we use PEMDAS.

Notice that ${7}^{-1}=\frac{1}{7}.$ So, we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}{7}^{-1}\times (2+\frac{1}{3}) &= \frac{1}{7}\times (2+\frac{1}{3}) \\ &= \frac{1}{7}\times \frac{6+1}{3} \\ &= \frac{1}{7}\times \frac{7}{3} \\ &= \frac{1\times 7}{7\times 3} \\ &= \frac{1\times \cancel{7}}{3\times \cancel{7}} \\ &= \frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186481357 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "7e360105-eb66-5367-814d-689677702f6e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1" :db/id 17592186480975} {:answer/id #uuid "9e9f7126-1aec-56cb-a084-4f34d28dafc8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{2}" :db/id 17592186481043} {:answer/id #uuid "a79440e4-ebcc-5811-a667-c1e64c7db96b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\pi " :db/id 17592186481055} {:answer/id #uuid "c27b400b-e962-57cc-9be7-11f6f93220fa" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0" :db/id 17592186481111} {:answer/id #uuid "d99527b4-de43-5d96-9eda-144ff935847e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186481146}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186480975} :answer-field/id #uuid "2a10b6cc-8155-5c1e-bf70-aecfcd94d2ca" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186481254}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "3b9226c2-67e0-5858-9c64-ae46c4147a95" :question/math-academy-id "q-163257" :question/problem "Find the average value of the function $f(x,y)={y}^{2}$ on the disk of radius $2$ centered at the origin." :question/worked-solution "First, notice that 

$$
\text{Area}(D)=\pi \cdot {2}^{2}=4\pi .
$$

The average value of the function over a region $D$ is given by

$$
{f}_{\text{ave}}=\frac{1}{\text{Area}(D)}\,{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

We will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

In polar coordinates $(r,\theta ),$ the region can be expressed as 

$$
Δ=\{(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 2,\,0\le \theta <2\pi \}.
$$

Using the change of variables formula, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}{y}^{2}\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{2}{r}^{3}{\sin }^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\sin }^{2}⁡\theta {\int }_{0}^{2}{r}^{3}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\sin }^{2}⁡\theta \,{[\frac{{r}^{4}}{4}]}_{0}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\sin }^{2}⁡\theta (4-0)\text{d}\theta  \\  & =4{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\sin }^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =4{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\frac{1}{2}(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2{[\theta -\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta ]}_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =2[(2\pi -0)-\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{sin}⁡4\pi -\operatorname{sin}⁡0)] \\  & =2\cdot 2\pi  \\  & =4\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
{f}_{\text{ave}}=\frac{1}{4\pi }\cdot 4\pi =1.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186481364 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "09a70e77-e143-5fe1-987f-6cf3d9622cb5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\operatorname{ln}⁡6" :db/id 17592186480759} {:answer/id #uuid "16926c3a-001d-572a-beb5-ac09cba7435e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2\operatorname{ln}⁡6" :db/id 17592186480780} {:answer/id #uuid "930bb660-443d-5920-8d2a-07cfdc6d0a50" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2\operatorname{ln}⁡3" :db/id 17592186481014} {:answer/id #uuid "943844b2-6990-576d-9141-b10699c96298" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4\operatorname{ln}⁡2" :db/id 17592186481018} {:answer/id #uuid "96c98676-4b18-52e8-baf0-b525847f1830" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\operatorname{ln}⁡3" :db/id 17592186481029}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186481014} :answer-field/id #uuid "1dca1b12-338a-5c5f-badf-6213000ef5a1" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186481249}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "4d5d128b-3cee-5601-8961-cb121a4bf681" :question/math-academy-id "q-160903" :question/problem "Use a change of variables to evaluate the double integral 

$$
{∬}_{D}\frac{{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}{(x-y)^{2}}\,dxdy,
$$

where $D$ is the quadrilateral region with vertices $(1,0),$ $(2,1),$ $(3,0),$ and $(2,-1).$" :question/worked-solution "Let's define a transformation $T$ as follows:

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}⟶\begin{bmatrix}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{bmatrix}
$$

This transformation maps some region $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane to our region $D$ in the $xy$-plane.

To compute the required integral, we can use the change of variables formula

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dxdy={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(x(u,v),y(u,v))\,|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\text{ }dudv
$$

where $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T.$

To compute the required integral, we proceed as follows:

**Step 1**: Find a suitable change of variables.

The integrand

$$
f(x,y)=\frac{{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}{(x-y)^{2}}=\frac{x+y}{x-y}
$$

suggests that we use the change of variables 

$$
u=x+y,\,v=x-y.
$$

This change of variables gives us the *inverse* function ${T}^{-1},$ that is

$$
{T}^{-1}:\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}u(x,y) \\ v(x,y)\end{bmatrix}.
$$

**Step 2**: Find $Δ,$ which is the image of $D$ under the action of ${T}^{-1}.$ 

The vertices of our domain $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane are as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{T}^{-1}(1,0) & =(1+0,1-0) \\  & =(1,1) \\ {T}^{-1}(2,1) & =(2+1,2-1) \\  & =(3,1) \\ {T}^{-1}(3,0) & =(3+0,3-0) \\  & =(3,3) \\ {T}^{-1}(2,-1) & =(2+(-1),2-(-1)) \\  & =(1,3)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our domain in the $uv$-plane is the following rectangle:

$$
Δ=\{(u,v)\,:\,1\le u\le 3,\,1\le v\le 3\}
$$

![](images/f3/f34926c196b850fa22e0f918b27c8d25e5deb7f6aa7ec232e2eeaf4e46dd309c.png)

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =-2.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 4**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T:$

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}={\left(\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)}\right)}^{-1}=-\frac{1}{2}
$$

Note that $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}\ne 0$ everywhere inside $Δ.$ In other words, $T$ has no critical points inside $Δ.$

**Step 5**: Perform the change of variables, and evaluate the integral:

Performing the change of variables, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\frac{{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}{(x-y)^{2}}\,\text{d}x\text{d}y & ={∬}_{D}\frac{x+y}{x-y}\,\text{d}x\text{d}y \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}\frac{u}{v}\,|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}\frac{u}{v}\,|-\frac{1}{2}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{1}^{3}{\int }_{1}^{3}\frac{u}{v}\,\text{d}u\,\text{d}v \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{1}^{3}\frac{1}{v}\,\text{d}v{\int }_{1}^{3}u\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot {[\operatorname{ln}⁡v]}_{1}^{3}\cdot {[\frac{1}{2}{u}^{2}]}_{1}^{3} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡3\cdot 4 \\  & =2\operatorname{ln}⁡3.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186481367 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0794f66a-f45d-5607-98bd-140c6175658d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1" :db/id 17592186480756} {:answer/id #uuid "2b32d836-4282-5cc7-9a51-0ec7993b4598" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{2}{3}" :db/id 17592186480819} {:answer/id #uuid "5932c544-2818-549e-b0bc-0ffb7089e13f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{5}{4}" :db/id 17592186480901} {:answer/id #uuid "bc7fc21c-1500-5e17-a1b2-d0a8f29d6724" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{3}" :db/id 17592186481099} {:answer/id #uuid "f814775e-bc0c-5f32-a98d-179b8afcfcc4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186481218}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186480819} :answer-field/id #uuid "421edb72-f508-5f8a-ab68-a626bb9c3ff3" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186481265}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "510822f4-2240-59da-8db4-5275b43b2562" :question/math-academy-id "q-163197" :question/problem "Consider the function $f(x,y)$ and the region $D$ given by

$$
f(x,y)=2xy,\,D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le \frac{y}{2},\,0\le y\le 4\}.
$$

According to the mean value theorem for double integrals, there exists a point $(a,b)\in D$ such that the volume of the solid enclosed between the surface $z=f(x,y)$ and the $xy$-plane over the region $D$ equals the volume of the right cylinder with base $D$ and height $f(a,b).$ Find $a$ given that $b=3.$" :question/worked-solution "According to the mean value theorem for double integrals, there exists a point $(a,b)\in D$ such that

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A=f(a,b)\cdot \text{Area}(D).
$$

Evaluating the integral on the left-hand side, we have

$$

\displaystyle 6{x}^{3}(\frac{x}{2}-\frac{{x}^{3}}{3})=
$$" :question/worked-solution "We multiply each term inside the parentheses by the term outside the parentheses, simplify using the rules of exponents, and then we add the results together:

$$
\begin{aligned}6{x}^{3}(\frac{x}{2}-\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}) &= (6{x}^{3})\left(\frac{x}{2}\right)+(6{x}^{3})\left(-\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}\right) \\ &= (6{x}^{3})(\frac{1}{2}x)+(6{x}^{3})(-\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3}) \\ &= (6\cdot \frac{1}{2})({x}^{3}\cdot x)+(6\cdot \left(-\frac{1}{3}\right))({x}^{3}\cdot {x}^{3}) \\ &= (3)({x}^{3+1})+(-2)\cdot ({x}^{3+3}) \\ &= 3{x}^{4}-2{x}^{6}\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186481371 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0f4c86f2-5cfb-5693-a142-edc6be59008a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2\operatorname{ln}⁡2" :db/id 17592186480767} {:answer/id #uuid "344eed9f-15e2-5d9d-a328-322b0adeb917" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{\ln }^{3}⁡2" :db/id 17592186480839} {:answer/id #uuid "68632396-ccfe-581e-8589-6ce419497b94" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2{\ln }^{3}⁡2" :db/id 17592186480933} {:answer/id #uuid "79ad7697-010f-568d-851d-4911a16f499a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{\ln }^{2}⁡2" :db/id 17592186480962} {:answer/id #uuid "95eca681-53e5-51f4-8569-95f9733c2dbe" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2{\ln }^{2}⁡2" :db/id 17592186481024}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186480933} :answer-field/id #uuid "f081c215-96de-53ac-b301-926b90ac00ff" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186481333}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "5de90e63-3afe-527a-b599-3cdcd703aa52" :question/math-academy-id "q-83656" :question/problem "Using the change of variables $u={e}^{x}$ and $v={e}^{y},$ evaluate the double integral

$$

where $D=\{(x,y)\,:\,1\le {e}^{x}\le 2,\,1\le {e}^{y}\le 4\}.$" :question/worked-solution "Let's define a transformation $T$ as follows:

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}⟶\begin{bmatrix}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{bmatrix}
$$

This transformation maps some region $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane to our region $D$ in the $xy$-plane.

To compute the required integral, we can use the change of variables formula

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,dx\,dy={∬}_{Δ}f(x(u,v),y(u,v))|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|du\,dv
$$

where $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T.$

Note that the change of variables

$$
u={e}^{x},\,v={e}^{y}
$$

 

gives us the *inverse* function ${T}^{-1},$ that is

$$
{T}^{-1}:\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}u(x,y) \\ v(x,y)\end{bmatrix}.
$$

To compute the required integral, we proceed as follows:

**Step 1**: Find $Δ,$ which is the image of $D$ under the action of ${T}^{-1}.$ 

Our domain in the $uv$-plane is

$$
\begin{aligned}Δ & =\{(u,v)\,:\,1\le u\le 2,\,1\le v\le 4\}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}{e}^{x} & 0 \\ 0 & \text{ }\text{ }{e}^{y}\end{vmatrix} \\  & ={e}^{x+y}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T$ is

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}={\left(\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)}\right)}^{-1}=\frac{1}{{e}^{x+y}}=\frac{1}{uv}.
$$

Note that $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}\ne 0$ everywhere inside $Δ.$ In other words, $T$ has no critical points inside $Δ.$

**Step 4**: Perform the change of variables:

Performing the change of variables, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}y\,dx\,dy & ={∬}_{Δ}\operatorname{ln}⁡v\,|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\text{d}u\,\text{d}v \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}\operatorname{ln}⁡v\cdot |\frac{1}{uv}|\,\text{d}u\,\text{d}v \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}\frac{1}{u}[{\int }_{1}^{4}\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡v}{v}\,dv]du \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}\frac{1}{u}{[\frac{{\ln }^{2}⁡v}{2}]}_{1}^{4}du \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{1}^{2}\frac{1}{u}[{\ln }^{2}⁡4-{\ln }^{2}⁡1]\,du \\  & =\frac{{\ln }^{2}⁡4}{2}{\int }_{1}^{2}\frac{1}{u}\,du \\  & =2{\ln }^{2}⁡2[\operatorname{ln}⁡u]_{1}^{2} \\  & =2{\ln }^{2}⁡2(\operatorname{ln}⁡2-\operatorname{ln}⁡1) \\  & =2{\ln }^{3}⁡2.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186481373 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "2f5e6d20-6d83-5a4b-9919-511354ddc37f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-87" :db/id 17592186480828} {:answer/id #uuid "76d69649-f0c6-5771-848d-71954873581b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "87" :db/id 17592186480957} {:answer/id #uuid "b381b4b1-c1bc-52ab-8b7e-21ef5860d874" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-89" :db/id 17592186481079} {:answer/id #uuid "e6602306-1f53-57b5-91c7-8b39e35659a8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "89" :db/id 17592186481178} {:answer/id #uuid "fdeff659-436b-5f34-ac81-a6409e40fce1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-121" :db/id 17592186481230}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186480828} :answer-field/id #uuid "93d546fe-e93e-5d3c-8f24-4f640019211e" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186481291}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "5e5e796d-b724-597d-a614-e8af03095fdf" :question/math-academy-id "q-100301" :question/problem "Calculate $$

$$" :question/worked-solution "To evaluate the given expression, we use PEMDAS.

is not zero. Any non-zero number raised to the power of $0$ equals $1.$ So, we have 

$$

$$

$$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}-2 & \text{ }\text{ }1 \\ 0 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =-2.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 4**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T:$

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}={\left(\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)}\right)}^{-1}=-\frac{1}{2}.
$$

Note that $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}\ne 0$ everywhere inside $Δ.$ In other words, $T$ has no critical points inside $Δ.$

**Step 5**: Perform the change of variables, and evaluate the integral:

Performing the change of variables, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡(y-2x)}{y-2x}\,\text{d}x\text{d}y & ={∬}_{Δ}\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡u}{u}\,|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡u}{u}\,|-\frac{1}{2}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}[{\int }_{1}^{4}\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡u}{u}\,du]dv \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}{[\frac{{\ln }^{2}⁡u}{2}]}_{1}^{4}dv \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{\int }_{0}^{2}({\ln }^{2}⁡4-{\ln }^{2}⁡1)\,dv \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{\ln }^{2}⁡4{\int }_{0}^{2}dv \\  & =\frac{1}{4}(2\operatorname{ln}⁡2)^{2}\cdot [v]_{0}^{2} \\  & ={\ln }^{2}⁡2\cdot (2-0) \\  & =2{\ln }^{2}⁡2.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186481399 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "50b7b909-d962-51d6-9392-bbe5c3a4f0d0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1" :db/id 17592186480886} {:answer/id #uuid "6bf4c5c6-de83-56d9-bcdb-6036594d8b2a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{3}{2}" :db/id 17592186480942} {:answer/id #uuid "95973894-ec85-559b-89b7-bafc61605c0f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{3}" :db/id 17592186481022} {:answer/id #uuid "e1ffe2e3-2de3-51af-a5e8-e086627cabd7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{2}" :db/id 17592186481165} {:answer/id #uuid "ea4ec8f7-1073-567c-82c5-5f1ecde10a3e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186481189}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186481189} :answer-field/id #uuid "db0e353a-fec5-5d61-839e-8dfe38eddf51" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186481324}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "a130ee36-c4fa-557a-b62c-af4b4bf44ed4" :question/math-academy-id "q-163151" :question/problem "Consider the function $f(x,y)$ and the region $D$ given by

$$
\mathbf{F}(x,y)=⟨x+\sqrt{y},\hspace{0.222em}y+\sqrt{x}⟩
$$

through the boundary of the region enclosed by the curve $y=\operatorname{cos}⁡x$ and the line $y=0$ for $-\frac{\pi }{2}\le x\le \frac{\pi }{2}.$" :question/worked-solution "Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $\mathbf{F}=P\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+Q\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j},$ and $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first derivatives on an open region containing $D,$ then the flux form of Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}\mathbf{F}\cdot \mathbf{n}\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}s={∬}_{D}\text{div}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{F}\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}A,
$$

which is equivalent to

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A.
$$

The region $D$ and the curve $C$ for this case are shown below.

![](images/e5/e570374b37c116e32c3a7762b8cf09a28bdbb3e06b5e67e25837902a89bcd264.png)

We have that $P(x,y)=x+\sqrt{y}$ and $Q(x,y)=y+\sqrt{x}.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}=1,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

We can express the region $D$ as a type I region as follows:

$$
D=\{(x,y):-\frac{\pi }{2}\le x\le \frac{\pi }{2},\,0\le y\le \operatorname{cos}⁡x\}
$$

Therefore, applying Green's theorem in flux form, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}\mathbf{F}\cdot \mathbf{n}\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\hspace{0.167em}\mathrm{d}y-Q\hspace{0.167em}\mathrm{d}x \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(1+1)\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}A \\  & =2{\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{cos}x}\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}y\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}x \\  & =2{\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}y\hspace{0.167em}{|}_{0}^{\operatorname{cos}x}\hspace{0.167em}\mathrm{d}x \\  & =2{\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{cos}x\hspace{0.167em}\mathrm{d}x \\  & =2\operatorname{sin}x\hspace{0.167em}{|}_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2} \\  & =2(1-(-1)) \\  & =4.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186481407 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "07e40d47-7a70-5f2c-ba24-6a855b1d6eb7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\frac{16}{3\pi }" :db/id 17592186480757} {:answer/id #uuid "43bff162-e0e6-5e6e-b559-7547ee7c72a5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\frac{8}{3}" :db/id 17592186480868} {:answer/id #uuid "e1b2263d-a0be-566e-8984-74cc5d983449" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\frac{16}{5\pi }" :db/id 17592186481164} {:answer/id #uuid "e83a9fc3-1293-5456-b3e0-ca1e41eb01ee" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\frac{32}{3}" :db/id 17592186481182} {:answer/id #uuid "e979451f-00ff-5ed9-83e8-7aff07a87414" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\frac{32}{3\pi }" :db/id 17592186481185}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186481185} :answer-field/id #uuid "7e8c2182-159c-53aa-a9ec-6a0270a24944" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186481282}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "b0a81f04-6f59-512d-aa20-c54e3b26a51d" :question/math-academy-id "q-163277" :question/problem "![](images/06/06a853735916ae3219eea02fa7e7e30d9e941106600cd5b642d951f553aace59.png)

Find the average value of the function $f(x,y)=5y({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})$ on the semicircle shown above." :question/worked-solution "First, notice that 

$$
\text{Area}(D)=\frac{1}{2}\cdot \pi \cdot {1}^{2}=\frac{\pi }{2}.
$$

The average value of the function over a region $D$ is given by

$$
{f}_{\text{ave}}=\frac{1}{\text{Area}(D)}\,{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

We will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

Notice that the region $D$ represents a portion of the disk of radius $1$ centered at 
$(1,0).$

Cartesian and polar coordinates are connected by the following equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x &=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \\ y &=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta\end{aligned}\right.
$$

With that is mind, let's now write the $y=-\sqrt{2x-{x}^{2}}$ in polar coordinates:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =-\sqrt{2x-{x}^{2}} \\ {y}^{2} & =2x-{x}^{2} \\ {x}^{2}+{y}^{2} & =2x \\ (r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2} & =2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ {r}^{2}({\cos }^{2}⁡\theta +{\sin }^{2}⁡\theta ) & =2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ {r}^{2} & =2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ {r}^{2}-2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =0 \\ r(r-2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

 

Since $r$ cannot be identical to zero on the entire semicircle, we must have $r=2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .$

Therefore, in polar coordinates $(r,\theta ),$ the region can be expressed as 

$$
Δ=\{(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,-\frac{\pi }{2}\le \theta \le 0\}.
$$

Therefore, we obtain

$$

$$"} {:db/id 17592186481408 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "3d66d8b4-c0c5-583c-9422-a56fec563fa4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\sqrt[8]{e}-2" :db/id 17592186480858} {:answer/id #uuid "9d49fd2e-9748-5870-a942-7855eab45dc3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2(\sqrt[4]{e}+1)" :db/id 17592186481041} {:answer/id #uuid "aaec5f62-9f91-57f5-b958-6eca6bd1c1da" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4(\sqrt[4]{e}-1)" :db/id 17592186481061} {:answer/id #uuid "c378d23d-c433-57b0-a302-3ca7d194c79d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4(\sqrt[2]{e}-1)" :db/id 17592186481117} {:answer/id #uuid "ff8cb142-efbd-5919-b474-a1189a94a948" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2(\sqrt[2]{e}+2)" :db/id 17592186481237}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186481061} :answer-field/id #uuid "d1136c19-2541-5007-b027-75b59e3253ba" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186481317}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "b2ff4fa5-a334-50b5-9869-f8e569ec5011" :question/math-academy-id "q-163256" :question/problem "Find the average value of the function $f(x,y)={e}^{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}$ on the disk of radius $\frac{1}{2}$ centered at the origin." :question/worked-solution "First, notice that 

$$
\text{Area}(D)=\pi \cdot {\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)}^{2}=\frac{\pi }{4}.

The average value of the function over a region $D$ is given by

$$
{f}_{\text{ave}}=\frac{1}{\text{Area}(D)}\,{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

We will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

In polar coordinates $(r,\theta ),$ the region can be expressed as 

$$
Δ=\{(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le \frac{1}{2},\,0\le \theta <2\pi \}.

Using the change of variables formula, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}{e}^{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}{e}^{(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}}\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}{e}^{{r}^{2}}\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,{[\frac{{e}^{{r}^{2}}}{2}]}_{0}^{1/2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(\frac{{e}^{1/4}}{2}-\frac{1}{2})\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{\sqrt[4]{e}-1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{\sqrt[4]{e}-1}{2}[\theta ]_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =\frac{\sqrt[4]{e}-1}{2}(2\pi -0) \\  & =(\sqrt[4]{e}-1)\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
{f}_{\text{ave}}=\frac{4}{\pi }\cdot (\sqrt[4]{e}-1)\pi =4(\sqrt[4]{e}-1).
$$"} {:db/id 17592186481410 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "11e03497-2478-5699-b8c8-60dc8393efd3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4" :db/id 17592186480771} {:answer/id #uuid "14aeda53-bc0f-5285-a152-aac2c1de7b55" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "24" :db/id 17592186480775} {:answer/id #uuid "31768ff6-9f0c-50bd-9796-46c6ac637b1f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "32" :db/id 17592186480835} {:answer/id #uuid "328e9ba1-7166-5fcf-9c18-bf5334f7dc30" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "8" :db/id 17592186480837} {:answer/id #uuid "c05027eb-9d67-552f-950c-d7aa5524cbba" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{2}" :db/id 17592186481107}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186480835} :answer-field/id #uuid "e051d3d7-1ee2-505b-957c-b010b42121b8" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186481326}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "b878a44e-123c-5f2f-a474-6dc1888b9c72" :question/math-academy-id "q-160938" :question/problem "Use a change of variables to evaluate the double integral 

$$
{∬}_{D}({x}^{2}-xy)\,dxdy,
$$

where $D$ is the quadrilateral region with vertices $(3,2),$ $(5,4),$ $(5,2),$ and $(3,0).$" :question/worked-solution "Let's define a transformation $T$ as follows:

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}⟶\begin{bmatrix}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{bmatrix}
$$

This transformation maps some region $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane to our region $D$ in the $xy$-plane.

To compute the required integral, we can use the change of variables formula

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dxdy={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(x(u,v),y(u,v))\,|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\text{ }dudv
$$

where $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T.$

To compute the required integral, we proceed as follows:

**Step 1**: Find a suitable change of variables.

The integrand

$$
f(x,y)={x}^{2}-xy=x(x-y)
$$

suggests that we use the change of variables 

$$
u=x,\,v=x-y.
$$

This change of variables gives us the *inverse* function ${T}^{-1},$ that is

$$
{T}^{-1}:\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}u(x,y) \\ v(x,y)\end{bmatrix}.
$$

**Step 2**: Find $Δ,$ which is the image of $D$ under the action of ${T}^{-1}.$ 

The vertices of our domain $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane are as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{T}^{-1}(3,2) & =(3,3-2) \\  & =(3,1) \\ {T}^{-1}(5,4) & =(5,5-4) \\  & =(5,1) \\ {T}^{-1}(5,2) & =(5,5-2) \\  & =(5,3) \\ {T}^{-1}(3,0) & =(3,3-0) \\  & =(3,3)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our domain in the $uv$-plane is the following rectangle:

$$
Δ=\{(u,v)\,:\,3\le u\le 5,\,1\le v\le 3\}
$$

![](images/e0/e0b810c03e7e3210fcff3a739e3781ad5ff694bfe44d5f73d7782c3b4108a286.png)

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 1 & -1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 4**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T:$

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}={\left(\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)}\right)}^{-1}=-1
$$

Note that $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}\ne 0$ everywhere inside $Δ.$ In other words, $T$ has no critical points inside $Δ.$

**Step 5**: Perform the change of variables, and evaluate the integral:

Performing the change of variables, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}({x}^{2}-xy)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y & ={∬}_{D}x(x-y)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}uv\,|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}uv\,|-1|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{3}{\int }_{3}^{5}uv\,\text{d}u\,\text{d}v \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{3}v\,\text{d}v{\int }_{3}^{5}u\,\text{d}u \\  & ={[\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}]}_{1}^{3}\cdot {[\frac{1}{2}{u}^{2}]}_{3}^{5} \\  & =4\cdot 8 \\  & =32.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186481411 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1b7b96a3-3ee8-51d8-bf7e-f10bc137dc77" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "6" :db/id 17592186480796} {:answer/id #uuid "5ea1906a-4d23-5e92-aa42-2516002c4c66" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{5}{2}" :db/id 17592186480915} {:answer/id #uuid "654022a5-61f4-581f-8b07-c11340a40a55" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4" :db/id 17592186480925} {:answer/id #uuid "e98d6b52-9796-58a4-ba09-031961cb2020" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{3}{2}" :db/id 17592186481186} {:answer/id #uuid "fc2a60a5-710d-5d16-938e-a0bd54aeac9c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3" :db/id 17592186481227}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186480925} :answer-field/id #uuid "da8ec83a-e269-5c73-bf54-b07a27aefc49" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186481322}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "bbfd9077-09aa-55c5-a7ec-ce238f7922af" :question/math-academy-id "q-163240" :question/problem "Find the average value of the function $f(x,y)=y+{x}^{2}$ on the region $D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 2,\,x\le y\le 2x\}$ given that the area of the region is $2.$" :question/worked-solution "Applying the average value formula, we find that the average value of the function is

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{\text{ave}} & =\frac{1}{\text{Area}(D)}\,{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{∬}_{D}y+{x}^{2}\,\text{d}A \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{x}^{2x}y+{x}^{2}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}[\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}+{x}^{2}y]_{y=x}^{y=2x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}[{x}^{3}+\frac{3{x}^{2}}{2}]\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[\frac{{x}^{4}}{4}+\frac{{x}^{3}}{2}]_{x=0}^{x=2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(8-0) \\  & =4.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186481418 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "062b1938-49ed-576d-84ed-09a8fb852cc9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1-\frac{{\pi }^{3}}{8}" :db/id 17592186480749} {:answer/id #uuid "34aac4ef-6b3d-5a11-9211-3216b95b6351" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{4}" :db/id 17592186480841} {:answer/id #uuid "365aa022-a66e-5c42-b417-e96430223091" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{{\pi }^{3}}{8}-1" :db/id 17592186480846} {:answer/id #uuid "9d25158d-398d-5c30-8fda-c6ddce1b0d76" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{16}-1" :db/id 17592186481040} {:answer/id #uuid "f17962e7-50b9-5445-bd8a-61e21702bfc0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{{\pi }^{3}}{16}" :db/id 17592186481208}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186481208} :answer-field/id #uuid "be68da14-ad39-5dd8-8b81-96f9bc5c3b1f" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186481309}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "c8466ab0-fd66-5adb-8220-fa89c46bae69" :question/math-academy-id "q-38309" :question/problem "Use a change of variables to evaluate the double integral

where $$
\displaystyle D=\{(x,y)\,:\,|y-x|\le \frac{\pi }{2},\,0\le y\le \frac{\pi }{2}\}.
$$" :question/worked-solution "Let's define a transformation $T$ as follows:

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}⟶\begin{bmatrix}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{bmatrix}
$$

This transformation maps some region $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane to our region $D$ in the $xy$-plane.

To compute the required integral, we can use the change of variables formula

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dxdy={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(x(u,v),y(u,v))\,|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\text{ }dudv
$$

where $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T.$

To compute the required integral, we proceed as follows:

**Step 1**: Find a suitable change of variables.

The inequalities that define the region $D,$

$$
\frac{\pi }{2}\le y-x\le \frac{\pi }{2},\,0\le y\le \frac{\pi }{2},
$$

suggest that we use the change of variables 

$$
u=y-x\,\text{and}\,v=y.
$$

This change of variables gives us the *inverse* function ${T}^{-1},$ that is

$$
{T}^{-1}:\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}u(x,y) \\ v(x,y)\end{bmatrix}.
$$

**Step 2**: Find $Δ,$ which is the image of $D$ under the action of ${T}^{-1}.$ 

Our domain in the $uv$-plane is

$$
\begin{aligned}Δ & =\{(u,v)\,:\,-\frac{\pi }{2}\le u\le \frac{\pi }{2},\,0\le v\le \frac{\pi }{2}\}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}-1 & \text{ }\text{ }1 \\ 0 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 4**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T:$

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}={\left(\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)}\right)}^{-1}=-1.
$$

Note that $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}\ne 0$ everywhere inside $Δ.$ In other words, $T$ has no critical points inside $Δ.$

**Step 5**: Perform the change of variables, and evaluate the integral:

Performing the change of variables, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}y{\cos }^{2}⁡(y-x)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y & ={∬}_{Δ}v{\cos }^{2}⁡u\,|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}v{\cos }^{2}⁡u\cdot |-1|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}v[{\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}{\cos }^{2}⁡u\,du]dv \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}v[{\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡2u+1)du]dv \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}v[\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡2u}{2}+u]_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}\,dv \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\pi v\,dv \\  & =\frac{\pi }{2}[\frac{{v}^{2}}{2}]_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =\frac{\pi }{2}\cdot \frac{{\pi }^{2}}{8} \\  & =\frac{{\pi }^{3}}{16}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186481421 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "2edca394-1295-57f0-b5af-ed3335a801ae" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{5}{2}" :db/id 17592186480827} {:answer/id #uuid "5a9d8a94-9534-5e68-924f-dcf67bae6e63" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4" :db/id 17592186480906} {:answer/id #uuid "9596a5ea-3eda-5d12-a885-036340592f59" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3" :db/id 17592186481021} {:answer/id #uuid "9993e960-d9b3-5a9c-a231-8dca7a1500f5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{14}{5}" :db/id 17592186481034} {:answer/id #uuid "c0180c32-42f3-525a-b857-b3753cd90618" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186481105}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186481021} :answer-field/id #uuid "6c26abb0-e3c4-5856-80ba-2321788c3c2b" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186481276}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "d1845eab-f52b-5f23-bd27-faf40f79c71a" :question/math-academy-id "q-163205" :question/problem "Consider the function $f(x,y)$ and the region $D$ given by

$$
f(x,y)=2x+y,\,D=\{(x,y)\,:\,\frac{y}{2}\le x\le y,\,\,0\le y\le 6\}.
$$

According to the mean value theorem for double integrals, there exists a point $(a,b)\in D$ such that the volume of the solid enclosed between the surface $z=f(x,y)$ and the $xy$-plane over the region $D$ equals the volume of the right cylinder with base $D$ and height $f(a,b).$ Find $a$ given that $b=4.$" :question/worked-solution "According to the mean value theorem for double integrals, there exists a point $(a,b)\in D$ such that

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A=f(a,b)\cdot \text{Area}(D).
$$

Evaluating the integral on the left-hand side, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{D}(2x+y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{6}{\int }_{y/2}^{y}(2x+y)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{6}[{x}^{2}+xy]_{x=y/2}^{x=y}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{6}([{y}^{2}+{y}^{2}]-[\frac{{y}^{2}}{4}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}])\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{6}\frac{5{y}^{2}}{4}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={[\frac{5{y}^{3}}{12}]}_{y=0}^{y=6} \\  & =90.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Area}(D) & ={∬}_{D}\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{6}{\int }_{y/2}^{y}\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{6}[x]_{x=y/2}^{x=y}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{6}\frac{y}{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={[\frac{{y}^{2}}{4}]}_{y=0}^{y=6} \\  & =9.\end{aligned}
$$

Also, we are told that $b=4.$ So, our initial equation simplifies to

$$
\begin{aligned}90 & =f(a,4)\cdot 9 \\ 90 & =(2a+4)\cdot 9 \\ 10 & =2a+4 \\ 6 & =2a \\ a & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that $(3,4)\in D.$ Therefore, the answer is $a=3.$"} {:db/id 17592186481423 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1761c3e4-c91a-57a8-9013-9b3654a234fa" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "10" :db/id 17592186480783} {:answer/id #uuid "47c7196f-be5c-55f4-aa25-27610bf7736c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{5}{8}" :db/id 17592186480875} {:answer/id #uuid "ae180a90-3ca2-5c61-ac30-22916f24dea1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{5}{2}" :db/id 17592186481065} {:answer/id #uuid "e5aa3207-9a4b-5442-a65a-773ebcb88f61" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\pi }{2}" :db/id 17592186481176} {:answer/id #uuid "f081f9d6-ce8e-5bb4-8583-a147cbb0c2be" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\pi " :db/id 17592186481202}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186480875} :answer-field/id #uuid "848b178b-00cd-5964-8724-b50b402d0b68" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186481285}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "d3e35845-58c1-5603-a038-b92edbbc2e02" :question/math-academy-id "q-160906" :question/problem "Use a change of variables to evaluate the double integral

**Step 1**: Find a suitable change of variables.

The integrand

$$
f(x,y)=2x\operatorname{cos}⁡(x+2y)
$$

suggests that we use the change of variables 

$$
u=2x,\,v=x+2y.
$$

This change of variables gives us the *inverse* function ${T}^{-1},$ that is

$$
{T}^{-1}:\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}u(x,y) \\ v(x,y)\end{bmatrix}.

**Step 2**: Find $Δ,$ which is the image of $D$ under the action of ${T}^{-1}.$

$$

First, let's find the slope ${m}_{1}$ of the line passing through the points $(1,5)$ and $(-3,-1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}m_1 &= \frac{y_2-y_1}{x_2-x_1} \\ &= \frac{-1-(5)}{-3-(1)} \\ &= \frac{-6}{-4} \\ &= \frac{3}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Since perpendicular lines have slopes that are negative reciprocals of each other, the slope of the new line should be the negative reciprocal of the slope of the given line. The given line has a slope of $\frac{3}{2},$ so our perpendicular line must have a slope of $-\frac{2}{3}.$

Our perpendicular line must have the slope $m=-\frac{2}{3}$ and pass through the point $(x_1,y_1)=(5,6).$ Using point-slope form and simplifying, we obtain the equation of the line in slope-intercept form:

$$
\begin{aligned}y-y_1 &= m(x-x_1) \\ y-(6) &= -\frac{2}{3}(x-(5)) \\ y-(6) &= \frac{10}{3} -\frac{2 x}{3} \\ y &= \frac{28}{3} -\frac{2 x}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

However, we want to write the equation in standard form. So, we will bring the $x$ term to the left-hand side and multiply both sides of the equation by $3:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y &= \frac{28}{3} -\frac{2 x}{3} \\ \frac{2 x}{3} + y &= \frac{28}{3} \\ 3(\frac{2 x}{3} + y) &= 3\left(\frac{28}{3}\right) \\ 2 x + 3 y &= 28\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186481762 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "02a656c4-82b8-5e88-8816-0dc0a192bb9e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186481753} {:answer/id #uuid "80096874-46a7-55a9-a918-5e3243f639ba" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186481758}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186481758} :answer-field/id #uuid "23c3cc50-8f49-5f0a-a0d2-109c1fb2b62f" :answer-field/key "${\int }_{-\infty }^{-1}\frac{1}{x}\,\text{d}x$" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186481755} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "145423fa-33a3-52aa-ae1d-b24235875c7c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186481754} {:answer/id #uuid "3630167e-491c-546f-ac6e-210342635c1e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186481756}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186481756} :answer-field/id #uuid "9525a6e4-2431-55ce-91b6-40d7a688e4cf" :answer-field/key "${\int }_{2}^{\infty }\frac{1}{\sqrt{x-1}}\,\text{d}x$" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186481759} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "775f0f81-df07-5d86-9ff9-7f28b4ccaf9a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186481757} {:answer/id #uuid "d1da4748-78a9-5547-93fa-277269ba94ff" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186481761}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186481761} :answer-field/id #uuid "b5ca4e79-9a78-5e09-ad2e-1b4358963f5c" :answer-field/key "${\int }_{1}^{\infty }\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x$" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186481760}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "e50acc57-5eee-5203-9dd8-5e7531f41fa1" :question/problem "Which of the following improper integrals are divergent?

Select all that apply." :question/worked-solution "Let's work out each integral.

For the first integral, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{2}^{\infty }\frac{1}{\sqrt{x-1}}\,\text{d}x & =\lim_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{2}^{a}\frac{1}{\sqrt{x-1}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\lim_{a\to \infty }{[2\sqrt{x-1}]}_{2}^{a} \\  & =\lim_{a\to \infty }(2\sqrt{a-1}-2\sqrt{2-1}) \\  & =\lim_{a\to \infty }(2\sqrt{a-1}-2) \\  & =\infty ,\end{aligned}
$$

so the integral diverges.

For the second integral, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{-1}\frac{1}{x}\,\text{d}x & =\lim_{a\to -\infty }{\int }_{a}^{-1}\frac{1}{x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\lim_{a\to -\infty }{[\operatorname{ln}⁡|x|]}_{a}^{-1} \\  & =\lim_{a\to -\infty }(\operatorname{ln}⁡|-1|-\operatorname{ln}⁡|a|) \\  & =-\infty ,\end{aligned}
$$

so the integral diverges.

For the third integral, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{\infty }\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =\lim_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{1}^{a}\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\lim_{a\to \infty }{[-\frac{1}{x}]}_{1}^{a} \\  & =\lim_{a\to \infty }(-\frac{1}{a}+\frac{1}{1}) \\  & =1,\end{aligned}
$$

so the integral is convergent.

In conclusion, only integrals $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{2}^{\infty }\frac{1}{\sqrt{x-1}}\,\text{d}x
$$ and $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{-\infty }^{-1}\frac{1}{x}\,\text{d}x
$$ are divergent."} {:answer/id #uuid "0a545db6-b2c1-5af7-bab8-a92a067e183d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{\int }_{1}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}{\int $$
f(x)=\left\{\begin{aligned}\frac{x}{2}-1,\, & 2<x<4, \\ 0,\, & \text{otherwise.}\end{aligned}\right.
$$" :question/worked-solution "The $100p$th percentile of a random variable $X$ is the number ${x}_{p}$ such that

$$
P(X\le {x}_{p})=p.
$$

In our case, we want to find the $25$th percentile, which corresponds to the decimal $p=0.25.$ We have

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X\le {x}_{0.25}) & ={\int }_{2}^{{x}_{0.25}}(\frac{x}{2}-1)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={(\frac{{x}^{2}}{4}-x)|}_{2}^{{x}_{0.25}} \\  & =\frac{{x}_{0.25}^{2}}{4}-{x}_{0.25}-(\frac{(2)^{2}}{4}-2) \\  & =\frac{{x}_{0.25}^{2}}{4}-{x}_{0.25}+1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the $25$th percentile is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{x}_{0.25}^{2}}{4}-{x}_{0.25}+1 & =0.25 \\ {x}_{0.25}^{2}-4{x}_{0.25}+3 & =0 \\ ({x}_{0.25}-3)({x}_{0.25}-1) & =0 \\ {x}_{0.25}=1,\,3.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that we take the root ${x}_{0.25}=3$ because $2<{x}_{0.25}<4.$"} {:db/id 17592186482523 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "25237418-8897-5984-a318-b9d6acfd3dbf" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{(p-\frac{9}{16})}^{2}" :db/id 17592186481872} {:answer/id #uuid "336a6d96-d960-535c-95fb-75d4c09869fb" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{(p-\frac{9}{4})}^{2}" :db/id 17592186481900} {:answer/id #uuid "4e12cabb-23ac-5417-9a7a-ef3c27b9cbcc" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{(p-\frac{3}{4})}^{2}" :db/id 17592186481965} {:answer/id #uuid "6481951b-42c4-5e4f-90f7-2774c2f713bb" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{(p-\frac{3}{16})}^{2}" :db/id 17592186482006} {:answer/id #uuid "8350d09e-a155-59ee-9cf8-3c2e7a019dc2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{(p-\frac{3}{2})}^{2}" :db/id 17592186482076}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186481965} :answer-field/id #uuid "68e62d53-fe58-5a69-aba9-9a9c52260323" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186482430}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "33ad6f1c-10b4-54e8-b066-192c2a7ae636" :question/math-academy-id "q-111620" :question/problem "Factor ${p}^{2}-\frac{3}{2}p+\frac{9}{16}.$" :question/worked-solution "The "square of a difference" formula states that

$$
{p}^{2}-2ap+{a}^{2}=(p-a)^{2}.
$$

We will use this formula to factor the given trinomial. Our trinomial is

$$
{p}^{2}-\frac{3}{2}p+\frac{9}{16}.
$$

First, we write the constant term as a perfect square:

$$
\begin{aligned}{p}^{2}-\frac{3}{2}p+{\left(\frac{3}{4}\right)}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we factor a $2$ out of the linear term:

$$
\begin{aligned}{p}^{2}-2\cdot \frac{3}{4}p+{\left(\frac{3}{4}\right)}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we factor the trinomial using the square of difference formula with $a=\frac{3}{4}.$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{(p-\frac{3}{4})}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186482529 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "12f1b3aa-ebc1-51c1-8273-c4b915d8ecf4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{(n+\frac{25}{16})}^{2}" :db/id 17592186481826} {:answer/id #uuid "3d534e72-0930-51b5-a1d0-f3aa1de73e46" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{(n+\frac{5}{4})}^{2}" :db/id 17592186481928} {:answer/id #uuid "7e777da0-d7e0-58cc-ba96-49a1a74e9598" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{(n+\frac{5}{16})}^{2}" :db/id 17592186482064} {:answer/id #uuid "898c7c3f-dd8f-5773-abc2-e29cff260011" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{(n+\frac{25}{4})}^{2}" :db/id 17592186482094} {:answer/id #uuid "9d033726-a4f4-50d9-b131-7a5467c7dc90" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{(n+\frac{5}{2})}^{2}" :db/id 17592186482148}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186481928} :answer-field/id #uuid "6650d077-6bfe-5e18-8868-b906e55313a6" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186482428}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "3ab2e3ce-42ef-5550-a256-e8688e7ed48b" :question/math-academy-id "q-111618" :question/problem "Factor the expression ${n}^{2}+\frac{5}{2}n+\frac{25}{16}.$" :question/worked-solution "The "square of a sum" formula states that

$$
{n}^{2}+2an+{a}^{2}=(n+a)^{2}.
$$

We will use this formula to factor the given trinomial. Our trinomial is

$$
{n}^{2}+\frac{5}{2}n+\frac{25}{16}.
$$

First, we write the constant term as a perfect square:

$$
\begin{aligned}{n}^{2}+\frac{5}{2}n+{\left(\frac{5}{4}\right)}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we factor a $2$ out of the linear term:

$$
\begin{aligned}{n}^{2}+2\cdot \frac{5}{4}n+{\left(\frac{5}{4}\right)}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we factor the trinomial using the square of sum formula with $a=\frac{5}{4}.$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{(n+\frac{5}{4})}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186482534 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0a545db6-b2c1-5af7-bab8-a92a067e183d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{\int }_{1}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{3w}\frac{1}{3}(u+\frac{vw}{u})\,dw\,dv\,du" :db/id 17592186481792} {:answer/id #uuid "68e6ba86-dd63-5072-80c7-8937c30e291d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{\int }_{1}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{v}(\frac{w}{u}+3vu)\,dw\,dv\,du" :db/id 17592186482015} {:answer/id #uuid "6c9f7ec3-cf1f-5f6e-8b5d-a4981ae3628c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{\int }_{1}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{3w}\frac{1}{3}(v+\frac{vw}{u})\,dw\,dv\,du" :db/id 17592186482026} {:answer/id #uuid "ad6f11e6-c760-5ae7-8acd-14a00b864038" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{\int }_{1}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{3}(\frac{u}{3}+\frac{vw}{u})\,dw\,dv\,du" :db/id 17592186482181} {:answer/id #uuid "e4dfc26b-d49c-54ee-9547-1ec07e222142" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{\int }_{1}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{3}\frac{1}{3}(v+\frac{vw}{u})\,dw\,dv\,du" :db/id 17592186482319}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186482319} :answer-field/id #uuid "176c3a3c-6656-5311-869f-fdb6f745be21" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186482389}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "46b1b539-1890-56ee-b628-8f298fa77da5" :question/math-academy-id "q-161871" :question/problem "Consider the finite region $R$ in the $xyz$-space, given by

$$
R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,1\le x\le 2,\,0\le xy\le 2,\,0\le z\le 1\}.
$$

By performing the change of variables

$$
u=x,\,v=xy,\,w=3z,
$$

 

the triple integral

$$
{∭}_{R}({x}^{2}y+3xyz)\,dV
$$

can be written in terms of $u,$ $v,$ and $w$ as" :question/worked-solution "Let's define a transformation $T$ as follows:

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v \\ w\end{bmatrix}⟶\begin{bmatrix}x(u,v,w) \\ y(u,v,w) \\ z(u,v,w)\end{bmatrix}
$$

This transformation maps some region $Δ$ in the $uvw$-space to our region $R$ in the $xyz$-space.

To find the required integral, we can use the change of variables formula

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\text{ }dV={∭}_{Δ}\text{ }f(x(u,v,w),y(u,v,w),z(u,v,w))\,|\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v\text{d}w
$$

where $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T.$

Note that the change of variables

$$
u=x,\,v=xy,\,w=3z,
$$

 

gives us the *inverse* function ${T}^{-1},$ that is

$$
{T}^{-1}:\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y \\ z\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}u(x,y,z) \\ v(x,y,z) \\ w(x,y,z)\end{bmatrix}.
$$

To find the required integral, we proceed in four steps:

**Step 1**: Find $Δ,$ which is the image of $R$ under the action of ${T}^{-1}.$ 

Our domain in the $uvw$-space is

$$
\begin{aligned}Δ & =\{(u,v,w)\,:\,1\le u\le 2,\,0\le v\le 2,\,0\le w\le 3\}.\end{aligned}
$$

 

**Step 2**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} & \frac{∂u}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y} & \frac{∂v}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & \frac{∂w}{∂y} & \frac{∂w}{∂z}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ y & x & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 3\end{vmatrix} \\  & =3\begin{vmatrix}1 & 0 \\ y & x\end{vmatrix} \\  & =3(x-0) \\  & =3x \\  & =3u.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T$ is

$$
\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}={\left(\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)}\right)}^{-1}=\frac{1}{3u}.
$$

Note that $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}\ne 0$ everywhere inside $Δ.$ In other words, $T$ has no critical points inside $Δ.$

**Step 4**: Perform the change of variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∭}_{R}({x}^{2}y+3xyz)\,dV & ={∭}_{Δ}(uv+vw)\cdot |\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}|\,du\,dv\,dw \\  & ={∭}_{Δ}(uv+vw)\cdot |\frac{1}{3u}|\,du\,dv\,dw \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{3}\,\frac{1}{3}(v+\frac{vw}{u})\,\,dw\,dv\,du\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186482535 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "71daa61c-f673-5487-82fd-dfae267f950a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "12\pi " :db/id 17592186482039} {:answer/id #uuid "84aa3c04-cf41-557b-8aea-45aea8b80596" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{9\pi }{4}" :db/id 17592186482082} {:answer/id #uuid "af8ed3a1-6f17-5628-a41f-6b72eaa00e2b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4\pi " :db/id 17592186482188} {:answer/id #uuid "e2f7ffd3-d593-5a78-9afb-ab0de4615675" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{16\pi }{3}" :db/id 17592186482312} {:answer/id #uuid "e76d4b36-6b12-5f00-85a3-5cc9eafa0940" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "8\pi " :db/id 17592186482329}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186482312} :answer-field/id #uuid "27ef04a2-40cf-5a45-9600-60f9cd13b11c" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186482401}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "4913e4d1-197e-5ba9-a574-72530dddbf74" :question/math-academy-id "q-161789" :question/problem "![](images/08/085e28508da725e445c410fedc08a1992dccc5e0a7b99b3248182f58ffae2c07.png)

Evaluate the triple integral

$$
{∭}_{R}\frac{1}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}}}\,\text{d}V
$$

over the region $R$ enclosed inside the sphere ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}=4z,$ shown above." :question/worked-solution "We will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\,dV={∭}_{Δ}\,f(\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ)\,{\rho }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ.
$$

If $(\rho ,\theta ,ϕ)$ are the spherical coordinates of a point, then its Cartesian coordinates $(x,y,z)$ can be found by using the following formulas:

$$
x=\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,y=\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,z=\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ
$$

Notice that the region $R$ represents the sphere of radius $2$ centered at $(0,0,2).$

With that in mind, let's now write the ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}=4z$ in spherical polar coordinates:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2} & =4z \\ {\rho }^{2} & =4\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ \\ \rho (\rho -4\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

 

Since $\rho $ cannot be identical to zero on the entire sphere, we must have $\rho =4\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ.$

![](images/8a/8a730a72fe9f3f69878ef647215e8ed05e913f23bf8e0fab01bad6271e860335.png)

 

As a result, we obtain that in spherical polar coordinates, our region can be expressed as 

$$
Δ=\{(\rho ,\theta ,ϕ)\,:\,0\le \rho \le 4\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ,\,0\le \theta \le 2\pi ,\,0\le ϕ\le \frac{\pi }{2}\}.
$$

Next, we substitute the spherical polar coordinates into the function $f(x,y,z)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}}}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =f(\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ) \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{{\rho }^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{1}{\rho }\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∭}_{R}\frac{1}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}}}\,\text{d}V & ={∭}_{Δ}\frac{1}{\rho }\cdot {\rho }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{4\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ}\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ{[\frac{1}{2}{\rho }^{2}]}_{\rho =0}^{\rho =4\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ}\,d\theta \,dϕ \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }8\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ{\cos }^{2}⁡ϕ\,d\theta \,dϕ \\  & =8{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ{\cos }^{2}⁡ϕ\,dϕ\cdot {\int }_{0}^{2\pi }d\theta  \\  & =8{[-\frac{1}{3}{\cos }^{3}⁡ϕ]}_{ϕ=0}^{ϕ=\pi /2}\cdot [\theta ]_{\theta =0}^{\theta =2\pi } \\  & =-\frac{8}{3}(0-1)\cdot (2\pi -0) \\  & =\frac{16\pi }{3}\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186482547 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0b43c30d-dbbd-56ae-bb9d-ec705a2a3b5c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "16" :db/id 17592186481795} {:answer/id #uuid "0d41d4b8-c95d-5007-abd0-08600085f08f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "32" :db/id 17592186481803} {:answer/id #uuid "11f2f0e2-ee85-5dc7-8bf8-e4bbb3c1a106" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4" :db/id 17592186481822} {:answer/id #uuid "e6ad71c3-d535-5d86-9412-6ac3d6c65116" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "48" :db/id 17592186482325} {:answer/id #uuid "f3d483b0-65b2-53a0-9add-ad98d8a18577" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "64" :db/id 17592186482353}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186481803} :answer-field/id #uuid "f6f66c5c-6087-5c29-8319-6c31eb512359" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186482500}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "7144ca6a-debb-5e59-baf7-8232b8798b6c" :question/math-academy-id "q-162183" :question/problem "Find the volume bounded by the region $R,$ given by

$$
R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,1\le y\le 3,\,-2\le x-z\le 0,\,1\le \frac{z-1}{y}\le 5\}.
$$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that the volume of $R$ can be found as 

$$
V={∭}_{R}\text{d}V.
$$

Let's define a transformation $T$ as follows:

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v \\ w\end{bmatrix}⟶\begin{bmatrix}x(u,v,w) \\ y(u,v,w) \\ z(u,v,w)\end{bmatrix}
$$

This transformation maps some region $Δ$ in the $uvw$-space to our region $R$ in the $xyz$-space.

To compute the required volume, we can use the change of variables formula

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\text{ }dV={∭}_{Δ}\text{ }f(x(u,v,w),y(u,v,w),z(u,v,w))\,|\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v\text{d}w
$$

where $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T.$

The inequalities that define the region $R,$

$$
1\le y\le 3,\,-2\le x-z\le 0,\,1\le \frac{z-1}{y}\le 5,
$$

suggest that we use the change of variables

$$
u=y,\,v=x-z,\,w=\frac{z-1}{y}.
$$

This change of variables gives us the *inverse* function ${T}^{-1},$ that is

$$
{T}^{-1}:\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y \\ z\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}u(x,y,z) \\ v(x,y,z) \\ w(x,y,z)\end{bmatrix}.
$$

To compute the required volume, we proceed in four steps:

**Step 1**: Find $Δ,$ which is the image of $R$ under the action of ${T}^{-1}.$ 

Our domain in the $uvw$-space is

$$
\begin{aligned}Δ & =\{(u,v,w)\,:\,1\le u\le 3,\,-2\le v\le 0,\,1\le w\le 5\}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} & \frac{∂u}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y} & \frac{∂v}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & \frac{∂w}{∂y} & \frac{∂w}{∂z}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}0 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & -1 \\ 0 & -\frac{z-1}{{y}^{2}} & \frac{1}{y}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =1(-1)^{1+2}\begin{vmatrix}1 & -1 \\ 0 & \frac{1}{y}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{y} \\  & =\frac{1}{u}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T$ is

$$
\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}={\left(\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)}\right)}^{-1}=u.
$$

Note that $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}\ne 0$ everywhere inside $Δ.$ In other words, $T$ has no critical points inside $Δ.$

**Step 4**: Perform the change of variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∭}_{R}dV & ={∭}_{Δ}1\cdot |u|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v\text{d}w \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{3}{\int }_{-2}^{0}{\int }_{1}^{5}u\,dw\,dv\,du \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{3}u\,du\cdot {\int }_{-2}^{0}dv\cdot {\int }_{1}^{5}dw \\  & ={[\frac{{u}^{2}}{2}]}_{u=1}^{u=3}\cdot [v]_{v=-2}^{v=0}\cdot [w]_{w=1}^{w=5} \\  & =(\frac{9}{2}-\frac{1}{2})\cdot (0-(-2))\cdot (5-1) \\  & =32.\end{aligned}

$$
u=y+z,\,v=x+4z,\,w=2y
$$

to evaluate the triple integral

$$
{∭}_{R}\,\frac{y+z}{x+4z}\,dV,
$$

 
where the region $R$ is given by

$$
R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,0\le y+z\le 2,\,1\le x+4z\le e,\,0\le y\le 1\}.
$$" :question/worked-solution "Let's define a transformation $T$ as follows:

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v \\ w\end{bmatrix}⟶\begin{bmatrix}x(u,v,w) \\ y(u,v,w) \\ z(u,v,w)\end{bmatrix}
$$

This transformation maps some region $Δ$ in the $uvw$-space to our region $R$ in the $xyz$-space.

To compute the required integral, we can use the change of variables formula

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\text{ }dV={∭}_{Δ}\text{ }f(x(u,v,w),y(u,v,w),z(u,v,w))\,|\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v\text{d}w
$$

where $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T.$

Note that the change of variables

$$
u=y+z,\,v=x+4z,\,w=2y
$$

gives us the *inverse* function ${T}^{-1},$ that is

$$
{T}^{-1}:\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y \\ z\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}u(x,y,z) \\ v(x,y,z) \\ w(x,y,z)\end{bmatrix}.
$$

To compute the required integral, we proceed in four steps:

**Step 1**: Find $Δ,$ which is the image of $R$ under the action of ${T}^{-1}.$ 

Our domain in the $uvw$-space is

$$
\begin{aligned}Δ & =\{(u,v,w)\,:\,0\le u\le 2,\,1\le v\le e,\,0\le w\le 2\}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} & \frac{∂u}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y} & \frac{∂v}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & \frac{∂w}{∂y} & \frac{∂w}{∂z}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}0 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 & 4 \\ 0 & 2 & 0\end{vmatrix} \\  & =2(-1)^{3+2}\begin{vmatrix}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 4\end{vmatrix} \\  & =2(-1)(-1). \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T$ is

$$
\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}={\left(\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)}\right)}^{-1}=\frac{1}{2}.
$$

Note that $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}\ne 0$ everywhere inside $Δ.$ In other words, $T$ has no critical points inside $Δ.$

**Step 4**: Perform the change of variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∭}_{R}\frac{y+z}{x+4z}\,dV & ={∭}_{Δ}\frac{u}{v}\cdot |\frac{1}{2}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v\text{d}w \\  & ={∭}_{Δ}\frac{u}{2v}\,\text{d}u\text{d}v\text{d}w \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{1}^{e}{\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{u}{2v}\,dw\,dv\,du \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{u}{2}\,du\cdot {\int }_{1}^{e}\frac{1}{v}\,dv\cdot {\int }_{0}^{2}dw \\  & =[\frac{{u}^{2}}{4}]_{u=0}^{u=2}\cdot {[\operatorname{ln}⁡v]}_{v=1}^{v=e}\cdot [w]_{w=0}^{w=2} \\  & =(1-0)\cdot (1-0)\cdot (2-0) \\  & =2\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186482601 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "107bc90b-168a-5ae7-9c1e-5151de594035" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\pi " :db/id 17592186481814} {:answer/id #uuid "1508999f-583d-5409-a945-a2774f7b6030" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\pi }{9}" :db/id 17592186481833} {:answer/id #uuid "1e78963c-6d08-52e4-886b-c299ac1eab3b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{3\pi }{2}" :db/id 17592186481855} {:answer/id #uuid "a5dfe954-7d04-5a12-8506-1f9267e2a525" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{5\pi }{8}" :db/id 17592186482169} {:answer/id #uuid "fdb401e4-0e59-57f0-b798-ca38f29d946f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3\pi " :db/id 17592186482375}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186481833} :answer-field/id #uuid "748331ec-5745-5dc8-9854-65c69f6cb19e" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186482439}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "ddc59e97-e243-5e27-9d57-5e0f9b714882" :question/math-academy-id "q-161777" :question/problem "![](images/90/90d5e9115d216f2a7f8fba49295a36b95cd932c4df7f8bace1b45e3542e9ae11.png)

Evaluate the triple integral

$$
{∭}_{R}{({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2})}^{3}\,\text{d}V
$$

over the region $R$ enclosed inside the sphere ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}=1$ for $x\ge 0$ and $z\ge 0,$ shown above." :question/worked-solution "We will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\,dV={∭}_{Δ}\,f(\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ)\,{\rho }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ.
$$

If $(\rho ,\theta ,ϕ)$ are the spherical coordinates of a point, then its Cartesian coordinates $(x,y,z)$ can be found by using the following formulas:

$$
x=\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,y=\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,z=\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ
$$

Notice that the region $R$ represents one-quarter of the sphere of radius $1$ centered at the origin.

![](images/ec/ec2f6c67eee7f836cc71efec2b17c2276aa8a9d397c632b3c499a46a75f7b95c.png)

 

As a result, we obtain that in spherical polar coordinates, our region can be expressed as 

$$
Δ=\{(\rho ,\theta ,ϕ)\,:\,0\le \rho \le 1,\,-\frac{\pi }{2}\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2},\,0\le ϕ\le \frac{\pi }{2}\}.
$$

Next, we substitute the spherical polar coordinates into the function $f(x,y,z)={({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2})}^{3}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =f(\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ) \\  & ={({\rho }^{2})}^{3} \\  & ={\rho }^{6}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∭}_{R}{({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2})}^{3}\,\text{d}V & ={∭}_{Δ}{\rho }^{6}\cdot {\rho }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\rho }^{8}\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\,dϕ\cdot {\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}d\theta \cdot {\int }_{0}^{1}{\rho }^{8}\,d\rho  \\  & =[-\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ]_{ϕ=0}^{ϕ=\pi /2}\cdot [\theta ]_{\theta =-\pi /2}^{\theta =\pi /2}\cdot {[\frac{1}{9}{\rho }^{9}]}_{\rho =0}^{\rho =1} \\  & =-(0-1)\cdot (\frac{\pi }{2}-\left(-\frac{\pi }{2}\right))\cdot \frac{1}{9}(1-0) \\  & =1\cdot \pi \cdot \frac{1}{9} \\  & =\frac{\pi }{9}\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186482606 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1ee0c1d0-b902-5d6e-9fd8-7baec2f61f9c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4" :db/id 17592186481859} {:answer/id #uuid "572c02e1-9d71-5b99-960a-6f12882be763" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "6" :db/id 17592186481981} {:answer/id #uuid "70ef93b1-e501-54d3-bcff-1f06883cd750" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "5" :db/id 17592186482035} {:answer/id #uuid "75475609-dfeb-560d-bc22-9379064434fc" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "8" :db/id 17592186482047} {:answer/id #uuid "8e5aafc8-ceba-5678-a412-98f1f904e581" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "9" :db/id 17592186482109}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186481859} :answer-field/id #uuid "3587c6f6-e4fb-567f-a4f3-80de70f97f45" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186482407}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "e662cc33-8ce5-5a82-9731-097b3595e6c3" :question/math-academy-id "q-162140" :question/problem "Use the change of variables 

$$

to evaluate the triple integral
