Round your answer to $3$ decimal places." :question/worked-solution "Let $A$ be the event that a light bulb is of type A, $D$ be the event that a light bulb is defective, and ${F}_{1},{F}_{2},{F}_{3}$ be the event that a light bulb is produced in factory $1,$ $2,$ or $3,$ respectively. 

Let's break down the information given in the problem statement:

- From the bullet points, we have the following information:

$$
\begin{aligned} & P({F}_{1})=0.45 &  & P(D|{F}_{1})=0.05 \\  & P({F}_{2})=0.45 \\  & P({F}_{3})=0.1 &  & P(D|{F}_{3})=0.01\end{aligned}
$$

The disjoint union ${F}_{1}⊔{F}_{2}⊔{F}_{3}$ covers the entire sample space, and we have

$$
P({F}_{1})+P({F}_{2})+P({F}_{3})=0.45+0.45+0.1=1.
$$

- Since $57\%$ of all light bulbs are of type A, we have

$$
P(A)=0.57.
$$

- Since $3\%$ of type A light bulbs are defective, we have

$$
P(D|A)=0.03.
$$

- Since $41\%$ of defective light bulbs are of type A, we have

$$
P(A|D)=0.41
$$

We want to find the probability that a randomly chosen light bulb from factory $2$ is defective, which is represented as $P(D|{F}_{2}).$ 

Using Bayes' theorem combined with the law of total probability, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}P(A|D) & =\frac{P(D|A)P(A)}{P(D)} \\ P(A|D) & =\frac{P(D|A)P(A)}{P(D|{F}_{1})P({F}_{1})+P(D|{F}_{2})P({F}_{2})+P(D|{F}_{3})P({F}_{3})} \\ 0.41 & =\frac{(0.03)(0.57)}{(0.05)(0.45)+P(D|{F}_{2})(0.45)+(0.01)(0.1)} \\ 0.41 & =\frac{0.0171}{0.0235+0.45P(D|{F}_{2})}\end{aligned}

\begin{aligned}0.41(0.0235+0.45P(D|{F}_{2})) & =0.0171 \\ 0.0235+0.45P(D|{F}_{2}) & =\frac{0.0171}{0.41} \\ 0.0235+0.45P(D|{F}_{2}) & =\frac{171}{4100} \\ 0.45P(D|{F}_{2}) & =\frac{171}{4100}-0.0235 \\ P(D|{F}_{2}) & =\frac{1}{0.45}(\frac{171}{4100}-0.0235) \\ P(D|{F}_{2}) & ≈0.040\end{aligned}
$$

| $\,0.8\,$ | $\,0.7881\,$ | $\,0.7910\,$ | $\,0.7939\,$ |" :question/worked-solution "Let $X$ represent the output voltage of a randomly selected AC adapter. Then we have $X∼N(19,{\sigma }^{2}),$ and we want to find $P(X>19.3).$ But first, we need to find the standard deviation $\sigma .$ 

We know that $P(X>20)=0.01.$ First, we convert this to a cumulative probability:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X\le 20) & =1-P(X>20) \\  & =1-0.01 \\  & =0.99\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we convert $X$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X\le 20) & =0.99 \\ P(Z\le \frac{20-19}{\sigma }) & =0.99 \\ Φ\left(\frac{1}{\sigma }\right) & =0.99 \\ \frac{1}{\sigma } & ={Φ}^{-1}(0.99)\end{aligned}
$$

From the table, 

$$

$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sigma } & =2.3263 \\ \sigma  & =\frac{1}{2.32639} \\  & ≈0.42985.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can solve for $P(X>19.3)$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X>19.3) & =1-P(X\le 19.3) \\  & =1-P(Z\le \frac{19.3-19}{0.42985}) \\  & ≈1-P(Z\le 0.70) \\  & =1-Φ(0.70) \\  & =1-0.7580 \\  & ≈24.2\%\end{aligned}
$$

$$
f(x,y,z)=x+2y+3z
$$

subject to the constraints 

$$
g(x,y,z)=x-y-z=0,\,h(x,y,z)=4{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=1.
$$

Since $f(x,y,z)$ is continuous and the constraint is closed and bounded, $f(x,y,z)$ reaches a global maximum and a global minimum on the constraint. 

Therefore, by the method of Lagrange multipliers, we must solve the following system:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) &=\lambda ∇g(x,y,z)+\mu ∇h(x,y,z) \\ g(x,y,z) &=0 \\ h(x,y,z) &=1\end{aligned}\right.
$$

We start by expanding the first equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & =\lambda ∇g(x,y,z)+\mu ∇h(x,y,z) \\ ⟨{f}_{x},{f}_{y},{f}_{z}⟩ & =\lambda ⟨{g}_{x},{g}_{y},{g}_{z}⟩+\mu ⟨{h}_{x},{h}_{y},{h}_{z}⟩ \\ ⟨1,2,3⟩ & =\lambda ⟨1,-1,-1⟩+\mu ⟨8x,2y,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, we have the following system:

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}1 &=\lambda +8\mu x \\ 2 &=-\lambda +2\mu y \\ 3 &=-\lambda\end{aligned}\right.\,⇒\,\left\{\begin{aligned}x &=\frac{1}{2\mu } \\ y &=-\frac{1}{2\mu } \\ \lambda &=-3\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that $\mu $ can't be zero since this leads to a contradiction.

Next, we substitute our expressions for $x$ and $y$ into the second constraint:

$$
\begin{aligned}4{x}^{2}+{y}^{2} & =1 \\ \frac{1}{{\mu }^{2}}+\frac{1}{4{\mu }^{2}} & =1 \\ \frac{5}{4{\mu }^{2}} & =1 \\ {\mu }^{2} & =\frac{5}{4} \\ \mu  & =\pm \frac{\sqrt{5}}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

As a result, 

$$
x=\pm \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}},\,y=∓\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}.
$$

Finally, we substitute $x$ and $y$ into the first constraint:

- If $x=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}$ and $y=-\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}x-y-z & =0 \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}-\left(-\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\right)-z & =0 \\ z & =\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}.\end{aligned}
$$

- If $x=-\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}$ and $y=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}x-y-z & =0 \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}-\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\right)-z & =0 \\ z & =-\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $f$ has possible extreme values at the points

$$
(\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}},-\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}},\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}),\,(-\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}},\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}},-\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}})
$$

We evaluate $f$ at each of these points. These are given in the following table:

| $(x,y,z)$ | $$
\displaystyle (\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}},-\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}},\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}})
$$ | $$
\displaystyle (-\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}},\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}},-\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}})
$$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x,y,z)$ | $\sqrt{5}$ | $-\sqrt{5}$ |

Therefore, the function reaches a maximum value at $$
\displaystyle (\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}},-\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}},\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}),
$$ and its   maximum value is $\sqrt{5}.$"} {:db/id 17592186493933 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "7ca77ecc-c1a9-5d9e-bb7f-432fe7a73841" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.21" :db/id 17592186493582} {:answer/id #uuid "8fda6180-a0df-5a37-bce4-0c0c1f2770b9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.19" :db/id 17592186493618} {:answer/id #uuid "9c1602bd-bf20-5b35-8c8b-08a20f5fd4ca" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.32" :db/id 17592186493634} {:answer/id #uuid "aed00733-48dd-5a2a-9f46-ede060604a30" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.24" :db/id 17592186493670} {:answer/id #uuid "b93831bc-3eb1-57b6-a625-ff14ad98c1fb" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.29" :db/id 17592186493694}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186493670} :answer-field/id #uuid "044df1b7-c311-5b38-a151-6ea7331c7eee" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186493803}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "865ccf64-fc88-5f41-a8ec-576978864deb" :question/math-academy-id "q-94978" :question/problem "The diastolic blood pressure of a group of people is normally distributed with a mean of $85\,\text{mm}\,\text{Hg}$ and a standard deviation of $14\,\text{mm}\,\text{Hg}.$ What is the probability that a randomly selected person from the group has a diastolic blood pressure greater than $77\,\text{mm}\,\text{Hg}$ and less than $86\,\text{mm}\,\text{Hg}?$ Round your answer to $2$ decimal places.

We want to find $P(77<X<86).$ First, we convert $X$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(77<X<86) & =P(\frac{77-85}{14}<Z<\frac{86-85}{14}) \\  & =P(-0.57<Z<0.07)\end{aligned}

Now, we express the required probability in terms of $Φ(z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}P(-0.57<Z<0.07) & =P(Z<0.07)-P(Z\le -0.57) \\  & =P(Z\le 0.07)-P(Z\le -0.57) \\  & =Φ(0.07)-Φ(-0.57)\end{aligned}
$$

From the table, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}Φ(0.07) & =0.5279 \\ Φ(-0.57) & =0.2843\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}P(-0.57<Z<0.07) & =Φ(0.07)-Φ(-0.57) \\  & =0.5279-0.2843 \\  & =0.2436.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the probability that the randomly selected person from the group has a diastolic blood pressure greater than $77\,\text{mm}\,\text{Hg}$ and less than $86\,\text{mm}\,\text{Hg}$ is approximately $0.24.$"} {:db/id 17592186493934 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "bfa1ad90-bf21-5bd7-9c4a-e2c278e3e210" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2x-5y" :db/id 17592186493706}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186493706} :answer-field/id #uuid "2578c7dc-df07-5c9f-9883-dccf1b4fa276" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186493811} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1900311e-ec2f-5a19-8cfb-a76c9ae262ca" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "15" :db/id 17592186493434}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186493434} :answer-field/id #uuid "adee3ac3-8ecd-58c3-a665-8c5d902d4cdf" :answer-field/key "field-2" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186493860}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "8d0eef6f-b433-56d1-a89d-4aab29bca392" :question/math-academy-id "q-214594" :question/problem "Express the equation of the line $y=\frac{2}{5}x-3$ in standard form.

{{field-1}}

$=$
{{field-2}}" :question/worked-solution "Our goal is to write the equation in the form $ax+by=c,$ where $a,b,$ and $c$ are integers with no common factors and $a\ge 0.$

We begin by moving all of the variables to the left-hand side and all of the constants to the right-hand side. This gives

$$
-\frac{2}{5}x+y=-3
$$

Now, we multiply both sides of the equation by $-1:$

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{2}{5}x+y & =-3 \\ (-1)\cdot (-\frac{2}{5}x+y) & =(-1)\cdot (-3) \\ \frac{2}{5}x-y & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we multiply both sides of the equation by $5:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{5}x-y & =3 \\ 5\cdot (\frac{2}{5}x-y) & =5\cdot (3) \\ 2x-5y & =15\end{aligned}
$$

Now, $a,b,$ and $c$ are integers with no common factors, and $a\ge 0.$ So we are done!

The standard form of the line is 

$$
2x-5y=15.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186493956 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0b6b5fe5-29d1-5793-a274-fa3b5699e913" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3({e}^{-1/2}-{e}^{-2})\operatorname{ln}⁡2" :db/id 17592186493410} {:answer/id #uuid "17dcff5e-6574-5e2e-be4c-22c67c1a31d5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{e}{8}" :db/id 17592186493432} {:answer/id #uuid "702b0bc2-ac10-5437-9f18-9fa877532a9e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{{e}^{-1}-{e}^{-2}}{4}" :db/id 17592186493554} {:answer/id #uuid "857734df-e10d-5568-a049-4e87b8b5c0d1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "8{e}^{2}" :db/id 17592186493601} {:answer/id #uuid "e162164d-9035-55fa-9f1c-b47ea0bae241" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "({e}^{2}-e)\operatorname{ln}⁡2" :db/id 17592186493747}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186493410} :answer-field/id #uuid "15ea503e-c96f-567a-8f89-cf26cc3e1193" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186493808}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "c5c02db8-6f5e-5ac6-a24e-9e9016b1082e" :question/math-academy-id "q-160899" :question/problem "Using the change of variables $u=\frac{y}{x}$ and $v=xy,$ evaluate the double integral

$$
{∬}_{D}{e}^{-xy/2}\,dx\,dy,
$$

where $D=\{(x,y)\,:\,\frac{x}{4}\le y\le 2x,\,1\le xy\le 4\}.$" :question/worked-solution "Let's define a transformation $T$ as follows:

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}⟶\begin{bmatrix}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{bmatrix}
$$

This transformation maps some region $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane to our region $D$ in the $xy$-plane.

To compute the required integral, we can use the change of variables formula

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,dx\,dy={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(x(u,v),y(u,v))|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|du\,dv
$$

where $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T.$

Note that the change of variables

$$
u=\frac{y}{x},\,v=xy
$$

 
gives us the *inverse* function ${T}^{-1},$ that is

$$
{T}^{-1}:\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}u(x,y) \\ v(x,y)\end{bmatrix}.
$$

To compute the required integral, we proceed as follows:

**Step 1**: Find $Δ,$ which is the image of $D$ under the action of ${T}^{-1}.$ 

Our domain in the $uv$-plane is

$$
\begin{aligned}Δ & =\{(u,v)\,:\,\frac{1}{4}\le u\le 2,\,1\le v\le 4\}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}-\frac{y}{{x}^{2}} & \frac{1}{x} \\ y & \text{ }\text{ }x\end{vmatrix} \\  & =-\frac{2y}{x}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T$ is

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}={\left(\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)}\right)}^{-1}=\frac{1}{\left(-\frac{2y}{x}\right)}=-\frac{1}{2u}.
$$

Note that $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}\ne 0$ everywhere inside $Δ.$ In other words, $T$ has no critical points inside $Δ.$

**Step 4**: Perform the change of variables:

Performing the change of variables, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}{e}^{-xy/2}\,dx\,dy & ={∬}_{Δ}{e}^{-v/2}|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\text{d}u\,\text{d}v \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}{e}^{-v/2}\cdot |-\frac{1}{2u}|\,\text{d}u\,\text{d}v \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{1}^{4}{\int }_{1/4}^{2}\frac{{e}^{-v/2}}{u}\,\text{d}u\,\text{d}v \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{1}^{4}{e}^{-v/2}[{\int }_{1/4}^{2}\frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u]\text{d}v \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{1}^{4}{e}^{-v/2}[\operatorname{ln}⁡|u|\,{|}_{1/4}^{2}]du \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{1}^{4}{e}^{-v/2}[\operatorname{ln}⁡2-\operatorname{ln}⁡\frac{1}{4}]\,du \\  & =\frac{3\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{2}{\int }_{1}^{4}{e}^{-v/2}\,du \\  & =\frac{3\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{2}\cdot {[-2{e}^{-v/2}]}_{1}^{4} \\  & =-3\operatorname{ln}⁡2\cdot ({e}^{-2}-{e}^{-1/2}) \\  & =3({e}^{-1/2}-{e}^{-2})\operatorname{ln}⁡2.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186493960 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "6da77181-6032-5e5c-929d-4a017fc0454f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-60" :db/id 17592186493553}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186493553} :answer-field/id #uuid "5932016c-ec0a-5d79-9f39-b11ee0e695a8" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186493826}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "d4dc1b86-0478-57c7-a48b-3ee42621256c" :question/math-academy-id "q-175957" :question/problem "Expressed as an integer, $(-4)÷\left(\frac{2}{5}\right)\times 6=${{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "To evaluate this expression, we use PEMDAS.

$$"} {:db/id 17592186493962 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "264f5867-7c47-5f07-9b9c-b3815c6cd840" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "53.10\,\text{cm}" :db/id 17592186493452} {:answer/id #uuid "73143a86-4466-59b0-9d13-697c03f90f7c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "40.50\,\text{cm}" :db/id 17592186493562} {:answer/id #uuid "975eb98b-4ab0-5014-8bea-9fcf9cfaaba5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "50.50\,\text{cm}" :db/id 17592186493630} {:answer/id #uuid "ec6926a3-0298-524c-9ffa-d17531745d04" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "52.15\,\text{cm}" :db/id 17592186493768} {:answer/id #uuid "ff5d72e2-1423-5d98-a00f-6cea45e898da" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "48.05\,\text{cm}" :db/id 17592186493801}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186493630} :answer-field/id #uuid "7782954d-0945-5a09-a4ad-d4eaf2acb6cc" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186493839}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "d916a01a-c116-520b-be92-bf93eddd6997" :question/math-academy-id "q-95126" :question/problem "The lengths of babies at birth in a given population are normally distributed with a mean of $\mu \,\text{cm}$ and a standard deviation of $6\,\text{cm}.$ Additionally, the length of $60\%$ of the newborns falls between $0.9\mu \,\text{cm}$ and $1.1\mu \,\text{cm}.$ Find the mean $\mu $ rounded to $2$ decimal places.

*Hint: A table of values of ${Φ}^{-1}(p)$ for different values of $p$ is given below, where $p=Φ(z)$ is the cumulative distribution function for the standard normal distribution.* 

| $p$ | $\,0.75\,$ | $\,0.80\,$ | $\,0.85\,$ | $\,0.90\,$ | $\,0.95\,$ | $\,0.97\,$ | $\,0.99\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| ${Φ}^{-1}(p)$ | $\,0.6745\,$ | $\,0.8416\,$ | $\,1.0364\,$ | $\,1.2816\,$ | $\,1.6449\,$ | $\,1.8808\,$ | $\,2.3263\,$ |" :question/worked-solution "Let $X$ represent the length of a randomly selected newborn. Then we have $X∼N(\mu ,{6}^{2}),$ and we want to find the mean $\mu .$ 

We know that $P(0.9\mu <X<1.1\mu )=0.6.$ First, we convert this to a cumulative probability:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(0.9\mu <X<1.1\mu ) & =0.6 \\ 2P(\mu <X<1.1\mu ) & =0.6 \\ P(\mu <X<1.1\mu ) & =0.3 \\ P(X<\mu )+P(\mu <X<1.1\mu ) & =0.5+0.3 \\ P(X<1.1\mu ) & =0.8\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we convert $X$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X<1.1\mu ) & =0.8 \\ P(Z<\frac{0.1\mu }{6}) & =0.8 \\ Φ\left(\frac{0.1\mu }{6}\right) & =0.8 \\ \frac{0.1\mu }{6} & ={Φ}^{-1}(0.8)\end{aligned}
$$

From the table, 

$$
{Φ}^{-1}(0.8)≈0.8416.
$$

Finally then,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{0.1\mu }{6} & =0.8416 \\ 0.1\mu  & =5.0496 \\ \mu  & =\frac{5.0496}{0.1} \\  & ≈50.50\,\text{cm}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186493964 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "3b33f311-775b-531d-a7c1-211917078fee" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-5" :db/id 17592186493491} {:answer/id #uuid "6cc52ef3-233d-50cf-981c-9d55c945e79b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-9" :db/id 17592186493551} {:answer/id #uuid "d635b4ea-d9c6-5d7b-b741-bd02b50aa24f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "10" :db/id 17592186493728} {:answer/id #uuid "fa2baa31-cb4e-5fc8-881b-3a0207f4db3c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "5" :db/id 17592186493796} {:answer/id #uuid "ffea41a4-e1d5-5dcb-a38a-77b3723e6c19" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "7" :db/id 17592186493802}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186493551} :answer-field/id #uuid "55f0be58-6264-52fc-81bc-9aa7d91e0659" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186493825}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "daa44e18-10db-5d53-b4fb-045b6b617679" :question/math-academy-id "q-162897" :question/problem "Use the method of Lagrange multipliers to find the minimum value of the function $f(x,y,z)=2x+4y-2z$ on the intersection of the plane $2x-4y-2z=1$ and the cylinder ${x}^{2}+{z}^{2}=2.$" :question/worked-solution "We need to find the minimum value of 

$$
f(x,y,z)=2x+4y-2z
$$

subject to the constraints 

$$
g(x,y,z)=2x-4y-2z=1,\,h(x,y,z)={x}^{2}+{z}^{2}=2.
$$

Since $f(x,y,z)$ is continuous and the constraint is closed and bounded, $f(x,y,z)$ reaches a global maximum and a global minimum on the constraint. 

Therefore, by the method of Lagrange multipliers, we must solve the following system:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) &=\lambda ∇g(x,y,z)+\mu ∇h(x,y,z) \\ g(x,y,z) &=1 \\ h(x,y,z) &=2\end{aligned}\right.
$$

We start by expanding the first equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & =\lambda ∇g(x,y,z)+\mu ∇h(x,y,z) \\ ⟨{f}_{x},{f}_{y},{f}_{z}⟩ & =\lambda ⟨{g}_{x},{g}_{y},{g}_{z}⟩+\mu ⟨{h}_{x},{h}_{y},{h}_{z}⟩ \\ ⟨2,4,-2⟩ & =\lambda ⟨2,-4,-2⟩+\mu ⟨2x,0,2z⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the following system:

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}2 &=2\lambda +2\mu x \\ 4 &=-4\lambda \\ -2 &=-2\lambda +2\mu z\end{aligned}\right.\,⇒\,\left\{\begin{aligned}x &=\frac{2}{\mu } \\ \lambda &=-1 \\ z &=-\frac{2}{\mu }\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that $\mu $ can't be zero since this leads to a contradiction.

Next, we substitute our expressions for $x$ and $z$ into the second constraint:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{z}^{2} & =2 \\ \frac{4}{{\mu }^{2}}+\frac{4}{{\mu }^{2}} & =2 \\ \frac{8}{{\mu }^{2}} & =2 \\ {\mu }^{2} & =4 \\ \mu  & =\pm 2\end{aligned}
$$

As a result, 

$$
x=\pm 1,\,z=∓1.
$$

Finally, we substitute $x$ and $z$ into the first constraint:

- If $x=1$ and $z=-1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}2x-4y-2z & =1 \\ 2(1)-4y-2(-1) & =1 \\ -4y & =-3 \\ y & =\frac{3}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

- If $x=-1$ and $z=1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}2x-4y-2z & =1 \\ 2(-1)-4y-2(1) & =1 \\ -4y & =5 \\ y & =-\frac{5}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $f$ has possible extreme values at the points

$$
(1,\frac{3}{4},-1),\,(-1,-\frac{5}{4},1).
$$

We evaluate $f$ at each of these points. These are given in the following table:

| $(x,y,z)$ | $(1,\frac{3}{4},-1)$ | $(-1,-\frac{5}{4},1)$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x,y,z)$ | $7$ | $-9$ |

Therefore, the function reaches a minimum value at $(-1,-\frac{5}{4},1),$ and its minimum value is $-9.$"} {:db/id 17592186493967 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "aad9a2ec-8c38-50c5-a148-e148cf1a201f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.307" :db/id 17592186493659} {:answer/id #uuid "cb08ac4c-bcdb-5bf3-803d-48abd3c44b23" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.546" :db/id 17592186493717} {:answer/id #uuid "db3514aa-7da2-58cd-a765-4883b4c73d8a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.135" :db/id 17592186493736} {:answer/id #uuid "e44bfd71-59f5-5456-8e29-b331fc4b994f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.398" :db/id 17592186493751} {:answer/id #uuid "e5ca70ca-440e-5d09-bd91-1a12c84d2bf9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.252" :db/id 17592186493758}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186493751} :answer-field/id #uuid "b2b5eda7-fc54-5354-9c43-01751b2546c8" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186493866}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "deb0627a-b1f4-5ecd-95e2-372ffa642f2c" :question/math-academy-id "q-149493" :question/problem "A volleyball school for children splits the players into three teams, team $1$, team $2,$ and team $3.$ 

- $44\%$ of children are in team $1,$ and $23\%$ of children in this team have been playing for over two years.

- $32\%$ of children are in team $2,$ and $26\%$ of children in this team have been playing for over two years.

- $24\%$ of children are in team $3.$

If $7\%$ of all children can play in the blocker position, $40\%$ of children who can play as blockers have been playing for over two years, and $10\%$ of children who have been playing for over two years can play as blockers, what is the probability that a randomly chosen child in team $3$ has been playing for over two years? Round your answer to $3$ decimal places." :question/worked-solution "Let $B$ be the event that a child can play in the blocker position, $I$ be the event that a child has been playing for over two years, and ${T}_{1},{T}_{2},{T}_{3}$ be the events that a child is in team $1,$ $2,$ or $3,$ respectively. 

Let's break down the information given in the problem statement:

- From the bullet points, we have the following information:

$$
\begin{aligned} & P({T}_{1})=0.44 &  & P(I|{T}_{1})=0.23 \\  & P({T}_{2})=0.32 &  & P(I|{T}_{2})=0.26 \\  & P({T}_{3})=0.24\end{aligned}
$$

The disjoint union ${T}_{1}⊔{T}_{2}⊔{T}_{3}$ covers the entire sample space, and we have

$$
P({T}_{1})+P({T}_{2})+P({T}_{3})=0.44+0.32+0.24=1.
$$

- Since $7\%$ of children can play in the blocker position, we have

$$
P(B)=0.07.
$$

- Since $40\%$ of children who can play as blockers have been playing for over two years, we have

$$
P(I|B)=0.4.
$$

- Since $10\%$ of children who have been playing for over two years can play as blockers, we have

$$
P(B|I)=0.1.
$$

We want to find the probability that a randomly chosen child in team 3 has been playing for over two years, which is represented as $P(I|{T}_{3}).$

Using Bayes' theorem combined with the law of total probability, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}P(B|I) & =\frac{P(I|B)P(B)}{P(I)} \\ P(B|I) & =\frac{P(I|B)P(B)}{P(I|{T}_{1})P({T}_{1})+P(I|{T}_{2})P({T}_{2})+P(I|{T}_{3})P({T}_{3})} \\ 0.1 & =\frac{(0.4)(0.07)}{(0.23)(0.44)+(0.26)(0.32)+P(I|{T}_{3})(0.24)} \\ 0.1 & =\frac{0.028}{0.1844+0.24P(I|{T}_{3})}.\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this equation for $P(I|{T}_{3}),$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}0.1(0.1844+0.24P(I|{T}_{3})) & =0.028 \\ 0.1844+0.24P(I|{T}_{3}) & =\frac{0.028}{0.1} \\ 0.1844+0.24P(I|{T}_{3}) & =\frac{7}{25} \\ 0.24P(I|{T}_{3}) & =\frac{7}{25}-0.1844 \\ P(I|{T}_{3}) & =\frac{1}{0.24}(\frac{7}{25}-0.1844) \\ P(I|{T}_{3}) & ≈0.398\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to three decimal places."} {:db/id 17592186493970 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "63e7cc4a-4887-5d31-b8e4-aff9bc110c7a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.24" :db/id 17592186493542}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186493542} :answer-field/id #uuid "97f65a01-cb5a-533f-b4b2-586e85f00033" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186493850}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "e22ccace-d75b-5bc7-acc2-7090937bcda1" :question/math-academy-id "q-324457" :question/problem "In a distribution center, the average weight of shipped packages is $2.5$ kilograms. However, $20\%$ of packages weigh no more than $2.3$ kilograms. Assuming that package weights are normally distributed, find the standard deviation, $\sigma ,$ of the package weights, **rounded to two decimal places.**

*Hint: A table of values of ${Φ}^{-1}(p)$ for different values of $p$ is given below, where $p=Φ(z)$ is the cumulative distribution function for the standard normal distribution.*

| ${Φ}^{-1}(p)$ | $\,-2.3263\,$ | $\,-1.8808\,$ | $\,-1.6449\,$ | $\,-1.2816\,$ | $\,-1.0364\,$ | $\,-0.8416\,$ | $\,-0.6745\,$ |

$\sigma ≈$

$kg$" :question/worked-solution "Let $X$ represent the package weight (in kilograms). Then we have $X∼N(2.5,{\sigma }^{2}),$ and we want to find the standard deviation $\sigma .$ 

We know that $P(X\le 2.3)=0.20.$ Converting $X$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X\le 2.3) & =0.20 \\ P(Z\le \frac{2.3-2.5}{\sigma }) & =0.20 \\ Φ\left(-\frac{0.2}{\sigma }\right) & =0.20 \\ -\frac{0.2}{\sigma } & ={Φ}^{-1}(0.20).\end{aligned}
$$

From the table, 

$$
{Φ}^{-1}(0.20)=-0.8416.
$$

Finally then, 

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{0.2}{\sigma } & =-0.8416 \\ \frac{0.2}{\sigma } & =0.8416 \\ \sigma  & =\frac{0.2}{0.8416} \\  & ≈0.24\,\text{kg}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186493971 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "7836d0df-6d0e-53c1-9b87-066f993123a0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.04" :db/id 17592186493572} {:answer/id #uuid "7f62054b-c721-5065-baa7-a2e088063d8b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.01" :db/id 17592186493589} {:answer/id #uuid "ad72aa07-660d-51b0-afc8-b41ca13de413" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.02" :db/id 17592186493664} {:answer/id #uuid "ae4692a1-b2be-56d2-9388-d0e19d2609ff" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.03" :db/id 17592186493667} {:answer/id #uuid "b79552a7-3376-5da8-91ca-17bece0d388e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.00" :db/id 17592186493688}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186493664} :answer-field/id #uuid "c5d04840-0a76-5834-bd32-257991f12cc2" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186493875}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "e312f711-a596-58e6-bba4-4f3bc71c5f9f" :question/math-academy-id "q-132434" :question/problem "The volume of soda in cans filled at a particular factory is normally distributed with a mean of $12$ ounces and a standard deviation of $0.1$ ounces. What is the probability that a randomly selected soda can contains more than $12.2$ ounces? Round your answer to $2$ decimal places.

*Hint: A table of values of $Φ(z)$ for different values of $z$ is given below, where $Φ(z)$ is the cumulative distribution function for the standard normal distribution.* 

| $z$ | $\,0.00\,$ | $\,0.01\,$ | $\,0.02\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\,2.0\,$ | $\,0.9772\,$ | $\,0.9778\,$ | $\,0.9783\,$ |
| $\,2.1\,$ | $\,0.9821\,$ | $\,0.9826\,$ | $\,0.9830\,$ |
| $\,2.2\,$ | $\,0.9861\,$ | $\,0.9864\,$ | $\,0.9868\,$ |" :question/worked-solution "Let $X$ represent the volume (in ounces) of soda in a randomly selected can. Then we have $X∼N(12,{0.1}^{2}).$

We want to find $P(X>12.2).$ Thus, we convert $X$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X>12.2) & =P(Z>\frac{12.2-12}{0.1}) \\  & =P(Z>2) \\  & =1-P(Z\le 2) \\  & =1-Φ(2)\end{aligned}
$$

From the $z$-table, we see that

$$

Therefore, the probability that a randomly selected soda can contains more than $12.2$ ounces is approximately $0.02.$"} {:db/id 17592186493973 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "143bd49e-b2ca-5b56-9eca-6d7751d7c1e3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2\operatorname{ln}⁡2" :db/id 17592186493428} {:answer/id #uuid "37392f66-38d1-5cf1-a83a-b61ffbecdc24" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\operatorname{ln}⁡3" :db/id 17592186493480} {:answer/id #uuid "3b9d745e-3b7a-5566-acd4-df51a55a0434" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186493492} {:answer/id #uuid "757701d0-e96c-58b7-9b6d-52ab1067ccc8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4" :db/id 17592186493565} {:answer/id #uuid "f8b8b11d-0fcd-5a7a-8d95-67c9db317553" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\operatorname{ln}⁡8" :db/id 17592186493793}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186493428} :answer-field/id #uuid "b260735c-8ce2-5820-82bd-e9db5e7533a8" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186493865}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "e9c37ee3-304c-5283-97a5-75391f3d1e94" :question/math-academy-id "q-82985" :question/problem "Using the change of variables $u=x+3y$ and $v=x+2y,$ evaluate the double integral

$$
{∬}_{D}\frac{x+3y}{x+2y}\,dx\,dy,
$$

where $D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le x+3y\le 2,\,2\le x+2y\le 4\}.$" :question/worked-solution "Let's define a transformation $T$ as follows:

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}⟶\begin{bmatrix}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{bmatrix}
$$

This transformation maps some region $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane to our region $D$ in the $xy$-plane.

To compute the required integral, we can use the change of variables formula

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,dx\,dy={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(x(u,v),y(u,v))|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|du\,dv
$$

where $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T.$

Note that the change of variables

$$
u=x+3y,\,v=x+2y
$$

 

gives us the *inverse* function ${T}^{-1},$ that is

$$
{T}^{-1}:\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}u(x,y) \\ v(x,y)\end{bmatrix}.
$$

To compute the required integral, we proceed as follows:

**Step 1**: Find $Δ,$ which is the image of $D$ under the action of ${T}^{-1}.$ 

Our domain in the $uv$-plane is

$$
\begin{aligned}Δ & =\{(u,v)\,:\,0\le u\le 2,\,2\le v\le 4\}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}1 & 3 \\ 1 & \text{ }\text{ }2\end{vmatrix} \\  & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T$ is

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}={\left(\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)}\right)}^{-1}=-1.
$$

Note that $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}\ne 0$ everywhere inside $Δ.$ In other words, $T$ has no critical points inside $Δ.$

**Step 4**: Perform the change of variables:

Performing the change of variables, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\frac{x+3y}{x+2y}\,dx\,dy & ={∬}_{Δ}\frac{u}{v}\cdot |\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\text{d}u\,\text{d}v \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}\frac{u}{v}\cdot |-1|\text{d}u\,\text{d}v \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{2}^{4}\frac{u}{v}\,\text{d}v\,\text{d}u \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}u[{\int }_{2}^{4}\frac{1}{v}\,dv]du \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}u[\operatorname{ln}⁡v]_{2}^{4}\,du \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}u(\operatorname{ln}⁡4-\operatorname{ln}⁡2)\,du \\  & =(2\operatorname{ln}⁡2-\operatorname{ln}⁡2){\int }_{0}^{2}u\,du \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡2[\frac{{u}^{2}}{2}]_{0}^{2} \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡2\cdot (2-0) \\  & =2\operatorname{ln}⁡2.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186493975 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "f4f2613b-7acb-5604-981e-e17f2565df89" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4.18" :db/id 17592186493785}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186493785} :answer-field/id #uuid "bee0cd22-295e-5274-8db9-3430efc1f645" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186493870}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "fe644563-13d6-5255-adb7-59462252c8b9" :question/math-academy-id "q-325123" :question/problem "The average amount of coffee dispensed into medium cups is $10$ ounces. | $\,0.1\,$ | $\,0.5398\,$ | $\,0.5438\,$ | $\,0.5478\,$ |" :question/worked-solution "Given a binomial random variable $X∼B(n,p),$ if 

- $np>5,$ and

- $n(1-p)>5,$

we can approximate $X$ as a normal random variable $Y$ with mean $\mu =np$ and variance ${\sigma }^{2}=np(1-p),$ that is, 

$$
Y∼N(np,np(1-p)).
$$

Here, we have $n=70$ and $p=0.52.$ Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}np & =70\cdot 0.52 \\  & =36.4 \\  & >5\,✓ \\ n(1-p) & =70\cdot (1-0.52) \\  & =33.6 \\  & >5.\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

So, we can approximate our binomial random variable $X$ with a normal random variable $Y$ with mean

$$
\mu =np=(70)(0.52)=36.4
$$

and variance

$$
{\sigma }^{2}=np(1-p)=(70)(0.52)(1-0.52)=17.472.
$$

That is, we can approximate $X$ by $Y∼N(36.4,17.472).$

Now, we can estimate the desired probability $P(X\ge 37).$ Using a continuity correction, we have

$$
P(X\ge 37)≈P(Y\ge 36.5).
$$

To compute this probability, we transform to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(Y\ge 36.5) & =P(Z\ge \frac{36.5-36.4}{\sqrt{17.472}}) \\  & ≈P(Z\ge 0.02) \\  & =1-P(Z<0.02) \\  & =1-P(Z\le 0.02) \\  & =1-Φ(0.02) \\  & =1-0.5080 \\  & =0.4920\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$

$$
{∬}_{D}\frac{y-2x}{y+2x}\,dxdy,
$$

where $D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le y-2x\le 2,\,2\le y+2x\le 6\}.$" :question/worked-solution "Let's define a transformation $T$ as follows:

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}⟶\begin{bmatrix}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{bmatrix}
$$

This transformation maps some region $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane to our region $D$ in the $xy$-plane.

To compute the required integral, we can use the change of variables formula

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dxdy={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(x(u,v),y(u,v))\,|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\text{ }dudv
$$

where $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T.$

To compute the required integral, we proceed as follows:

**Step 1**: Find a suitable change of variables.

The inequalities that define the region $D,$

$$
0\le y-2x\le 2,\,2\le y+2x\le 6,
$$

suggest that we use the change of variables 

$$
u=y-2x\,\text{and}\,v=y+2x.
$$

This change of variables gives us the *inverse* function ${T}^{-1},$ that is

$$
{T}^{-1}:\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}u(x,y) \\ v(x,y)\end{bmatrix}.
$$

**Step 2**: Find $Δ,$ which is the image of $D$ under the action of ${T}^{-1}.$ 

Our domain in the $uv$-plane is

$$
\begin{aligned}Δ & =\{(u,v)\,:\,0\le u\le 2,\,2\le v\le 6\}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}-2 & 1 \\ \text{ }\text{ }\text{ }2 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =-4.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 4**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T:$

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}={\left(\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)}\right)}^{-1}=-\frac{1}{4}
$$

Note that $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}\ne 0$ everywhere inside $Δ.$ In other words, $T$ has no critical points inside $Δ.$

**Step 5**: Perform the change of variables, and evaluate the integral:

Performing the change of variables, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\frac{y-2x}{y+2x}\,\text{d}x\text{d}y & ={∬}_{Δ}\frac{u}{v}\,|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}\frac{u}{v}|-\frac{1}{4}|\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{\int }_{0}^{2}u[{\int }_{2}^{6}\frac{1}{v}\,dv]du \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{\int }_{0}^{2}u[\operatorname{ln}⁡|v|]_{2}^{6}\,du \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{\int }_{0}^{2}u(\operatorname{ln}⁡6-\operatorname{ln}⁡2)\,du \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{\int }_{0}^{2}u\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡3\,du \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}{4}{[\frac{1}{2}{u}^{2}]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186495068 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "35350a1f-7895-51fc-8e71-c814db467aef" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.583" :db/id 17592186494424} {:answer/id #uuid "54feab7b-9521-5920-abd6-97ca8ad85f0c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.587" :db/id 17592186494490} {:answer/id #uuid "65d9e86c-9f69-5f93-b937-a18b030341ef" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.626" :db/id 17592186494523} {:answer/id #uuid "d9bdf78a-e3f2-5b0b-8bcf-024af2813423" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.663" :db/id 17592186494834} {:answer/id #uuid "dd5d40eb-d6c1-59c7-b0ed-ebf1039c7633" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.579" :db/id 17592186494844}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186494490} :answer-field/id #uuid "00cb2415-3f5b-552e-bb6f-9f456d752a78" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186494917}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "212cd403-0726-5b1b-ae69-c8952ab761bd" :question/math-academy-id "q-132503" :question/problem "In a math test, a student has a $55\%$ probability of correctly answering each question. $k=$
{{field-1}}${\text{kg/s}}^{2}$" :question/worked-solution "The equation of motion for a particle of mass $m$ moving with forced harmonic motion without damping under the action of a spring with spring constant $k$ and external force $F(t)$ is given by

$$
m{y}^{″}=-ky+F(t).
$$

Substituting our values for $m$ and $F(t)$ gives

$$
0.8{y}^{″}=-ky+(4{cos}^{2}\,(\frac{5}{2}t)-2).
$$

Simplifying and rearranging the above equation, we get

$$
{y}^{″}+\frac{5k}{4}y=\frac{5}{2}(2{cos}^{2}\,(\frac{5}{2}t)-1).
$$

The complementary solution ${y}_{c}$ here represents simple harmonic motion, and it can be written as

$$
{y}_{c}=A\operatorname{cos}⁡\omega t+B\operatorname{sin}⁡\omega t,
$$

where $A$ and $B$ are arbitrary constants of integration, and $\omega $ is the system's internal frequency.

In our case,

$$
{\omega }^{2}=\frac{5k}{4}\,⟹\,k=\frac{4}{5}{\omega }^{2}.
$$

The oscillator experiences resonance when the frequency of the external periodic force $$
\displaystyle f(t)=\frac{5}{2}(2{cos}^{2}\,(\frac{5}{2}t)-1)
$$ is equal to the frequency of the complementary solution $\omega .$ Since

$$
f(t)=\frac{5}{2}(2{cos}^{2}\,(\frac{5}{2}t)-1)=\frac{5}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t),
$$

the frequency of the external periodic force is $5.$

Therefore,

$$
k=\frac{4}{5}{\omega }^{2}=\frac{4}{5}\cdot {5}^{2}=20\,{\text{kg/s}}^{2}.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186495097 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1b511858-4818-5d57-8bd8-1fe8930c3764" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.037" :db/id 17592186494372} {:answer/id #uuid "5e2bb00f-cdb9-563a-8c96-93286f07eecc" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.055" :db/id 17592186494512} {:answer/id #uuid "715cf66d-11dd-57af-bac0-c97174f16e01" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.046" :db/id 17592186494560} {:answer/id #uuid "8dcc2491-00c7-5189-9306-0c2b27964cda" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.051" :db/id 17592186494640} {:answer/id #uuid "b203c66c-4318-5382-af46-3a61a328e257" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.035" :db/id 17592186494732}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186494560} :answer-field/id #uuid "ee77bc02-a4f1-5565-b42d-e9a68c8e93d4" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186495034}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "6b518eb4-0e6a-5c41-b563-8246f9c1143e" :question/math-academy-id "q-132269" :question/problem "Given that the random variable $X∼B(150,0.48),$ use the normal approximation to the binomial distribution to approximate $P(X=67).$ Give your final answer to three decimal places.

*Hint: The data below is taken from the table of values of the cumulative distribution function $Φ(z)$ for the standard normal distribution.* 

| $z$ | $\,0.00\,$ | $\,0.01\,$ | $\,0.02\,$ | $\,0.03\,$ | $\,0.04\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\,-0.9\,$ | $\,0.1841\,$ | $\,0.1814\,$ | $\,0.1788\,$ | $\,0.1762\,$ | $\,0.1736\,$ |
| $\,-0.8\,$ | $\,0.2119\,$ | $\,0.2090\,$ | $\,0.2061\,$ | $\,0.2033\,$ | $\,0.2005\,$ |
| $\,-0.7\,$ | $\,0.2420\,$ | $\,0.2389\,$ | $\,0.2358\,$ | $\,0.2327\,$ | $\,0.2297\,$ |" :question/worked-solution "Given a binomial random variable $X∼B(n,p),$ if 

- $np>5,$ and

- $n(1-p)>5,$

we can approximate $X$ as a normal random variable $Y$ with mean $\mu =np$ and variance ${\sigma }^{2}=np(1-p),$ that is, 

$$
Y∼N(np,np(1-p)).
$$

Here, we have $n=150$ and $p=0.48.$ Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}np & =150\cdot 0.48 \\  & =72 \\  & >5\,✓ \\ n(1-p) & =150\cdot (1-0.48) \\  & =78 \\  & >5.\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

So, we can approximate our binomial random variable $X$ with a normal random variable $Y$ with mean

$$
\mu =np=(150)(0.48)=72
$$

and variance

$$
{\sigma }^{2}=np(1-p)=(150)(0.48)(1-0.48)=37.44.
$$

That is, we can approximate $X$ by $Y∼N(72,37.44).$

Now, we can approximate the desired probability $P(X=67).$ Using a continuity correction, we have

$$
P(X=67)≈P(66.5\le Y\le 67.5).
$$

To compute this probability, we transform to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(66.5\le Y\le 67.5) & =P(\frac{66.5-72}{\sqrt{37.44}}\le Z\le \frac{67.5-72}{\sqrt{37.44}}) \\  & ≈P(-0.90\le Z\le -0.74) \\  & =P(Z\le -0.74)-P(Z<-0.90) \\  & =P(Z\le -0.74)-P(Z\le -0.90) \\  & =Φ(-0.74)-Φ(-0.90) \\  & =0.2297-0.1841 \\  & =0.046\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
P(X=67)≈0.046.
$$

Note: Using a software package for the approximation gives a probability of $0.0468.$"} {:db/id 17592186495099 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "68c0ec99-c2fb-58f7-b7f5-fb61baf0c84f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\pi }{2}+\frac{\pi n}{2}" :db/id 17592186494528} {:answer/id #uuid "7d3756b0-b0a2-556a-be88-863ea77b203d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\pi }{4}+\frac{\pi n}{2}" :db/id 17592186494588} {:answer/id #uuid "8da11eb5-91be-5bf3-9fcf-acbbb9eaa5a1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\pi }{2}+\pi n" :db/id 17592186494639} {:answer/id #uuid "c6b7976b-3f51-5c07-8e0f-1d2e78e5cbc1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\pi n}{4}" :db/id 17592186494786} {:answer/id #uuid "cdf2e835-db95-5864-affb-01ff7cb2c729" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\pi }{4}+\pi n" :db/id 17592186494807}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186494807} :answer-field/id #uuid "5e73b358-a22b-50ef-9592-ee78086917fe" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186494958}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "743cb560-d24b-5701-9107-2d76831f26b0" :question/math-academy-id "q-162648" :question/problem "The domain of the vector-valued function $$
\displaystyle f(t)=\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+(1+t)\,j+\operatorname{cot}⁡(t-\frac{\pi }{4})\,k
$$ is 

$$
t\in (-\infty ,\infty ),\,t\ne \bbox[5pt,border:1pt solid black]{\phantom{AAAAA}}.
$$

What is the missing expression? You may assume that $n$ is an integer." :question/worked-solution "To find the domain of $f$, we need the intersection of the domains of the individual components.

- The domain of the 1st component $\operatorname{sin}⁡t$ is $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).$

- The domain of the 2nd component $1+t$ is $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).$

- The domain of the 3rd component $\operatorname{cot}⁡(t-\frac{\pi }{4})$ is $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ),$ except for the values of $t$ for which

$$
t-\frac{\pi }{4}=\pi n\,⟹\,t=\frac{\pi }{4}+\pi n,
$$

where $n$ is an integer.

Therefore, the domain of the vector-valued function $f(t)$ is 

$$
t\in (-\infty ,\infty ),\,t\ne \frac{\pi }{4}+\pi n,
$$

where $n$ is an integer."} {:db/id 17592186495100 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "36ad6cac-d25a-50df-a71c-ff5530463782" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3-4\pi " :db/id 17592186494431} {:answer/id #uuid "377131c4-9276-5492-90f4-5fe9f9ea094b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\frac{3}{2\pi }" :db/id 17592186494433} {:answer/id #uuid "389c158d-eca4-5138-ade2-702a2174ac43" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3(2\pi -1)" :db/id 17592186494436} {:answer/id #uuid "76f8296f-42f1-5d17-a5c6-7274b014898c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\frac{12}{\pi }" :db/id 17592186494571} {:answer/id #uuid "adfbcfe0-1ed2-552d-9eab-c92cbe93246a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{7}{6\pi }" :db/id 17592186494723}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186494571} :answer-field/id #uuid "caaee621-928c-5865-8689-d0a675bcc7ba" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186495012}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "75903bf3-d1b7-5813-a3cf-49663583fcbd" :question/math-academy-id "q-160915" :question/problem "Use a change of variables to evaluate the double integral 

$$
{∬}_{D}\frac{{y}^{2}}{{x}^{2}}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi xy)\,dxdy,
$$

where $D=\{(x,y)\,:\,1\le xy\le 4,\,1\le \frac{y}{x}\le 5\}.$" :question/worked-solution "Let's define a transformation $T$ as follows:

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}⟶\begin{bmatrix}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{bmatrix}
$$

This transformation maps some region $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane to our region $D$ in the $xy$-plane.

To compute the required integral, we can use the change of variables formula

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dxdy={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(x(u,v),y(u,v))\,|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\text{ }dudv
$$

where $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T.$

To compute the required integral, we proceed as follows:

**Step 1**: Find a suitable change of variables.

The inequalities that define the region $D,$

$$
1\le xy\le 4,\,1\le \frac{y}{x}\le 5,
$$

suggest that we use the change of variables 

$$
u=xy\,\text{and}\,v=\frac{y}{x}.
$$

This change of variables gives us the *inverse* function ${T}^{-1},$ that is

$$
{T}^{-1}:\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}u(x,y) \\ v(x,y)\end{bmatrix}.
$$

**Step 2**: Find $Δ,$ which is the image of $D$ under the action of ${T}^{-1}.$ 

Our domain in the $uv$-plane is

$$
\begin{aligned}Δ & =\{(u,v)\,:\,1\le u\le 4,\,1\le v\le 5\}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}\text{ }\text{ }\text{ }y & x \\ -\frac{y}{{x}^{2}} & \frac{1}{x}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\frac{2y}{x}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 4**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T:$

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}={\left(\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)}\right)}^{-1}=\frac{1}{\left(\frac{2y}{x}\right)}=\frac{1}{2v}
$$

Note that $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}\ne 0$ everywhere inside $Δ.$ In other words, $T$ has no critical points inside $Δ.$

**Step 5**: Perform the change of variables, and evaluate the integral:

Performing the change of variables, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\frac{{y}^{2}}{{x}^{2}}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi xy)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y & ={∬}_{D}{\left(\frac{y}{x}\right)}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi xy)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}{v}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi u)|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}{v}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi u)|\frac{1}{2v}|\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{1}^{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi u)[{\int }_{1}^{5}v\,dv]du \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{1}^{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi u){[\frac{1}{2}\,{v}^{2}]}_{1}^{5}\,du \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{1}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi u)\cdot 12\,du \\  & =6{\int }_{1}^{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi u)\,du \\  & =6{[-\frac{1}{\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi u)]}_{1}^{4} \\  & =-\frac{6}{\pi }(1-(-1)) \\  & =-\frac{12}{\pi }.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186495106 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "691a66a6-f8a5-5d42-a44a-c4fd56f19ebc" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.834" :db/id 17592186494530} {:answer/id #uuid "7c83485f-fc05-527b-8ac5-652edd3cc5b9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.837" :db/id 17592186494586} {:answer/id #uuid "83023c61-f5a8-5b7f-a11e-887b7484c4ba" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.830" :db/id 17592186494605} {:answer/id #uuid "88f1ea9b-fe91-518b-836c-b738ddcb3eb1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.805" :db/id 17592186494622} {:answer/id #uuid "dbc223ef-5e68-57a9-8abb-0d5420360510" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.808" :db/id 17592186494837}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186494530} :answer-field/id #uuid "cbe948d3-cf3f-5d7a-a051-dde7f129c617" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186495013}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "865aae44-8837-5a5c-9a79-489c7c05763a" :question/math-academy-id "q-132495" :question/problem "Given that the random variable $X∼B(240,0.45),$ use the normal approximation to the binomial distribution to approximate $P(X>100).$ Round your final answer to three decimal places.

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =-6t\,i+3{t}^{2}\,j+{t}^{3}\,k \\ T(t) & =\frac{1}{{t}^{2}+2}(-2\,i+2t\,j+{t}^{2}\,k) \\ N(t) & =\frac{1}{{t}^{2}+2}[2t\,i+(2-{t}^{2})\,j+2t\,k].\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $T$ and $N$ denote the unit tangent and principal normal, respectively." :question/worked-solution "First, notice that the unit tangent and the principal normal at the point where $t=1$ are

$$
\begin{aligned}T(1) & =\frac{1}{(1)^{2}+2}(-2\,i+2(1)\,j+(1)^{2}\,k)=\frac{1}{3}(-2\,i+2\,j+k) \\ N(1) & =\frac{1}{(1)^{2}+2}[2(1)\,i+(2-(1)^{2})\,j+2(1)\,k]=\frac{1}{3}[2\,i+j+2\,k].\end{aligned}
$$

Also, the position vector of the point where $t=1$ is

$$
p=r(1)=-6(1)\,i+3(1)^{2}\,j+(1)^{3}\,k=⟨-6,3,1⟩.
$$

Now, we need to find a vector that's perpendicular to the osculating plane. To do that, we use the cross product of the unit tangent $T(1)$ and the principal normal $N(1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}T(1)\times N(1) & =(\frac{1}{3}(-2\,i+2\,j+k))\times (\frac{1}{3}[2\,i+j+2\,k]) \\  & =(\frac{1}{3}\cdot \frac{1}{3})\cdot \begin{vmatrix}i & j & k \\ -2 & 2 & 1 \\ 2 & 1 & 2\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{9}\left[\text{ }\begin{vmatrix}2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{vmatrix}\,i-\begin{vmatrix}-2 & 1 \\ 2 & 2\end{vmatrix}\,j+\begin{vmatrix}-2 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{vmatrix}\,k\text{ }\right] \\  & =\frac{1}{9}(3\,i+6\,j-6\,k)\end{aligned}
$$

Since we are interested only in the direction of the above vector, let's write our perpendicular vector $n$ as 

$$
n=3\cdot (T(1)\times N(1))=i+2\,j-2\,k=⟨1,2,-2⟩.
$$

Finally, let $⟨x,y,z⟩$ denote the position vector of a point on the osculating plane. Since the plane is perpendicular to $n$ and passes through the tip of the position vector $p$, its Cartesian equation can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}(⟨x,y,z⟩-p)\cdot n & =0 \\ ⟨x,y,z⟩\cdot n-p\cdot n & =0 \\ ⟨x,y,z⟩\cdot n & =p\cdot n \\ ⟨x,y,z⟩\cdot ⟨1,2,-2⟩ & =⟨-6,3,1⟩\cdot ⟨1,2,-2⟩ \\ 1\cdot x+2\cdot y+(-2)\cdot z & =-2 \\ x+2y-2z+2 & =0.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186495132 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "52c6a4e9-74ca-5582-b0af-97d3ec19601a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.070" :db/id 17592186494482} {:answer/id #uuid "821cd6eb-46cd-5eb8-b1a0-1a9aa204f81f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.073" :db/id 17592186494601} {:answer/id #uuid "87c0932e-63f4-5bb4-a48c-af20cb5ab96a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.066" :db/id 17592186494617} {:answer/id #uuid "eaf79bda-c742-597d-9104-da468519214c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.082" :db/id 17592186494874} {:answer/id #uuid "f90fc399-9a07-50e3-a059-9866e338d3fe" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.079" :db/id 17592186494904}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186494601} :answer-field/id #uuid "f507c9e1-30ff-5ca4-a4e4-d03f72191b3d" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186495038}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "b726722f-b10f-58df-8eed-f61e3c1a5880" :question/math-academy-id "q-132275" :question/problem "Given that the random variable $X∼B(85,0.56),$ use the normal approximation to the binomial distribution to approximate $P(X=50).$ Give your final answer to three decimal places.

\displaystyle {\int }_{2}^{\infty }\frac{3}{\sqrt{(3t-2)^{5}}}\,\text{d}t.
$$" :question/worked-solution "First, we substitute $u=3t-2.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}t}=3\,⟹\,\text{d}u=3\text{d}t.
$$

Since $u\to \infty $ when $t\to \infty ,$ the table for the limits of integration using the rule $u=3t-2$ is as follows:

| $t$ | $2$ | $\infty $ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $4$ | $\infty $ |

So, the integral in terms of the new variable $u$ is

$$
{\int }_{2}^{\infty }\frac{3}{\sqrt{(3t-2)^{5}}}\,\text{d}t={\int }_{4}^{\infty }\frac{1}{\sqrt{{u}^{5}}}\,\text{d}u
$$

Finally, we proceed by setting the upper bound equal to some parameter $a,$ integrating as usual, and then taking the limit as $a\to \infty .$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{2}^{\infty }\frac{3}{\sqrt{(3t-2)^{5}}}\,\text{d}t & ={\int }_{4}^{\infty }\frac{1}{\sqrt{{u}^{5}}}\,\text{d}u \\  & ={\int }_{4}^{\infty }{u}^{-5/2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\lim_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{4}^{a}{u}^{-5/2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\cdot {lim}_{a\to \infty }{[-\frac{2}{3}{u}^{-3/2}]}_{4}^{a} \\  & =-\frac{2}{3}\cdot {lim}_{a\to \infty }{[{u}^{-3/2}]}_{4}^{a} \\  & =-\frac{2}{3}\cdot {lim}_{a\to \infty }[\frac{1}{(a)^{3/2}}-\frac{1}{(4)^{3/2}}] \\  & =-\frac{2}{3}\cdot (0-\frac{1}{8}) \\  & =\frac{1}{12}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186495164 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "87044dd2-9dec-5037-baed-466b750f914c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.014" :db/id 17592186494616} {:answer/id #uuid "99750630-e4cc-503e-9185-a49d3e7b138b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.041" :db/id 17592186494667} {:answer/id #uuid "a666113c-0a9a-5270-8a84-1103dd3a6c70" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.401" :db/id 17592186494699} {:answer/id #uuid "aa306e23-7ca1-53c8-939a-84d254417478" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.011" :db/id 17592186494711} {:answer/id #uuid "aad33263-b593-5f72-9670-762a2eec16d3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.141" :db/id 17592186494713}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186494667} :answer-field/id #uuid "55e37936-2de1-5d34-8dd5-3c2259d1d17c" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186494955}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "ed942805-cf1d-5ddc-afc6-5eb5833ba5cd" :question/math-academy-id "q-95743" :question/problem "In an airport, $58\%$ of the flights arrive early. $$
\begin{aligned}x\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+2y & =24 x^{2} \\ \frac{1}{x}\left(x\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+2y\right) & =\frac{1}{x}\cdot 24 x^{2} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+\frac{2}{x}y & =24 x\end{aligned}
$$

This equation is in the standard form

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+P(x)y=Q(x),
$$

with $P(x)=\frac{2}{x}$ and $Q(x)=24 x.$

We compute an integrating factor using the definition:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x) & =e^{\int P(x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & =e^{\int \frac{2}{x}\,\text{d}x} \\  & =e^{2 \ln{\left(x \right)}} \\  & =x^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}x^{2}\cdot (\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+\frac{2}{x}y) & =x^{2}\cdot 24 x \\ x^{2}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+2 xy & =24 x^{3} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(yx^{2}) & =24 x^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(yx^{2})\,\text{d}x & =\int 24 x^{3}\,\text{d}x \\ yx^{2} & =6 x^{4}+C \\ y & =\frac{C + 6 x^{4}}{x^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

This is the general solution. To find the value of $C$ corresponding to the specific solution, we apply the initial condition $y(1)=-6$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}y(1) & =\frac{(6 (1)^{4})+C}{((1)^{2})} \\ -6 & =\frac{6+C}{1} \\ C & =-12\end{aligned}
$$

$$

:question/math-academy-id "q-181149" :question/problem "Consider the following system of equations:

$$

$(u,v)=($

$)$" :question/worked-solution "We will isolate a variable in one of the equations and then substitute it into the other equation. It so happens that the second equation is already solved for $u:$

$$
u=-v-2
$$

So, we replace $u$ with $-v-2$ in the first equation and solve for $v:$

$$
\begin{aligned}4u-6v & =-3 \\ 4(-v-2)-6v & =-3 \\ -4v-8-6v & =-3 \\ -10v & =5 \\ v & =-\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

If we now substitute $v=-\frac{1}{2}$ into $u=-v-2,$ then we can find the value of $u:$

$$
\begin{aligned}u & =-v-2 \\ u & =-\left(-\frac{1}{2}\right)-2 \\ u & =-\frac{3}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the system of equations is $u=-\frac{3}{2},\,v=-\frac{1}{2},$ which can be expressed as $(-\frac{3}{2},-\frac{1}{2}).$"} {:db/id 17592186496228 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "24120408-2087-55b0-b11d-72781143b0e9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.1093" :db/id 17592186495590} {:answer/id #uuid "85c254a0-62c2-59a8-886c-22c3f672d045" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.1112" :db/id 17592186495799} {:answer/id #uuid "9eff9744-fffc-5560-b024-8d235dec8231" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.1335" :db/id 17592186495866} {:answer/id #uuid "a4b71db8-fce7-543b-b560-c183dd798dc6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.1357" :db/id 17592186495879} {:answer/id #uuid "bee4b9cc-203d-5c1c-bc20-21d933ffd030" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.1587" :db/id 17592186495930}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186495930} :answer-field/id #uuid "b619dfd9-b2dd-59c0-870d-da366a920039" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186496165}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "0c9343e5-40f1-5766-8346-83637c7ee445" :question/math-academy-id "q-109759" :question/problem "In a technical support call center, waiting times are normally distributed with a mean of $15$ minutes and a standard deviation of $3$ minutes. The conversation times are normally distributed with a mean of $10$ minutes and a standard deviation of $4$ minutes. The time to solve a problem is the sum of the waiting time and the conversation time. What is the probability that it took more than $30$ minutes to solve the problem of a randomly selected caller? You may assume that waiting and conversation times are independent.

*Hint: A table of values of $Φ(z)$ for different values of $z$ is given below, where $Φ(z)$ is the cumulative distribution function for the standard normal distribution.* 

| $z$ | $\,0.00\,$ | $\,0.01\,$ | $\,0.02\,$ | $\,0.03\,$ | $\,0.04\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\,1.0\,$ | $\,0.8413\,$ | $\,0.8438\,$ | $\,0.8461\,$ | $\,0.8485\,$ | $\,0.8508\,$ |
| $\,1.1\,$ | $\,0.8643\,$ | $\,0.8665\,$ | $\,0.8686\,$ | $\,0.8708\,$ | $\,0.8729\,$ |
| $\,1.2\,$ | $\,0.8849\,$ | $\,0.8869\,$ | $\,0.8888\,$ | $\,0.8907\,$ | $\,0.8925\,$ |" :question/worked-solution "Let $X$ denote the waiting time, and let $Y$ denote the conversation time. We want to find 

$$
P(X+Y>30).
$$

Since $X$ and $Y$ are independent random variables such that $X∼N(15,{3}^{2})$ and $Y∼N(10,{4}^{2})$, then 

$$
\begin{aligned}X+Y & ∼N(15+10,{3}^{2}+{4}^{2}) \\  & ∼N(25,25).\end{aligned}
$$

So, the variable $X+Y$ is normally distributed with mean $\mu =25$ and standard deviation $\sigma =\sqrt{25}=5.$

In order to find $P(X+Y>30),$ we convert $X+Y$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X+Y>30) & =P(Z>\frac{30-25}{5}) \\  & ≈P(Z>1) \\  & =1-P(Z\le 1) \\  & =1-Φ(1)\end{aligned}
$$

Using the $z$-table, we see that

$$
Φ(1)≈0.8413.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X+Y>30) & =1-Φ(1) \\  & ≈1-0.8413 \\  & ≈0.1587.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186496233 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "157119ad-5b76-548f-a94f-bee7025201f7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(3,-5)" :db/id 17592186495555} {:answer/id #uuid "46e470ef-ca26-51e5-aee3-653cf87f3e09" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(-1,\frac{5}{2})" :db/id 17592186495673} {:answer/id #uuid "86ec9541-d0b1-50d6-838f-9aff4b8c683d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(1,-5)" :db/id 17592186495802} {:answer/id #uuid "a10f0a61-fc58-5d61-b389-91be03e48828" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(-4,1)" :db/id 17592186495868} {:answer/id #uuid "fa2621a8-8093-5de7-9d44-d7db4e9d303f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(-\frac{3}{2},\frac{5}{2})" :db/id 17592186496060}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186496060} :answer-field/id #uuid "07c72b37-51b5-51e6-86af-9356a0461011" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186496075}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "19d2dbdd-1890-5f16-8c5e-f4b760789d4e" :question/math-academy-id "q-170022" :question/problem "Consider the following system of equations.

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}3u+z &=-2 \\ 3u-5z &=-17\end{aligned}\right.
$$

The variable $u$ can be eliminated from the system using the following two steps:

1\. Multiply the second equation by $-1$ and obtain

  $$
  \begin{aligned}-3u+5z=17.\end{aligned}
  $$

2\. Add the multiplied equation to the first equation to get

  $$
  \begin{aligned}⋯\,\,?\,\,⋯\,\,=15.\end{aligned}
  $$

Find the missing expression, and hence find the solution $(u,z)$ of the system." :question/worked-solution "Let's follow the steps provided:

**Step 1**: Multiplying the second equation by $-1$ yields the following equivalent system:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}3u+z &=-2 \\ (\,3u-5z &=-17\,)\,\times (-1)\end{aligned}\right.\,⟹\,\left\{\begin{aligned}3u+z &=-2 \\ -3u+5z &=17\end{aligned}\right.
$$

**Step 2**: Next, we add these two equations together, *eliminate* the variable $u,$ and solve the resulting equation for $z:$

$$
\begin{array}{rl}\cancel{3u}+z & =-2 \\ -\cancel{3u}+5z & =17 \\ \hline (z+5z) & =(-2+17) \\ 6z & =15 \\ z & =\frac{15}{6} \\ z & =\frac{5}{2}\end{array}
$$

So, the solution must have $z=\frac{5}{2}.$ However, we still need to find $u.$ To do this, we substitute $z=\frac{5}{2}$ back into one of the equations. Let's choose the first equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}3u+z & =-2 \\ 3u+\frac{5}{2} & =-2 \\ 3u & =-\frac{9}{2} \\ u & =-\frac{3}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the system of equations is $u=-\frac{3}{2},\,z=\frac{5}{2},$ which can be expressed as $(-\frac{3}{2},\frac{5}{2}).$"} {:db/id 17592186496238 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "2c3d3836-b51f-5e7c-a7a9-704639b3e9bf" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3" :db/id 17592186495608} {:answer/id #uuid "528dca58-912a-5c4e-81e7-257ba6b0db7e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{2}{3}" :db/id 17592186495698} {:answer/id #uuid "6b4182f5-2803-552b-853e-c778c967ac69" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{3}{5}" :db/id 17592186495746} {:answer/id #uuid "c37c19ae-e778-56f2-937e-0465119bfe29" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{6}" :db/id 17592186495938} {:answer/id #uuid "c8690093-4909-568c-bd3a-20b77037a0fe" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186495948}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186495938} :answer-field/id #uuid "5a78871b-3da5-52c1-a57c-cb87914fafa1" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186496119}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "2f22631e-a7c9-5925-8b08-e1ce77a0788a" :question/math-academy-id "q-163499" :question/problem "A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis. When the displacement of $P$ from the origin is $x\,m,$ the velocity is $v\,m/s,$ and the acceleration is $k{x}^{2}(x-5)\,{m/s}^{2},$ where $k$ is a positive constant. If $P$ has velocity $v=2\sqrt{3}\,m/s$ at the origin and the particle is at rest when its displacement is $6\,m,$ find the value of $k.$" :question/worked-solution "![](images/9a/9ac139d8823f326f32869f308cb2d04cdc9e0d86dba7d4a11b66955afd665da3.png)

Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ is $k{x}^{2}(x-5)\,{m/s}^{2},$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=k{x}^{2}(x-5).
$$

Using the fact that

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}),
$$

we can rewrite our equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=k{x}^{2}(x-5).
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\text{d}x=\int k({x}^{3}-5{x}^{2})\,\text{d}x
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=k(\frac{{x}^{4}}{4}-\frac{5{x}^{3}}{3})+C.
$$

Now, since $v=2\sqrt{3}\,m/s$ when $x=0\,m,$ we can find the value of the constant $C,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =k(\frac{{x}^{4}}{4}-\frac{5{x}^{3}}{3})+C \\ \frac{1}{2}(2\sqrt{3})^{2} & =k(\frac{(0)^{4}}{4}-\frac{5(0)^{3}}{3})+C \\ C & =6\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=k(\frac{{x}^{4}}{4}-\frac{5{x}^{3}}{3})+6.
$$

Finally, since $v=0\,m/s$ when $x=6\,m,$ we can find the value of the positive constant $k,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =k(\frac{{x}^{4}}{4}-\frac{5{x}^{3}}{3})+6 \\ \frac{1}{2}(0)^{2} & =k(\frac{(6)^{4}}{4}-\frac{5(6)^{3}}{3})+6 \\ 0 & =k(324-360)+6 \\ 0 & =-36k+6 \\ 36k & =6 \\ k & =\frac{1}{6}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186496244 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1f39b3f3-f271-59a4-bf86-3f809a0727f9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4\,m/s" :db/id 17592186495577} {:answer/id #uuid "45fc70ca-1697-5db6-b1f1-c08ca6e6db5c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\sqrt{65}\,m/s" :db/id 17592186495667} {:answer/id #uuid "6b84233d-39b9-5907-bb7e-b896ae67e3f1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\sqrt{53}\,m/s" :db/id 17592186495748} {:answer/id #uuid "b2128b20-1288-5387-bc4f-30b80ffe9c21" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "8\,m/s" :db/id 17592186495911} {:answer/id #uuid "f55ad6c7-9522-5c97-be01-f1f507abc917" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4\sqrt{5}\,m/s" :db/id 17592186496043}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186495667} :answer-field/id #uuid "096d2af6-6379-5a37-9ed1-9857796a70e5" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186496076}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "3aa3a140-5e95-5af8-9fd5-684dff535064" :question/math-academy-id "q-163561" :question/problem "A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis in the direction of increasing $x$ where $x\ge 0.$ When the displacement of $P$ from the origin is $x\,m,$ the velocity is $v\,m/s,$ and the acceleration is $k(7-x)\,{m/s}^{2},$ where $k$ is a positive constant. If $P$ has velocity $v=4\,m/s$ at the origin and has velocity $v=2\sqrt{10}\,m/s$ when its displacement is $2\,m,$ find the maximum velocity of the particle." :question/worked-solution "![](images/60/602ef5480fe59ccf921d17a19d10848a1a8a04a1fc3fb3181b8e9b17ebe81fad.png)

The extrema of the velocity occur at the critical points of $v.$ Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ is $k(7-x)\,{m/s}^{2},$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=k(7-x).
$$

To find the moments where $v$ is a maximum, we need to solve $\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=0$ and test each solution using the first derivative test.

Solving $\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=0$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}k(7-x) & =0 \\ 7-x & =0 \\ x & =7.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the extremum of the velocity function occurs when $x=7\,m.$

We now test the extreme value using the first derivative test. We summarize the necessary information in a table, shown below.

| $x$ | $(0,7)$ | $7$ | $(7,\infty )$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Test Point | $6$ |  | $8$ |
| $\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}$ | $k>0$ | $0$ | $-k<0$ |
| $v$ | $↗$ | max | $↘$ |

We conclude that the velocity is maximized when $x=7\,m.$

Next, using the fact that

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}),
$$

we can rewrite our initial equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=k(7-x).
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\text{d}x=\int k(7-x)\,\text{d}x
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=k(7x-\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2})+C.
$$

Now, since $v=4\,m/s$ when $x=0\,m,$ we can find the value of the constant $C,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =k(7x-\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2})+C \\ \frac{1}{2}(4)^{2} & =k(7(0)-\frac{1}{2}(0)^{2})+C \\ C & =8\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=k(7x-\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2})+8.
$$

Also, since $v=2\sqrt{10}\,m/s$ when $x=2\,m,$ we can find the value of the positive constant $k,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =k(7x-\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2})+8 \\ \frac{1}{2}(2\sqrt{10})^{2} & =k(7(2)-\frac{1}{2}{(2)}^{2})+8 \\ 20 & =12k+8 \\ 12k & =12 \\ k & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =1(7x-\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2})+8 \\ {v}^{2} & =14x-{x}^{2}+16 \\ v & =\pm \sqrt{-{x}^{2}+14x+16}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the particle is moving in the direction of increasing $x,$ we have that $v(x)>0,$ so we can disregard the negative square root. Therefore,

$$
v(x)=\sqrt{-{x}^{2}+14x+16}.
$$

Finally, we calculate the maximum velocity:

$$
{v}_{max}=v(7)=\sqrt{-(7)^{2}+14(7)+16}=\sqrt{65}\,m/s
$$"} {:db/id 17592186496264 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "80350002-a1a3-5d74-bd16-1ec73fee04f4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{3},-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{3},\frac{\sqrt{2}}{3})$ and $(-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{3},\frac{\sqrt{2}}{3},-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{3})$" :db/id 17592186495786} {:answer/id #uuid "8f8e83f7-8310-58f5-9c73-52c7cc216ae6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$(\frac{-\sqrt{2}}{3},-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{3},-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{3})$ and $(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{3},\frac{\sqrt{2}}{3},\frac{\sqrt{2}}{3})$" :db/id 17592186495826} {:answer/id #uuid "9823e226-22f2-5864-b4b5-cc7c8eaef60c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{3},-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{3},-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{3})$ only" :db/id 17592186495852} {:answer/id #uuid "9d651deb-dd53-5f49-8875-9a85b310492f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{3},-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{3},-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{3})$ and $(-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{3},\frac{\sqrt{2}}{3},\frac{\sqrt{2}}{3})$" :db/id 17592186495860} {:answer/id #uuid "ce78662c-56d5-5bd3-8e1e-31dfb2b4b788" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$(-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{3},\frac{\sqrt{2}}{3},\frac{\sqrt{2}}{3})$ only" :db/id 17592186495958}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186495860} :answer-field/id #uuid "e1dd5380-2900-5587-97bf-5ddd6b25c63f" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186496200}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "6022ca77-a6e7-5c06-a55c-446e2e02d3c5" :question/math-academy-id "q-71123" :question/problem "Find the point(s) of the intersection of the ellipsoid $\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}+{y}^{2}+3{z}^{2}=1$ and the line 
$$
\displaystyle \left\{\begin{aligned}x &=-t \\ y &=t, \\ z &=t\end{aligned}\right.
$$ where $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).$" :question/worked-solution "Substituting the expressions for $x$, $y$, and $z$ from the parametric equation of the line into the equation of the ellipsoid, we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}+{y}^{2}+3{z}^{2} & =1 \\ {x}^{2}+2{y}^{2}+6{z}^{2} & =2 \\ (-t)^{2}+2(t)^{2}+6(t)^{2} & =2 \\ {t}^{2}+2{t}^{2}+6{t}^{2} & =2 \\ 9{t}^{2} & =2 \\ {t}^{2} & =\frac{2}{9}\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, we get the solutions $t=-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{3}$ and $t=\frac{\sqrt{2}}{3}.$ 

Now, we substitute our solutions back into the equations of the line.

- For $t=-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{3}$, we have

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x &=-\left(-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{3}\right)=\frac{\sqrt{2}}{3} \\ y &=-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{3} \\ z &=-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{3},\end{aligned}\right.
$$

so the first point is $$
\displaystyle (\frac{\sqrt{2}}{3},-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{3},-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{3}).
$$

*Hint: A table of values of $Φ(z)$ for different values of $z$ is given below, where $Φ(z)$ is the cumulative distribution function for the standard normal distribution.* 

| $z$ | $\,0.05\,$ | $\,0.06\,$ | $\,0.07\,$ | $\,0.08\,$ | $\,0.09\,$ |

| $\,0.4\,$ | $\,0.6736\,$ | $\,0.6772\,$ | $\,0.6808\,$ | $\,0.6844\,$ | $\,0.6879\,$ |
| $\,0.5\,$ | $\,0.7088\,$ | $\,0.7123\,$ | $\,0.7157\,$ | $\,0.7190\,$ | $\,0.7224\,$ |" :question/worked-solution "Recall that if ${X}_{1}$ and ${X}_{2}$ are independent random variables, where ${X}_{1}∼N({\mu }_{1},{\sigma }_{1}^{2})$ and ${X}_{2}∼N({\mu }_{2},{\sigma }_{2}^{2})$, and $a$ and $b$ are constants, then 

$$
a{X}_{1}+b{X}_{2}∼N(a{\mu }_{1}+b{\mu }_{2},{a}^{2}{\sigma }_{1}^{2}+{b}^{2}{\sigma }_{2}^{2}).
$$

Since ${X}_{1}$ and ${X}_{2}$ are independent, the distribution of $Y$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}Y={X}_{1}-{X}_{2} & ∼N({\mu }_{1}-{\mu }_{2},{\sigma }_{1}^{2}+{\sigma }_{2}^{2}) \\  & ∼N(7-6,1+3) \\  & ∼N(1,4).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $Y$ is normally distributed with mean $\mu =1$ and standard deviation $\sigma =\sqrt{4}=2.$

$$
\begin{aligned}P(Y\le 2.1) & =P(Z\le \frac{2.1-1}{2}) \\  & =P(Z\le 0.55) \\  & =Φ(0.55)\end{aligned}
$$

Using the $z$-table, we see that

$$
Φ(0.55)≈0.7088.
$$

Therefore,

$$
P(Y\le 2.1)≈0.71.

The weight of a blade is normally distributed with a mean of $80\,\text{g}$ and a variance of $31\,{\text{g}}^{2}.$ The weight of the rubber is normally distributed with a mean of $45\,\text{g}$ grams and a variance of $50\,{\text{g}}^{2}.$ If one racket is randomly selected, what is the probability that it weighs more than $128\,\text{g}?$ You may assume that the weights are independent.

*Hint: A table of values of $Φ(z)$ for different values of $z$ is given below, where $Φ(z)$ is the cumulative distribution function for the standard normal distribution.*

| $\,0.2\,$ | $\,0.5793\,$ | $\,0.5832\,$ | $\,0.5871\,$ | $\,0.5910\,$ | $\,0.5948\,$ |
| $\,0.3\,$ | $\,0.6179\,$ | $\,0.6217\,$ | $\,0.6255\,$ | $\,0.6293\,$ | $\,0.6331\,$ |" :question/worked-solution "Let $X$ denote the weight of the blade, and let $Y$ denote the weight of the rubber. We want to find 

$$
P(X+Y>128).
$$

Since $X$ and $Y$ are  independent random variables such that $X∼N(80,31)$ and $Y∼N(45,50),$ then 

$$
\begin{aligned}X+Y & ∼N(80+45,31+50) \\  & ∼N(125,81).\end{aligned}
$$

So, the variable $X+Y$ is normally distributed with mean $\mu =125$ and standard deviation $\sigma =\sqrt{81}=9.$

In order to find $P(X+Y>128),$ we convert $X+Y$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X+Y>128) & =P(Z>\frac{128-125}{9}) \\  & ≈P(Z>0.33) \\  & =1-P(Z\le 0.33) \\  & =Φ(0.33)\end{aligned}
$$

Using the $z$-table, we see that

$$
Φ(0.33)≈0.6293.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X+Y>128) & ≈1-Φ(0.33) \\  & ≈1-0.6293 \\  & ≈0.3707.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186496273 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "00242b83-572e-53ab-ab15-9ac11dfbe5eb" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{2}{3}\,i-\frac{2}{3}\,i+\frac{1}{3}\,k" :db/id 17592186495510} {:answer/id #uuid "894bdd9e-e9ef-5b86-8bbe-ae7c9838996f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\frac{1}{3}\,i+\frac{2}{3}\,j+\frac{2}{3}\,k" :db/id 17592186495810} {:answer/id #uuid "b0f9e00c-950f-52ef-bbb0-f302706bc8e3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "i+\frac{2}{3}\,j+k" :db/id 17592186495907} {:answer/id #uuid "da523dad-c39c-5d16-88c2-713bc37dc420" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\frac{1}{3}\,i-\frac{1}{3}\,j" :db/id 17592186495991} {:answer/id #uuid "ea456b64-55aa-56ac-80e7-2621dd218995" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\frac{2}{3}\,i+\frac{2}{3}\,k" :db/id 17592186496026}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186496026} :answer-field/id #uuid "3fb741de-a765-5845-9e59-3f7b8e4242c7" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186496102}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "773cbe61-ec11-5375-8f39-d897f1cb3120" :question/math-academy-id "q-64333" :question/problem "Find $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{0}^{1}c\times f(t)\,\text{d}t

$c=i+k.$" :question/worked-solution "The cross-product rule states that

$$
{\int }_{0}^{1}c\times f(t)\,\text{d}t=c\times {\int }_{0}^{1}f(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

Applying the cross-product rule, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}c\times f(t)\,dt & =c\times {\int }_{0}^{1}f(t)\,dt \\  & =(i+k)\times (i+\frac{2}{3}\,j+k) \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}i & j & k \\ 1 & 0 & 1 \\ 1 & \frac{2}{3} & 1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}0 & 1 \\ \frac{2}{3} & 1\end{vmatrix}i-\begin{vmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{vmatrix}j+\begin{vmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 1 & \frac{2}{3}\end{vmatrix}k \\  & =(0-\frac{2}{3})i-(1-1)j+(\frac{2}{3}-0)k \\  & =-\frac{2}{3}\,i+\frac{2}{3}\,k.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186496278 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "00c0bdf1-ca0d-5a57-8521-96c07af1afa4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.88" :db/id 17592186495512} {:answer/id #uuid "51759a7d-87c9-562a-8312-f8b6d8fc5142" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.86" :db/id 17592186495695} {:answer/id #uuid "59500d77-cde2-5c82-b94d-9272e1f58b92" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.84" :db/id 17592186495712} {:answer/id #uuid "8b96a22a-c2c5-5cc0-ac69-7def23646d93" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.87" :db/id 17592186495817} {:answer/id #uuid "95e8df01-f50d-5ef6-8b62-b148b070af96" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.89" :db/id 17592186495845}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186495695} :answer-field/id #uuid "c622c6db-0cfb-5314-962b-7b684cde7e09" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186496175}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "7e624f6f-227d-5bbb-b9ec-897830d915af" :question/math-academy-id "q-109668" :question/problem "If ${X}_{1}∼N(1,0.4)$ and ${X}_{2}∼N(4,6)$ are independent and $Y=5{X}_{1}+{X}_{2},$ calculate $P(Y<13.4).$ Round your final answer to two decimal places.
