</tbody></table>" :question/worked-solution "Recall that if ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},$ and ${X}_{3}$ are mutually independent random variables, where 

$$
{X}_{1}∼N({\mu }_{1},{\sigma }_{1}^{2}),\,{X}_{2}∼N({\mu }_{2},{\sigma }_{2}^{2}),\,{X}_{3}∼N({\mu }_{3},{\sigma }_{3}^{2}),
$$

and ${a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}$ are real constants,  then 

$$
\begin{aligned}Y & ={a}_{1}{X}_{1}+{a}_{2}{X}_{2}+{a}_{3}{X}_{3} \\  & ∼N({a}_{1}{\mu }_{1}+{a}_{2}{\mu }_{2}+{a}_{3}{\mu }_{3},\,{a}_{1}^{2}{\sigma }_{1}^{2}+{a}_{2}^{2}{\sigma }_{2}^{2}+{a}_{3}^{2}{\sigma }_{3}^{2}).\end{aligned}
$$

In our case, we have

$$
{X}_{1}∼N(2,2),\,{X}_{2}∼N(1,{3}^{2}),\,{X}_{3}∼N(3,8),
$$

and

$$
Y=4{X}_{1}+3{X}_{2}-{X}_{3}.
$$

Since ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},$ and ${X}_{3}$ are mutually independent, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[Y] & ={a}_{1}{\mu }_{1}+{a}_{2}{\mu }_{2}+{a}_{3}{\mu }_{3} \\  & =4\cdot 2+3\cdot 1+(-1)\cdot 3 \\  & =8, \\ \text{Var}[Y] & ={a}_{1}^{2}{\sigma }_{1}^{2}+{a}_{2}^{2}{\sigma }_{2}^{2}+{a}_{3}^{2}{\sigma }_{3}^{2} \\  & ={4}^{2}\cdot 2+{3}^{2}\cdot {3}^{2}+(-1)^{2}\cdot 8 \\  & =16\cdot 2+9\cdot 9+1\cdot 8 \\  & =121.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}Y∼N(8,121).\end{aligned}
$$

We want to find $P(5<Y<10).$ Thus, we convert $Y$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(5<Y<10) & =P(\frac{5-8}{\sqrt{121}}<Z<\frac{10-8}{\sqrt{121}}) \\  & ≈P(-0.27<Z<0.18) \\  & =P(Z<0.18)-P(Z<-0.27) \\  & =Φ(0.18)-Φ(-0.27)\end{aligned}
$$

Using the $z$-table, we see that

$$
\begin{aligned}Φ(-0.27)≈0.3936,\,Φ(0.18)≈0.5714.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(5<Y<10) & =Φ(0.18)-Φ(-0.27) \\  & ≈0.5714-0.3936 \\  & =0.1778.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186499442 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "2e6e465a-f17e-50bb-b46b-f276dcc9ca53" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{{d}^{2}I}{d{t}^{2}}+2\,\frac{dI}{dt}+\frac{500}{9}I=3\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)" :db/id 17592186498833} {:answer/id #uuid "4e4787a7-f87e-55ab-8bcb-ef502674a203" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{{d}^{2}I}{d{t}^{2}}+4\,\frac{dI}{dt}+\frac{500}{9}I=3\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)" :db/id 17592186498912} {:answer/id #uuid "7e3396b7-b378-5d68-b0be-22381f3e75bc" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{{d}^{2}I}{d{t}^{2}}+2\,\frac{dI}{dt}+\frac{500}{9}I=27\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)" :db/id 17592186499014} {:answer/id #uuid "f4c03e75-17fb-5d9c-ab12-407c389dfc74" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{{d}^{2}I}{d{t}^{2}}+18\,\frac{dI}{dt}+500I=27\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)" :db/id 17592186499278} {:answer/id #uuid "ff9fcca2-a6ca-5520-8419-d82dbb197ec4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{{d}^{2}I}{d{t}^{2}}+2\,\frac{dI}{dt}+\frac{500}{9}I=3\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)" :db/id 17592186499305}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186499305} :answer-field/id #uuid "681c0005-a3b7-59a8-ba88-7bdafd30a043" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186499365}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "00663209-74b8-5c10-8a0a-2c782390f942" :question/math-academy-id "q-345269" :question/problem "A series RCL circuit has a source electromotive force (EMF) of $9\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)\,\text{V},$ a resistance of $18\,Ω,$ a capacitance of $0.002\,\text{F},$ and an inductance of $L=9\,\text{H}.$ Find the differential equation governing the amount of current $I$ (in amperes) in the circuit at time $t$ (in seconds).

*Hint: The voltage drop ${V}_{C}$ across the capacitor is related to its charge by $q=C{V}_{C},$ where $C$ is the capacitance measured in Farads.*" :question/worked-solution "The diagram for our circuit is shown below.

![](images/a3/a3bbe131778b11fe61a7e436d3d4729958bb207961ca9faaac91250cf4f2dde0.png)

The current $I,$ measured in amperes, is defined as the rate of flow of charge $q,$ measured in coulombs.

$$
I=\frac{dq}{dt}
$$

Kirchhoff's voltage law states that in a series circuit, the source voltage (EMF) equals the sum of the voltage drops.

In an RCL circuit, there are three voltage drops:

- The voltage drop across the resistor is proportional to the current, with a constant of proportionality $R=18\,Ω.$ So,

$$
{V}_{R}=18I.
$$

- The voltage drop across the capacitor is related to its charge by $q=C{V}_{C}.$ Therefore,

$$
{V}_{C}=\frac{q}{C}=\frac{q}{0.002}=500q.
$$

- The voltage drop across the inductor is proportional to the rate of change of current, with a constant of proportionality $L=9\,\text{H}.$ Hence,

$$
{V}_{L}=9\,\frac{dI}{dt}.
$$

Therefore, by Kirchhoff's voltage law, these values are related by the equation

$$
9\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)=18I+500q+9\,\frac{dI}{dt}.
$$

Differentiating with respect to $t,$ the differential equation governing the current in the circuit is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{d}{dt}(9\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)) & =\frac{d}{dt}(18I+500q+9\,\frac{dI}{dt}) \\ 27\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t) & =18\,\frac{dI}{dt}+500\,\frac{dq}{dt}+9\,\frac{{d}^{2}I}{d{t}^{2}},\end{aligned}
$$

which, when substituting in $I=\frac{dq}{dt},$ gives

$$
\frac{{d}^{2}I}{d{t}^{2}}+2\,\frac{dI}{dt}+\frac{500}{9}I=3\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t).
$$"} {:db/id 17592186499449 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0c97c988-3336-5cff-9def-ec7413102202" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "6(u+w)" :db/id 17592186498757} {:answer/id #uuid "1c002a85-7881-5d55-b3a3-c0858f2a52d4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{6}(u+v-w)" :db/id 17592186498789} {:answer/id #uuid "449afe6a-6893-523f-8969-4d9facf23e7a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "6(v-w)" :db/id 17592186498886} {:answer/id #uuid "5760564c-6d75-5aa4-a9ab-7873348de3bc" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(u-w-v)" :db/id 17592186498930} {:answer/id #uuid "9cc9fd42-c83a-5ec5-bb24-9d73b0ba363e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{6}(v-w)" :db/id 17592186499061}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186498757} :answer-field/id #uuid "219a7147-3bde-5244-974f-5c2639b194f2" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186499325}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "21557ab9-79b3-55a0-a104-51c3d273599e" :question/math-academy-id "q-161868" :question/problem "Consider the finite region $R$ in the $xyz$-space, given by

$$
R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,0\le \frac{2x-y}{2}\le 1,\,0\le \frac{y}{2}\le 2,\,0\le z\le 3\}.
$$

Given the change of variables

$$
u=\frac{2x-y}{2},\,v=\frac{y}{2},\,w=\frac{z}{3},
$$

which of the following could be the missing part of the expression below?

$$
{∭}_{R}(\frac{2x-y}{2}+\frac{z}{3})\,dV={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}\bbox[3pt,border:1pt solid black]{\phantom{AAAAAA}}\,dw\,dv\,du
$$" :question/worked-solution "Let's define a transformation $T$ as follows:

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v \\ w\end{bmatrix}⟶\begin{bmatrix}x(u,v,w) \\ y(u,v,w) \\ z(u,v,w)\end{bmatrix}
$$

This transformation maps some region $Δ$ in the $uvw$-space to our region $R$ in the $xyz$-space.

To find the required integral, we can use the change of variables formula

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\text{ }dV={∭}_{Δ}\text{ }f(x(u,v,w),y(u,v,w),z(u,v,w))\,|\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v\text{d}w
$$

where $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T.$

Note that the change of variables

$$
u=\frac{2x-y}{2},\,v=\frac{y}{2},\,w=\frac{z}{3},
$$

gives us the *inverse* function ${T}^{-1},$ that is

$$
{T}^{-1}:\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y \\ z\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}u(x,y,z) \\ v(x,y,z) \\ w(x,y,z)\end{bmatrix}.
$$

To find the required integral, we proceed in four steps:

**Step 1**: Find $Δ,$ which is the image of $R$ under the action of ${T}^{-1}.$ 

Our domain in the $uvw$-space is

$$
\begin{aligned}Δ & =\{(u,v,w)\,:\,0\le u\le 1,\,0\le v\le 2,\,0\le w\le 1\}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} & \frac{∂u}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y} & \frac{∂v}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & \frac{∂w}{∂y} & \frac{∂w}{∂z}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}1 & -\frac{1}{2} & 0 \\ 0 & \,\,\,\frac{1}{2} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & \frac{1}{3}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\begin{vmatrix}1 & -\frac{1}{2} \\ 0 & \,\,\,\frac{1}{2}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}(\frac{1}{2}-0) \\  & =\frac{1}{6}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T$ is

$$
\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}={\left(\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)}\right)}^{-1}=6.
$$

Note that $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}\ne 0$ everywhere inside $Δ.$ In other words, $T$ has no critical points inside $Δ.$

**Step 4**: Perform the change of variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∭}_{R}(\frac{2x-y}{2}+\frac{z}{3})\,dV & ={∭}_{Δ}(u+w)\cdot |\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v\text{d}w \\  & ={∭}_{Δ}(u+w)\cdot |6|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v\text{d}w \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}\,6(u+w)\,dw\,dv\,du\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186499451 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "127b87a9-3547-5f82-8e20-56536f5209a6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.3065" :db/id 17592186498767} {:answer/id #uuid "3a96e61e-0735-50a9-af65-701f136638b0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.2513" :db/id 17592186498864} {:answer/id #uuid "3b99f153-049c-5318-b515-99bf33b57b7b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.3136" :db/id 17592186498866} {:answer/id #uuid "4e061e8a-a2dc-5eee-8491-ea1fb94a6785" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.2815" :db/id 17592186498910} {:answer/id #uuid "78f2e606-2657-5beb-94bd-946cdd13f94f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.2997" :db/id 17592186499001}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186498910} :answer-field/id #uuid "a1570c35-d982-5bc7-9620-251ec85f03df" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186499389}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "23386dfb-4266-50f7-b8bd-add2ea98080d" :question/math-academy-id "q-143499" :question/problem "Let ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{40}$ be a random sample of size $n=40$ from a population with probability density function

</tbody></table>" :question/worked-solution "Suppose that ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{n}$ is a random sample of size $n$ from a population with population mean $\mu $ and population standard deviation $\sigma .$ The central limit theorem (or CLT) states that for sufficiently large $n,$ the distribution of the sample mean $\overset{―}{X}$ can be approximated as 

$$
\overset{―}{X}∼N\,(\mu ,\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n}).
$$

In our case:

- the sample size is

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =40,\end{aligned}
$$

- the population mean is

$$
\begin{aligned}\mu  & =\text{E}[X] \\  & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }x\,f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}x\cdot 1\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}\,{|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{2} \\  & =0.5,\end{aligned}
$$

- the population variance is ${\sigma }^{2}=0.08.$

Therefore, by the CLT, we have that the distribution of the sample mean can be approximated as

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{―}{X} & ∼N\,(\mu ,\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n}) \\  & ∼N\,(0.5,\frac{0.08}{40}) \\  & ∼N(0.5,0.002).\end{aligned}
$$

We want to find $P(0.51<\overset{―}{X}<0.55).$ So, we convert $\overset{―}{X}$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(0.51<\overset{―}{X}<0.55) & =P(\frac{0.51-0.5}{\sqrt{0.002}}<Z<\frac{0.55-0.5}{\sqrt{0.002}}) \\  & ≈P(0.22<Z<1.12) \\  & =P(Z<1.12)-P(Z<0.22) \\  & =Φ(1.12)-Φ(0.22)\end{aligned}
$$

From the tables, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Φ(0.22)=0.5871, \\ Φ(1.12)=0.8686.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(0.51<\overset{―}{X}<0.55) & =Φ(1.12)-Φ(0.22) \\  & =0.8686-0.5871 \\  & =0.2815.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186499454 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "01216357-33ad-5489-97fe-d40f92097dc2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{{d}^{2}I}{d{t}^{2}}+5\,\frac{dI}{dt}+25I=-10.5\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)" :db/id 17592186498731} {:answer/id #uuid "12ad58da-5be4-5d5f-a731-caa6425b7700" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{{d}^{2}I}{d{t}^{2}}+5\,\frac{dI}{dt}+25I=10.5\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)" :db/id 17592186498769} {:answer/id #uuid "1426eb8c-723b-599f-b12f-5067b673a38d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{{d}^{2}I}{d{t}^{2}}+10\,\frac{dI}{dt}+25I=-21\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)" :db/id 17592186498774} {:answer/id #uuid "ae1b529d-6fba-5b9f-866e-68a9138f76fa" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{{d}^{2}I}{d{t}^{2}}+5\,\frac{dI}{dt}+25I=-10.5\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)" :db/id 17592186499113} {:answer/id #uuid "e39b6a92-dada-5fdc-ac3e-bc73303d026b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{{d}^{2}I}{d{t}^{2}}+5\,\frac{dI}{dt}+50I=-10.5\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)" :db/id 17592186499243}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186498731} :answer-field/id #uuid "4fc2413c-734a-5d54-94fc-67baf81cb38a" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186499352}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "2ce9d0ba-72fa-5144-a2b0-16cd598fe603" :question/math-academy-id "q-345414" :question/problem "![](images/df/dfe6902183d348f21d053acce448bd5012d190b6b678f406099ef9d0a2c83374.png)

Find the differential equation governing the current $I$ (in amperes) at time $t$ (in seconds) in the circuit given in the diagram above.

*Hint: The voltage drop ${V}_{C}$ across the capacitor is related to its charge by $q=C{V}_{C},$ where $C$ is the capacitance measured in Farads.*" :question/worked-solution "The diagram shows a series RCL circuit with a source electromotive force (EMF) of $7\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)\,\text{V},$ a resistor of resistance $10\,Ω,$ a capacitor of capacitance $0.02\,\text{F},$ and an inductor of inductance $2\,\text{H}.$

The current $I,$ measured in amperes, is defined as the rate of flow of charge $q,$ measured in coulombs.

$$
I=\frac{dq}{dt}
$$

Kirchhoff's voltage law states that in a series circuit, the source voltage (EMF) equals the sum of the voltage drops.

In an RCL circuit, there are three voltage drops:

- The voltage drop across the resistor is proportional to the current, with a constant of proportionality $R=10\,Ω.$ So,

$$
{V}_{R}=10I.
$$

- The voltage drop across the capacitor is related to its charge by $q=C{V}_{C}.$ Therefore,

$$
{V}_{C}=\frac{q}{C}=\frac{q}{0.02}=50q.
$$

- The voltage drop across the inductor is proportional to the rate of change of current, with a constant of proportionality $L=2\,\text{H}.$ Hence,

$$
{V}_{L}=2\,\frac{dI}{dt}.
$$

Therefore, by Kirchhoff's voltage law, these values are related by the equation

$$
7\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)=10I+50q+2\,\frac{dI}{dt}.
$$

Differentiating with respect to $t,$ the differential equation governing the current in the circuit is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{d}{dt}(7\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)) & =\frac{d}{dt}(10I+50q+2\,\frac{dI}{dt}) \\ -21\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t) & =10\,\frac{dI}{dt}+50\,\frac{dq}{dt}+2\,\frac{{d}^{2}I}{d{t}^{2}},\end{aligned}
$$

which, when substituting in $I=\frac{dq}{dt},$ gives

$$
\frac{{d}^{2}I}{d{t}^{2}}+5\,\frac{dI}{dt}+25I=-10.5\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t).
$$"} {:db/id 17592186499460 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "d23c71b1-938d-5c3c-896d-64a1b9e36fad" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "6" :db/id 17592186499197}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186499197} :answer-field/id #uuid "6ead61a9-5da2-511e-a657-d00ea95b48b4" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186499369}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "3d1e7c48-2675-551e-94d8-a9622a621313" :question/math-academy-id "q-345097" :question/problem "The charge $q(t)$ on the capacitor, in coulombs, in a series RCL circuit at time $t$ seconds is

amperes." :question/worked-solution "The current $I$ measured in amperes, is defined as the rate of flow of charge $q$ measured in coulombs.

$$
I=\frac{dq}{dt}
$$

Differentiating the given expression for $q(t),$ we obtain the following expression for $I,$ in amperes:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(t) & =\frac{d}{dt}(-{e}^{-4t}+3{e}^{-2t}+\frac{7}{25}\operatorname{cos}⁡(6t)+\frac{24}{25}\operatorname{sin}⁡(6t)) \\  & =4{e}^{-4t}-6{e}^{-2t}-\frac{42}{25}\operatorname{sin}⁡(6t)+\frac{144}{25}\operatorname{cos}⁡(6t).\end{aligned}
$$

Note the following:

- The quantity ${I}_{c}(t)=4{e}^{-4t}-6{e}^{-2t}$ is the *transient current*, since it goes to zero as $t\to \infty .$

- The function $$
\displaystyle {I}_{p}(t)=-\frac{42}{25}\operatorname{sin}⁡(6t)+\frac{144}{25}\operatorname{cos}⁡(6t)
$$ is the *steady-state current*. It governs the current's long-term behavior.

Therefore, as $t\to \infty ,$ we have

$$
I(t)≈{I}_{p}(t)=-\frac{42}{25}\operatorname{sin}⁡(6t)+\frac{144}{25}\operatorname{cos}⁡(6t).
$$

Finally, the amplitude of the steady-state current, in amperes, is given by

$$
\sqrt{{\left(-\frac{42}{25}\right)}^{2}+{\left(\frac{144}{25}\right)}^{2}}=\sqrt{\frac{1764+20736}{625}}=\sqrt{\frac{22500}{625}}=6.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186499462 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "2705d98a-25ec-5969-a29d-c332f4d288ab" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.6879" :db/id 17592186498814} {:answer/id #uuid "5fe3f48b-7c14-53ba-b3fd-bbec7ac1ee02" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.7190" :db/id 17592186498950} {:answer/id #uuid "b742ff69-3bac-5abb-b927-7a4fa661d8ef" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.6480" :db/id 17592186499137} {:answer/id #uuid "d15ccfd9-6d0f-59d8-a94c-08cca8b6e6ce" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.6517" :db/id 17592186499195} {:answer/id #uuid "e6cc3768-66dc-5f5e-be89-3a0ad7d4c68f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.7157" :db/id 17592186499254}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186498814} :answer-field/id #uuid "84e05cf2-3838-56c6-aae2-6436bc5d9b0d" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186499380}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "404778b6-2da1-56e5-aa20-574c3d5c8b29" :question/math-academy-id "q-143485" :question/problem "Let ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{148}$ be a random sample of size $n=148$ from a population with a population mean $\mu =98$ and population standard deviation $\sigma =74.$ Find an approximation for the probability that the sample mean is greater than $95.$

*Hint: A table of values of $Φ(z)$ for different values of $z$ is given below, where $Φ(z)$ is the cumulative distribution function for the standard normal distribution.*

| $\,-0.3\,$ | $\,0.3557\,$ | $\,0.3520\,$ | $\,0.3483\,$ |" :question/worked-solution "Suppose that ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{n}$ is a random sample of size $n$ from a population with a population mean $\mu $ and population standard deviation $\sigma .$ The central limit theorem (or CLT) states that for sufficiently large $n,$ the distribution of the sample mean $\overset{―}{X}$ can be approximated as 

$$
\overset{―}{X}∼N\,(\mu ,\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n}).
$$

In our case, we have

$$
n=148,\,\mu =98,\,\sigma =74.
$$

Therefore, by the CLT, we have that the distribution of the sample mean can be approximated as

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{―}{X} & ∼N\,(\mu ,\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n}) \\  & ∼N\,(98,\frac{{74}^{2}}{148}) \\  & ∼N(98,37).\end{aligned}
$$

We want to find $P(\overset{―}{X}>95).$ So, we convert $\overset{―}{X}$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(\overset{―}{X}>95) & =P(Z>\frac{95-98}{\sqrt{37}}) \\  & =P(Z>-\frac{3}{\sqrt{37}}) \\  & ≈P(Z>-0.49)\end{aligned}
$$

Using the complement of the normal distribution, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}P(Z>-0.49) & =1-P(Z<-0.49) \\  & =1-Φ(-0.49).\end{aligned}
$$

From the table, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Φ(-0.49)=0.3121.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(\overset{―}{X}>95) & =1-Φ(-0.49) \\  & =1-0.3121 \\  & =0.6879.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186499467 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "762a8247-a61f-554d-9284-b315dcdad86d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "I(t)=\frac{3}{4}{e}^{-4t}-\frac{1}{4}{e}^{-2t}" :db/id 17592186498995} {:answer/id #uuid "936e54df-c6a4-517d-aecf-8dc308a9634b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "I(t)=\frac{3}{4}{e}^{-4t}+\frac{1}{4}{e}^{-2t}" :db/id 17592186499051} {:answer/id #uuid "a427506f-ef7d-5ee2-9914-6c5fd3720316" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "I(t)=\frac{1}{4}{e}^{-4t}+\frac{3}{4}{e}^{-2t}" :db/id 17592186499085} {:answer/id #uuid "d4e5b1c1-6827-5f0e-8851-ce5fba6646cb" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "I(t)=\frac{3}{4}{e}^{-2t}+\frac{1}{4}{e}^{-4t}" :db/id 17592186499205} {:answer/id #uuid "d93500c5-93ce-5509-abb5-158f5bb08d21" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "I(t)=\frac{7}{4}{e}^{-4t}+\frac{1}{4}{e}^{-2t}" :db/id 17592186499215}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186499051} :answer-field/id #uuid "2cc4a8f1-8e79-5bf4-8c50-2960fd5aec31" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186499336}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "4f1e7e70-00e5-5263-ad86-e1c271d552fe" :question/math-academy-id "q-345169" :question/problem "![](images/d3/d34d844ed99307f03ff2454f8916efa91738d7b967f546ef6e516e003d4fc481.png)

Find an equation for the current (in amperes) in the circuit given in the diagram above, expressing your answer in terms of time $t$ (in seconds) only, and given that the initial charge on the capacitor is $\frac{1}{4}\,\text{C}$ and the initial current is $1\,\text{A}.$

*Hint: The voltage drop ${V}_{C}$ across the capacitor is related to its charge by $q=C{V}_{C},$ where $C$ is the capacitance measured in Farads.*" :question/worked-solution "The diagram shows a series RCL circuit with a source electromotive force (EMF) of $9\,\text{V},$ a resistor of resistance $12\,Ω,$ a capacitor of capacitance $0.0625\,\text{F},$ and an inductor of inductance $2\,\text{H}.$

The current $I,$ measured in amperes, is defined as the rate of flow of charge $q,$ measured in coulombs.

$$
I=\frac{dq}{dt}
$$

Kirchhoff's voltage law states that in a series circuit, the source voltage (EMF) equals the sum of the voltage drops.

In an RCL circuit, there are three voltage drops:

- The voltage drop across the resistor is proportional to the current, with a constant of proportionality $R=12\,Ω.$ So,

$$
{V}_{R}=12I.
$$

- The voltage drop across the capacitor is related to its charge by $q=C{V}_{C}.$ Therefore,

$$
{V}_{C}=\frac{q}{C}=\frac{q}{0.0625}=16q.
$$

- The voltage drop across the inductor is proportional to the rate of change of current, with a constant of proportionality $L=2\,\text{H}.$ Hence,

$$
{V}_{L}=2\,\frac{dI}{dt}.
$$

Therefore, by Kirchhoff's voltage law, these values are related by the equation

$$
9=12I+16q+2\,\frac{dI}{dt}.
$$

Differentiating with respect to $t,$ the differential equation governing the current in the circuit is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{d}{dt}(9) & =\frac{d}{dt}(12I+16q+2\,\frac{dI}{dt}) \\ 0 & =12\,\frac{dI}{dt}+16\,\frac{dq}{dt}+2\,\frac{{d}^{2}I}{d{t}^{2}},\end{aligned}
$$

which, when substituting in $I=\frac{dq}{dt},$ gives

$$
\frac{{d}^{2}I}{d{t}^{2}}+6\,\frac{dI}{dt}+8I=0.
$$

The given equation is a second-order linear homogeneous equation with constant coefficients. To find the general solution, we must take a linear combination of two linearly independent solutions.

Assuming the solutions take the form $I={e}^{\lambda t},$ we obtain two solutions, namely, $I={e}^{-4t}$ and $I={e}^{-2t}.$
So, the general solution in our case is

$$
I(t)=A{e}^{-4t}+B{e}^{-2t}.
$$

We're told that the circuit starts with an initial charge of $\frac{1}{4}\,\text{C}$ on the capacitor and an initial current of $1\,\text{A}.$
Now, solving the Kirchhoff's law equation for $\frac{dI}{dt},$ we have

$$
\frac{dI}{dt}=\frac{9}{2}-6I-8q.
$$

So, we can apply the initial conditions $I(0)=1$ and 

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}^{′}(0) & =\frac{9}{2}-6I(0)-8q(0) \\  & =\frac{9}{2}-6\cdot 1-8\cdot \frac{1}{4} \\  & =-\frac{7}{2},\end{aligned}
$$

and solve for $A$ and $B.$

- Substituting $I(0)=1$ into our general solution gives

$$
\begin{aligned}1 & =A{e}^{-4(0)}+B{e}^{-2(0)} \\ 1 & =A+B.\end{aligned}
$$

- Differentiating $I,$ we get

$$
{I}^{′}=-4A{e}^{-4t}-2B{e}^{-2t}
$$

Substituting in ${I}^{′}(0)=-\frac{7}{2}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{7}{2} & =-4A{e}^{-4(0)}-2B{e}^{-2(0)} \\ -\frac{7}{2} & =-4A-2B.\end{aligned}
$$

Putting the two equations in $A$ and $B$ together gives the following system:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}1 &=A+B \\ -\frac{7}{2} &=-4A-2B\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Solving this system gives $A=\frac{3}{4}$ and $B=\frac{1}{4}.$ Therefore, the equation for the current (in amperes) in the circuit is

$$
I(t)=\frac{3}{4}{e}^{-4t}+\frac{1}{4}{e}^{-2t}.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186499470 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "668253cd-0144-5b80-9229-3e2e29fffd88" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "I(t)=\frac{4}{3}{e}^{-4t}+\frac{5}{2}{e}^{-t}" :db/id 17592186498958} {:answer/id #uuid "77b92a32-a4d2-5d8e-9427-ff367d4abcae" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "I(t)=-\frac{4}{3}{e}^{-4t}+\frac{17}{6}{e}^{-t}" :db/id 17592186498998} {:answer/id #uuid "b8b8f8c9-3ee9-577d-9ca4-85115a991a46" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "I(t)=-\frac{5}{2}{e}^{-4t}+\frac{17}{6}{e}^{-t}" :db/id 17592186499143} {:answer/id #uuid "bfbacf7e-f6d5-59fb-8037-235e5b941105" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "I(t)=\frac{4}{3}{e}^{-4t}-\frac{17}{6}{e}^{-t}" :db/id 17592186499154} {:answer/id #uuid "c371254f-a58d-5c4b-9b11-45959b0a4872" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "I(t)=\frac{17}{6}{e}^{-4t}+\frac{4}{3}{e}^{-t}" :db/id 17592186499160}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186498998} :answer-field/id #uuid "8ebb9408-4bb6-577b-a3e1-f2b37a11a6a2" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186499384}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "5218de49-0b02-5048-960b-3418b12d24b2" :question/math-academy-id "q-345162" :question/problem "The charge $q(t),$ in coulombs, and current $I(t),$ in amperes, in a series RCL circuit are related by the equation

$$
\frac{dI}{dt}+5I+4q=11.
$$

Find an equation for the current in the circuit, expressing your answer in terms of time $t$ (in seconds) only, and given that the initial charge on the capacitor is $\frac{1}{4}\,\text{C}$ and the initial current is $\frac{3}{2}\,\text{A}.$" :question/worked-solution "The current $I,$ measured in amperes, is defined as the rate of flow of charge $q,$ measured in coulombs.

$$
I=\frac{dq}{dt}
$$

Differentiating the given relation with respect to $t,$ the differential equation governing the current in the circuit is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{d}{dt}(\frac{dI}{dt}+5I+4q) & =\frac{d}{dt}(11) \\ \frac{{d}^{2}I}{d{t}^{2}}+5\,\frac{dI}{dt}+4\,\frac{dq}{dt} & =0,\end{aligned}
$$

which, when substituting in $I=\frac{dq}{dt},$ gives

$$
\frac{{d}^{2}I}{d{t}^{2}}+5\,\frac{dI}{dt}+4I=0.
$$

The given equation is a second-order linear homogeneous equation with constant coefficients. To find the general solution, we must take a linear combination of two linearly independent solutions.

Assuming the solutions take the form $I={e}^{\lambda t},$ we obtain two solutions, namely, $I={e}^{-4t}$ and $I={e}^{-t}.$
So, the general solution in our case is

$$
I(t)=A{e}^{-4t}+B{e}^{-t}.
$$

We're told that the circuit starts with an initial charge of $\frac{1}{4}\,\text{C}$ on the capacitor and an initial current of $\frac{3}{2}\,\text{A}.$
Now, solving the given relation for $\frac{dI}{dt},$ we have

$$
\frac{dI}{dt}=11-5I-4q.
$$

So, we can apply the initial conditions $I(0)=\frac{3}{2}$ and 

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}^{′}(0) & =11-5I(0)-4q(0) \\  & =11-5\cdot \frac{3}{2}-4\cdot \frac{1}{4} \\  & =\frac{5}{2},\end{aligned}
$$

and solve for $A$ and $B.$

- Substituting $I(0)=\frac{3}{2}$ into our general solution gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{2} & =A{e}^{-4(0)}+B{e}^{-1(0)} \\ \frac{3}{2} & =A+B.\end{aligned}
$$

- Differentiating $I,$ we get

$$
{I}^{′}=-4A{e}^{-4t}-B{e}^{-t}
$$

Substituting in ${I}^{′}(0)=\frac{5}{2}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{5}{2} & =-4A{e}^{-4(0)}-B{e}^{-1(0)} \\ \frac{5}{2} & =-4A-B.\end{aligned}
$$

Putting the two equations in $A$ and $B$ together gives the following system:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{2} &=A+B \\ \frac{5}{2} &=-4A-B\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Solving this system gives $A=-\frac{4}{3}$ and $B=\frac{17}{6}.$ Therefore, the equation for the current (in amperes) in the circuit is

$$
I(t)=-\frac{4}{3}{e}^{-4t}+\frac{17}{6}{e}^{-t}.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186499476 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "41216090-a989-57ea-9a0f-6de131ddbc5b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.4873" :db/id 17592186498881} {:answer/id #uuid "671c8ecd-1582-5061-be4f-2c20b3d551bd" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.5646" :db/id 17592186498962} {:answer/id #uuid "a4e395ad-d4a8-5689-9848-88a1b4b68ab2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.5366" :db/id 17592186499087} {:answer/id #uuid "a73252f2-f336-5a10-bbe0-1689a2bfb15b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.5011" :db/id 17592186499098} {:answer/id #uuid "d051cc40-58a5-56ad-9a15-8c97eac88c9e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.4942" :db/id 17592186499190}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186498962} :answer-field/id #uuid "7c0a2054-e571-5c46-8a14-d732f5257c7a" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186499379}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "5ae46753-9928-51e1-ad50-7c5a5efcdfe5" :question/math-academy-id "q-143476" :question/problem "Let ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{90}$ be a random sample of size $n=90$ from a population with a population mean $\mu =92$ and population standard deviation $\sigma =30.$ Find an approximation for the probability that the sample mean is between $90$ and $95.$

*Hint: A table of values of $Φ(z)$ for different values of $z$ is given below, where $Φ(z)$ is the cumulative distribution function for the standard normal distribution.* 

| $z$ | $\,0.03\,$ | $\,0.04\,$ | $\,0.05\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\,0.6\,$ | $\,0.7357\,$ | $\,0.7389\,$ | $\,0.7422\,$ |
| $\,0.7\,$ | $\,0.7673\,$ | $\,0.7704\,$ | $\,0.7734\,$ |
| $\,0.8\,$ | $\,0.7967\,$ | $\,0.7995\,$ | $\,0.8023\,$ |
| $\,0.9\,$ | $\,0.8238\,$ | $\,0.8264\,$ | $\,0.8289\,$ |" :question/worked-solution "Suppose that ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{n}$ is a random sample of size $n$ from a population with a population mean $\mu $ and population standard deviation $\sigma .$ The central limit theorem (or CLT) states that for sufficiently large $n,$ the distribution of the sample mean $\overset{―}{X}$ can be approximated as 

$$
\overset{―}{X}∼N\,(\mu ,\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n}).
$$

In our case, we have

$$
n=90,\,\mu =92,\,\sigma =30.
$$

Therefore, by the CLT, we have that the distribution of the sample mean can be approximated as

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{―}{X} & ∼N\,(\mu ,\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n}) \\  & ∼N\,(92,\frac{{30}^{2}}{90}) \\  & ∼N(92,10).\end{aligned}
$$

We want to find $P(90<\overset{―}{X}<95).$ So, we convert $\overset{―}{X}$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(90<\overset{―}{X}<95) & =P(\frac{90-92}{\sqrt{10}}<Z<\frac{95-92}{\sqrt{10}}) \\  & =P(-\frac{2}{\sqrt{10}}<Z<\frac{3}{\sqrt{10}}) \\  & ≈P(-0.63<Z<0.95) \\  & =P(Z<0.95)-P(Z<-0.63) \\  & =Φ(0.95)-Φ(-0.63)\end{aligned}
$$

From the table, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Φ(0.95) & =0.8289 \\ Φ(0.63) & =0.7357.\end{aligned}
$$

Also, by the symmetry of the normal distribution, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Φ(-0.63) & =1-Φ(0.63) \\  & =1-0.7357 \\  & =0.2643.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(90<\overset{―}{X}<95) & =Φ(0.95)-Φ(-0.63) \\  & =0.8289-0.2643 \\  & =0.5646.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186499479 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "17418eda-e303-583e-abb8-8163f34cf65c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{5}{12}" :db/id 17592186498779} {:answer/id #uuid "3b1f2bf6-1e84-5da8-8223-f7a8617abe63" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{12}" :db/id 17592186498865} {:answer/id #uuid "aaa17f5a-3932-5a85-be4a-9e7f8aca50c3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{3}" :db/id 17592186499103} {:answer/id #uuid "af9d5967-0e62-5e9c-80be-bb9563606efe" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{6}" :db/id 17592186499116} {:answer/id #uuid "e507ffc4-50dc-56ba-8db0-2ce573a2305a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{4}" :db/id 17592186499248}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186498865} :answer-field/id #uuid "06575685-8b6e-5313-b708-d919a2eb705b" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186499310}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "5e32ec93-9a95-5b63-b1e8-8733a4d5c7af" :question/math-academy-id "q-82910" :question/problem "Using the change of variables 

$$
u=x+y,\,v=y,
$$

calculate the area of the finite region $D$ bounded by the curves $(x+y)^{3}-y=0$ and $(x+y)^{2}-y=0.$" :question/worked-solution "The area of the required region is given by

$$
{∬}_{D}dxdy.
$$

Let's define a transformation $T$ as follows: 

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{bmatrix}
$$

This transformation maps some region $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane to our region $D$ in the $xy$-plane.

To compute the required area, we will use the change of variables formula

$$
{∬}_{D}dxdy={∬}_{Δ}|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\text{ }dudv
$$

where $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T.$  

Note that the changes of variables

$$
u=x+y,\,v=y
$$

 

gives us the *inverse* function ${T}^{-1},$ that is

$$
{T}^{-1}:\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}u(x,y) \\ v(x,y)\end{bmatrix}.
$$

To compute the required area, we proceed in four steps:

**Step 1**: Find $Δ,$ which is the image of $D$ under the action of ${T}^{-1}.$ 

Substituting $x+y=u$ and $y=v$ into the equation of the first curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}(x+y)^{3}-y=0\,⟹\,{u}^{3}-v=0\,⟹\,v={u}^{3},\end{aligned}
$$

while substituting $x+y=u$ and $y=v$ into the equation of the second curve, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}(x+y)^{2}-y=0\,⟹\,{u}^{2}-v=0\,⟹\,v={u}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the intersections of the curves in the $uv$-plane, we solve the following system:

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}v &={u}^{3} \\ v &={u}^{2}\end{aligned}\right.\,⟹\,\left\{\begin{aligned}{u}^{2}(u-1) &=0 \\ v &=u.\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the intersection points are $(0,0)$ and $(1,1).$

Therefore, our domain in the $uv$-plane has the type I representation 

$$
Δ=\{(u,v)\,:\,0\le u\le 1,\,{u}^{3}\le v\le {u}^{2}\}.
$$

![](images/a8/a8d2549c665a918cc8d69c69136fcb49e654ebb9aa5e53611155798e791b36a9.png)

   

**Step 2**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T$ is

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}={\left(\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)}\right)}^{-1}=(1)^{-1}=1.
$$

Note that $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}\ne 0$ everywhere inside $Δ.$  In other words, $T$ has no critical points inside $Δ.$

**Step 4**: Compute the required area.

We calculate the required area by performing the change of variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\text{d}x\text{d}y & ={∬}_{Δ}|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}|1|\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[{\int }_{{u}^{3}}^{{u}^{2}}\,dv]du \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}v{|}_{{u}^{3}}^{{u}^{2}}\,du \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}({u}^{2}-{u}^{3})du \\  & ={[\frac{{u}^{3}}{3}-\frac{{u}^{4}}{4}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}-\frac{1}{4} \\  & =\frac{1}{12}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186499482 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0cc4a8d6-eafc-5ee6-a82e-90d6cd839dc1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "I(t)=-\frac{43}{4}{e}^{-6t}+\frac{73}{12}{e}^{-3t}" :db/id 17592186498758} {:answer/id #uuid "6301bea8-0af2-5e55-a95e-0ba3af21f105" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "I(t)=\frac{73}{12}{e}^{-6t}-\frac{29}{6}{e}^{-3t}" :db/id 17592186498953} {:answer/id #uuid "74463303-feaf-5f41-b2a1-22eec88e4e26" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "I(t)=\frac{29}{6}{e}^{-6t}+\frac{43}{4}{e}^{-3t}" :db/id 17592186498986} {:answer/id #uuid "912374b9-7fc1-5b10-9f21-b7d793054f6c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "I(t)=-\frac{29}{6}{e}^{-6t}+\frac{73}{12}{e}^{-3t}" :db/id 17592186499046} {:answer/id #uuid "ca9ccf40-b7ff-525d-9971-a897975f15a0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "I(t)=\frac{73}{12}{e}^{-6t}+\frac{29}{6}{e}^{-3t}" :db/id 17592186499175}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186499046} :answer-field/id #uuid "985290a4-113d-5a11-a0ec-110811ffe0e8" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186499387}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "62aefe8f-6088-586d-94c3-d6e202d70a8e" :question/math-academy-id "q-345164" :question/problem "The charge $q(t),$ in coulombs, and current $I(t),$ in amperes, in a series RCL circuit are related by the equation

$$
\frac{dI}{dt}+9I+18q=25.
$$

Find an equation for the current in the circuit, expressing your answer in terms of time $t$ (in seconds) only, and given that the initial charge on the capacitor is $\frac{1}{6}\,\text{C}$ and the initial current is $\frac{5}{4}\,\text{A}.$" :question/worked-solution "The current $I,$ measured in amperes, is defined as the rate of flow of charge $q,$ measured in coulombs.

$$
I=\frac{dq}{dt}
$$

Differentiating the given relation with respect to $t,$ the differential equation governing the current in the circuit is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{d}{dt}(\frac{dI}{dt}+9I+18q) & =\frac{d}{dt}(25) \\ \frac{{d}^{2}I}{d{t}^{2}}+9\,\frac{dI}{dt}+18\,\frac{dq}{dt} & =0,\end{aligned}
$$

which, when substituting in $I=\frac{dq}{dt},$ gives

$$
\frac{{d}^{2}I}{d{t}^{2}}+9\,\frac{dI}{dt}+18I=0.
$$

The given equation is a second-order linear homogeneous equation with constant coefficients. To find the general solution, we must take a linear combination of two linearly independent solutions.

Assuming the solutions take the form $I={e}^{\lambda t},$ we obtain two solutions, namely, $I={e}^{-6t}$ and $I={e}^{-3t}.$
So, the general solution in our case is

$$
I(t)=A{e}^{-6t}+B{e}^{-3t}.
$$

We're told that the circuit starts with an initial charge of $\frac{1}{6}\,\text{C}$ on the capacitor and an initial current of $\frac{5}{4}\,\text{A}.$
Now, solving the given relation for $\frac{dI}{dt},$ we have

$$
\frac{dI}{dt}=25-9I-18q.
$$

So, we can apply the initial conditions $I(0)=\frac{5}{4}$ and 

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}^{′}(0) & =25-9I(0)-18q(0) \\  & =25-9\cdot \frac{5}{4}-18\cdot \frac{1}{6} \\  & =\frac{43}{4},\end{aligned}
$$

and solve for $A$ and $B.$

- Substituting $I(0)=\frac{5}{4}$ into our general solution gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{5}{4} & =A{e}^{-6(0)}+B{e}^{-3(0)} \\ \frac{5}{4} & =A+B.\end{aligned}
$$

- Differentiating $I,$ we get

$$
{I}^{′}=-6A{e}^{-6t}-3B{e}^{-3t}
$$

Substituting in ${I}^{′}(0)=\frac{43}{4}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{43}{4} & =-6A{e}^{-6(0)}-3B{e}^{-3(0)} \\ \frac{43}{4} & =-6A-3B.\end{aligned}
$$

Putting the two equations in $A$ and $B$ together gives the following system:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}\frac{5}{4} &=A+B \\ \frac{43}{4} &=-6A-3B\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Solving this system gives $A=-\frac{29}{6}$ and $B=\frac{73}{12}.$ Therefore, the equation for the current (in amperes) in the circuit is

$$
I(t)=-\frac{29}{6}{e}^{-6t}+\frac{73}{12}{e}^{-3t}.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186499485 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "5e7704d1-16de-5f57-9381-77fa91a75339" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "I(t)=\frac{7}{4}{e}^{-t}-\frac{3}{4}{e}^{-5t}" :db/id 17592186498946} {:answer/id #uuid "65e56828-40a4-5c88-88b8-dc7bcfb344e2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "I(t)=-\frac{3}{4}{e}^{-t}+\frac{7}{4}{e}^{-5t}" :db/id 17592186498957} {:answer/id #uuid "74d13041-41ad-5e74-9ece-8544d7624726" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "I(t)=\frac{7}{4}{e}^{-5t}-\frac{3}{4}{e}^{-t}" :db/id 17592186498988} {:answer/id #uuid "ae716747-adb4-5e5e-89d4-b2a39710996d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "I(t)=\frac{7}{4}{e}^{-t}+\frac{3}{4}{e}^{-5t}" :db/id 17592186499114} {:answer/id #uuid "b83a0cfa-c6af-5ba3-83d9-9e7b4d506e58" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "I(t)=\frac{3}{4}{e}^{-t}-\frac{7}{4}{e}^{-5t}" :db/id 17592186499142}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186498946} :answer-field/id #uuid "ebb96b46-f989-5842-a663-f156f4929adf" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186499420}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "676e6c66-ab4f-5266-9314-934677a34712" :question/math-academy-id "q-345156" :question/problem "The charge $q(t),$ in coulombs, and current $I(t),$ in amperes, in a series RCL circuit are related by the equation

$$
\frac{dI}{dt}+6I+5q=\frac{21}{2}.
$$

Find an equation for the current in the circuit, expressing your answer in terms of time $t$ (in seconds) only, and given that the initial charge on the capacitor is $\frac{1}{2}\,\text{C}$ and the initial current is $1\,\text{A}.$" :question/worked-solution "The current $I,$ measured in amperes, is defined as the rate of flow of charge $q,$ measured in coulombs.

$$
I=\frac{dq}{dt}
$$

Differentiating the given relation with respect to $t,$ the differential equation governing the current in the circuit is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{d}{dt}(\frac{dI}{dt}+6I+5q) & =\frac{d}{dt}\left(\frac{21}{2}\right) \\ \frac{{d}^{2}I}{d{t}^{2}}+6\,\frac{dI}{dt}+5\,\frac{dq}{dt} & =0,\end{aligned}
$$

which, when substituting in $I=\frac{dq}{dt},$ gives

$$
\frac{{d}^{2}I}{d{t}^{2}}+6\,\frac{dI}{dt}+5I=0.
$$

The given equation is a second-order linear homogeneous equation with constant coefficients. To find the general solution, we must take a linear combination of two linearly independent solutions.

Assuming the solutions take the form $I={e}^{\lambda t},$ we obtain two solutions, namely, $I={e}^{-t}$ and $I={e}^{-5t}.$
So, the general solution in our case is

$$
I(t)=A{e}^{-t}+B{e}^{-5t}.
$$

We're told that the circuit starts with an initial charge of $\frac{1}{2}\,\text{C}$ on the capacitor and an initial current of $1\,\text{A}.$
Now, solving the given relation for $\frac{dI}{dt},$ we have

$$
\frac{dI}{dt}=\frac{21}{2}-6I-5q.
$$

So, we can apply the initial conditions $I(0)=1$ and 

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}^{′}(0) & =\frac{21}{2}-6I(0)-5q(0) \\  & =\frac{21}{2}-6\cdot 1-5\cdot \frac{1}{2} \\  & =\frac{21}{2}-\frac{12}{2}-\frac{5}{2} \\  & =2,\end{aligned}
$$

and solve for $A$ and $B.$

- Substituting $I(0)=1$ into our general solution gives

$$
\begin{aligned}1 & =A{e}^{-(0)}+B{e}^{-5(0)} \\ 1 & =A+B.\end{aligned}
$$

- Differentiating $I,$ we get

$$
{I}^{′}=-A{e}^{-t}-5B{e}^{-5t}
$$

Substituting in ${I}^{′}(0)=2$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}2 & =-A{e}^{-(0)}-5B{e}^{-5(0)} \\ 2 & =-A-5B.\end{aligned}
$$

Putting the two equations in $A$ and $B$ together gives the following system:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}1 &=A+B \\ 2 &=-A-5B\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Solving this system gives $A=\frac{7}{4}$ and $B=-\frac{3}{4}.$ Therefore, the equation for the current (in amperes) in the circuit is

$$
I(t)=\frac{7}{4}{e}^{-t}-\frac{3}{4}{e}^{-5t}.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186499491 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1784c964-2bd8-551a-9e62-6cb6f2560ce3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3e" :db/id 17592186498780} {:answer/id #uuid "255b1548-0862-5d3a-8e4b-d22ea5aa0f02" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{e-1}{3}" :db/id 17592186498812} {:answer/id #uuid "4f74f069-41cb-54fc-8a9a-08d22d7c1865" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{3e}{2}" :db/id 17592186498916} {:answer/id #uuid "7d9780c4-afc1-59e7-ac65-84b80ad23ee1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{9}{4}(e-1)" :db/id 17592186499011} {:answer/id #uuid "903bd708-b320-50fc-b991-e52faae4df28" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3e+2" :db/id 17592186499042}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186499011} :answer-field/id #uuid "2030cf44-2880-55da-b8da-7f5dffbc7894" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186499324}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "787730fc-5924-57cd-ac3a-f6e87e085583" :question/math-academy-id "q-161893" :question/problem "Use the change of variables 

$$
u=x+y,\,v=y-x,\,w=z,
$$

to evaluate the triple integral

$$
∭(x+y){e}^{y-x}\,dV,
$$

 
where the region $R$ is given by

$$
R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,1\le x+y\le 2,\,0\le y-x\le 1,\,0\le z\le 3\}.
$$" :question/worked-solution "Let's define a transformation $T$ as follows:

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v \\ w\end{bmatrix}⟶\begin{bmatrix}x(u,v,w) \\ y(u,v,w) \\ z(u,v,w)\end{bmatrix}
$$

This transformation maps some region $Δ$ in the $uvw$-space to our region $R$ in the $xyz$-space.

To compute the required integral, we can use the change of variables formula

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\text{ }dV={∭}_{Δ}\text{ }f(x(u,v,w),y(u,v,w),z(u,v,w))\,|\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v\text{d}w
$$

where $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T.$

Note that the change of variables

$$
u=x+y,\,v=y-x,\,w=z,
$$

gives us the *inverse* function ${T}^{-1},$ that is

$$
{T}^{-1}:\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y \\ z\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}u(x,y,z) \\ v(x,y,z) \\ w(x,y,z)\end{bmatrix}.
$$

To compute the required integral, we proceed in four steps:

**Step 1**: Find $Δ,$ which is the image of $R$ under the action of ${T}^{-1}.$ 

Our domain in the $uvw$-space is

$$
\begin{aligned}Δ & =\{(u,v,w)\,:\,1\le u\le 2,\,0\le v\le 1,\,0\le w\le 3\}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} & \frac{∂u}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y} & \frac{∂v}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & \frac{∂w}{∂y} & \frac{∂w}{∂z}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}1 & 1 & 0 \\ -1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =1(-1)^{3+3}\begin{vmatrix}1 & 1 \\ -1 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =1-(-1) \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T$ is

$$
\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}={\left(\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)}\right)}^{-1}=\frac{1}{2}.
$$

Note that $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}\ne 0$ everywhere inside $Δ.$ In other words, $T$ has no critical points inside $Δ.$

**Step 4**: Perform the change of variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∭}_{R}(x+y){e}^{y-x}\,dV & ={∭}_{Δ}u{e}^{v}\cdot |-\frac{1}{2}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v\text{d}w \\  & ={∭}_{Δ}\frac{u{e}^{v}}{2}\,\text{d}u\text{d}v\text{d}w \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{3}\frac{u{e}^{v}}{2}\,dw\,dv\,du \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{1}^{2}u\,du\cdot {\int }_{0}^{1}{e}^{v}\,dv\cdot {\int }_{0}^{3}dw \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot [\frac{{u}^{2}}{2}]_{u=1}^{u=2}\cdot {[{e}^{v}]}_{v=0}^{v=1}\cdot [w]_{w=0}^{w=3} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(2-\frac{1}{2})\cdot (e-1)\cdot (3-0) \\  & =\frac{9}{4}(e-1)\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186499534 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "453ad036-0136-573d-a854-e752d1240d93" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.9693" :db/id 17592186498888} {:answer/id #uuid "757bd7db-06f3-5391-932a-f85a5a835619" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.9525" :db/id 17592186498993} {:answer/id #uuid "7f11626b-a94c-59c3-845b-e27cfd30e095" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.9616" :db/id 17592186499017} {:answer/id #uuid "a3e99088-b1c1-5c8b-b459-a6d83a427867" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.9515" :db/id 17592186499084} {:answer/id #uuid "d9d51ccd-7b14-576e-8104-0ce48692c5e8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.9625" :db/id 17592186499217}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186499017} :answer-field/id #uuid "906ebcc0-b9ec-5434-848f-edcd08786742" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186499386}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "c5ea7895-e704-5589-b13a-69dbf76447fe" :question/math-academy-id "q-143482" :question/problem "Let ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{128}$ be a random sample of size $n=128$ from a population with a population mean $\mu =250$ and population standard deviation $\sigma =64.$ Find an approximation for the probability that the sample mean is less than $260.$

| $\,1.8\,$ | $\,0.9686\,$ | $\,0.9693\,$ | $\,0.9699\,$ |" :question/worked-solution "Suppose that ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{n}$ is a random sample of size $n$ from a population with a population mean $\mu $ and population standard deviation $\sigma .$ The central limit theorem (or CLT) states that for sufficiently large $n,$ the distribution of the sample mean $\overset{―}{X}$ can be approximated as

$$
f(x)=\left\{\begin{aligned}4{x}^{3}, & 0\le x\le 1, \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}.\end{aligned}\right.

Given that the population variance ${\sigma }^{2}=0.03,$ calculate $P(\overset{―}{X}>0.7).$

*Hint: A table of values of $Φ(z)$ for different values of $z$ is given below, where $Φ(z)$ is the cumulative distribution function for the standard normal distribution.*

| $\,-3.0\,$ | $\,0.0012\,$ | $\,0.0011\,$ | $\,0.0011\,$ |" :question/worked-solution "Suppose that ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{n}$ is a random sample of size $n$ from a population with population mean $\mu $ and population standard deviation $\sigma .$ The central limit theorem (or CLT) states that for sufficiently large $n,$ the distribution of the sample mean $\overset{―}{X}$ can be approximated as 

$$
\overset{―}{X}∼N\,(\mu ,\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n}).
$$

In our case:

- the sample size is

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =30,\end{aligned}
$$

- the population mean is

$$
\begin{aligned}\mu  & =\text{E}[X] \\  & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }x\,f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}x\cdot 4{x}^{3}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}4{x}^{4}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[\frac{4{x}^{5}}{5}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{4}{5} \\  & =0.8,\end{aligned}
$$

- the population variance is ${\sigma }^{2}=0.03.$

Therefore, by the CLT, we have that the distribution of the sample mean can be approximated as

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{―}{X} & ∼N\,(\mu ,\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n}) \\  & ∼N\,(0.8,\frac{0.03}{30}) \\  & ∼N(0.8,0.001).\end{aligned}
$$

We want to find $P(\overset{―}{X}>0.7).$ So, we convert $\overset{―}{X}$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(\overset{―}{X}>0.7) & =P(Z>\frac{0.7-0.8}{\sqrt{0.001}}) \\  & ≈P(Z>-3.16)\end{aligned}
$$

Using the complement of the normal distribution, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}P(Z>-3.16) & =1-P(Z<-3.16) \\  & =1-Φ(-3.16).\end{aligned}
$$

From the table, we have that

$$
Φ(-3.16)=0.0008.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(\overset{―}{X}>0.7) & =1-Φ(-3.16) \\  & =1-0.0008 \\  & =0.9992.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186499538 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1ebdcf1b-f76b-580c-8aa4-70ac17e6facc" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.3897" :db/id 17592186498796} {:answer/id #uuid "2d9fafad-5bf3-5710-99f5-3681e44187d4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.5411" :db/id 17592186498831} {:answer/id #uuid "39c5c463-edf8-5fec-9f6c-d5356a716684" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.3091" :db/id 17592186498859} {:answer/id #uuid "7a81f9c2-6bc9-52a7-b4de-4afc2f00e62d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.4641" :db/id 17592186499003} {:answer/id #uuid "9cdc3eca-7006-5354-9681-ab500004c7a8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.4721" :db/id 17592186499062}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186498796} :answer-field/id #uuid "01f05f01-de9e-58d6-bfff-58ec49139415" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186499308}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "cb19bbbb-4b9e-595b-b617-d56f35ac7f98" :question/math-academy-id "q-143484" :question/problem "Let ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{98}$ be a random sample of size $n=98$ from a population with a population mean $\mu =180$ and population standard deviation $\sigma =70.$ Find an approximation for the probability that the sample mean is greater than $182.$

Find, in amperes, the amplitude of the steady state current for the RCL circuit shown above, rounded to two decimal places.

*Hint: The voltage drop ${V}_{C}$ across the capacitor is related to its charge by $q=C{V}_{C},$ where $C$ is the capacitance measured in Farads.*" :question/worked-solution "The diagram shows a series RCL circuit with a source electromotive force (EMF) of $40\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\,\text{V},$ a resistor of resistance $90\,Ω,$ a capacitor of capacitance $\frac{1}{200}\,\text{F},$ and an inductor of inductance $10\,\text{H}.$

The current $I,$ measured in amperes, is defined as the rate of flow of charge $q,$ measured in coulombs.

$$
I=\frac{dq}{dt}
$$

Kirchhoff's voltage law states that in a series circuit, the source voltage (EMF) equals the sum of the voltage drops.

In an RCL circuit, there are three voltage drops:

- The voltage drop across the resistor is proportional to the current, with a constant of proportionality $R=90\,Ω.$ So,

$$
{V}_{R}=90I=90\,\frac{dq}{dt}.
$$

- The voltage drop across the capacitor is related to its charge by $q=C{V}_{C}.$ Therefore,

$$
{V}_{C}=\frac{q}{C}=\frac{q}{(1/200)}=200q.
$$

- The voltage drop across the inductor is proportional to the rate of change of current, with a constant of proportionality $L=10\,\text{H}.$ Hence,

$$
{V}_{L}=10\,\frac{dI}{dt}=10\,\frac{d}{dt}\left(\frac{dq}{dt}\right)=10\,\frac{{d}^{2}q}{d{t}^{2}}.
$$

Therefore, by Kirchhoff's voltage law, the differential equation governing the amount of charge $q$ on the capacitor is

$$
40\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)=90\,\frac{dq}{dt}+200q+10\,\frac{{d}^{2}q}{d{t}^{2}},
$$

which gives

$$
\frac{{d}^{2}q}{d{t}^{2}}+9\cdot \frac{dq}{dt}+20q=4\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t).
$$

The given equation is a second-order linear equation with constant coefficients. To find the general solution, we must sum the complementary and particular solutions.

- To find the complementary solution ${q}_{c},$ we solve the corresponding homogeneous equation, given by

$$
\frac{{d}^{2}{q}_{c}}{d{t}^{2}}+9\cdot \frac{d{q}_{c}}{dt}+20{q}_{c}=0.
$$

Solving using an integration technique, such as a trial solution, we obtain the complementary solution

$$
{q}_{c}(t)=A{e}^{-4t}+B{e}^{-5t},
$$

where $A$ and $B$ are constants.

- Next, we find the particular solution. Note that the right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is sinusoidal with argument $2t.$ So, we assume that the particular solution is also a sinusoidal with argument $2t,$ i.e.,

$$
{q}_{p}(t)=\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t).
$$

To find the values of $\alpha $ and $\beta ,$ we substitute

$$
\begin{aligned}{q}_{p} & =\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t), \\ \frac{d{q}_{p}}{dt} & =-2\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+2\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t), \\ \frac{{d}^{2}{q}_{p}}{d{t}^{2}} & =-4\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)-4\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t),\end{aligned}
$$

into the inhomogeneous equation and group like terms on the left-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,(-4\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)-4\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t))+9(-2\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+2\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t))\,\, &  \\ +20(\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)) & =4\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\ (16\alpha +18\beta )\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+(-18\alpha +16\beta )\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) & =4\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the coefficients, we get the following system of equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}16\alpha +18\beta &=0\, && (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)) \\ -18\alpha +16\beta &=4\, && (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t))\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Solving this system gives $\alpha =-\frac{18}{145},$ $\beta =\frac{16}{145}.$ Therefore, the particular solution is

$$
{q}_{p}(t)=-\frac{18}{145}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\frac{16}{145}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t).
$$

Now, since the general solution is given by the sum of the complementary solution and the particular solution, the general solution in our case is

$$
q(t)={q}_{c}(t)+{q}_{p}(t)=A{e}^{-4t}+B{e}^{-5t}-\frac{18}{145}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\frac{16}{145}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t).
$$

Differentiating this expression for $q(t),$ we obtain the following expression for $I$ in amperes:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(t) & =\frac{d}{dt}(A{e}^{-4t}+B{e}^{-5t}-\frac{18}{145}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\frac{16}{145}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)) \\  & =-4A{e}^{-4t}-5B{e}^{-5t}+\frac{36}{145}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+\frac{32}{145}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t).\end{aligned}
$$

Note the following:

- The quantity ${I}_{c}(t)=-4A{e}^{-4t}-5B{e}^{-5t}$ is the *transient current*, since it goes to zero as $t\to \infty .$

- The function $$
\displaystyle {I}_{p}(t)=\frac{36}{145}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+\frac{32}{145}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)
$$ is the *steady-state current*. It governs the current's long-term behavior.

Therefore, as $t\to \infty ,$ we have

$$
I(t)≈{I}_{p}(t)=\frac{36}{145}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+\frac{32}{145}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t).
$$

Finally, the amplitude of the steady-state current, in amperes, is given by

$$
\sqrt{{\left(\frac{36}{145}\right)}^{2}+{\left(\frac{32}{145}\right)}^{2}}≈0.33,
$$

rounded to two decimal places."} {:db/id 17592186499542 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0c6717c0-172d-55ad-8cdc-fb5fc434994c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "9" :db/id 17592186498756} {:answer/id #uuid "7214b0d8-e012-5439-9dec-14fa7390b7eb" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3" :db/id 17592186498984} {:answer/id #uuid "7b063c59-3e26-51c8-a0e3-18f8e69e895a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-6" :db/id 17592186499005} {:answer/id #uuid "a2d6bad6-25fd-50f1-873b-d472676fc497" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "6" :db/id 17592186499080} {:answer/id #uuid "ce426131-c353-59ac-95f1-7e7323260cef" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "12" :db/id 17592186499184}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186499080} :answer-field/id #uuid "467b7751-c11a-52b3-bf8c-2a1c44044541" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186499347}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "d36cf0d0-fde1-5898-8003-f96433332315" :question/math-academy-id "q-345277" :question/problem "![](images/3c/3c08141f91eea5b2d2006926de5239f91630de139fae970147d8267d46429392.png)

Consider the RCL circuit shown above. Given that the current $I(t)$ in the circuit at time $t$ seconds is given by

where $A,$ $B,$ $P,$ and $Q$ are constants, find the value of $P+Q.$

*Hint: The voltage drop ${V}_{C}$ across the capacitor is related to its charge by $q=C{V}_{C},$ where $C$ is the capacitance measured in Farads.*" :question/worked-solution "The diagram shows a series RCL circuit with a source electromotive force (EMF) of $20\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)\,\text{V},$ a resistor of resistance $6\,Ω,$ a capacitor of capacitance $0.25\,\text{F},$ and an inductor of inductance $2\,\text{H}.$

The current $I,$ measured in amperes, is defined as the rate of flow of charge $q,$ measured in coulombs.

$$
I=\frac{dq}{dt}
$$

Kirchhoff's voltage law states that in a series circuit, the source voltage (EMF) equals the sum of the voltage drops.

In an RCL circuit, there are three voltage drops:

- The voltage drop across the resistor is proportional to the current, with a constant of proportionality $R=6\,Ω.$ So,

$$
{V}_{R}=6I.
$$

- The voltage drop across the capacitor is related to its charge by $q=C{V}_{C}.$ Therefore,

$$
{V}_{C}=\frac{q}{C}=\frac{q}{0.25}=4q.
$$

- The voltage drop across the inductor is proportional to the rate of change of current, with a constant of proportionality $L=2\,\text{H}.$ Hence,

$$
{V}_{L}=2\,\frac{dI}{dt}.
$$

Therefore, by Kirchhoff's voltage law, these values are related by the equation

$$
20\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)=6I+4q+2\,\frac{dI}{dt}.
$$

Differentiating with respect to $t,$ the differential equation governing the current in the circuit is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{d}{dt}(20\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)) & =\frac{d}{dt}(6I+4q+2\,\frac{dI}{dt}) \\ 60\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t) & =6\,\frac{dI}{dt}+4I+2\,\frac{{d}^{2}I}{d{t}^{2}},\end{aligned}
$$

which, when substituting in $I=\frac{dq}{dt},$ gives

$$
\frac{{d}^{2}I}{d{t}^{2}}+3\cdot \frac{dI}{dt}+2I=30\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t).
$$

The given equation is a second-order linear equation with constant coefficients. To find the general solution, we must sum the complementary and particular solutions.

- To find the complementary solution ${I}_{c},$ we solve the corresponding homogeneous equation, given by

$$
\frac{{d}^{2}{I}_{c}}{d{t}^{2}}+3\cdot \frac{d{I}_{c}}{dt}+2{I}_{c}=0.
$$

Solving using an integration technique, such as a trial solution, we obtain the complementary solution

$$
{I}_{c}(t)=A{e}^{-2t}+B{e}^{-t},

where $A$ and $B$ are constants.

into the inhomogeneous equation and group like terms on the left-hand side:

Find, in amperes, the amplitude of the steady state current for the RCL circuit shown above, rounded to two decimal places.

*Hint: The voltage drop ${V}_{C}$ across the capacitor is related to its charge by $q=C{V}_{C},$ where $C$ is the capacitance measured in Farads.*" :question/worked-solution "The diagram shows a series RCL circuit with a source electromotive force (EMF) of $16\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)\,\text{V},$ a resistor of resistance $25\,Ω,$ a capacitor of capacitance $0.05\,\text{F},$ and an inductor of inductance $5\,\text{H}.$

The current $I,$ measured in amperes, is defined as the rate of flow of charge $q,$ measured in coulombs.

$$
I=\frac{dq}{dt}
$$

Kirchhoff's voltage law states that in a series circuit, the source voltage (EMF) equals the sum of the voltage drops.

In an RCL circuit, there are three voltage drops:

- The voltage drop across the resistor is proportional to the current, with a constant of proportionality $R=25\,Ω.$ So,

$$
{V}_{R}=25I=25\,\frac{dq}{dt}.
$$

- The voltage drop across the capacitor is related to its charge by $q=C{V}_{C}.$ Therefore,

$$
{V}_{C}=\frac{q}{C}=\frac{q}{0.05}=20q.
$$

- The voltage drop across the inductor is proportional to the rate of change of current, with a constant of proportionality $L=5\,\text{H}.$ Hence,

$$
{V}_{L}=5\,\frac{dI}{dt}=5\,\frac{d}{dt}\left(\frac{dq}{dt}\right)=5\,\frac{{d}^{2}q}{d{t}^{2}}.
$$

Therefore, by Kirchhoff's voltage law, the differential equation governing the amount of charge $q$ on the capacitor is

$$
16\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)=25\,\frac{dq}{dt}+20q+5\,\frac{{d}^{2}q}{d{t}^{2}},
$$

which gives

$$
\frac{{d}^{2}q}{d{t}^{2}}+5\cdot \frac{dq}{dt}+4q=\frac{16}{5}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t).
$$

The given equation is a second-order linear equation with constant coefficients. To find the general solution, we must sum the complementary and particular solutions.

- To find the complementary solution ${q}_{c},$ we solve the corresponding homogeneous equation, given by

$$
\frac{{d}^{2}{q}_{c}}{d{t}^{2}}+5\cdot \frac{d{q}_{c}}{dt}+4{q}_{c}=0.
$$

Solving using an integration technique, such as a trial solution, we obtain the complementary solution

$$
{q}_{c}(t)=A{e}^{-4t}+B{e}^{-t},
$$

where $A$ and $B$ are constants.

- Next, we find the particular solution. Note that the right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is sinusoidal with argument $3t.$ So, we assume that the particular solution is also a sinusoidal with argument $3t,$ i.e.,

$$
{q}_{p}(t)=\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(3t).
$$

To find the values of $\alpha $ and $\beta ,$ we substitute

$$
\begin{aligned}{q}_{p} & =\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(3t), \\ \frac{d{q}_{p}}{dt} & =-3\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)+3\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡(3t), \\ \frac{{d}^{2}{q}_{p}}{d{t}^{2}} & =-9\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)-9\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(3t),\end{aligned}
$$

into the inhomogeneous equation and group like terms on the left-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,(-9\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)-9\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(3t))+5(-3\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)+3\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡(3t))\,\, &  \\ +\,4(\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)) & =\frac{16}{5}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t) \\ (-5\alpha +15\beta )\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+(-15\alpha -5\beta )\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t) & =\frac{16}{5}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the coefficients, we get the following system of equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}-5\alpha +15\beta &=0\, && (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)) \\ -15\alpha -5\beta &=\frac{16}{5}\, && (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t))\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Solving this system gives $\alpha =-\frac{24}{125},$ $\beta =-\frac{8}{125}.$ Therefore, the particular solution is

$$
{q}_{p}(t)=-\frac{24}{125}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)-\frac{8}{125}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t).
$$

Now, since the general solution is given by the sum of the complementary solution and the particular solution, the general solution in our case is

$$
q(t)={q}_{c}(t)+{q}_{p}(t)=A{e}^{-4t}+B{e}^{-t}-\frac{24}{125}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)-\frac{8}{125}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t).
$$

Differentiating this expression for $q(t),$ we obtain the following expression for $I$ in amperes:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(t) & =\frac{d}{dt}(A{e}^{-4t}+B{e}^{-t}-\frac{24}{125}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)-\frac{8}{125}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)) \\  & =-4A{e}^{-4t}-B{e}^{-t}+\frac{72}{125}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)-\frac{24}{125}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t).\end{aligned}
$$

Note the following:

- The quantity ${I}_{c}(t)=-4A{e}^{-4t}-B{e}^{-t}$ is the *transient current*, since it goes to zero as $t\to \infty .$

- The function $$
\displaystyle {I}_{p}(t)=\frac{72}{125}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)-\frac{24}{125}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)
$$ is the *steady-state current*. It governs the current's long-term behavior.

Therefore, as $t\to \infty ,$ we have

$$
I(t)≈{I}_{p}(t)=\frac{72}{125}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)-\frac{24}{125}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t).
$$

Finally, the amplitude of the steady-state current, in amperes, is given by

$$
\sqrt{{\left(\frac{72}{125}\right)}^{2}+{\left(\frac{24}{125}\right)}^{2}}≈0.61,
$$

rounded to two decimal places."} {:db/id 17592186499561 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0d7b7bfd-bb55-564e-9903-0d5b6e678486" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.7173" :db/id 17592186498759} {:answer/id #uuid "5bb173f3-e4b4-5ccd-a8d7-911db39988bc" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.7985" :db/id 17592186498938} {:answer/id #uuid "6a74c583-3769-5c0f-b18c-c5ebd3d2f5a5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.7713" :db/id 17592186498971} {:answer/id #uuid "abe25544-5aa0-54fe-bd59-001ab2d00a9e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.7413" :db/id 17592186499109} {:answer/id #uuid "b0081045-ba39-5996-b207-6c0dcb67bc89" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.7333" :db/id 17592186499118}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186499118} :answer-field/id #uuid "851c3373-8dc4-5b32-bf52-e856ed7d70a8" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186499381}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "f56d1332-6e08-590b-aa4f-b85bae891009" :question/math-academy-id "q-143517" :question/problem "| $x$ | $1$ | $4$ | $6$ | $8$ |

</tbody></table>" :question/worked-solution "Suppose that ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{n}$ is a random sample of size $n$ from a population with population mean $\mu $ and population standard deviation $\sigma .$ The central limit theorem (or CLT) states that for sufficiently large $n,$ the distribution of the sample mean $\overset{―}{X}$ can be approximated as 

$$
\overset{―}{X}∼N\,(\mu ,\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n}).
$$

In our case:

- the sample size is 

$$
n=128,
$$

- the population mean is

$$
\begin{aligned}\mu  & =\text{E}[X] \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}f({x}_{i}) \\  & =1\cdot 0.4+4\cdot 0.25+6\cdot 0.1+8\cdot 0.25 \\  & =0.4+1+0.6+2 \\  & =4,\end{aligned}
$$

- the population variance is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sigma }^{2} & =\text{Var}[X] \\  & =\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2} \\  & =({1}^{2}\cdot 0.4+{4}^{2}\cdot 0.25+{6}^{2}\cdot 0.1+{8}^{2}\cdot 0.25)-{4}^{2} \\  & =(0.4+4+3.6+16)-16 \\  & =8.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, by the CLT, we have that the distribution of the sample mean can be approximated as

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{―}{X} & ∼N\,(\mu ,\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n}) \\  & ∼N\,(4,\frac{8}{128}) \\  & ∼N(4,0.0625).\end{aligned}
$$

We want to find $P(3.6<\overset{―}{X}<4.2).$ So, we convert $\overset{―}{X}$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(3.6<\overset{―}{X}<4.2) & ≈-P(\frac{3.6-4}{\sqrt{0.0625}}<Z<\frac{4.2-4}{\sqrt{0.0625}}) \\  & ≈-P(-1.6<Z<0.8) \\  & =P(Z<0.8)-P(Z<-1.6) \\  & =Φ(0.8)-Φ(-1.6).\end{aligned}
$$

From the tables, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Φ(0.8)=0.7881, \\ Φ(-1.6)=0.0548.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(3.6<\overset{―}{X}<4.2) & =Φ(0.8)-Φ(-1.6) \\  & =0.7881-0.0548 \\  & =0.7333.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186499563 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0963b04a-28a1-576f-8d9c-d59f7978d23d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{{d}^{2}I}{d{t}^{2}}+4\,\frac{dI}{dt}+25I=0" :db/id 17592186498745} {:answer/id #uuid "1a6e5911-1c62-5f6d-a491-64465fb439aa" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{{d}^{2}I}{d{t}^{2}}+4\,\frac{dI}{dt}+25I=\frac{5}{4}" :db/id 17592186498786} {:answer/id #uuid "2c282b5e-3565-5127-bf53-9f9794f22673" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{{d}^{2}I}{d{t}^{2}}+2\,\frac{dI}{dt}+25I=0" :db/id 17592186498826} {:answer/id #uuid "4ac9e8b9-f649-56b4-9e7c-ffb7818bc817" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{{d}^{2}I}{d{t}^{2}}+4\,\frac{dI}{dt}+100I=0" :db/id 17592186498904} {:answer/id #uuid "b1d098b4-b771-53c7-8448-cd7fd9aac848" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{{d}^{2}I}{d{t}^{2}}+2\,\frac{dI}{dt}+25I=\frac{5}{4}" :db/id 17592186499127}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186498745} :answer-field/id #uuid "133dfe6a-631c-5fea-b4cf-98feb476123f" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186499321}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "f79f0727-9270-5c79-bad1-22894e26808b" :question/math-academy-id "q-345057" :question/problem "A series RCL circuit has a source electromotive force (EMF) of $10\,\text{V},$ a resistance of $32\,Ω,$ a capacitance of $0.005\,\text{F},$ and an inductance of $L=8\,\text{H}.$ Find the differential equation governing the amount of current $I$ (in amperes) in the circuit at time $t$ (in seconds).

Of this amount, he uses $3\,\frac{3}{10}$ liters. How much paint did Mike have left over when he finished? Express your answer as a mixed number in its lowest terms.

{{field-1}}
$\,$liters of paint left." :question/worked-solution "After finishing, Mike had $(4\,\frac{4}{5}-3\,\frac{3}{10})$ liters of paint left.

Writing $4\,\frac{4}{5}$ as an improper fraction, we have

$$
4\,\frac{4}{5}=\frac{4\times 5+4}{5}=\frac{24}{5}.
$$

Writing $3\,\frac{3}{10}$ as an improper fraction, we have

$$
3\,\frac{3}{10}=\frac{3\times 10+3}{10}=\frac{33}{10}.
$$

Therefore, our problem now is to work out the following:

$$
\frac{24}{5}-\frac{33}{10}
$$

To subtract two fractions with unlike denominators, we need to express each fraction as an equivalent fraction with a common denominator.

In this question, we can make a common denominator of $10.$

To put $\frac{24}{5}$ over a denominator of $10,$ we multiply the numerator and denominator by $2:$

$$
\frac{24}{5}=\frac{24\times 2}{5\times 2}=\frac{48}{10}
$$

We can now subtract the fractions. We keep the denominator the same, and we subtract the numerators:

$$
\frac{48}{10}-\frac{33}{10}=\frac{15}{10}
$$

Simplifying, we have

$$
\frac{15}{10}=\frac{15÷5}{10÷5}=\frac{3}{2}.
$$

Finally, we convert back to a mixed number:

$$
\frac{3}{2}=1\,\text{R}\,1=1\,\frac{1}{2}
$$

Therefore, Mike had $1\,\frac{1}{2}$ liters of paint left."} {:db/id 17592186500293 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0e338a7c-f5c5-55b6-800b-47f10296b1d7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{112}{729}" :db/id 17592186499686} {:answer/id #uuid "4673f4bc-028d-52bd-b6cb-43a313197f90" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{23}{1458}" :db/id 17592186499785} {:answer/id #uuid "60d5eb82-e934-5a50-abfb-6bb988e212e5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{230}{729}" :db/id 17592186499844} {:answer/id #uuid "aa8b3642-18a5-59b9-ba90-c44b1dc2ff93" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{130}{729}" :db/id 17592186499989} {:answer/id #uuid "b05849a6-fd14-5761-ac6a-f3df6f46c897" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{113}{1458}" :db/id 17592186500007}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186499844} :answer-field/id #uuid "ecc71117-bad7-5cf6-bbde-8b45ac8873de" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186500274}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "2175ed2b-85f5-5f4e-9b21-fd44965b957e" :question/math-academy-id "q-126173" :question/problem "Given that the random variable $X$ has the cumulative distribution function

$$
