</tbody></table>" :question/worked-solution "Given a population in which a proportion $p$ of the population has a particular characteristic, the sampling distribution of the sample proportion $\widehat{\,p}$ can be approximated as

$$
\widehat{\,p}∼N(p,\frac{p(1-p)}{n}),
$$

where the sample size $n$ is much smaller than the population size, $np>5,$ and $n(1-p)>5.$

In our case

- the sample size is $n=125,$ and

- the population proportion is $p=0.75.$

Now, since

$$
np=125(0.75)=93.75>5
$$

and

$$
n(1-p)=125(1-0.75)=31.25>5,
$$

and $n=125$ is much smaller than the population size, we can apply the above approximation.

The sampling distribution of the sample proportion, in this case, can be approximated as

$$
\begin{aligned}\widehat{\,p} & ∼N(p,\frac{p(1-p)}{n}) \\  & ∼N(0.75,\frac{0.75(1-0.75)}{125}) \\  & ∼N(0.75,0.0015).\end{aligned}
$$

The probability we wish to find is
$P(0.65<\widehat{\,p}\le 0.72).$
So, we convert $\widehat{\,p}$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(0.65<\widehat{\,p}<0.72) & =P(\frac{0.65-0.75}{\sqrt{0.0015}}<Z\le \frac{0.72-0.75}{\sqrt{0.0015}}) \\  & ≈P(-2.58<Z\le -0.77) \\  & =P(Z\le -0.77)-P(Z\le -2.58) \\  & =Φ(-0.77)-Φ(-2.58)\end{aligned}
$$

From the table, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Φ(-0.77) & =0.2206 \\ Φ(-2.58) & =0.0049.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(0.65<\widehat{\,p}<0.72) & =Φ(-0.77)-Φ(-2.58) \\  & =0.2206-0.0049 \\  & =0.2157.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186502114 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0cd46750-aab1-5ab4-8f35-4bb7abe41d55" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "I only" :db/id 17592186501490} {:answer/id #uuid "508c1697-4000-5926-99b2-497ea4d6c810" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "I and II only" :db/id 17592186501612} {:answer/id #uuid "6ad952b8-2ed2-584a-967d-7f752886a23d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "II and III only" :db/id 17592186501664} {:answer/id #uuid "d6c31986-9c09-50b3-be41-6a9593a36e04" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "I and III only" :db/id 17592186501892} {:answer/id #uuid "e34c4d92-333e-5b82-80d3-ad763eae7cfc" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "III only" :db/id 17592186501921}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186501664} :answer-field/id #uuid "fa3a4acb-3217-5494-99eb-6860b8a21200" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186502063}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "75b5d8b1-9316-5672-a007-ededd1581f02" :question/math-academy-id "q-146819" :question/problem "For which of the following situations can the distribution of the sample proportion $\widehat{\,p}$ be approximated as

$$
\widehat{\,p}∼N(p,\frac{p(1-p)}{n}),
$$

where $P$ is the population proportion?

I. A sample of size $n=200$ from a population of size $N=1\,000$ in which $90\%$ of the population has a particular characteristic.

II. A sample of size $n=40$ from a population of size $N=1\,000$ in which $80\%$ of the population has a particular characteristic.

III. A sample of size $n=30$ from a population of size $N=1\,000$ in which $70\%$ of the population has a particular characteristic." :question/worked-solution "Given a population in which a proportion $p$ of the population has a particular characteristic, the sampling distribution of the sample proportion $\widehat{\,p}$ can be approximated as

$$
\widehat{\,p}∼N(p,\frac{p(1-p)}{n}),
$$

where 

- $n\le 5\%\cdot N$ (the sample size is less than (or equal to) $5\%$ of the population size),

- $np>5$ (more than $5$ sample elements have the characteristic), and

- $n(1-p)>5$ (more than $5$ sample elements do not have the characteristic).

Let's now examine each situation.

- In situation I, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =200 \\ 5\%\cdot N & =0.05\cdot 1\,000 \\  & =50 \\  & <200\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

Since the sample size is more than $5\%$ of the population size, we *cannot* approximate the distribution of $\widehat{\,p}$ using the given model.

- In situation II, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =40 \\  & \le 5\%\cdot N \\  & =0.05\cdot 1\,000 \\  & =50\,✓ \\ np & =40(0.8) \\  & =32 \\  & >5\,✓ \\ n(1-p) & =40(1-0.8) \\  & =8 \\  & >5.\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can approximate the distribution of $\widehat{\,p}$ using the given model.

- In situation III, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =30 \\  & \le 5\%\cdot N \\  & =0.05\cdot 1\,000 \\  & =50\,✓ \\ np & =30(0.7) \\  & =21 \\  & >5\,✓ \\ n(1-p) & =30(1-0.7) \\  & =9 \\  & >5.\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can approximate the distribution of $\widehat{\,p}$ using the given model.

Therefore, the correct answer is "II and III only.""} {:db/id 17592186502115 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0227caa1-4c42-5eb8-ac85-3986c6a9d588" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{dQ}{dt}+\frac{1}{20}Q=3.2" :db/id 17592186501469} {:answer/id #uuid "2b05d523-77bc-5466-bb19-c3abe62adb5c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{dQ}{dt}-\frac{2}{35}Q=3.2" :db/id 17592186501542} {:answer/id #uuid "43ec94b3-4df2-52b9-a2ad-f9deb82de611" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{dQ}{dt}-\frac{1}{20}Q=3.2" :db/id 17592186501591} {:answer/id #uuid "520f62b8-d63d-5371-96d8-62c3e5df7765" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{dQ}{dt}+\frac{2}{35}Q=3.2" :db/id 17592186501616} {:answer/id #uuid "7b78dea8-b14f-5f74-a0d7-da6c0fe28734" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{dQ}{dt}+\frac{2}{35}Q=0" :db/id 17592186501695}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186501616} :answer-field/id #uuid "23c464d0-a940-5cbe-ac3b-db43ce37099c" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186501988}] :question/id #uuid "787955c7-f519-56e2-a7ff-67abb164ab3b" :question/math-academy-id "q-336622" :question/problem "A tank initially holds $280\,\text{L}$ of a chemical solution containing $4\,\text{kg}$ of dissolved chemical.
A chemical solution containing $0.20\,\text{kg}$ of dissolved chemical per liter is poured into the tank at a rate of $16\,\text{L/min},$ while the completely mixed solution leaves the tank at a rate of $16\,\text{L/min}.$ Which differential equation best describes the amount of dissolved chemical $Q,$ in kilograms, in the tank $t$ minutes after the solution begins to be added?" :question/worked-solution "Since $Q$ is the amount of dissolved chemical in the tank at time $t,$ the derivative 

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}
$$

describes how this amount changes with respect to time $t,$ in minutes. This is equal to the rate at which dissolved chemical enters the tank minus the rate at which dissolved chemical leaves the tank.

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}
$$

Note that the units of $\frac{dQ}{dt},{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}$ and ${Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}$ are $\text{kg}/\text{min}.$ Now, let's compute the required rates of change in steps.

**Step 1**: Calculating the rate at which dissolved chemical enters the tank.

First, note that a chemical solution containing $0.20\,\text{kg/L}$ of dissolved chemical enters the tank at a rate of $16\,\text{L/min}.$ So, the rate at which the *dissolved chemical* enters the tank is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′} & =(0.20\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{L}})\cdot (16\,\frac{\text{L}}{\text{min}}) \\  & =(0.20\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\cancel{\text{L}}})\cdot (16\,\frac{\cancel{\text{L}}}{\text{min}}) \\  & =3.2\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Calculating the rate at which dissolved chemical exits the tank.

Now, to find the rate at which dissolved chemical leaves the tank, we must first determine the volume of solution in the tank at time $t.$

- The tank initially contains $280\,\text{L}$ of solution.

- Chemical solution enters the tank at a rate of $16\,\text{L/min}.$ So, after $t$ minutes, $16t\,\text{L}$ have entered the tank.

- The completely mixed solution leaves the tank at a rate of $16\,\text{L/min}.$ So, after $t$ minutes, $16t\,\text{L}$ have left the tank.

As a result, the volume of solution in the tank after $t$ minutes is 

$$
280+16t-16t=280\,\text{L}.
$$

Since $Q$ is the mass of dissolved chemical in the tank, the *concentration* of the solution at time $t$ is

$$
\frac{Q}{280}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{L}}.
$$

Therefore, as the completely mixed solution leaves at a rate of $16\,\text{L/min},$ *dissolved chemical* leaves at a rate of

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} & =(16\,\frac{\text{L}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{280}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{L}}) \\  & =(16\,\frac{\cancel{\text{L}}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{280}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\cancel{\text{L}}}) \\  & =\frac{16Q}{280}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{min}} \\  & =\frac{2Q}{35}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Calculate the overall rate of change.

Finally, the rate of change equals the rate of entry minus the rate of exit: 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dQ}{dt} & ={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} \\  & =3.2-\frac{2Q}{35}\end{aligned}
$$

which finally gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dQ}{dt}+\frac{2}{35}Q=3.2.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186502117 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "07440603-54b5-5976-899e-ae9b9661d017" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "Φ(1.81)" :db/id 17592186501483} {:answer/id #uuid "32730632-54f9-51bd-9b77-5eb922390acc" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "Φ(1.47)" :db/id 17592186501559} {:answer/id #uuid "4f8d336e-ed5a-5688-ade1-9317c97d93ce" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "Φ(0.97)" :db/id 17592186501610} {:answer/id #uuid "e4626d23-d099-557f-8b2c-0a74d5d57629" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "Φ(2.11)" :db/id 17592186501926} {:answer/id #uuid "f139c347-a6cc-572a-946f-3b855b388e8a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "Φ(1.65)" :db/id 17592186501950}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186501483} :answer-field/id #uuid "6c885ba5-a648-5bca-b5b2-398b1f373335" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186502012}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "7a5fcfb6-efc6-55da-8a4d-4dde0bab77e9" :question/math-academy-id "q-147448" :question/problem "An amusement park knows that $25\%$ of its visitors ride the rollercoaster. A pure solvent is poured into the reactor at a rate of $16\,\text{L/min},$ while the completely mixed solution leaves the reactor at a rate of $20\,\text{L/min}.$ Which differential equation best describes the amount of reactant $Q,$ in kilograms, in the reactor $t$ minutes after the solvent begins to be added?" :question/worked-solution "Since $Q$ is the amount of reactant in the reactor at time $t,$ the derivative 

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}
$$

describes how this amount changes with respect to time $t,$ in minutes. This is equal to the rate at which reactant enters the reactor minus the rate at which reactant leaves the reactor.

$$

$$

Note that the units of $\frac{dQ}{dt},{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}$ and ${Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}$ are $\text{kg}/\text{min}.$ Now, let's compute the required rates of change in steps.

**Step 1**: Calculating the rate at which reactant enters the reactor.

First, note that the incoming solvent (i.e., a solution containing $0\,\text{kg/L}$ of reactant) enters the reactor at a rate of $16\,\text{L/min}.$ So, the rate at which the *reactant* enters the reactor is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′} & =(0\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{L}})\cdot (16\,\frac{\text{L}}{\text{min}}) \\  & =(0\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\cancel{\text{L}}})\cdot (16\,\frac{\cancel{\text{L}}}{\text{min}}) \\  & =0\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Calculating the rate at which reactant exits the reactor.

Now, to find the rate at which reactant leaves the reactor, we must first determine the volume of solution in the reactor at time $t.$

- The reactor initially contains $520\,\text{L}$ of solution.

- Solvent enters the reactor at a rate of $16\,\text{L/min}.$ So, after $t$ minutes, $16t\,\text{L}$ have entered the reactor.

As a result, the volume of solution in the reactor after $t$ minutes is 

$$
520+16t-20t=(520-4t)\,\text{L}.
$$

Since $Q$ is the mass of reactant in the reactor, the *concentration* of the solution at time $t$ is

$$
\frac{Q}{520-4t}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{L}}.
$$

Therefore, as the completely mixed solution leaves at a rate of $20\,\text{L/min},$ *reactant* leaves at a rate of

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} & =(20\,\frac{\text{L}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{520-4t}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{L}}) \\  & =(20\,\frac{\cancel{\text{L}}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{520-4t}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\cancel{\text{L}}}) \\  & =\frac{20Q}{520-4t}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{min}} \\  & =\frac{5Q}{130-t}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Calculate the overall rate of change.

Finally, the rate of change equals the rate of entry minus the rate of exit: 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dQ}{dt} & ={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} \\  & =0-\frac{5Q}{130-t}\end{aligned}
$$

which finally gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dQ}{dt}+\frac{5}{130-t}Q=0.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186502123 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "56867d82-3d07-5414-9450-8f0c79240546" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "Φ(0.78)-Φ(-0.78)" :db/id 17592186501624} {:answer/id #uuid "68727b43-f29b-53a1-a5d7-6dcd49a3a034" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "Φ(0.36)-Φ(-0.36)" :db/id 17592186501657} {:answer/id #uuid "a3dbdab0-ba6b-5637-9d3a-42a4f9671754" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "Φ(0.96)-Φ(-0.69)" :db/id 17592186501782} {:answer/id #uuid "aa9cff08-4800-5f04-8bf4-570544c083f1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "Φ(0.80)-Φ(-0.80)" :db/id 17592186501801} {:answer/id #uuid "fc19f28c-42f1-5740-9078-6e1e7a33e836" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "Φ(0.88)-Φ(-0.88)" :db/id 17592186501968}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186501968} :answer-field/id #uuid "3db1ac1a-fba9-53f0-abaa-ce90a089ca8c" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186501995}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "84cf65c5-831d-5253-bb62-b35c4c8f232c" :question/math-academy-id "q-146942" :question/problem "Suppose we take a random sample of size $n=50$ from a population where $20\%$ of the population has a particular characteristic. Find a normal approximation for the probability that between $15\%$ and $25\%$ of the sample have the characteristic. You may assume that the population size is significantly larger than the sample size.

*Hint: $Φ(z)$ is the cumulative distribution function for the standard normal distribution.*" :question/worked-solution "Given a population in which a proportion $p$ of the population has a particular characteristic, the sampling distribution of the sample proportion $\widehat{\,p}$ can be approximated as

$$
\widehat{\,p}∼N(p,\frac{p(1-p)}{n}),
$$

where the sample size $n$ is much smaller than the population size, $np>5,$ and $n(1-p)>5.$

In our case

- the sample size is $n=50,$ and

- the population proportion is $p=0.2.$

Now, since

$$
np=50(0.2)=10>5
$$

and

$$
n(1-p)=50(1-0.2)=40>5,
$$

and $n=50$ is much smaller than the population size, we can apply the above approximation.

The sampling distribution of the sample proportion, in this case, can be approximated as

$$
\begin{aligned}\widehat{\,p} & ∼N(p,\frac{p(1-p)}{n}) \\  & ∼N(0.2,\frac{0.2(1-0.2)}{50}) \\  & ∼N(0.2,0.0032).\end{aligned}
$$

The probability we wish to find is
$P(0.15\le \widehat{\,p}\le 0.25).$
So, we convert $\widehat{\,p}$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(0.15\le \widehat{\,p}\le 0.25) & =P(\frac{0.15-0.2}{\sqrt{0.0032}}\le Z\le \frac{0.25-0.2}{\sqrt{0.0032}}) \\  & ≈P(-0.88\le Z\le 0.88) \\  & =P(Z\le 0.88)-P(Z\le -0.88) \\  & =Φ(0.88)-Φ(-0.88)\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186502130 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1fd464ab-03dd-5c29-a547-e17631549a84" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "16.20\,\text{lb}" :db/id 17592186501521} {:answer/id #uuid "41e819ff-cd32-5d60-ba16-54665c890b1d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "15.84\,\text{lb}" :db/id 17592186501588} {:answer/id #uuid "8ba3054a-6459-569b-81c3-907904cb6174" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "16.78\,\text{lb}" :db/id 17592186501735} {:answer/id #uuid "91dfca2e-8991-5e9e-966d-e682738680c3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "15.12\,\text{lb}" :db/id 17592186501745} {:answer/id #uuid "92fa06dd-98f7-529e-8d06-b10b01e3a805" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "17.05\,\text{lb}" :db/id 17592186501747}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186501521} :answer-field/id #uuid "396eb760-1ba4-5c61-a4fd-b36963318cca" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186501992}] :question/id #uuid "9f051584-9c22-538b-be73-a90ad4399f9f" :question/math-academy-id "q-336843" :question/problem "A $300\,\text{gal}$-capacity tank initially holds $180\,\text{gal}$ of water containing $45\,\text{lb}$ of dissolved contaminant. Clean water begins to flow into the tank at a rate of $6\,\text{gal/min},$ while the completely mixed water flows out at a rate of $4\,\text{gal/min}.$ Find the amount of contaminant in the tank at the moment it begins to overflow." :question/worked-solution "Let $Q$ be the amount of contaminant in the tank at time $t.$ Then, the derivative 

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}
$$

describes how this amount changes with respect to time $t,$ in minutes. This is equal to the rate at which contaminant enters the tank minus the rate at which contaminant leaves the tank.

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}
$$

Note that the units of $\frac{dQ}{dt},{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}$ and ${Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}$ are $\text{lb}/\text{min}.$ Now, let's compute the required rates of change in steps.

**Step 1**: Calculating the rate at which contaminant enters the tank.

First, note that clean water (i.e., water containing $0\,\text{lb/gal}$ of contaminant) enters the tank at a rate of $6\,\text{gal/min}.$ So, the rate at which the *contaminant* enters the tank is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′} & =(0\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{gal}})\cdot (6\,\frac{\text{gal}}{\text{min}}) \\  & =(0\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\cancel{\text{gal}}})\cdot (6\,\frac{\cancel{\text{gal}}}{\text{min}}) \\  & =0\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Calculating the rate at which contaminant exits the tank.

To find the rate at which contaminant leaves the tank, we must first determine the volume of water in the tank at time $t.$

The tank initially contains $180\,\text{gal}$ of water; clean water enters at $6\,\text{gal/min},$ and mixed water leaves at $4\,\text{gal/min}.$
As a result, the amount of water in the tank after $t$ minutes is 

$$
V(t)=180+6t-4t=(180+2t)\,\text{gal}.
$$

Note that $V(t)$ is an increasing function, so the tank is filling.

Since $Q$ is the amount of contaminant in the tank, the concentration of the water at time $t$ is

$$
\frac{Q}{180+2t}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{gal}}.
$$

Therefore, as the completely mixed water leaves at a rate of $4\,\text{gal/min},$ *contaminant* leaves at a rate of

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} & =(4\,\frac{\text{gal}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{180+2t}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{gal}}) \\  & =(4\,\frac{\cancel{\text{gal}}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{180+2t}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\cancel{\text{gal}}}) \\  & =\frac{4Q}{180+2t}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{min}} \\  & =\frac{2Q}{90+t}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Calculate the overall rate of change.

The rate of change equals the rate of entry minus the rate of exit. Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dQ}{dt} & ={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} \\  & =0-\frac{2Q}{90+t}\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the equation

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}=-\frac{2}{90+t}\,Q.
$$

**Step 4**: Integrate the equation

Separating variables and integrating both sides with respect to $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{Q}\cdot \frac{dQ}{dt} & =-\frac{2}{90+t} \\ \int \frac{1}{Q}\cdot \frac{dQ}{dt}dt & =\int \left(-\frac{2}{90+t}\right)\,dt \\ \int \frac{1}{Q}\cdot \,dQ & =-2\int \frac{1}{90+t}\,dt \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|Q| & =-2(\operatorname{ln}⁡|90+t|)+C \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|Q| & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|(90+t)^{-2}|+C \\ |Q| & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡|(90+t)^{-2}|+C} \\ Q(t) & =\frac{A}{(90+t)^{2}},\end{aligned}
$$

where $A=\pm {e}^{C}$ is a constant of integration.

We're told that the tank initially contains $45\,\text{lb}$ of contaminant. So, we can apply the initial condition $Q(0)=45,$ and solve for $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(0) & =45 \\ \frac{A}{(90+0)^{2}} & =45 \\ A & =45(90)^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we obtain the following expression for $Q(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(t) & =\frac{45(90)^{2}}{(90+t)^{2}} \\  & =45{\left(\frac{90}{90+t}\right)}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let ${t}_{o}$ be the time when the tank begins to overflow. The tank has a capacity of $300\,\text{gal},$ so we can use the condition $V({t}_{o})=300$ to solve for ${t}_{o}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}V({t}_{o}) & =300 \\ 180+2{t}_{o} & =300 \\ 2{t}_{o} & =120 \\ {t}_{o} & =60\,\text{min}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the amount of contaminant in the tank at the moment it begins to overflow is

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(60) & =45{\left(\frac{90}{90+60}\right)}^{2} \\  & =45{\left(\frac{90}{150}\right)}^{2} \\  & =45{\left(\frac{3}{5}\right)}^{2} \\  & =16.20\,\text{lb}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186502131 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "3009884b-eaac-58c4-9dd7-476278e483b9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.2626" :db/id 17592186501550} {:answer/id #uuid "43b7b2e8-0dd0-53f5-a8d4-5c5d905e9b5a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.1112" :db/id 17592186501590} {:answer/id #uuid "88a07982-8bca-5d34-ba03-ad213b50a5ca" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.0808" :db/id 17592186501728} {:answer/id #uuid "a5ecc379-ae54-5c46-b4ed-94535e2a2e81" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.2121" :db/id 17592186501788} {:answer/id #uuid "b0d11df6-7dc5-50f2-bbd9-0d41650103a0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.1615" :db/id 17592186501818}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186501590} :answer-field/id #uuid "fa9ea89e-2b67-50ed-9875-e233798706d2" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186502064}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "a0e2a9c0-d660-51ad-8aa9-baeec300d0b3" :question/math-academy-id "q-146975" :question/problem "Suppose we take a random sample of size $n=76$ from a population where $24\%$ of the population has a particular characteristic. | $\,1.4\,$ | $\,0.9192\,$ | $\,0.9207\,$ | $\,0.9222\,$ | $\,0.9236\,$ |" :question/worked-solution "Given a population in which a proportion $p$ of the population has a particular characteristic, the sampling distribution of the sample proportion $\widehat{\,p}$ can be approximated as

$$
\widehat{\,p}∼N(p,\frac{p(1-p)}{n}),
$$

where the sample size $n$ is much smaller than the population size, $np>5,$ and $n(1-p)>5.$

In our case

- the sample size is $n=76,$ and

- the population proportion is $p=0.24.$

Now, since

$$
np=76(0.24)=18.24>5
$$

and

$$
n(1-p)=76(1-0.24)=57.76>5,
$$

and $n=76$ is much smaller than the population size, we can apply the above approximation.

The sampling distribution of the sample proportion, in this case, can be approximated as

$$
\begin{aligned}\widehat{\,p} & ∼N(p,\frac{p(1-p)}{n}) \\  & ∼N(0.24,\frac{0.24(1-0.24)}{76}) \\  & ∼N(0.24,0.0024).\end{aligned}
$$

The probability we wish to find is
$P(\widehat{\,p}>0.3).$
So, we convert $\widehat{\,p}$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(\widehat{\,p}>0.3) & =P(Z>\frac{0.3-0.24}{\sqrt{0.0024}}) \\  & ≈P(Z>1.22) \\  & =1-P(Z<1.22) \\  & =1-Φ(1.22).\end{aligned}
$$

From the table, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Φ(1.22) & =0.8888.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(\widehat{\,p}>0.3) & =1-Φ(1.22) \\  & =1-0.8888 \\  & =0.1112.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186502132 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "4116f3f0-c977-5e04-8b37-cfee23a31d33" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "III only" :db/id 17592186501586} {:answer/id #uuid "56fb8155-120b-5170-9145-1fd130c2ec2e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "I and III only" :db/id 17592186501627} {:answer/id #uuid "619c4398-31f6-54ae-99e8-d78d34165a47" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "I and II only" :db/id 17592186501648} {:answer/id #uuid "ac32c0bc-5323-5faa-b8d5-33267bce243a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "II only" :db/id 17592186501808} {:answer/id #uuid "e8ba3ea6-389e-54cf-a4c9-3ac81a2a28ba" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "II and III only" :db/id 17592186501936}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186501627} :answer-field/id #uuid "e00782d6-c22d-5c54-843e-daefb08e60d9" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186502051}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "ab0bcefd-4d59-56aa-b8ec-f3d0b1dc4757" :question/math-academy-id "q-146838" :question/problem "For which of the following situations can the distribution of the sample proportion $\widehat{\,p}$ be approximated as

where $p$ is the population proportion?

I. A sample of $50$ recently caught shrimps, where $55\%$ of the shrimps in the sea weigh more than $10\,\text{g}.$

II. A sample of $27$ companies, where $82\%$ of the companies in the country employ more than $100$ people.

III. A sample of $100$ songs in a streaming service, given that $92\%$ of the songs last less than $3$ minutes.

*Hint: In each case, you may assume that the population size is significantly larger than the sample size.*" :question/worked-solution "Given a population in which a proportion $p$ of the population has a particular characteristic, the sampling distribution of the sample proportion $\widehat{\,p}$ can be approximated as

$$

$$

where 

- $n\le 5\%\cdot N$ (the sample size is less than (or equal to) $5\%$ of the population size),

- $np>5$ (more than $5$ sample elements have the characteristic), and

- $n(1-p)>5$ (more than $5$ sample elements do not have the characteristic).

We're given that the population is significantly larger than the sample size in each case. Therefore, we may assume that the first condition is satisfied in each case.

Let's now examine each situation.

- In situation I, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}np & =50(0.55) \\  & =27.5 \\  & >5\,✓ \\ n(1-p) & =50(1-0.55) \\  & =22.5 \\  & >5.\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can approximate the distribution of $\widehat{\,p}$ using the given model.

- In situation II, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}np & =27(0.82) \\  & =22.14 \\  & >5\,✓ \\ n(1-p) & =27(1-0.82) \\  & =4.86 \\  & ≯5.\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

Since $n(1-p)≯5,$ we *cannot* approximate the distribution of $\widehat{\,p}$ using the given model.

- In situation III, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}np & =100(0.92) \\  & =92 \\  & >5\,✓ \\ n(1-p) & =100(1-0.92) \\  & =8 \\  & >5.\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can approximate the distribution of $\widehat{\,p}$ using the given model.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only.""} {:db/id 17592186502141 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "03359e21-7a1b-5dec-803d-c1cd7423ca1d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.5329" :db/id 17592186501470} {:answer/id #uuid "45e1015c-d45f-5639-97c2-7d9314f8ad2e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.4275" :db/id 17592186501593} {:answer/id #uuid "7eb8dfe6-123f-5cfc-a78b-fa1793a96281" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.4884" :db/id 17592186501703} {:answer/id #uuid "bd4a2dca-96f1-5a35-91e8-35bd1ef6be15" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.2687" :db/id 17592186501846} {:answer/id #uuid "e120a658-b96e-5c48-8cf4-5d70b8be76ed" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.3954" :db/id 17592186501915}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186501703} :answer-field/id #uuid "f514e27c-296f-5be6-8d4d-2642d4f0a3fa" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186502061}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "c30b7d81-9bb5-5e5f-938c-eb285e73259b" :question/math-academy-id "q-147482" :question/problem "A smartphone app has $500\,000$ users, $150\,000$ of which have a paid account. $$
\widehat{\,p}∼N(p,\frac{p(1-p)}{n}),
$$

where the sample size $n$ is much smaller than the population size, $np>5,$ and $n(1-p)>5.$

In our case

- the sample size is $n=300,$ and

- the population proportion is $p=\frac{150\,000}{500\,000}=0.3.$

Now, since

$$
np=300(0.3)=90>5
$$

and

$$
n(1-p)=300(1-0.3)=210>5,
$$

and the $n=300$ is much smaller than the population size, we can apply the above approximation.

The sampling distribution of the sample proportion, in this case, can be approximated as

$$
\begin{aligned}\widehat{\,p} & ∼N(p,\frac{p(1-p)}{n}) \\  & ∼N(0.3,\frac{0.3(1-0.3)}{300}) \\  & ∼N(0.3,0.0007).\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we determine the probability we wish to find. If between $72$ and $90$ of users in the sample have a paid account, then

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{72}{300}\le \widehat{\,p} & \le \frac{90}{300} \\ 0.24\le \widehat{\,p} & \le 0.3.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the probability we wish to find is
$P(0.24\le \widehat{\,p}\le 0.3).$
So, we convert $\widehat{\,p}$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(0.24\le \widehat{\,p}\le 0.3) & =P(\frac{0.24-0.3}{\sqrt{0.0007}}\le Z\le \frac{0.3-0.3}{\sqrt{0.0007}}) \\  & ≈P(-2.27\le Z\le 0) \\  & =P(Z\le 0)-P(Z\le -2.27) \\  & =Φ(0)-Φ(-2.27)\end{aligned}
$$

From the table, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Φ(0)=0.5000,\,Φ(-2.27)=0.0116.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(0.24\le \widehat{\,p}\le 0.3) & =Φ(0)-Φ(-2.27) \\  & =0.5000-0.0116 \\  & =0.4884.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186502142 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0112f1fc-6de5-513e-87f9-3b66ed92fd30" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "100.8\,\text{lb}" :db/id 17592186501465} {:answer/id #uuid "26fdd352-98f8-5049-9bca-4712271dc3ef" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "99.2\,\text{lb}" :db/id 17592186501536} {:answer/id #uuid "5cc4d99a-a70c-5a49-aae0-f3604e67d27f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "100.4\,\text{lb}" :db/id 17592186501638} {:answer/id #uuid "c69e4261-0557-5f97-9e81-25b3bb4c21af" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "99.6\,\text{lb}" :db/id 17592186501861} {:answer/id #uuid "f1dcaab2-0d10-522e-bd0f-9e9fdbc1a915" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "100.0\,\text{lb}" :db/id 17592186501952}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186501952} :answer-field/id #uuid "507a90fb-d7f1-59f5-8df1-dc619644c3da" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186502000}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "c3e80580-6c31-591c-a6d6-df75a9aede3a" :question/math-academy-id "q-336503" :question/problem "A fertilizer tank for an irrigation system can hold up to $210\,\text{gal}$ of solution. Initially, it contains $90\,\text{gal}$ of fertilizer solution with $18\,\text{lb}$ of dissolved fertilizer. A more concentrated solution with concentration $0.5\,\text{lb/gal}$ flows into the tank at a rate of $18\,\text{gal/min},$ while the completely mixed solution drains out at a rate of $12\,\text{gal/min}.$ Rounded to one decimal place, find the amount of fertilizer in the tank at the moment it begins to overflow." :question/worked-solution "Since $Q$ is the amount of fertilizer in the tank at time $t,$ the derivative 

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}
$$

describes how this amount changes with respect to time $t,$ in minutes. This is equal to the rate at which fertilizer enters the tank minus the rate at which fertilizer leaves the tank.

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}
$$

Note that the units of $\frac{dQ}{dt},{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}$ and ${Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}$ are $\text{lb}/\text{min}.$ Now, let's compute the required rates of change in steps.

**Step 1**: Calculating the rate at which fertilizer enters the tank.

First, note that a solution containing $0.5\,\text{lb/gal}$ of fertilizer enters the tank at a rate of $18\,\text{gal/min}.$ So, the rate at which the *fertilizer* enters the tank is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′} & =(0.5\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{gal}})\cdot (18\,\frac{\text{gal}}{\text{min}}) \\  & =(0.5\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\cancel{\text{gal}}})\cdot (18\,\frac{\cancel{\text{gal}}}{\text{min}}) \\  & =9\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Calculating the rate at which fertilizer exits the tank.

To find the rate at which fertilizer leaves the tank, we must first determine the volume of solution in the tank at time $t.$

The tank initially contains $90\,\text{gal}$ of solution; solution enters at $18\,\text{gal/min}$ and mixed solution leaves at $12\,\text{gal/min}.$
As a result, the amount of solution in the tank after $t$ minutes is 

$$
V(t)=90+18t-12t=6(15+t)\,\text{gal}.
$$

Note that $V(t)$ is an increasing function, so the tank is filling.

Since $Q$ is the amount of fertilizer in the tank, the concentration of the solution at time $t$ is

$$
\frac{Q}{6(15+t)}\,\text{lb/gal}.
$$

Therefore, as the completely mixed solution leaves at a rate of $12\,\text{gal/min},$ *fertilizer* leaves at a rate of

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} & =(12\,\frac{\text{gal}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{6(15+t)}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{gal}}) \\  & =(12\,\frac{\cancel{\text{gal}}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{6(15+t)}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\cancel{\text{gal}}}) \\  & =\frac{12Q}{6(15+t)}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{min}} \\  & =\frac{2Q}{15+t}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Calculate the overall rate of change.

The rate of change equals the rate of entry minus the rate of exit. Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dQ}{dt} & ={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} \\  & =9-\frac{2Q}{15+t}\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the equation

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}+\frac{2}{15+t}\,Q=9.
$$

**Step 4**: Integrate the equation.

This is a first-order linear equation with variable coefficients. So we find the general solution using an integrating factor:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(t) & ={e}^{\int 2/(15+t)\,dt} \\  & ={e}^{2\operatorname{ln}⁡|15+t|} \\  & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(15+t)^{2}} \\  & =(15+t)^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying both sides of the differential equation by $I(t)=(15+t)^{2}$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}(15+t)^{2}\cdot (\frac{dQ}{dt}+\frac{2}{15+t}\,Q) & =(15+t)^{2}\cdot 9 \\ (15+t)^{2}\frac{dQ}{dt}+2(15+t)Q & =9(15+t)^{2} \\ \frac{d}{dt}(Q(15+t)^{2}) & =9(15+t)^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate with respect to $t:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{d}{dt}(Q(15+t)^{2})\,dt & =\int 9(15+t)^{2}\,dt \\ Q(15+t)^{2} & =9\cdot \frac{1}{3}(15+t)^{3}+C \\ Q(t) & =3(15+t)+\frac{C}{(15+t)^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

We're told that the tank initially contains $18\,\text{lb}$ of fertilizer. So, we can apply the initial condition $Q(0)=18,$ and solve for $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(0) & =18 \\ 3(15+0)+\frac{C}{(15+0)^{2}} & =18 \\ 45+\frac{C}{(15)^{2}} & =18 \\ \frac{C}{{15}^{2}} & =-27 \\ C & =-27(15)^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we obtain the following expression for $Q(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(t) & =3(15+t)-\frac{27(15)^{2}}{(15+t)^{2}} \\  & =3(15+t)-27{\left(\frac{15}{15+t}\right)}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let ${t}_{o}$ be the time when the tank begins to overflow. The tank has a capacity of $210\,\text{gal},$ so we can use the condition $V({t}_{o})=210$ to solve for ${t}_{o}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}V({t}_{o}) & =210 \\ 90+18{t}_{o}-12{t}_{o} & =210 \\ 90+6{t}_{o} & =210 \\ 6{t}_{o} & =120 \\ {t}_{o} & =20\,\text{min}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, rounded to one decimal place, the amount of fertilizer in the tank at the moment it begins to overflow is

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(20) & =3(15+20)-27{\left(\frac{15}{15+20}\right)}^{2} \\  & =105-27{\left(\frac{15}{35}\right)}^{2} \\  & ≈100.0\,\text{lb}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186502148 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "19631a4f-fc75-5f16-94d0-c840626309aa" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4.48\,\text{kg}" :db/id 17592186501515} {:answer/id #uuid "409f3cff-59d6-5382-900e-2722da60aa57" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3.09\,\text{kg}" :db/id 17592186501584} {:answer/id #uuid "5688b277-ef03-5eaf-8c63-160fb654c7c9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3.62\,\text{kg}" :db/id 17592186501625} {:answer/id #uuid "5f94b143-c3c7-545e-847d-30ec918b7ae6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4.90\,\text{kg}" :db/id 17592186501641} {:answer/id #uuid "a0b4fa8a-26bd-5a01-bcb0-d0ebf5922738" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4.01\,\text{kg}" :db/id 17592186501768}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186501768} :answer-field/id #uuid "71c957ef-ec71-5945-b112-c39defc2facc" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186502016}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "d0340e70-b947-5b25-8e24-a63ff0f87f38" :question/math-academy-id "q-339403" :question/problem "A wastewater treatment basin initially holds $320\,\text{L}$ of liquid containing $2.2\,\text{kg}$ of dissolved neutralizing agent.
A feed solution containing $0.05\,\text{kg/L}$ of the agent is pumped into the basin at a rate of $8\,\text{L/min},$ while the completely mixed liquid is drained out at a rate of $4\,\text{L/min}.$
Find, rounded to two decimal places, the amount of agent in the basin $5$ minutes after pumping begins." :question/worked-solution "Let $Q$ be the amount of agent in the basin at time $t,$ in minutes. Then, the derivative 

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}
$$

describes how this amount changes with respect to time $t.$ This is equal to the rate at which agent enters the tank minus the rate at which agent leaves the tank.

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}
$$

Note that the units of $\frac{dQ}{dt},{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}$ and ${Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}$ are $\text{kg}/\text{min}.$ Now, let's compute the required rates of change in steps.

**Step 1**: Calculating the rate at which agent enters the basin.

Note that a feed solution containing $0.05\,\text{kg/L}$ of the agent enters the basin at a rate of $8\,\text{L/min}.$ So, the rate at which the *agent* enters the basin is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′} & =(0.05\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{L}})\cdot (8\,\frac{\text{L}}{\text{min}}) \\  & =(0.05\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\cancel{\text{L}}})\cdot (8\,\frac{\cancel{\text{L}}}{\text{min}}) \\  & =0.4\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Calculating the rate at which agent exits the basin.

To find the rate at which agent leaves the basin, we must first determine the volume of liquid in the basin at time $t.$

The basin initially contains $320\,\text{L}$ of liquid; a solution enters at $8\,\text{L/min}$ and leaves at $4\,\text{L/min}.$
As a result, the volume of liquid in the basin after $t$ minutes is 

$$
320+8t-4t=(320+4t)\,\text{L}.
$$

Since $Q$ is the amount of agent in the basin, the *concentration* of the mixed solution at time $t$ is

$$
\frac{Q}{320+4t}\,\text{kg/L}.
$$

Therefore, as the completely mixed liquid leaves at a rate of $4\,\text{L/min},$ *agent* leaves at a rate of

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} & =(4\,\frac{\text{L}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{320+4t}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{L}}) \\  & =(4\,\frac{\cancel{\text{L}}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{320+4t}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\cancel{\text{L}}}) \\  & =\frac{4Q}{320+4t}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{min}} \\  & =\frac{Q}{80+t}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Calculate the overall rate of change.

The rate of change equals the rate of entry minus the rate of exit. Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dQ}{dt} & ={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} \\  & =0.4-\frac{Q}{80+t}\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the equation

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dQ}{dt}+\frac{1}{80+t}Q=0.4.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 4**: Integrate the equation.

This is a first-order linear equation with variable coefficients. So we find the general solution using an integrating factor:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(t) & ={e}^{\int 1/(80+t)\,dt} \\  & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡|80+t|} \\  & =80+t\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying both sides of the differential equation by $I(t)=80+t$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}(80+t)\cdot (\frac{dQ}{dt}+\frac{1}{80+t}Q) & =(80+t)\cdot 0.4 \\ (80+t)\frac{dQ}{dt}+Q & =0.4(80+t) \\ \frac{d}{dt}(Q(80+t)) & =0.4(80+t).\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate with respect to $t:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{d}{dt}(Q(80+t))\,dt & =\int 0.4(80+t)\,dt \\ Q(80+t) & =0.4\cdot \frac{1}{2}(80+t)^{2}+C \\ Q(t) & =0.2(80+t)+\frac{C}{80+t}\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $C$ is a constant of integration.

We're told that the basin initially contains $2.2\,\text{kg}$ of agent. So, we can apply the initial condition $Q(0)=2.2,$ and solve for $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(0) & =2.2 \\ 0.2(80+0)+\frac{C}{80+0} & =2.2 \\ 16+\frac{C}{80} & =2.2 \\ \frac{C}{80} & =-13.8 \\ C & =-1104\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we obtain the following expression for $Q(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(t) & =0.2(80+t)-\frac{1104}{80+t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,  the amount of agent in the basin $5$ minutes after pumping begins is

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(5) & =0.2(80+5)-\frac{1104}{80+5} \\  & =17-\frac{1104}{85} \\  & ≈4.01\,\text{kg},\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to two decimal places."} {:db/id 17592186502151 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "2f6ee384-815c-53b4-9f2d-c31907cf3c91" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "I and II only" :db/id 17592186501548} {:answer/id #uuid "4c291cdc-8fdf-5b18-b158-8a4495491a8c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "II only" :db/id 17592186501604} {:answer/id #uuid "82d21d0a-8fa8-5493-aa93-34dbcc67ac2e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "I only" :db/id 17592186501716} {:answer/id #uuid "d97cc3ab-896e-5f3e-bae3-64970cbcd952" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "III only" :db/id 17592186501899} {:answer/id #uuid "f9a565c8-6e99-5075-9f5d-a43101206bcd" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "I and III only" :db/id 17592186501964}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186501604} :answer-field/id #uuid "9a7338c4-7992-59c5-b27c-44f71458a952" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186502032}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "d6efb51f-1cc6-56d3-90b2-77b3cfdb82a3" :question/math-academy-id "q-146816" :question/problem "For which of the following situations can the distribution of the sample proportion $\widehat{\,p}$ be approximated as

$$
\widehat{\,p}∼N(p,\frac{p(1-p)}{n}),
$$

where $p$ is the population proportion?

I. A sample of size $n=100$ from a population of size $N=500$ in which $90\%$ of the population has a particular characteristic.

II. A sample of size $n=60$ from a population of size $N=1\,500$ in which $90\%$ of the population has a particular characteristic.

III. A sample of size $n=40$ from a population of size $N=1\,500$ in which $90\%$ of the population has a particular characteristic." :question/worked-solution "Given a population in which a proportion $p$ of the population has a particular characteristic, the sampling distribution of the sample proportion $\widehat{\,p}$ can be approximated as

$$
\widehat{\,p}∼N(p,\frac{p(1-p)}{n}),
$$

where 

- $n\le 5\%\cdot N$ (the sample size is less than (or equal to) $5\%$ of the population size),

- $np>5$ (more than $5$ sample elements have the characteristic), and

- $n(1-p)>5$ (more than $5$ sample elements do not have the characteristic).

Let's now examine each situation.

- In situation I, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =100, \\ 5\%\cdot N & =0.05\cdot 500 \\  & =25 \\  & <100.\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

Since  the sample size is more than $5\%$ of the population size, we *cannot* approximate the distribution of $\widehat{\,p}$ using the given model.

- In situation II, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =60 \\  & \le 5\%\cdot N \\  & =0.05\cdot 1\,500 \\  & =75\,✓ \\ np & =60(0.90) \\  & =54 \\  & >5\,✓ \\ n(1-p) & =60(1-0.90) \\  & =6 \\  & >5.\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can approximate the distribution of $\widehat{\,p}$ using the given model.

- In situation III, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =40 \\  & \le 5\%\cdot N \\  & =0.05\cdot 1\,500 \\  & =75\,✓ \\ np & =40(0.9) \\  & =36 \\  & >5\,✓ \\ n(1-p) & =40(1-0.9) \\  & =4 \\  & ≯5.\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

Since $n(1-p)≯5,$ we *cannot* approximate the distribution of $\widehat{\,p}$ using the given model.

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only.""} {:db/id 17592186502154 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "2ff494bd-0b9f-5135-9d18-50e3d2df3439" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "Φ(0.71)" :db/id 17592186501549} {:answer/id #uuid "50ba5d47-3502-5e34-8efb-9b1500551a36" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "Φ(0.79)" :db/id 17592186501613} {:answer/id #uuid "729c9ecc-6c95-5e5f-ad08-f8c44fba093f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "Φ(0.93)" :db/id 17592186501676} {:answer/id #uuid "8b101809-2ccd-5ced-a664-5deefedab9db" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "Φ(0.64)" :db/id 17592186501732} {:answer/id #uuid "9dca0f89-0c53-5160-acd7-38acb63d1d3b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "Φ(0.87)" :db/id 17592186501763}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186501763} :answer-field/id #uuid "b081ec7e-333d-5dd4-a804-4e114c60c34a" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186502038}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "d98ad49e-5d4d-5c1b-b380-745357c60a55" :question/math-academy-id "q-146972" :question/problem "Suppose we take a random sample of size $n=75$ from a population where $45\%$ of the population has a particular characteristic. Find a normal approximation for the probability that less than $50\%$ of the sample has the characteristic. You may assume that the population size is significantly larger than the sample size.

*Hint: $Φ(z)$ is the cumulative distribution function for the standard normal distribution.*" :question/worked-solution "Given a population in which a proportion $p$ of the population has a particular characteristic, the sampling distribution of the sample proportion $\widehat{\,p}$ can be approximated as

$$
\widehat{\,p}∼N(p,\frac{p(1-p)}{n}),
$$

where the sample size $n$ is much smaller than the population size, $np>5,$ and $n(1-p)>5.$

In our case

- the sample size is $n=75,$ and

- the population proportion is $p=0.45.$

Now, since

$$
np=75(0.45)=33.75>5
$$

and

$$
n(1-p)=75(1-0.45)=41.25>5,
$$

and $n=75$ is much smaller than the population size, we can apply the above approximation.

The sampling distribution of the sample proportion, in this case, can be approximated as

$$
\begin{aligned}\widehat{\,p} & ∼N(p,\frac{p(1-p)}{n}) \\  & ∼N(0.45,\frac{0.45(1-0.45)}{75}) \\  & ∼N(0.45,0.0033).\end{aligned}
$$

The probability we wish to find is
$P(\widehat{\,p}<0.5).$
So, we convert $\widehat{\,p}$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(\widehat{\,p}\le 0.5) & =P(Z\le \frac{0.5-0.45}{\sqrt{0.0033}}) \\  & ≈P(Z\le 0.87) \\  & =Φ(0.87)\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186502157 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "78a9c22a-d2cf-5556-83bc-973ce5081e81" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "98.74\,\text{g}" :db/id 17592186501692} {:answer/id #uuid "af336e1d-577f-5f06-a6fb-d40be71dd596" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "94.90\,\text{g}" :db/id 17592186501812} {:answer/id #uuid "db9870bb-ca97-5434-9e2f-f0f1821c5287" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "102.12\,\text{g}" :db/id 17592186501907} {:answer/id #uuid "dc627a42-82c5-5373-81cf-850a6f244c32" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "96.83\,\text{g}" :db/id 17592186501909} {:answer/id #uuid "f405b4b6-a9a5-5b98-9592-9a6a03980d43" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "100.65\,\text{g}" :db/id 17592186501955}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186501692} :answer-field/id #uuid "4dc2b09f-c2d7-5d6c-8b4d-48c2f11ae6c3" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186501998}] :question/id #uuid "ea65973e-51d0-5969-ad2d-3fe183a87ba6" :question/math-academy-id "q-336840" :question/problem "A $10\,500\,\text{mL}$-capacity water tank initially holds $7\,200\,\text{mL}$ of water containing $210\,\text{g}$ of dissolved contaminant. $$

$$

Note that the units of $\frac{dQ}{dt},{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}$ and ${Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}$ are $\text{g}/\text{s}.$ Now, let's compute the required rates of change in steps.

**Step 1**: Calculating the rate at which contaminant enters the tank.

First, note that clean water (i.e., water containing $0\,\text{g/mL}$ of contaminant) enters the tank at a rate of $90\,\text{mL/s}.$ So, the rate at which the *contaminant* enters the tank is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′} & =(0\,\frac{\text{g}}{\text{mL}})\cdot (90\,\frac{\text{mL}}{\text{s}}) \\  & =(0\,\frac{\text{g}}{\cancel{\text{mL}}})\cdot (90\,\frac{\cancel{\text{mL}}}{\text{s}}) \\  & =0\,\frac{\text{g}}{\text{s}}.\end{aligned}

**Step 2**: Calculating the rate at which contaminant exits the tank.

To find the rate at which contaminant leaves the tank, we must first determine the volume of water in the tank at time $t.$

The tank initially contains $7\,200\,\text{mL}$ of water; clean water enters at $90\,\text{mL/s},$ and mixed water leaves at $60\,\text{mL/s}.$
As a result, the amount of water in the tank after $t$ seconds is 

$$
V(t)=7\,200+90t-60t=30(240+t)\,\text{mL}.
$$

Note that $V(t)$ is an increasing function, so the tank is filling.

Since $Q$ is the amount of contaminant in the tank, the concentration of the water at time $t$ is

$$
\frac{Q}{30(240+t)}\,\frac{\text{g}}{\text{mL}}.
$$

Therefore, as the completely mixed water leaves at a rate of $60\,\text{mL/s},$ *contaminant* leaves at a rate of

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} & =(60\,\frac{\text{mL}}{\text{s}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{30(240+t)}\,\frac{\text{g}}{\text{mL}}) \\  & =(60\,\frac{\cancel{\text{mL}}}{\text{s}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{30(240+t)}\,\frac{\text{g}}{\cancel{\text{mL}}}) \\  & =\frac{2Q}{240+t}\,\frac{\text{g}}{\text{s}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Calculate the overall rate of change.

The rate of change equals the rate of entry minus the rate of exit. Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dQ}{dt} & ={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} \\  & =0-\frac{2Q}{240+t}\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the equation

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}=-\frac{2}{240+t}\,Q.
$$

**Step 4**: Integrate the equation

Separating variables and integrating both sides with respect to $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{Q}\cdot \frac{dQ}{dt} & =-\frac{2}{240+t} \\ \int \frac{1}{Q}\cdot \frac{dQ}{dt}dt & =\int \left(-\frac{2}{240+t}\right)\,dt \\ \int \frac{1}{Q}\cdot \,dQ & =-2\int \frac{1}{240+t}\,dt \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|Q| & =-2(\operatorname{ln}⁡|240+t|)+C \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|Q| & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|(240+t)^{-2}|+C \\ |Q| & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡|(240+t)^{-2}|+C} \\ Q(t) & =\frac{A}{(240+t)^{2}},\end{aligned}
$$

where $A=\pm {e}^{C}$ is a constant of integration.

We're told that the tank initially contains $210\,\text{g}$ of contaminant. So, we can apply the initial condition $Q(0)=210,$ and solve for $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(0) & =210 \\ \frac{A}{(240+0)^{2}} & =210 \\ A & =210(240)^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we obtain the following expression for $Q(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(t) & =\frac{210(240)^{2}}{(240+t)^{2}} \\  & =210{\left(\frac{240}{240+t}\right)}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let ${t}_{o}$ be the time when the tank begins to overflow. The tank has a capacity of $10\,500\,\text{mL},$ so we can use the condition $V({t}_{o})=10\,500$ to solve for ${t}_{o}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}V({t}_{o}) & =10\,500 \\ 30(240+{t}_{o}) & =10\,500 \\ 240+{t}_{o} & =350 \\ {t}_{o} & =110\,\text{s}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the amount of contaminant in the tank at the moment it begins to overflow is

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(110) & =210{\left(\frac{240}{240+110}\right)}^{2} \\  & =210{\left(\frac{24}{35}\right)}^{2} \\  & ≈98.74\,\text{g},\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to two decimal places."} {:db/id 17592186502158 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "2878ec78-2159-5e78-bce0-0d1fc6bda183" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{dQ}{dt}-\frac{1}{125}Q=108" :db/id 17592186501538} {:answer/id #uuid "57ee86c4-0d10-514b-b039-aff2c42d25db" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{dQ}{dt}+\frac{1}{125}Q=18" :db/id 17592186501632} {:answer/id #uuid "85f04d18-e494-5d62-84fa-11120096dd73" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{dQ}{dt}-\frac{1}{750}Q=108" :db/id 17592186501722} {:answer/id #uuid "af3af680-805e-5037-96ce-f61a6f8c4eb4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{dQ}{dt}+\frac{1}{750}Q=108" :db/id 17592186501813} {:answer/id #uuid "cc3c4ce1-d24f-5575-8831-e677209a91ea" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{dQ}{dt}+\frac{1}{125}Q=108" :db/id 17592186501872}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186501872} :answer-field/id #uuid "7ae92825-baa7-50ef-a722-e714030d9c79" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186502019}] :question/id #uuid "ee7a7310-6a9a-5bb5-9fe8-376a138abe62" :question/math-academy-id "q-336490" :question/problem "A processing tank initially holds $750\,\text{L}$ of water containing $900\,\text{g}$ of dissolved sugar.
A solution containing $18\,\text{g/L}$ of dissolved sugar is pumped into the tank at a rate of $6\,\text{L/min},$ while the completely mixed water is drained out at a rate of $6\,\text{L/min}.$ Which differential equation best describes the amount of sugar $Q$ in the tank $t$ minutes after pumping begins?" :question/worked-solution "Since $Q$ is the mass of sugar in the tank at time $t,$ the derivative 

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}
$$

describes how this amount changes. This is equal to the rate at which sugar enters the tank minus the rate at which sugar leaves the tank.

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}
$$

Note that the units of $\frac{dQ}{dt},{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}$ and ${Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}$ are $\text{g}/\text{min}.$ Now, let's compute the required rates of change in steps.

**Step 1**: Calculating the rate at which sugar enters the tank.

First, note that a water solution containing $18\,\text{g/L}$ of sugar enters the tank at a rate of $6\,\text{L/min}.$ So, the rate at which the *sugar* enters the tank is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′} & =(18\,\frac{\text{g}}{\text{L}})\cdot (6\,\frac{\text{L}}{\text{min}}) \\  & =(18\,\frac{\text{g}}{\cancel{\text{L}}})\cdot (6\,\frac{\cancel{\text{L}}}{\text{min}}) \\  & =108\,\frac{\text{g}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Calculating the rate at which sugar exits the tank.

Now, to find the rate at which sugar leaves the tank, we must first determine the volume of water in the tank at time $t.$

- The tank initially contains $750\,\text{L}$ of water.

- A solution enters the tank at a rate of $6\,\text{L/min}.$ So, after $t$ minutes, $6t\,\text{L}$ have entered the tank.

- The completely mixed water solution leaves the tank at a rate of $6\,\text{L/min}.$ So, after $t$ minutes, $6t\,\text{L}$ have left the tank.

As a result, the volume of water in the tank after $t$ minutes is 

$$
750+6t-6t=750\,\text{L}.
$$

Since $Q$ is the amount of sugar in the tank, the *concentration* of the water solution at time $t$ is 

$$
\frac{Q}{750}\,\frac{\text{g}}{\text{L}}.
$$

Therefore, as the completely mixed water leaves at a rate of $6\,\text{L/min},$ *sugar* leaves at a rate of

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} & =(6\,\frac{\text{L}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{750}\,\frac{\text{g}}{\text{L}}) \\  & =(6\,\frac{\cancel{\text{L}}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{750}\,\frac{\text{g}}{\cancel{\text{L}}}) \\  & =\frac{6Q}{750}\,\frac{\text{g}}{\text{min}} \\  & =\frac{Q}{125}\,\frac{\text{g}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Calculate the overall rate of change.

Finally, the rate of change equals the rate of entry minus the rate of exit: 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dQ}{dt} & ={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} \\  & =108-\frac{Q}{125}\end{aligned}
$$

which finally gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dQ}{dt}+\frac{1}{125}Q=108.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186502161 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "2c028762-bdd0-5cdd-bfee-795ad4f58f1a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{dQ}{dt}-\frac{1}{25}Q=2.4" :db/id 17592186501544} {:answer/id #uuid "46ba7316-4366-577b-b9c9-597098084ad0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{dQ}{dt}+\frac{1}{25}Q=2.4" :db/id 17592186501595} {:answer/id #uuid "6749d971-1ea4-5ebc-8ae4-5383ae7d993c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{dQ}{dt}+\frac{1}{25}Q=0" :db/id 17592186501656} {:answer/id #uuid "8e81d3f3-a95d-5bda-9070-b35e77fae07c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{dQ}{dt}+\frac{1}{30}Q=2.4" :db/id 17592186501741} {:answer/id #uuid "9e610baf-df41-5215-9dbb-da365544c39b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{dQ}{dt}-\frac{1}{30}Q=2.4" :db/id 17592186501764}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186501595} :answer-field/id #uuid "3cab02cb-f822-5c64-8397-0b6ad78c90d0" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186501993}] :question/id #uuid "f1d959d4-e84b-537b-9d31-22a9bf3bca3a" :question/math-academy-id "q-336618" :question/problem "A tank initially holds $500\,\text{L}$ of a brine (salt-water) solution containing $18\,\text{kg}$ of salt.
A brine solution containing $0.12\,\text{kg}$ of salt per liter is poured into the tank at a rate of $20\,\text{L/min},$ while the completely mixed brine leaves the tank at a rate of $20\,\text{L/min}.$ Which differential equation best describes the amount of salt $Q,$ in kilograms, in the tank $t$ minutes after the brine begins to be added?" :question/worked-solution "Since $Q$ is the amount of salt in the tank at time $t,$ the derivative 

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}
$$

describes how this amount changes with respect to time $t,$ in minutes. This is equal to the rate at which salt enters the tank minus the rate at which salt leaves the tank.

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}
$$

Note that the units of $\frac{dQ}{dt},{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}$ and ${Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}$ are $\text{kg}/\text{min}.$ Now, let's compute the required rates of change in steps.

**Step 1**: Calculating the rate at which salt enters the tank.

First, note that a brine solution containing $0.12\,\text{kg/L}$ of salt enters the tank at a rate of $20\,\text{L/min}.$ So, the rate at which the *salt* enters the tank is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′} & =(0.12\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{L}})\cdot (20\,\frac{\text{L}}{\text{min}}) \\  & =(0.12\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\cancel{\text{L}}})\cdot (20\,\frac{\cancel{\text{L}}}{\text{min}}) \\  & =2.4\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Calculating the rate at which salt exits the tank.

Now, to find the rate at which salt leaves the tank, we must first determine the volume of brine in the tank at time $t.$

- The tank initially contains $500\,\text{L}$ of brine.

- Brine enters the tank at a rate of $20\,\text{L/min}.$ So, after $t$ minutes, $20t\,\text{L}$ have entered the tank.

- The completely mixed brine leaves the tank at a rate of $20\,\text{L/min}.$ So, after $t$ minutes, $20t\,\text{L}$ have left the tank.

As a result, the volume of brine in the tank after $t$ minutes is 

$$
500+20t-20t=500\,\text{L}.
$$

Since $Q$ is the mass of salt in the tank, the *concentration* of the brine at time $t$ is

$$
\frac{Q}{500}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{L}}.
$$

Therefore, as the completely mixed brine leaves at a rate of $20\,\text{L/min},$ *salt* leaves at a rate of

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} & =(20\,\frac{\text{L}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{500}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{L}}) \\  & =(20\,\frac{\cancel{\text{L}}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{500}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\cancel{\text{L}}}) \\  & =\frac{20Q}{500}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{min}} \\  & =\frac{Q}{25}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Calculate the overall rate of change.

Finally, the rate of change equals the rate of entry minus the rate of exit: 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dQ}{dt} & ={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} \\  & =2.4-\frac{Q}{25}\end{aligned}
$$

which finally gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dQ}{dt}+\frac{1}{25}Q=2.4.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186502164 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "2443380b-5fb7-5644-9da4-9247216c51c7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "Φ(-2.45)" :db/id 17592186501531} {:answer/id #uuid "250e3fc3-8889-5bac-9379-1c96182f3fda" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "Φ(-1.62)" :db/id 17592186501534} {:answer/id #uuid "47f4e987-a1cd-511c-b8f3-f4bb08cf984c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "Φ(-1.85)" :db/id 17592186501599} {:answer/id #uuid "7f968a03-d0e7-595f-852d-c5d8937237d8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "Φ(-2.25)" :db/id 17592186501709} {:answer/id #uuid "d26bcec2-8907-5cfb-9e9c-5911985e9883" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "Φ(-2.78)" :db/id 17592186501882}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186501531} :answer-field/id #uuid "f3a76ecc-0207-5bbe-bd7d-f25da682e7e4" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186502057}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "fff0efc8-e9b9-52d5-b287-771e1cbfdc28" :question/math-academy-id "q-147479" :question/problem "A dried apricot producer knows that $70\%$ of apricots weigh more than $40$ g. If the factory randomly samples $350$ apricots, find a normal approximation for the probability that fewer than $224$ apricots weigh more than $40$ g. You may assume that the population size is significantly larger than the sample size.

*Note: $Φ(z)$ is the cumulative distribution function for the standard normal distribution.*" :question/worked-solution "Given a population in which a proportion $p$ of the population has a particular characteristic, the sampling distribution of the sample proportion $\widehat{\,p}$ can be approximated as

$$
\widehat{\,p}∼N(p,\frac{p(1-p)}{n}),
$$

where the sample size $n$ is much smaller than the population size, $np>5,$ and $n(1-p)>5.$

In our case

- the sample size is $n=350,$ and

- the population proportion is $p=0.7.$

Now, since

$$
np=350(0.7)=245>5
$$

and

$$
n(1-p)=350(1-0.7)=105>5,
$$

and $n=350$ is much smaller than the population size, we can apply the above approximation.

The sampling distribution of the sample proportion, in this case, can be approximated as

$$
\begin{aligned}\widehat{\,p} & ∼N(p,\frac{p(1-p)}{n}) \\  & ∼N(0.7,\frac{0.7(1-0.7)}{350}) \\  & ∼N(0.7,0.0006).\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we determine the probability we wish to find. If fewer than $224$ apricots in the sample weigh more than $40$ g, then 

$$
\widehat{\,p}<\frac{224}{350}=0.64.
$$

Hence, the probability we wish to find is
$P(\widehat{\,p}<0.64).$
So, we convert $\widehat{\,p}$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(\widehat{\,p}<0.64) & =P(Z<\frac{0.64-0.7}{\sqrt{0.0006}}) \\  & ≈P(Z<-2.45) \\  & =Φ(-2.45).\end{aligned}
$$"} {:answer/id #uuid "0084fe3c-7796-5a7f-bc12-dda369bedd8d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "u ∈ [- \frac{11}{2}, - \frac{1}{2}]" :db/id 17592186502538} {:answer/id #uuid "03170e0b-03b4-594f-b02a-0f35c65f1cbb" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "u ∈ (- \frac{11}{2}, - \frac{1}{2})" :db/id 17592186502539} {:answer/id #uuid "1f4bf33e-6bd1-5354-964f-f8a39e42ddc4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "t ∈ [- \frac{11}{2}, \frac{1}{2}]" :db/id 17592186502548} {:answer/id #uuid "7da62bfb-0d5f-538d-8129-90809aec4692" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "t ∈ (- \frac{11}{2}, \frac{1}{2})" :db/id 17592186502583} {:answer/id #uuid "45fabf12-9638-54bd-8f03-9388c5ea08d3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(- \sqrt{3}, \frac{3}{2})" :db/id 17592186502652} {:db/id 17592186502670 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "2d43e79f-3992-5d9f-b443-a9d5ff9a6c98" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "[-  \sqrt{3}, \frac{3}{2})" :db/id 17592186502642} {:answer/id #uuid "45fabf12-9638-54bd-8f03-9388c5ea08d3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(- \sqrt{3}, \frac{3}{2})" :db/id 17592186502652} {:answer/id #uuid "7a66a741-7cf0-5533-9f70-69723c8733c9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(- \sqrt{3}, \frac{3}{2}]" :db/id 17592186502678} {:answer/id #uuid "8141ce48-f13d-5d83-9da9-39610932de2c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(- ∞, \frac{3}{2}]" :db/id 17592186502681} {:answer/id #uuid "8572c164-14af-5bdd-a1b3-cc37efd5dbb0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "[-  \sqrt{3}, \frac{3}{2}]" :db/id 17592186502684}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186502684} :answer-field/id #uuid "9390ea5c-5cd9-5d46-a3e4-ba395d381922" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186502688}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "6923fc2f-fb4f-5d6f-a023-ed2ad4ba88da" :question/problem "The inequality $- \sqrt{3} \le x \le \frac{3}{2}$ can be expressed in interval notation as" :question/worked-solution "Every inequality can be expressed as an interval. We use the following notations:

- Parentheses ${\color{red}{(}}\phantom{0} \phantom{0}{\color{red}{)}}$ if the endpoints are *not* included.
- Brackets ${\color{blue}{[}}\phantom{0} \phantom{0}{\color{blue}{]}}$ if the endpoints *are* included.

Our inequality contains only "or equal to" symbols. So, the endpoints $- \sqrt{3}$ and $\frac{3}{2}$ *are* included.

$$
- \sqrt{3}\,\, {\color{blue}{\le}} \,\, x \,\, {\color{blue}{\le}} \,\, \frac{3}{2}
$$

Therefore, we can express our inequality in interval notation as follows:

$$
{\color{blue}{[}}- \sqrt{3},\frac{3}{2}{\color{blue}{]}}
$$

More formally, we can also write

$$
x\in [- \sqrt{3},\frac{3}{2}]
$$"} {:answer/id #uuid "841548ef-c306-578f-8df2-b22c2958c708" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(- \frac{2}{5}, \frac{1}{3})" :db/id 17592186502683} {:answer/id #uuid "8572c164-14af-5bdd-a1b3-cc37efd5dbb0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "[-  \sqrt{3}, \frac{3}{2}]" :db/id 17592186502684} {:db/id 17592186502690 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "666f7356-397c-5191-b9fd-d3d736122e06" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "- 2 \sqrt{5} \le x < - \frac{4}{3}" :db/id 17592186502667} {:answer/id #uuid "7490c675-fbb1-5ffb-9df0-c35aa2edee95" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$x < -  2 \sqrt{5}$ or $x > - \frac{4}{3}$" :db/id 17592186502675} {:answer/id #uuid "b8c693d8-1bca-5189-a689-17d9d90da545" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "- 2 \sqrt{5} < x < - \frac{4}{3}" :db/id 17592186502696} {:answer/id #uuid "cafc93dc-0f51-5df8-8648-b40d7015c6e2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "- 2 \sqrt{5} < x \le - \frac{4}{3}" :db/id 17592186502700} {:answer/id #uuid "d304e79c-381f-5c76-be1f-c4f8014e4e00" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "- 2 \sqrt{5} \le x \le - \frac{4}{3}" :db/id 17592186502704}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186502704} :answer-field/id #uuid "a20951e6-e74f-5cd0-b54a-9d7f776f9ac6" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186502694}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "95e19b06-6468-5678-a8fa-e4ba4e2a42c0" :question/problem "Which inequality corresponds to the interval $x ∈ [-  2 \sqrt{5}, - \frac{4}{3}]$?" :question/worked-solution "Every interval can be expressed as an inequality. We use the following notations:

- Parentheses ${\color{red}{(}}\phantom{0} \phantom{0}{\color{red}{)}}$ to indicate that the endpoints are *not* included.
- Brackets ${\color{blue}{[}}\phantom{0} \phantom{0}{\color{blue}{]}}$ to indicate that the endpoints *are* included.

Our interval contains only brackets. So, the endpoints are *included*.

$$
x\in {\color{blue}{[}}- 2 \sqrt{5}, - \frac{4}{3}{\color{blue}{]}}
$$

Therefore, our interval can be expressed as the following inequality:

Find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$ for the ellipse shown above." :question/worked-solution "Since our ellipse is centered at $(-1,2)$ and has semiaxes $4$ and $2,$ its equation is given by

$$

Now, to calculate $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x},$ we use implicit differentiation:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{(x+1)^{2}}{16}+\frac{(y-2)^{2}}{4}) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(1) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}\left(\frac{(x+1)^{2}}{16}\right)+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}\left(\frac{(y-2)^{2}}{4}\right) & =0 \\ \frac{2(x+1)}{16}+\frac{2(y-2)}{4}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =0 \\ \frac{y-2}{2}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-\frac{x+1}{8} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-\frac{x+1}{4(y-2)}\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186503664 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "43fca01d-214c-5770-b687-855abe991a41" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x^{3}-1" :db/id 17592186503112}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186503112} :answer-field/id #uuid "a268cdd9-081d-55c2-903c-5d29e55e0ccc" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186503598}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "1e63bbce-6bf5-50ed-a823-bd6bd4ad0965" :question/math-academy-id "q-342673" :question/problem "Simplify $\tanh \,(\frac{3}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡x)$ using the definition of the hyperbolic tangent.

{{field-1}}." :question/worked-solution "The horizontal asymptote is $y=\lim_{x\to \infty }f(x).$ To find the horizontal asymptote, we apply the usual procedure of dividing the numerator and denominator by the highest power of $x$ in the denominator, which is ${x}^{5}.$

$$
\operatorname{sinh}⁡x=\frac{1}{2}({e}^{x}-{e}^{-x}).
$$

Substituting the above definition into the equation $4\operatorname{sinh}⁡x=-3,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}4\cdot (\frac{1}{2}({e}^{x}-{e}^{-x})) & =-3 \\ 2({e}^{x}-{e}^{-x}) & =-3 \\ 2{e}^{x}-2{e}^{-x} & =-3.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we multiply both sides of the equation by ${e}^{x},$ and simplify:

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{x}\cdot (2{e}^{x}-2{e}^{-x}) & ={e}^{x}\cdot (-3) \\ 2{e}^{2x}-2 & =-3{e}^{x} \\ 2{e}^{2x}+3{e}^{x}-2 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

This is a quadratic equation in ${e}^{x}$ that we can factor as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}(2{e}^{x}-1)({e}^{x}+2) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

By the zero-product property, we have to solve two equations:

$$
2{e}^{x}-1=0,\,{e}^{x}+2=0
$$

Solving the two equations above for $x,$ we get:

$$
\begin{aligned}2{e}^{x}-1 & =0 &  & \, & {e}^{x}+2 & =0 \\ {e}^{x} & =\frac{1}{2} &  & \, & {e}^{x} & =-2 \\ x & =\operatorname{ln}⁡\left(\frac{1}{2}\right) &  & \, & \end{aligned}
$$

There are no real values of $x$ for which ${e}^{x}=-2.$ Therefore, $x=\operatorname{ln}⁡\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)$ is the only real solution to the equation."} {:db/id 17592186503687 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "4bc45995-cc23-5f2f-95dc-adb53fd70390" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{3}{e}" :db/id 17592186503122} {:answer/id #uuid "7d02c22e-415b-580d-b404-ffc0a846300a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{3}^{9}" :db/id 17592186503238} {:answer/id #uuid "9b48a15c-7746-52d0-ab31-148949b28472" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{e}{3}" :db/id 17592186503291} {:answer/id #uuid "a689aded-b802-5144-9786-711cd58ea390" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{e}^{-3}" :db/id 17592186503317} {:answer/id #uuid "b1c13605-3b15-5441-9ad6-991d71ce870e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{e}^{3}" :db/id 17592186503342}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186503342} :answer-field/id #uuid "c41454b8-a54a-5924-9bf1-be03ac5b4d5e" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186503612}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "55d1a1bd-c8eb-5ee7-88d6-a44ae7dc2c96" :question/math-academy-id "q-118710" :question/problem "Evaluate $\lim_{x\to \infty }{\left(\frac{x}{x-1}\right)}^{3x-3}.$" :question/worked-solution "Notice that as $x\to \infty ,$ 

- the expression inside the parentheses approaches $1,$ while

- the exponent approaches $\infty .$

So, if we attempt to evaluate the limit directly, we get

$$
\lim_{x\to \infty }{\left(\frac{x}{x-1}\right)}^{3x-3}={1}^{\infty },
$$

which is an indeterminate form.

Instead, let's recall the following special limit:

$$
\lim_{n\to \infty }{(1+\frac{1}{n})}^{n}=e
$$

We rewrite the given limit as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\lim_{x\to \infty }{\left(\frac{x}{x-1}\right)}^{3x-3} & =\lim_{x\to \infty }{\left(\frac{(x-1)+1}{x-1}\right)}^{3x-3} \\  & =\lim_{x\to \infty }{(1+\frac{1}{x-1})}^{3(x-1)}\end{aligned}
$$

Let $x-1=n.$ Therefore, since $n\to \infty $ as $x\to \infty ,$ we rewrite the limit using the algebra of limits, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\lim_{x\to \infty }{\left(\frac{x}{x-1}\right)}^{3x-3} & =\lim_{x\to \infty }{(1+\frac{1}{x-1})}^{3(x-1)} \\  & =\lim_{n\to \infty }{(1+\frac{1}{n})}^{3n} \\  & =\lim_{n\to \infty }{[{(1+\frac{1}{n})}^{n}]}^{3} \\  & ={[\lim_{n\to \infty }{(1+\frac{1}{n})}^{n}]}^{3} \\  & ={e}^{3}\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186503695 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "15d8b909-cd88-5396-a3e4-015217208b7b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{2}{7}" :db/id 17592186503025} {:answer/id #uuid "41ecd6aa-d66a-5b26-b453-6eb1d066f99c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{4}" :db/id 17592186503106} {:answer/id #uuid "5addda90-5bb8-5856-90d0-53bbb72f42a3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{7}" :db/id 17592186503157} {:answer/id #uuid "7f50f9e1-dab7-5e4d-9b55-64e931613784" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{3}{4}" :db/id 17592186503244} {:answer/id #uuid "ca2ee2e6-f6b2-50ac-81bf-610eca1b4575" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{2}" :db/id 17592186503387}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186503025} :answer-field/id #uuid "25b205bf-9311-59ed-b707-a4ae58c7b68e" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186503533}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "6487d2c0-d995-5efa-98e2-2110fb813c4e" :question/math-academy-id "q-158455" :question/problem "Compute $P(-1<X<1)$ given that the random variable $X$ has the probability density function

$$
f(x)=\left\{\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{28}({x}^{2}+1),\, & -2\le x\le 2, \\ 0,\, & \text{otherwise.}\end{aligned}\right.
$$" :question/worked-solution "If a continuous random variable $X$ has the probability density function $f(x),$ then 

$$
P(a<X<b)={\int }_{a}^{b}f(x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

So, in our case, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}P(-1<X<1) & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}\frac{3}{28}({x}^{2}+1)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{3}{28}{\int }_{-1}^{1}{x}^{2}+1\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{3}{28}{[\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3}+x]}_{-1}^{1} \\  & =\frac{3}{28}([\frac{1}{3}(1)^{3}+(1)]-[\frac{1}{3}(-1)^{3}+(-1)]) \\  & =\frac{3}{28}([\frac{1}{3}+1]-[-\frac{1}{3}-1]) \\  & =\frac{3}{28}\cdot \frac{8}{3} \\  & =\frac{2}{7}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186503699 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "232a1cb8-318a-56a7-b2b6-605efb1a56ca" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(0,8,6)" :db/id 17592186503049} {:answer/id #uuid "ad2eb325-c967-59e3-9afe-820fcadec04f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(-6,8,0)" :db/id 17592186503330} {:answer/id #uuid "d01c36cd-cab4-5b08-a618-0ee3882f5a91" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(1,2,3)" :db/id 17592186503396} {:answer/id #uuid "e04ebf57-2b2b-5f5a-87ee-ffb6237367bd" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(-3,2,1)" :db/id 17592186503439} {:answer/id #uuid "ebba451e-a3c1-5c1d-bba8-34bb410134dd" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(0,0,0)" :db/id 17592186503462}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186503396} :answer-field/id #uuid "840864ff-e144-58cd-b587-882bc625e5ec" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186503581}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "6fb5b9b2-b9ce-5495-8ebc-1c2e3903a753" :question/math-academy-id "q-75204" :question/problem "Given the curve $r(t)=⟨2t-{t}^{2}\,,\,2{t}^{2}\,,\,2t+{t}^{2}⟩,$ find the point at which the tangent to the curve is parallel to the vector $⟨0\,,\,1\,,\,1⟩.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we calculate the derivative of $r(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t-{t}^{2}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2{t}^{2}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t+{t}^{2})⟩ \\  & =⟨2-2t,\,4t,\,2+2t⟩\end{aligned}

The vectors ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $⟨0\,,\,1\,,\,1⟩$ are parallel for some specific value ${t}_{0}$ of the parameter $t$ if and only if there exists a constant $c$ such that ${r}^{′}({t}_{0})=c\,⟨0\,,\,1\,,\,1⟩.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =c\,⟨0\,,\,1\,,\,1⟩ \\ ⟨2-2t,\,4t,\,2+2t⟩ & =c\,⟨0\,,\,1\,,\,1⟩ \\ ⟨2-2t,\,4t,\,2+2t⟩ & =⟨0\,,\,c\,,\,c⟩.\end{aligned}

$$
