we conclude that $⟨0\,,\,1\,,\,1⟩$ and ${r}^{′}(t)$ are parallel at the point $(1,2,3).$"} {:db/id 17592186503718 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "07554fcf-2e2c-5e04-b659-229769d5a42f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{{z}^{2}-1}{{z}^{2}}" :db/id 17592186502996} {:answer/id #uuid "59dc9393-aba4-55f1-a33b-edbc6a5c7c71" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{{z}^{4}-1}{2{z}^{2}}" :db/id 17592186503154} {:answer/id #uuid "c9ac03e5-f4b2-5887-ba43-a82100a8936e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{{z}^{4}+1}{2{z}^{2}}" :db/id 17592186503384} {:answer/id #uuid "cef8d180-cb9e-5d9e-bd31-7ec2446df85d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{{z}^{2}-1}{4{z}^{2}}" :db/id 17592186503395} {:answer/id #uuid "ed0f0085-d2a8-5d8d-9d1f-f807dca76f30" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{{z}^{2}+1}{{z}^{2}}" :db/id 17592186503467}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186503154} :answer-field/id #uuid "1c5c7ef5-8ca5-5c12-9d79-8a62b31c25ba" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186503531}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "958048ce-f9d1-5782-ad7f-1bcc0753619d" :question/math-academy-id "q-95492" :question/problem "Given that $z>0,$ which of the following is equivalent to $\operatorname{sinh}⁡(2\operatorname{ln}⁡z)?$" :question/worked-solution "The definition of $\operatorname{sinh}⁡x$ is 

$$
\operatorname{sinh}⁡x=\frac{1}{2}({e}^{x}-{e}^{-x}).

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sinh}⁡(2\operatorname{ln}⁡z) & =\frac{1}{2}({e}^{2\operatorname{ln}⁡z}-{e}^{-2\operatorname{ln}⁡z}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}({e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡{z}^{2}}-{e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡{z}^{-2}}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}({z}^{2}-{z}^{-2}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}({z}^{2}-\frac{1}{{z}^{2}}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{{z}^{4}-1}{{z}^{2}}\right) \\  & =\frac{{z}^{4}-1}{2{z}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186503740 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "12c051ac-16d1-53b0-af08-3845e1f80fcd" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "y=0" :db/id 17592186503020} {:answer/id #uuid "716a5576-1477-5d48-9fac-ce2b26ac1535" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "y=9" :db/id 17592186503210} {:answer/id #uuid "c22ddc25-362a-57ac-b9a3-be8479d6a75e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "y=\frac{3}{2}" :db/id 17592186503371} {:answer/id #uuid "d43bf7b4-779c-5786-81da-db083c00f923" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "y=1" :db/id 17592186503403} {:answer/id #uuid "fe457f6b-9fd9-5669-9e55-7cc5d248f357" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "No horizontal asymptote" :db/id 17592186503507}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186503020} :answer-field/id #uuid "8358f70b-40f4-51c5-ad82-e863f6db2422" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186503579}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "c664e1c1-92ad-575b-bafc-9b1ddd2a888d" :question/math-academy-id "q-35762" :question/problem "Find the horizontal asymptote of the function $f(x)=\frac{9}{{x}^{2}-6}.$" :question/worked-solution "The horizontal asymptote is $y=\lim_{x\to \infty }f(x).$ To find the horizontal asymptote, we apply the usual procedure of dividing the numerator and denominator by the highest power of $x$ in the denominator, which is ${x}^{2}.$

$$
\begin{aligned}\lim_{x\to \infty }f(x) & =\lim_{x\to \infty }\frac{9}{{x}^{2}-6} \\  & =\lim_{x\to \infty }\frac{\left(\frac{9}{{x}^{2}}\right)}{(\frac{{x}^{2}}{{x}^{2}}-\frac{6}{{x}^{2}})} \\  & =\lim_{x\to \infty }\frac{\left(\frac{9}{{x}^{2}}\right)}{(1-\frac{6}{{x}^{2}})} \\  & =\frac{0}{1-0} \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, the horizontal asymptote of $f(x)$ is $y=0.$"} {:db/id 17592186503745 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0b600bcd-5006-5baf-9dca-4aab5033031d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{32}+\frac{25y}{8}+125{y}^{2}" :db/id 17592186503008} {:answer/id #uuid "4c839c43-5c26-510d-85ac-e2e3c39a216c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{32}+\frac{25y}{4}+145{y}^{2}" :db/id 17592186503128} {:answer/id #uuid "4fb998d5-d716-53e2-a50b-72e1271eb277" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{32}+\frac{25y}{8}-100{y}^{2}" :db/id 17592186503133} {:answer/id #uuid "5135b701-cd58-5dde-8d9b-989995318cb4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{32}+\frac{25y}{4}+100{y}^{2}" :db/id 17592186503136} {:answer/id #uuid "9799692b-0119-5014-ae4f-3ef5e9145c63" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{32}+\frac{25y}{8}+145{y}^{2}" :db/id 17592186503281}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186503008} :answer-field/id #uuid "ef1b5443-9d42-51aa-ac69-73ecc6958d74" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186503635}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "d6a9fa51-d96f-5308-9675-af7e9df7f105" :question/math-academy-id "q-3563" :question/problem "Find, in ascending powers of $y,$ the first three terms of the binomial expansion of ${(10y+\frac{1}{2})}^{5}.$" :question/worked-solution "First, let's compare our expression with the binomial

$$
(a+b)^{n}.
$$

Here we have that $n=5,$ $a=10y,$ and $b=\frac{1}{2}.$ So, the exponents of the binomial expansion must follow the pattern

$$
{a}^{5}{b}^{0},\,{a}^{4}{b}^{1},\,{a}^{3}{b}^{2},\,{a}^{2}{b}^{3},\,{a}^{1}{b}^{4},\,{a}^{0}{b}^{5}.
$$

The $5$th row in Pascal's Triangle is $(1,5,10,10,5,1).$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{(10y+\frac{1}{2})}^{5} & =1{a}^{5}+5{a}^{4}b+10{a}^{3}{b}^{2}+10{a}^{2}{b}^{3}+5a{b}^{4}+1{b}^{5} \\  & =1(10y)^{5}{\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)}^{0}+5(10y)^{4}{\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)}^{1}+10(10y)^{3}{\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)}^{2} \\  & \,+10(10y)^{2}{\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)}^{3}+5(10y)^{1}{\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)}^{4}+1(10y)^{0}{\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)}^{5} \\  & =1(100\,000{y}^{5})(1)+5(10\,000{y}^{4})\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)+10(1\,000{y}^{3})\left(\frac{1}{4}\right) \\  & \,+10(100{y}^{2})\left(\frac{1}{8}\right)+5(10y)\left(\frac{1}{16}\right)+1(1)\left(\frac{1}{32}\right) \\  & =100\,000{y}^{5}+\frac{50\,000{y}^{4}}{2}+\frac{10\,000{y}^{3}}{4}+\frac{1\,000{y}^{2}}{8}+\frac{50y}{16}+\frac{1}{32} \\  & =100\,000{y}^{5}+25\,000{y}^{4}+2\,500{y}^{3}+125{y}^{2}+\frac{25y}{8}+\frac{1}{32}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, in ascending powers of $y$, the first three terms are

$$
\frac{1}{32}+\frac{25y}{8}+125{y}^{2}.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186503747 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0d7df223-f754-5f11-b22a-77fb8e7962f2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(-\frac{2}{3},-1)" :db/id 17592186503014} {:answer/id #uuid "14919ef8-67c2-5133-aecb-d8b884b8e383" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$(-\frac{2}{3},-1)$ and $(-\frac{16}{3},4)$" :db/id 17592186503024} {:answer/id #uuid "4bcbc09b-35ca-5198-901e-f6baf95cdd47" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$(\frac{2}{3},7)$ and $(-\frac{2}{3},-1)$" :db/id 17592186503123} {:answer/id #uuid "74935c6a-47ac-531f-891d-589f038c3aaf" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$(\frac{2}{3},7)$ and $(\frac{16}{3},20)$" :db/id 17592186503216} {:answer/id #uuid "dc388b50-c7a3-5df5-b75c-72786abab2b5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(-\frac{16}{3},4)" :db/id 17592186503423}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186503024} :answer-field/id #uuid "6e7d6d7e-b60a-5f83-9ecc-1a604f1140c7" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186503566}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "da548a97-bf75-53d6-96e0-6ed458e117e2" :question/math-academy-id "q-165036" :question/problem "Given the curve $r(t)=⟨\frac{2}{3}{t}^{3},3{t}^{2}+4t⟩,$ find the point at which the tangent to the curve is parallel to the vector $⟨1,-1⟩.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we calculate the derivative of $r(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{2}{3}{t}^{3}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3{t}^{2}+4t)⟩ \\  & =⟨2{t}^{2},6t+4⟩\end{aligned}
$$

The vectors ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $⟨0\,,\,1\,,\,3⟩$ are parallel for some specific value ${t}_{0}$ of the parameter $t$ if and only if there exists a constant $c$ such that ${r}^{′}({t}_{0})=c⟨1,-1⟩.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =c⟨1,-1⟩ \\ ⟨2{t}^{2},6t+4⟩ & =c⟨1,-1⟩ \\ ⟨2{t}^{2},6t+4⟩ & =⟨c,-c⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the components gives:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}2{t}^{2} &=c \\ 6t+4 &=-c\end{aligned}\right.
$$

From the first equation, we obtain that $c=2{t}^{2}.$ Substituting $c=2{t}^{2}$ into the second equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}6t+4 & =-2{t}^{2} \\ 2{t}^{2}+6t+4 & =0 \\ {t}^{2}+3t+2 & =0 \\ (t+2)(t+1) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $⟨1,-1⟩$ and ${r}^{′}$ are parallel at the points corresponding to $t=-2$ and $t=-1.$

Finally, since

$$
\begin{aligned}r(-1) & =⟨\frac{2}{3}(-1)^{3},3(-1)^{2}+4(-1)⟩=⟨-\frac{2}{3},-1⟩, \\ r(-2) & =⟨\frac{2}{3}(-2)^{3},3(-2)^{2}+4(-2)⟩=⟨-\frac{16}{3},4⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

we conclude that $⟨1,-1⟩$ and ${r}^{′}(t)$ are parallel at the points $(-\frac{2}{3},-1)$ and $(-\frac{16}{3},4).$"} {:db/id 17592186503750 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "d555f50e-bb12-5374-8350-a9ef5d7a920d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\infty" :db/id 17592186503405}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186503405} :answer-field/id #uuid "1152ef23-8437-51aa-a9aa-c16e05bf2bcd" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186503522}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "e026e16b-5d19-5563-a374-d9f17e04bfda" :question/math-academy-id "q-339604" :question/problem "Evaluate the limit:

$\lim_{x\to \infty }\,\,\frac{{x}^{5}+5x+3}{{x}^{4}-2}=$

{{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "First, we divide both the numerator and the denominator by the highest power of $x$ in the denominator, which is ${x}^{4}.$ Then, by noting that the reciprocals shrink to $0$ in the limit, we can then evaluate the resulting expression.

$$
\begin{aligned}\lim_{x\to \infty }\,\,\frac{{x}^{5}+5x+3}{{x}^{4}-2} & =\lim_{x\to \infty }\,\,\frac{(\frac{{x}^{5}}{{x}^{4}}+\frac{5x}{{x}^{4}}+\frac{3}{{x}^{4}})}{(\frac{{x}^{4}}{{x}^{4}}-\frac{2}{{x}^{4}})} \\  & =\lim_{x\to \infty }\,\,\frac{(x+\frac{5}{{x}^{3}}+\frac{3}{{x}^{4}})}{(1-\frac{2}{{x}^{4}})} \\  & =\lim_{x\to \infty }\,\text{ }\frac{x+0+0}{1-0} \\  & =\lim_{x\to \infty }\,\,x \\  & =\infty .\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186503848 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "2d6ad986-0c26-5cd6-9cd3-04a7be56d694" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{x^{6}}{7}+C" :db/id 17592186503846} {:answer/id #uuid "4ec8b324-f032-547f-97d9-6c73f80f4440" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x^{7}+C" :db/id 17592186503850} {:answer/id #uuid "7fe67df0-46d1-5acd-abf6-e732a8688e8c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{x^{8}}{8}+C" :db/id 17592186503855} {:answer/id #uuid "b8b1f0d3-bec7-598d-ba2e-a3f438f06ce3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "7x^{7}+C" :db/id 17592186503868} {:answer/id #uuid "fa59a2a3-a8ed-5b0b-abda-91a9bba04e9d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{x^{7}}{7}+C" :db/id 17592186503875}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186503875} :answer-field/id #uuid "b67f2104-8e47-50cd-b752-fad1aa17e5ed" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186503867}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "4194dc2e-82ad-5109-91f4-d383eed4b18e" :question/problem "Calculate $$
\displaystyle \int {x}^{6}\,\text{d}x.
$$" :question/worked-solution "We apply the power rule with $n=6$, and we get

$$
\int {x}^{6}\,\text{d}x=\frac{{x}^{6+1}}{6+1}+C=\frac{{x}^{7}}{7}+C.
$$

Let's check by differentiating:

$$

$$"} {:db/id 17592186503851 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "01b9bd22-8b41-542b-82ba-62e400af4a02" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{x^{8}}{8} + C" :db/id 17592186503842} {:answer/id #uuid "0b7b7de0-eaf8-57d9-8475-c23f72194dd2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "8x^{8}" :db/id 17592186503844} {:answer/id #uuid "a5bb73e6-3ec8-51dd-ad3b-1cd6d6243b7a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "8 + C" :db/id 17592186503862} {:answer/id #uuid "b52194ac-60ec-5ec7-91b2-c8a58426c3e5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{x^{8}}{8}" :db/id 17592186503866} {:answer/id #uuid "f1d839d9-d182-5a2a-8ca4-8961f79ffaae" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x^{8} + C" :db/id 17592186503874}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186503842} :answer-field/id #uuid "88eaa69f-9171-51b9-9926-45e937a2ad36" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186503859}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "4fc55d29-07c8-58f3-8bc8-d1223d0589d0" :question/problem "Calculate $$

$$ Include the arbitrary constant of integration." :question/worked-solution "We apply the power rule with $n=7$, and we get

$\cdot \,\frac{\pi }{6n}$" :question/worked-solution "The definite integral can be defined in terms of the limit of a right Riemann sum as

$$
{\int }_{a}^{b}f(x)\,\text{d}x=\lim_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}f({x}_{i})\cdot Δx,
$$

where ${x}_{i}=a+iΔx$ and $Δx=\frac{b-a}{n}.$

In the definite integral

$$
{\int }_{0}^{\pi /6}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x,
$$

the function is $f(x)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x),$ the lower bound is $a=0$ and the upper bound is $b=\pi /6.$ So, we have

$$
Δx=\frac{\pi /6-0}{n}=\frac{\pi }{6n}.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /6}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x & =\lim_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}f({x}_{i})\cdot Δx \\  & =\lim_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}f(0+i\cdot \frac{\pi }{6n})\cdot \frac{\pi }{6n} \\  & =\lim_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}f\left(\frac{\pi i}{6n}\right)\cdot \frac{\pi }{6n} \\  & =\lim_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\cdot \frac{\pi i}{6n})\cdot \frac{\pi }{6n} \\  & =\lim_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\,\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{\pi i}{2n}\right)\cdot \frac{\pi }{6n}.\end{aligned}

Find the function $g(x).$" :question/worked-solution "We have the function 

$$
y=(\sqrt{x})^{x}.
$$

First, we take the natural logarithm of both sides:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡((\sqrt{x})^{x}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =x\operatorname{ln}⁡(\sqrt{x})\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we differentiate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(x\operatorname{ln}⁡(\sqrt{x})) \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot {y}^{′} & =(x)^{′}\cdot (\operatorname{ln}⁡(\sqrt{x}))+(x)\cdot {(\operatorname{ln}⁡(\sqrt{x}))}^{′} \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot {y}^{′} & =1\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡(\sqrt{x})+x\cdot (\frac{1}{\sqrt{x}}\cdot \frac{1}{2\sqrt{x}}) \\ \frac{{y}^{′}}{y} & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\sqrt{x})+\frac{1}{2} \\ \frac{{y}^{′}}{y} & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)+\frac{1}{2} \\ \frac{{y}^{′}}{y} & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)+1)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve for ${y}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =\frac{1}{2}y(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)+1)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $g(x)=(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)+1).$"} {:db/id 17592186504618 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "16cac734-0892-5ff2-a1ff-c0fbd3626b86" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "10{x}^{2}+10x\operatorname{ln}⁡x+1" :db/id 17592186504073} {:answer/id #uuid "6ba48682-04f1-5b7d-a7ef-91546e9c66ac" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "10{x}^{2}+2x\operatorname{ln}⁡x-1" :db/id 17592186504221} {:answer/id #uuid "76897061-1d77-5f85-af3e-f9654624d9fb" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "5{x}^{2}+10\operatorname{ln}⁡x+4" :db/id 17592186504234} {:answer/id #uuid "c1cc2afd-bb0e-5601-811e-65ad382a5a7f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "5{x}^{2}+10{x}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡x-2" :db/id 17592186504363} {:answer/id #uuid "f73153f7-d5e1-5b7b-8f5c-b7bd0c550c73" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "5{x}^{2}-2x+10x\operatorname{ln}⁡x" :db/id 17592186504461}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186504363} :answer-field/id #uuid "a560e212-9ade-5ff3-a8f4-f653183e4352" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186504552}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "358ad886-8781-5867-add0-1dfbbd99e7fd" :question/math-academy-id "q-138791" :question/problem "Consider the function $y={x}^{5{x}^{2}-2}.$ Its derivative is given by

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}={x}^{5{x}^{2}-3}\cdot g(x).
$$

Find the function $g(x).$" :question/worked-solution "We have the function 

$$
y={x}^{5{x}^{2}-2}.
$$

First, we take the natural logarithm of both sides:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{5{x}^{2}-2}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =(5{x}^{2}-2)\operatorname{ln}⁡x\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we differentiate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}((5{x}^{2}-2)\operatorname{ln}⁡x) \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(5{x}^{2}-2)\cdot (\operatorname{ln}⁡x)+(5{x}^{2}-2)\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡x) \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =10x\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡x+(5{x}^{2}-2)\cdot \frac{1}{x} \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =10x\operatorname{ln}⁡x+\frac{5{x}^{2}-2}{x}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve for $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =y(\frac{5{x}^{2}-2}{x}+10x\operatorname{ln}⁡x)\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute $y={x}^{5{x}^{2}-2}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & ={x}^{5{x}^{2}-2}(\frac{5{x}^{2}-2}{x}+10x\operatorname{ln}⁡x) \\  & ={x}^{5{x}^{2}-2}(\frac{5{x}^{2}-2}{x}+\frac{10{x}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{x}) \\  & ={x}^{5{x}^{2}-3}(5{x}^{2}+10{x}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡x-2)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $g(x)=5{x}^{2}+10{x}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡x-2.$"} {:db/id 17592186504619 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "07485527-04b3-57d3-a577-5a960471513a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\log_2(5x)" :db/id 17592186504042}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186504042} :answer-field/id #uuid "1ce33564-9610-5802-9f60-271794918cb3" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186504489} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1a12617f-583b-5e92-913a-797edfec8b26" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "7" :db/id 17592186504079}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186504079} :answer-field/id #uuid "3d2f8892-a963-5ac4-967b-d51cd720e5b7" :answer-field/key "field-2" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186504504}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "368aa1bb-68dd-5e11-83de-3c6725fca7d6" :question/math-academy-id "q-346198" :question/problem "Find the function $f(x)$ and the value of $b,$ given that

$$
{\int }_{3}^{b}f(x)\,\text{d}x=\lim_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=0}^{n-1}[{log}_{2}\,(5(3+\frac{4k}{n}))\cdot \frac{4}{n}].
$$

$\,f(x)=$

{{field-2}}" :question/worked-solution "A definite integral can be defined as the limit of a left Riemann sum as follows:

$$
{\int }_{a}^{b}f(x)\,\text{d}x=\lim_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=0}^{n-1}f({x}_{k})\cdot Δx
$$

where $Δx=\frac{b-a}{n}$ and ${x}_{k}=a+kΔx.$

Notice that we're given that the lower limit $a=3.$ 

Comparing the given summation with the general expression above, we see that $Δx=\frac{4}{n}.$ Therefore, 

$$
\frac{4}{n}=\frac{b-3}{n}\,⟹\,b=7.
$$

Consequently, ${x}_{k}=3+\frac{4k}{n}$ and $f({x}_{k})={log}_{2}\,(5{x}_{k}).$ By replacing the sample point ${x}_{k}$ with the variable $x,$ we find the original function.

Hence,

$$
{\int }_{3}^{7}{\log }_{2}⁡(5x)\,\text{d}x=\lim_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=0}^{n-1}[{log}_{2}\,(5(3+\frac{4k}{n}))\cdot \frac{4}{n}].
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is 

$$
f(x)={\log }_{2}⁡(5x)\,\text{and}\,b=7.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186504621 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "059675b4-5317-52c5-9e12-a825b02e678a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "27" :db/id 17592186504041} {:answer/id #uuid "331d3ba3-7d70-552c-9017-a789e832ecce" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "81" :db/id 17592186504119} {:answer/id #uuid "9d3dc435-4333-5003-b8cf-c80d000a682d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "64" :db/id 17592186504309} {:answer/id #uuid "a1847f87-ec08-58e3-8324-c070554a3699" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "25" :db/id 17592186504321} {:answer/id #uuid "ffa20eb0-d1e6-5ca7-86c5-1fe41e49f4b3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "34" :db/id 17592186504478}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186504119} :answer-field/id #uuid "fe2b2c06-359a-556f-b20c-5c316319fefe" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186504600}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "3c7cc171-f78e-5279-bfdd-075dc2385743" :question/math-academy-id "q-48417" :question/problem "The function $f(x)$ is given by

$$
f(x)=\left\{\begin{aligned}\frac{x}{\sqrt{x+k}-\sqrt{k}}, & x\ne 0, \\ 18, & x=0.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

If $f(x)$ is continuous at $x=0$, what is the value of $k?$" :question/worked-solution "From the definition of $f(x),$

$$
\begin{aligned}\lim_{x\to 0}f(x) & =\lim_{x\to 0}\frac{x}{\sqrt{x+k}-\sqrt{k}} \\  & =\lim_{x\to 0}(\frac{x}{\sqrt{x+k}-\sqrt{k}}\cdot \frac{\sqrt{x+k}+\sqrt{k}}{\sqrt{x+k}+\sqrt{k}}) \\  & =\lim_{x\to 0}\frac{x(\sqrt{x+k}+\sqrt{k})}{x+k-k} \\  & =\lim_{x\to 0}\frac{\cancel{x}(\sqrt{x+k}+\sqrt{k})}{\cancel{x}} \\  & =\lim_{x\to 0}(\sqrt{x+k}+\sqrt{k}) \\  & =\sqrt{0+k}+\sqrt{k} \\  & =2\sqrt{k}.\end{aligned}
$$

In order for $f(x)$ to be continuous at $x=0,$ we must have 

$$
\begin{aligned}\lim_{x\to 0}f(x) & =f(0) \\ 2\sqrt{k} & =18 \\ \sqrt{k} & =9 \\ k & =81.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186504627 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0d51a417-8cbd-5ff9-b30d-7d51a8e9f118" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$(0,1,-3)$ only" :db/id 17592186504060} {:answer/id #uuid "20488b98-fd63-5cb6-8e3f-219b6a0e9f1d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$(-2,3,1)$ and $(1,1,-5)$" :db/id 17592186504089} {:answer/id #uuid "42b18104-44f7-5697-9199-5fc61fed95d2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$(1,1,-5)$ only" :db/id 17592186504148} {:answer/id #uuid "80a1254f-1f1b-53be-aa01-60c2de725f39" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$(1,1,-5)$ and $(0,1,-3)$" :db/id 17592186504255} {:answer/id #uuid "f7eb6bd3-275d-5d82-a1bd-18241d86be15" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$(-2,3,1)$ only" :db/id 17592186504465}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186504465} :answer-field/id #uuid "39660287-438d-544e-a034-60a0f0a153f9" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186504501}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "540d859a-8179-5e53-b6ff-389c30bf0b61" :question/math-academy-id "q-129552" :question/problem "At which points on the surface $z=xy-3x+2y-5$ is the tangent plane horizontal?" :question/worked-solution "The Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the surface $z=f(x,y)$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ on the surface can be written as

$$
z-{z}_{0}=(x-{x}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0})+(y-{y}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),
$$

where $$
\displaystyle ⟨\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),-1⟩
$$ represents a normal vector to the tangent plane.

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(xy-3x+2y-5)=y-3 \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(xy-3x+2y-5)=x+2\end{aligned}
$$

 

Hence, the normal vector to the tangent plane is 

$$
⟨y-3,\,x+2,\,-1⟩.
$$

Note that the tangent plane is horizontal if and only if the normal vector is vertical. This means that the $x$- and $y$-components of the vector must be $0:$

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} &=0 \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} &=0\end{aligned}\right.\,⟹\,\left\{\begin{aligned}y-3 &=0 \\ x+2 &=0\end{aligned}\right.
$$

 

From the second equation we get $x=-2,$ while the first equation gives $y=3.$ 

Finally, substituting $x=-2$ and $y=3$ into our function, we get

$$
z=(-2)(3)-3(-2)+2(3)-5=1.
$$

Therefore, the point where the tangent plane is horizontal is $(-2,3,1).$"} {:db/id 17592186504629 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "07850059-ddb8-59d8-9ab0-8177d5206ad1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\frac{1}{2}" :db/id 17592186504046} {:answer/id #uuid "4d11d421-27fe-5c53-897b-17c35864bd3f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\pi }{2}" :db/id 17592186504171} {:answer/id #uuid "c141ccd2-2281-55be-a7bc-e600a17abbd9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1" :db/id 17592186504361} {:answer/id #uuid "c969f3b4-9799-57d4-a8f4-6cf2a9b701dd" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0" :db/id 17592186504372} {:answer/id #uuid "f5168c4d-1a9d-5db6-b1eb-f2e01f7135ac" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{2}" :db/id 17592186504459}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186504361} :answer-field/id #uuid "65db8db6-731c-5056-8281-d2ccd26fd053" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186504522}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "55ce71ca-d33d-5c8b-9d05-07e0dca2765b" :question/math-academy-id "q-152891" :question/problem "$$
\displaystyle \lim_{x\to \,3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{3}{2}\operatorname{arctan}⁡\left(\frac{x}{\sqrt{3}}\right))=
$$" :question/worked-solution "First, let's sketch the graph of  $$
\displaystyle y=\frac{3}{2}\operatorname{arctan}⁡\left(\frac{x}{\sqrt{3}}\right):
$$   

![](images/4a/4abceba56f404b0b39fbde4b1f7da0ec36e69a496c4ef52d3bebfbcb8c7d3380.png)

The domain of   $$
\displaystyle \frac{3}{2}\operatorname{arctan}⁡\left(\frac{x}{\sqrt{3}}\right)
$$ is $(-\infty ,\infty ).$    

Now, substituting $x=3$ directly into the limit, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\lim_{x\to \,3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{3}{2}\operatorname{arctan}⁡\left(\frac{x}{\sqrt{3}}\right)) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{3}{2}\operatorname{arctan}⁡\left(\frac{3}{\sqrt{3}}\right)) \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{3}{2}\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\sqrt{3})) \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{3}{2}\cdot \frac{\pi }{3}) \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right) \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186504632 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "3773932e-fae8-57ab-a030-de021b53748f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\lim_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=0}^{n-1}[{(2+\frac{i}{n})}^{4}\cdot \frac{1}{n}]" :db/id 17592186504128} {:answer/id #uuid "947fa02e-9a14-57a5-985e-c7e642d3bff6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\lim_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=0}^{n-1}[{(1+\frac{i}{n})}^{4}\cdot \frac{2}{n}]" :db/id 17592186504295} {:answer/id #uuid "9ddf0c06-3e13-5114-ae8a-765ff61402f7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\lim_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=0}^{n-1}[{(1+\frac{i}{n})}^{4}\cdot \frac{1}{n}]" :db/id 17592186504311} {:answer/id #uuid "ea0a3613-4a32-5b89-8a35-66e90173d741" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\lim_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=0}^{n-1}[{(1+\frac{i}{n})}^{4}\cdot \frac{4}{n}]" :db/id 17592186504437} {:answer/id #uuid "f561ae55-84c0-546c-9312-d11812ce786d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\lim_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=0}^{n-1}[{(2+\frac{i}{n})}^{4}\cdot \frac{2}{n}]" :db/id 17592186504460}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186504311} :answer-field/id #uuid "f3299ff3-e06a-576d-9e6b-49153eef928c" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186504596}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "5b26923d-aa9d-5c1e-919b-9d716067cb9d" :question/math-academy-id "q-113883" :question/problem "What is $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{1}^{2}{x}^{4}\,\text{d}x
$$ expressed as the limit of a left Riemann sum?" :question/worked-solution "The definite integral can be defined in terms of the limit of a left Riemann sum as

$$
{\int }_{a}^{b}f(x)\,\text{d}x=\lim_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=0}^{n-1}f({x}_{i})\cdot Δx,
$$

    

where $Δx=\frac{b-a}{n}$ and ${x}_{i}=a+iΔx.$

In the definite integral

$$
{\int }_{1}^{2}{x}^{4}\,\text{d}x,
$$

the function is $f(x)={x}^{4},$ the lower bound is $a=1,$ and the upper bound is $b=2.$ So, we have

$$
Δx=\frac{2-1}{n}=\frac{1}{n},
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{2}{x}^{4}\,\text{d}x & =\lim_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=0}^{n-1}f({x}_{i})\cdot Δx \\  & =\lim_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=0}^{n-1}[f(1+i\cdot \frac{1}{n})\,\cdot \frac{1}{n}] \\  & =\lim_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=0}^{n-1}[f(1+\frac{i}{n})\cdot \frac{1}{n}] \\  & =\lim_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=0}^{n-1}[{(1+\frac{i}{n})}^{4}\cdot \frac{1}{n}].\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186504637 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "9bdcbb96-5ec9-5007-b256-214fc5f8397c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{e}{3}" :db/id 17592186504308}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186504308} :answer-field/id #uuid "36d45e39-f71d-51b2-ae6d-2faee3a34b79" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186504499}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "650ff22d-86ac-5784-9e2d-04a2cd40b0db" :question/math-academy-id "q-341951" :question/problem "Find the slope $m$ of the tangent line to the curve $y=(\operatorname{ln}⁡(3x))^{{x}^{2}}$ at $x=\frac{e}{3}.$

$m=$
{{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "The slope of the tangent to the curve at $x=\frac{e}{3}$ equals the function's derivative at the corresponding point.

We have the function 

$$
y=(\operatorname{ln}⁡(3x))^{{x}^{2}}.
$$

First, we take the natural logarithm of both sides:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡((\operatorname{ln}⁡(3x))^{{x}^{2}}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & ={x}^{2}\,\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡(3x))\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we differentiate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2}\,\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡(3x))) \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot {y}^{′} & =({x}^{2})^{′}\cdot (\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡(3x)))+({x}^{2})\cdot {(\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡(3x)))}^{′} \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot {y}^{′} & =2x\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡(3x))+{x}^{2}\cdot (\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(3x)}\cdot \frac{1}{x}) \\ \frac{{y}^{′}}{y} & =2x\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡(3x))+\frac{x}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(3x)}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve for ${y}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =y(2x\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡(3x))+\frac{x}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(3x)})\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute $y=(\operatorname{ln}⁡(3x))^{{x}^{2}}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =(\operatorname{ln}⁡(3x))^{{x}^{2}}(2x\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡(3x))+\frac{x}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(3x)})\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of $y=(\operatorname{ln}⁡(3x))^{{x}^{2}}$ at $x=\frac{e}{3}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}m={y}^{′}{|}_{x=e/3} & =(\operatorname{ln}⁡(e))^{(e/3)^{2}}(2\left(\frac{e}{3}\right)\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡(e))+\frac{\left(\frac{e}{3}\right)}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(e)}) \\  & =(1)^{(e/3)^{2}}(2\left(\frac{e}{3}\right)\operatorname{ln}⁡(1)+\frac{\left(\frac{e}{3}\right)}{1}) \\  & =1\cdot (0+\frac{e}{3}) \\  & =\frac{e}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186504641 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "182d4fea-cab3-5c77-92d8-85665c78e002" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{tan}⁡x)+x\operatorname{csc}⁡x{\sec }^{2}⁡x" :db/id 17592186504074} {:answer/id #uuid "420d139d-afbe-5844-a8dd-8419647c77a8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{tan}⁡x)-\operatorname{csc}⁡x\operatorname{sec}⁡x" :db/id 17592186504145} {:answer/id #uuid "65ad5bd6-c5c9-54e5-bc74-3bf9d08af3ff" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{tan}⁡x)+x\operatorname{csc}⁡x\operatorname{sec}⁡x" :db/id 17592186504207} {:answer/id #uuid "86880236-33cf-5fe7-ad90-0ffd13b9f4a4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{tan}⁡x)+x\operatorname{sec}⁡x" :db/id 17592186504266} {:answer/id #uuid "d5c9c22c-95a4-5257-aadf-de4e6f6689bc" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{tan}⁡x)+\operatorname{tan}⁡x\operatorname{sec}⁡x" :db/id 17592186504403}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186504207} :answer-field/id #uuid "49f97b4d-3e4e-5d71-8051-0c4a12624cb5" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186504508}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "73c29bd9-9c93-5235-9a81-b902322f8bb3" :question/math-academy-id "q-138837" :question/problem "Consider the function $y=(\operatorname{tan}⁡x)^{x}.$ Its derivative is given by  

$$

$$

Find the function $g(x).$" :question/worked-solution "We have the function 

$$
y=(\operatorname{tan}⁡x)^{x}.
$$

First, we take the natural logarithm of both sides:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡((\operatorname{tan}⁡x)^{x}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =x\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{tan}⁡x)\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we differentiate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(x\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{tan}⁡x)) \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(x)\cdot (\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{tan}⁡x))+(x)\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{tan}⁡x)) \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =1\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{tan}⁡x)+x\cdot (\frac{1}{\operatorname{tan}⁡x}\cdot {\sec }^{2}⁡x) \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{tan}⁡x)+x\operatorname{csc}⁡x\operatorname{sec}⁡x\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve for $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =y(\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{tan}⁡x)+x\operatorname{csc}⁡x\operatorname{sec}⁡x)\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute $y=(\operatorname{tan}⁡x)^{x}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =(\operatorname{tan}⁡x)^{x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{tan}⁡x)+x\operatorname{csc}⁡x\operatorname{sec}⁡x)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $g(x)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{tan}⁡x)+x\operatorname{csc}⁡x\operatorname{sec}⁡x.$"} {:db/id 17592186504644 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "20c2c4de-610f-51d5-844f-c2ff3be490af" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1" :db/id 17592186504090}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186504090} :answer-field/id #uuid "d1fc9040-4cdf-577b-b242-fcc38c2ab2bd" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186504582}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "78505148-e7b2-516b-80ad-17e7629d4193" :question/math-academy-id "q-302680" :question/problem "Evaluate the following limit:

$$
z-{z}_{0}=(x-{x}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0})+(y-{y}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),
$$

where $$
\displaystyle ⟨\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),-1⟩
$$ represents a normal vector to the tangent plane.

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({e}^{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}) \\  & ={e}^{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\cdot 2x \\  & =2x{e}^{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({e}^{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}) \\  & ={e}^{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\cdot 2y \\  & =2y{e}^{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Hence, the normal vector to the tangent plane is 

$$
⟨2x{e}^{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}},\,2y{e}^{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}},\,-1⟩.
$$

Note that the tangent plane is horizontal if and only if the normal vector is vertical. This means that the $x$- and $y$-components of the vector must be $0:$

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} &=0 \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} &=0\end{aligned}\right.\,⟹\,\left\{\begin{aligned}2x{e}^{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}} &=0 \\ 2y{e}^{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}} &=0\end{aligned}\right.
$$

 

From the first equation, we get $x=0$ while the second equation gives $y=0.$ 

Finally, substituting $x=0$ and $y=0$ into our function, we get

$$
z={e}^{{0}^{2}+{0}^{2}}=1.
$$

Therefore, the point where the tangent plane is horizontal is $(0,0,1).$"} {:db/id 17592186504654 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "80e91b06-f9f7-58e7-9b93-fa4bf08254ae" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3" :db/id 17592186504257}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186504257} :answer-field/id #uuid "02fa8ffe-84d7-5a81-9584-e9e83fe39768" :answer-field/key "field-2" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186504479} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "e9b4387d-0850-5ada-aa3a-96062914b732" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "7x^{-3}" :db/id 17592186504436}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186504436} :answer-field/id #uuid "a295c97d-d2d9-5a3d-9891-87fc0cfd77f6" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186504549}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "92db8444-ee84-5a2b-a100-391911e28dfc" :question/math-academy-id "q-346192" :question/problem "Find the function $f(x)$ and the value of $b,$ given that

{{field-2}}" :question/worked-solution "A definite integral can be defined as the limit of a left Riemann sum as follows:

$$
{\int }_{a}^{b}f(x)\,\text{d}x=\lim_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=0}^{n-1}f({x}_{k})\cdot Δx
$$

where $Δx=\frac{b-a}{n}$ and ${x}_{k}=a+kΔx.$

Notice that we're given that the lower limit $a=1.$ 

Comparing the given summation with the general expression above, we see that $Δx=\frac{2}{n}.$ Therefore, 

$$
\frac{2}{n}=\frac{b-1}{n}\,⟹\,b=3.
$$

Consequently, ${x}_{k}=1+\frac{2k}{n}$ and $f({x}_{k})=7{x}_{k}^{-3}.$

Hence,

$$
{\int }_{1}^{3}7{x}^{-3}\,\text{d}x=\lim_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=0}^{n-1}[7{(1+\frac{2k}{n})}^{-3}\cdot \frac{2}{n}].
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is 

$$
f(x)=7{x}^{-3}\,\text{and}\,b=3.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186504655 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0a4055cd-dc46-58cf-9414-ebd3aeced26d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2\,i-\sqrt{\pi }\,j" :db/id 17592186504052} {:answer/id #uuid "169a9454-865f-5c99-afad-24018fd51b22" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\pi \,i-j" :db/id 17592186504072} {:answer/id #uuid "24013cd6-fd21-5ea4-a444-92864f2d2b61" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\pi \,j" :db/id 17592186504094} {:answer/id #uuid "24c7ddcb-f4c6-55ee-80f6-45bc59cf1057" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2\sqrt{\pi }\,i+2\,j" :db/id 17592186504096} {:answer/id #uuid "2fefcbb7-1707-5b33-9ea0-368b42c461ec" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-2\,i" :db/id 17592186504115}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186504096} :answer-field/id #uuid "ba947109-a6e8-5648-9e45-f1bf117b385d" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186504568}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "93366598-9424-5753-a6aa-f85435a0ef2f" :question/math-academy-id "q-130279" :question/problem "In what direction does the function $f(x,y)={e}^{2y}\operatorname{tan}⁡({x}^{2})$ increase most rapidly at the point $(\frac{\sqrt{\pi }}{2},0)?$" :question/worked-solution "At a given point, a function $f(x,y)$ increases most rapidly in the direction of its gradient at that point.

So, we compute $∇f(x,y)$ and evaluate it at the point $(1,-1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({e}^{2y}\operatorname{tan}⁡({x}^{2}))\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({e}^{2y}\operatorname{tan}⁡({x}^{2}))\,j \\  & =2x{e}^{2y}{\sec }^{2}⁡({x}^{2})\,i+2{e}^{2y}\operatorname{tan}⁡({x}^{2})\,j \\ ∇f(\frac{\sqrt{\pi }}{2},0) & =2\left(\frac{\sqrt{\pi }}{2}\right){e}^{0}{\sec }^{2}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right)\,i+2{e}^{0}\operatorname{tan}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right)\,j \\  & =2\sqrt{\pi }\,i+2\,j\end{aligned}

Therefore, the function increases most rapidly in the direction of $2\sqrt{\pi }\,i+2\,j.$"} {:db/id 17592186504656 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "b71b8dc8-607f-5822-afac-e0d10c462052" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\sin(x)\tan(x)" :db/id 17592186504349}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186504349} :answer-field/id #uuid "d1418ec4-9e2c-5aec-b01d-aff904f686c2" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186504581}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "965ab36a-7265-52be-bed3-0fcb25681407" :question/math-academy-id "q-341907" :question/problem "Given that $y=(\operatorname{sec}⁡(x))^{\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)}$, find ${y}^{′}.$

{{field-1}}$)$" :question/worked-solution "We have the function

$\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=(5{x}^{2}+2x)^{x-1}\cdot ($
{{field-1}}$+10{x}^{2}+2x)$" :question/worked-solution "We have the function 

$$
y=(5{x}^{2}+2x)^{x}.
$$

First, we take the natural logarithm of both sides:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡((5{x}^{2}+2x)^{x}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =x\operatorname{ln}⁡(5{x}^{2}+2x)\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we differentiate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(x\operatorname{ln}⁡(5{x}^{2}+2x)) \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(x)\cdot (\operatorname{ln}⁡(5{x}^{2}+2x))+(x)\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(5{x}^{2}+2x)) \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =1\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡(5{x}^{2}+2x)+x\cdot (\frac{1}{5{x}^{2}+2x}\cdot (10x+2)) \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(5{x}^{2}+2x)+\frac{10{x}^{2}+2x}{5{x}^{2}+2x}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve for $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =y(\operatorname{ln}⁡(5{x}^{2}+2x)+\frac{10{x}^{2}+2x}{5{x}^{2}+2x})\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute $y=(5{x}^{2}+2x)^{x}:$

We have the function 

$$

First, we take the natural logarithm of both sides:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡((\operatorname{ln}⁡x)^{5x}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =5x\,\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we differentiate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(5x\,\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)) \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot {y}^{′} & =(5x)^{′}\cdot (\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡x))+(5x)\cdot {(\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡x))}^{′} \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot {y}^{′} & =5\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)+5x\cdot (\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}\cdot \frac{1}{x}) \\ \frac{{y}^{′}}{y} & =5\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)+\frac{5}{\operatorname{ln}⁡x} \\ \frac{{y}^{′}}{y} & =5(\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)+\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡x})\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve for ${y}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =y(5(\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)+\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}))\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute $y=(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)^{5x}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =5(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)^{5x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)+\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡x})\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of $y=(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)^{5x}$ at $x=e$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}{|}_{x=e} & =5(\operatorname{ln}⁡e)^{5\cdot e}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡e)+\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡e}) \\  & =5(1)^{5e}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(1)+\frac{1}{1}) \\  & =5.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186504672 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "2c9696ed-0cf7-51a5-ab03-f99476ed2805" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1+\frac{4i}{n}" :db/id 17592186504110}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186504110} :answer-field/id #uuid "f2252516-11cb-503e-94e5-fbb51ee360c4" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186504594}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "bacd6074-8287-5758-9454-33c120a66361" :question/math-academy-id "q-346173" :question/problem "Express $$

$$
z-{z}_{0}=(x-{x}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0})+(y-{y}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),
$$

where $$
\displaystyle ⟨\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),-1⟩
$$ represents a normal vector to the tangent plane.

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(x\operatorname{ln}⁡y)=\operatorname{ln}⁡y \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(x\operatorname{ln}⁡y)=\frac{x}{y}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Hence, the normal vector to the tangent plane is 

$$
⟨\operatorname{ln}⁡y,\,\frac{x}{y},\,-1⟩.
$$

Note that the tangent plane is horizontal if and only if the normal vector is vertical. This means that the $x$- and $y$-components of the vector must be $0:$

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} &=0 \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} &=0\end{aligned}\right.\,⟹\,\left\{\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡y &=0 \\ \frac{x}{y} &=0\end{aligned}\right.
$$

 

From the first equation we get $y=1,$ while the second equation gives $x=0.$ 

Finally, substituting $x=0$ and $y=1$ into our function, we get

$$
z=0\operatorname{ln}⁡1=0.
$$

Therefore, the point where the tangent plane is horizontal is $(0,1,0).$"} {:db/id 17592186504692 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "016328d0-e890-5f0f-acd5-5481d9b4f783" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1+x\tan x\ln x" :db/id 17592186504033}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186504033} :answer-field/id #uuid "a32a9416-0150-598e-ac86-6202b9e0f123" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186504550}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "d597eea3-7247-5548-9071-6c8d8bbf677d" :question/math-academy-id "q-341717" :question/problem "Given that $y={x}^{\operatorname{sec}⁡x}$, find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}.$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{sec}⁡x\operatorname{ln}⁡x) \\ \frac{1}{y}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =(\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}\operatorname{sec}⁡x)\operatorname{ln}⁡x+\operatorname{sec}⁡x(\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}\operatorname{ln}⁡x) \\ \frac{1}{y}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =(\operatorname{sec}⁡x\operatorname{tan}⁡x)\operatorname{ln}⁡x+\operatorname{sec}⁡x\cdot \frac{1}{x}\end{aligned}

$$
{\int }_{0}^{2}(x+2)^{3}\,\text{d}x,

the function is $f(x)=(x+2)^{3},$ the lower bound is $a=0$ and the upper bound is $b=2.$ So, we have

$$

$$"} {:db/id 17592186504703 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "5de69524-b32f-529b-907d-70d9251c90c0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1-\ln x" :db/id 17592186504194}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186504194} :answer-field/id #uuid "8cbd0b0a-4f04-5099-bf6e-7a48a06d53ff" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186504543}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "e9eb4864-b21d-5e66-84e3-4be25804889c" :question/math-academy-id "q-341713" :question/problem "Given that $y=5e{x}^{1/x}$, find ${y}^{′}.$

{{field-1}}$)$" :question/worked-solution "The definition of $\operatorname{arsinh}⁡x$ is 

$$

$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{arsinh}⁡\left(\frac{4-{m}^{2}}{4m}\right) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{4-{m}^{2}}{4m}+\sqrt{{\left(\frac{4-{m}^{2}}{4m}\right)}^{2}+1}) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{4-{m}^{2}}{4m}+\sqrt{\frac{16-8{m}^{2}+{m}^{4}}{16{m}^{2}}+1}) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{4-{m}^{2}}{4m}+\sqrt{\frac{16+8{m}^{2}+{m}^{4}}{16{m}^{2}}}) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{4-{m}^{2}}{4m}+\sqrt{{\left(\frac{{m}^{2}+4}{4m}\right)}^{2}}) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{4-{m}^{2}}{4m}+|\frac{{m}^{2}+4}{4m}|)\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$"} {:db/id 17592186505756 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "dbc88f9e-cecb-5783-82a0-96646abc8723" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1\frac{1}{6}" :db/id 17592186505528}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186505528} :answer-field/id #uuid "83ca6591-abdc-5db7-b63f-855da19951b8" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186505667}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "34a9113a-d903-5269-9893-62edd17b6695" :question/math-academy-id "q-166822" :question/problem "In preparation for his entire week's work, the painter purchased $8\,\frac{5}{6}$ liters of thinner. $\,$liters of thinner left over." :question/worked-solution "The painter had $(8\,\frac{5}{6}-7\,\frac{2}{3})$ liters of thinner left over.

Writing $8\,\frac{5}{6}$ as an improper fraction, we have

$$
8\,\frac{5}{6}=\frac{8\times 6+5}{6}=\frac{53}{6}.
$$

Writing $7\,\frac{2}{3}$ as an improper fraction, we have

$$
7\,\frac{2}{3}=\frac{7\times 3+2}{3}=\frac{23}{3}.
$$

Therefore, our problem now is to work out the following:

$$
\frac{53}{6}-\frac{23}{3}
$$

To subtract two fractions with unlike denominators, we need to express each fraction as an equivalent fraction with a common denominator.

In this question, we can make a common denominator of $6.$

To put $\frac{23}{3}$ over a denominator of $6,$ we multiply the numerator and denominator by $2:$

$$
\frac{23}{3}=\frac{23\times 2}{3\times 2}=\frac{46}{6}
$$

We can now subtract the fractions. We keep the denominator the same, and we subtract the numerators:

$$
\frac{53}{6}-\frac{46}{6}=\frac{7}{6}
$$

Finally, we convert back to a mixed number:

$$
\frac{7}{6}=1\,\text{R}\,1=1\,\frac{1}{6}
$$

Therefore, the painter had $1\,\frac{1}{6}$ liters of thinner left over."} {:db/id 17592186505757 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "39889727-a276-5682-8ef7-8911020878d8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "xz(3xz+\operatorname{ln}⁡x)" :db/id 17592186505204} {:answer/id #uuid "4441e299-9c2b-5890-9b2f-cf910acd93da" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "xz(1+xz+\operatorname{ln}⁡x)" :db/id 17592186505243} {:answer/id #uuid "5670544a-efa4-5dea-bb60-d1317fd8ae11" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "xz(1+3yxz+2y\operatorname{ln}⁡x)" :db/id 17592186505277} {:answer/id #uuid "b1f47d0b-4c4f-560a-896d-281726884e02" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "xz(1+3{x}^{2}{z}^{2}+2xz\operatorname{ln}⁡x)" :db/id 17592186505452} {:answer/id #uuid "c2a78d89-bcff-52b4-a64b-a195e189c0f8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "xz(1+3xz+2\operatorname{ln}⁡x)" :db/id 17592186505481}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186505481} :answer-field/id #uuid "8ba8f018-adaf-5841-94d1-797bd241ddf9" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186505670}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "37458a2a-1dd8-5f4b-97d7-084609fd0a20" :question/math-academy-id "q-131291" :question/problem "Given that $F(x,y,z)=⟨\operatorname{ln}⁡x,x{z}^{3},{z}^{2}⟩$ and $f(x,y,z)={x}^{2}z,$ calculate $∇\cdot (f\,F).$" :question/worked-solution "We will use the following identity:

\displaystyle {\int }_{\pi /12}^{\pi /4}\frac{\operatorname{cot}⁡(2x)}{{\sin }^{4}⁡(2x)}\,\text{d}x=
$$" :question/worked-solution "We use the identity $$
\displaystyle \operatorname{cot}⁡2x=\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡2x}{\operatorname{sin}⁡2x}
$$ and rewrite the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{\pi /12}^{\pi /4}\frac{\operatorname{cot}⁡(2x)}{{\sin }^{4}⁡(2x)}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{\pi /12}^{\pi /4}\frac{1}{{\sin }^{4}⁡(2x)}\cdot \frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡2x}{\operatorname{sin}⁡2x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /12}^{\pi /4}\frac{1}{{\sin }^{5}⁡(2x)}\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡2x\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve this by substitution. Let $u=\operatorname{sin}⁡2x.$ Then 

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=2\operatorname{cos}⁡2x\,⟹\,\frac{1}{2}\text{d}u=\operatorname{cos}⁡2x\,\text{d}x.
$$

Now, we fill the table for the limits of integration, according to the rule $u=\operatorname{sin}⁡2x.$

| $x$ | $\frac{\pi }{12}$ | $\frac{\pi }{4}$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $\frac{1}{2}$ | $1$ |

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(({x}^{2}+2x)^{6}(\operatorname{sin}⁡x)^{1/3}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(({x}^{2}+2x)^{6})+\operatorname{ln}⁡((\operatorname{sin}⁡x)^{1/3}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =6\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+2x)+\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{sin}⁡x)\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we differentiate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(6\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+2x)+\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{sin}⁡x)) \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot {y}^{′} & =6\cdot \frac{1}{{x}^{2}+2x}\cdot (2x+2)+\frac{1}{3}\cdot \frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡x) \\ \frac{{y}^{′}}{y} & =\frac{12(x+1)}{{x}^{2}+2x}+\frac{\operatorname{cot}⁡x}{3}\end{aligned}

Now, we solve for ${y}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =y(\frac{12(x+1)}{{x}^{2}+2x}+\frac{\operatorname{cot}⁡x}{3})\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute $y=({x}^{2}+2x)^{6}\sqrt{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}:$

$$

$$

What is the variance of the number of times the spinner lands on blue?" :question/worked-solution "Let the random variable $X$ be equal to the number of times the spinner lands on blue.

Here, we have the following information:

- there are $n=21$ trials

- the probability of landing on blue is

$$
p=\frac{1}{3}.
$$

So, $X$ follows a binomial distribution, where $X∼B(21,\frac{1}{3}).$

For a binomial random variable $X,$ the variance is given by

$$
\text{Var}[X]=np(1-p),
$$

where $n$ is the number of experiments and $p$ is the probability of success on each experiment.

So, the variance of the number of times the spinner lands on blue is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X] & =np(1-p) \\  & =21\cdot \frac{1}{3}\cdot (1-\frac{1}{3}) \\  & =7\cdot \frac{2}{3} \\  & =\frac{14}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186506513 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "39eac370-b597-5b13-a139-ed248af8a490" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4" :db/id 17592186506009} {:answer/id #uuid "3e37cd6e-52b0-57de-acb7-d9a7a4ef0fe1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-4" :db/id 17592186506014} {:answer/id #uuid "6c234f23-48fe-556c-a0b1-24c477bfbdfa" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1" :db/id 17592186506100} {:answer/id #uuid "d2bacdde-7997-50ac-944f-7a50e4a49e86" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0" :db/id 17592186506288} {:answer/id #uuid "deac3608-20ae-52c0-97b0-276c7fcb4d55" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-1" :db/id 17592186506310}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186506288} :answer-field/id #uuid "c3dff71e-7253-5db5-a8db-526f8787e942" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186506474}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "11c48698-c6fd-5725-a4b0-1737e6fdc309" :question/math-academy-id "q-138831" :question/problem "Consider the function $y=\frac{(x+6)^{3}{\cos }^{4}⁡x}{(x-1)^{7}}.$  The derivative of this function is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}A(t)\,dt & =A(t)(-\frac{1}{s}{e}^{-st})\,{|}_{0}^{\infty }-{\int }_{0}^{\infty }({{field-4}}){A}^{′}(t)\,dt\end{aligned}
$$

." :question/worked-solution "Let $A(t)$ be the anti-derivative of $f(t)$ such that ${A}^{′}(t)=f(t)$ and $A(0)=0.$ Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{t}f(τ)\,dτ & =A(τ)\,{|}_{0}^{t} \\  & =A(t)-A(0) \\  & =A(t).\end{aligned}
$$

By definition of the Laplace transform, we can write

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{{\int }_{0}^{t}f(τ)\,\text{d}τ\} & =L\{A(t)\}={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}A(t)\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's use integration by parts:

$$
\begin{aligned}u=A(t) & \,⇒\, & du={A}^{′}(t)\,dt \\ dv={e}^{-st}\,dt & ⇒ & v=-\frac{1}{s}{e}^{-st}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting into the integration by parts formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}A(t)\,dt & =A(t)(-\frac{1}{s}{e}^{-st})\,{|}_{0}^{\infty }-{\int }_{0}^{\infty }(-\frac{1}{s}{e}^{-st}){A}^{′}(t)\,dt.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $A(0)=0$ and $\frac{1}{s}{e}^{-st}\to 0$ as $t\to \infty ,$ we have $-\frac{1}{s}A(t){e}^{-st}{|}_{0}^{\infty }=0$ and

$$
{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}A(t)\,dt=\frac{1}{s}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}{A}^{′}(t)\,dt.
$$

Finally, using that ${A}^{′}(t)=f(t),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{s}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}{A}^{′}(t)\,dt & =\frac{1}{s}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}f(t)\,dt \\  & =\frac{1}{s}\cdot F(s) \\  & =\frac{F(s)}{s}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186506525 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "6fc9c0e4-94e6-5a58-b402-1569ccdf0546" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$p+q=\frac{19}{4},\,z=-4$ and $z=1$" :db/id 17592186506114} {:answer/id #uuid "854c086c-10d6-59fc-a728-734ed635b82f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$p+q=-\frac{19}{4},\,z=4$ and $z=-1$" :db/id 17592186506144} {:answer/id #uuid "9dedfe61-c595-5e0a-ab8d-634757cce0c0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$p+q=\frac{25}{4},\,z=-4$ and $z=-1$" :db/id 17592186506189} {:answer/id #uuid "a3b96d21-d357-5674-892a-42feaf9e8b50" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$p+q=\frac{3}{4},\,z=4$ and $z=-7$" :db/id 17592186506208} {:answer/id #uuid "f0eb231a-0f38-50bf-8cf9-3768fa9ab226" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$p+q=\frac{19}{4},\,z=4$ and $z=-1$" :db/id 17592186506356}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186506356} :answer-field/id #uuid "9418bd8b-7dee-502f-b277-9872940fd25e" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186506447}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "2236615a-502f-5e6f-8a3b-d0bb2e05f4c6" :question/math-academy-id "q-35049" :question/problem "The equation $3{z}^{2}-12=9z$ can be written in the form $(z+p)^{2}=q.$ Find $\,p+q,$ and solve the equation." :question/worked-solution "First, we complete the square on the left-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}3{z}^{2}-12 & =9z \\ 3{z}^{2}-9z-12 & =0 \\ 3({z}^{2}-3z-4) & =0 \\ {z}^{2}-3z-4 & =0 \\ {z}^{2}-2\cdot z\cdot \frac{3}{2} & =4 \\ {z}^{2}-2\cdot z\cdot \frac{3}{2}+{\left(\frac{3}{2}\right)}^{2}-{\left(\frac{3}{2}\right)}^{2} & =-4 \\ [{z}^{2}-2\cdot z\cdot \frac{3}{2}+{\left(\frac{3}{2}\right)}^{2}]-{\left(\frac{3}{2}\right)}^{2} & =-4 \\ {(z-\frac{3}{2})}^{2}-{\left(\frac{3}{2}\right)}^{2} & =4 \\ {(z-\frac{3}{2})}^{2}-\frac{25}{4} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we isolate the perfect square:

$$
\begin{aligned}{(z-\frac{3}{2})}^{2}-{\left(\frac{3}{2}\right)}^{2} & =4 \\ {(z-\frac{3}{2})}^{2} & =\frac{25}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

So, $p=-\frac{3}{2},q=\frac{25}{4}$ and $p+q=\frac{19}{4}.$

Now, we solve the equation using the square-root method:

$$
\begin{aligned}{(z-\frac{3}{2})}^{2} & =\frac{25}{4} \\ \sqrt{{(z-\frac{3}{2})}^{2}} & =\sqrt{\frac{25}{4}} \\ |z-\frac{3}{2}| & =\frac{5}{2} \\ z-\frac{3}{2} & =\pm \frac{5}{2} \\ z & =\frac{3}{2}\pm \frac{5}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

We simplify the two solutions:

$$
\begin{aligned}z & =\frac{3}{2}+\frac{5}{2}=4 \\ z & =\frac{3}{2}-\frac{5}{2}=-1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solutions are $z=4$ and $z=-1.$"} {:db/id 17592186506527 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "419792fe-6389-5363-a771-125381c66945" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "8x^3+8x" :db/id 17592186506021}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186506021} :answer-field/id #uuid "b1cca9dd-6ad8-57a8-a947-88e8f34aa52d" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186506463}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "254041d3-aef5-5074-80f4-67b8b1344bc0" :question/math-academy-id "q-312672" :question/problem "Given that $y=\sqrt{\frac{{({x}^{4}+2{x}^{2}+8)}^{2}}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}},$ find ${y}^{′}.$

${y}^{′}=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}}($
{{field-1}}$+\,\operatorname{tan}⁡x({x}^{4}+2{x}^{2}+8))$" :question/worked-solution "Our function can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =\sqrt{\frac{{({x}^{4}+2{x}^{2}+8)}^{2}}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{{({x}^{4}+2{x}^{2}+8)}^{2}}}{\sqrt{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}} \\  & =\frac{{x}^{4}+2{x}^{2}+8}{(\operatorname{cos}⁡x)^{1/2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

First, we take the natural logarithm of both sides and use the quotient and power rules for logarithms:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡\left(\frac{{x}^{4}+2{x}^{2}+8}{(\operatorname{cos}⁡x)^{1/2}}\right) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{4}+2{x}^{2}+8)-\operatorname{ln}⁡((\operatorname{cos}⁡x)^{1/2}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{4}+2{x}^{2}+8)-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{cos}⁡x)\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we differentiate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{4}+2{x}^{2}+8)-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{cos}⁡x)) \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot {y}^{′} & =\frac{1}{{x}^{4}+2{x}^{2}+8}\cdot (4{x}^{3}+4x)-\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡x) \\ \frac{{y}^{′}}{y} & =\frac{4{x}^{3}+4x}{{x}^{4}+2{x}^{2}+8}+\frac{\operatorname{tan}⁡x}{2} \\ \frac{{y}^{′}}{y} & =\frac{1}{2}(\frac{8{x}^{3}+8x}{{x}^{4}+2{x}^{2}+8}+\operatorname{tan}⁡x)\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we solve for ${y}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =\frac{y}{2}(\frac{8{x}^{3}+8x}{{x}^{4}+2{x}^{2}+8}+\operatorname{tan}⁡x)\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute $y=\sqrt{\frac{{({x}^{4}+2{x}^{2}+8)}^{2}}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =\sqrt{\frac{{({x}^{4}+2{x}^{2}+8)}^{2}}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}}\cdot \frac{1}{2}(\frac{8{x}^{3}+8x}{{x}^{4}+2{x}^{2}+8}+\operatorname{tan}⁡x) \\  & =\frac{|{x}^{4}+2{x}^{2}+8|}{2\sqrt{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}}(\frac{8{x}^{3}+8x}{{x}^{4}+2{x}^{2}+8}+\operatorname{tan}⁡x)\end{aligned}
$$

Since ${x}^{4}+2{x}^{2}+8>0\text{ }∀x\in R$, so $|{x}^{4}+2{x}^{2}+8|={x}^{4}+2{x}^{2}+8$ and we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =\frac{{x}^{4}+2{x}^{2}+8}{2\sqrt{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}}(\frac{8{x}^{3}+8x}{{x}^{4}+2{x}^{2}+8}+\operatorname{tan}⁡x) \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}}[\frac{8{x}^{3}+8x}{{x}^{4}+2{x}^{2}+8}\cdot ({x}^{4}+2{x}^{2}+8)+\operatorname{tan}⁡x({x}^{4}+2{x}^{2}+8)] \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}}(8{x}^{3}+8x+\operatorname{tan}⁡x({x}^{4}+2{x}^{2}+8))\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186506532 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "4ebc9a01-e27f-509b-a68a-42b56dc2ad7d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\ln(6)" :db/id 17592186506045}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186506045} :answer-field/id #uuid "7487540a-070b-5d24-9ba2-dc636972e043" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186506432} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "ec54cd01-acca-5a25-833a-60eab750baf4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "18" :db/id 17592186506345}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186506345} :answer-field/id #uuid "a0efc8ad-b4c8-5f06-a724-3416448817ff" :answer-field/key "field-3" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186506453} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "97af42c5-8f26-50fc-a29e-fb1a80f1a04f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "7" :db/id 17592186506175}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186506175} :answer-field/id #uuid "d150bf24-0895-5aa8-98a7-c4a97ebe264b" :answer-field/key "field-2" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186506482}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "310e9298-b624-54d9-ac03-bed77b7fdecc" :question/math-academy-id "q-343350" :question/problem "Consider the function $y=\frac{{6}^{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}}{(x-2)^{4}(3-x)^{3}}.$  Find ${y}^{′}.$

y=\frac{{6}^{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}}{(x-2)^{4}(3-x)^{3}}.
$$

First, we take the natural logarithm of both sides and use the quotient, product, and power rules for logarithms:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡\left(\frac{{6}^{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}}{(x-2)^{4}(3-x)^{3}}\right) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({6}^{\operatorname{cos}⁡x})-\operatorname{ln}⁡((x-2)^{4}(3-x)^{3}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\operatorname{ln}⁡6-(\operatorname{ln}⁡((x-2)^{4})+\operatorname{ln}⁡((3-x)^{3})) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\operatorname{ln}⁡6-4\operatorname{ln}⁡(x-2)-3\operatorname{ln}⁡(3-x)\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we differentiate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\operatorname{ln}⁡6)-\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(4\operatorname{ln}⁡(x-2))-\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(3\operatorname{ln}⁡(3-x)) \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot {y}^{′} & =-(\operatorname{ln}⁡6)\operatorname{sin}⁡x-4\cdot \frac{1}{x-2}-3\cdot \frac{-1}{3-x} \\ \frac{{y}^{′}}{y} & =-(\operatorname{ln}⁡6)\operatorname{sin}⁡x-\frac{4}{x-2}+\frac{3}{3-x}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve for ${y}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =y(-(\operatorname{ln}⁡6)\operatorname{sin}⁡x-\frac{4}{x-2}+\frac{3}{3-x})\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute $y=\frac{{6}^{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}}{(x-2)^{4}(3-x)^{3}}:$

Remember, when multiplying or dividing an inequality by a negative number, we need to flip the inequality sign:

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{a}{4}\,\, & >\,\,-2 \\ (-4)\cdot \left(-\frac{a}{4}\right)\,\, & <\,\,(-4)\cdot (-2) \\ (-4)\cdot \left(-\frac{a}{4}\right)\,\, & <\,\,8\end{aligned}
$$

Since two negative numbers multiply to give a positive number, we first cancel the negatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}(-4)\cdot \left(-\frac{a}{4}\right) & <8 \\ (\cancel{-}4)\cdot (\cancel{-}\frac{a}{4}) & <8 \\ 4\cdot \frac{a}{4} & <8\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can cancel a common factor of $4$ from both the numerator and denominator.

$$
\begin{aligned}4\cdot \frac{a}{4} & <8 \\ \frac{4a}{4} & <8 \\ \frac{\cancel{4}a}{\cancel{4}} & <8 \\ a & <8\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution is $a<8.$ The solution can be expressed on a number line, as shown below.

$$
\begin{aligned}(-1)\cdot (-4{x}^{2}-6x+10) & =(-1)\cdot 0 \\ 4{x}^{2}+6x-10 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Now we move the constant term to the right-hand side and complete the square on the left-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}4{x}^{2}+6x-10 & =0 \\ 4{x}^{2}+6x & =10 \\ 4{x}^{2}+6x & =10 \\ 4({x}^{2}+\frac{3}{2}x) & =10 \\ 4[{x}^{2}+2\cdot \frac{3}{4}x+{\left(\frac{3}{4}\right)}^{2}-{\left(\frac{3}{4}\right)}^{2}] & =10 \\ 4[{(x+\frac{3}{4})}^{2}-\frac{9}{16}] & =10\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we expand the brackets, and write the equation in the required form:

$$
\begin{aligned}4{(x+\frac{3}{4})}^{2}-4\cdot \frac{9}{16} & =10 \\ 4{(x+\frac{3}{4})}^{2}-\frac{9}{4} & =10 \\ 4{(x+\frac{3}{4})}^{2} & =10+\frac{9}{4} \\ 4{(x+\frac{3}{4})}^{2} & =\frac{49}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $p=\frac{3}{4}.$ We now solve the equation using the square root method:

$$
\begin{aligned}4{(x+\frac{3}{4})}^{2} & =\frac{49}{4} \\ {(x+\frac{3}{4})}^{2} & =\frac{49}{16} \\ \sqrt{{(x+\frac{3}{4})}^{2}} & =\sqrt{\frac{49}{16}} \\ |x+\frac{3}{4}| & =\frac{7}{4} \\ x+\frac{3}{4} & =\pm \frac{7}{4} \\ x & =-\frac{3}{4}\pm \frac{7}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

We simplify the two solutions:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =-\frac{3}{4}-\frac{7}{4}=-\frac{10}{4}=-\frac{5}{2} \\ x & =-\frac{3}{4}+\frac{7}{4}=1\end{aligned}
$$

So, the solutions are $x=-\frac{5}{2}$ and $x=1.$"} {:db/id 17592186506552 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "04c28e5d-0de9-502d-81aa-7351f4920069" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-2" :db/id 17592186505924} {:answer/id #uuid "90c27865-1c0b-519b-81bb-de523a0ce9d7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "5" :db/id 17592186506157} {:answer/id #uuid "93851dca-79be-57a5-b496-18ef7187487f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "14" :db/id 17592186506161} {:answer/id #uuid "b193db5a-f715-5820-8744-ed3301ee43c4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "18" :db/id 17592186506234} {:answer/id #uuid "ebacda43-d38a-518b-8124-0083b7f84186" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186506342}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186506342} :answer-field/id #uuid "1d436c14-aa02-5c1c-8f96-e30ae5edad2a" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186506389}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "76085196-6a2f-5c76-90cb-5c742aa98a2b" :question/math-academy-id "q-138849" :question/problem "Consider the function $y=\sqrt{({x}^{2}+1)^{3}(x-3)^{8}}.$ The derivative of this function is given by

$$
{y}^{′}=\sqrt{{x}^{2}+1}(x-3)^{3}(a{x}^{2}+bx+c).

Find the value of $a+b+c.$" :question/worked-solution "Our function can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =\sqrt{({x}^{2}+1)^{3}(x-3)^{8}} \\  & =\sqrt{({x}^{2}+1)^{3}}\cdot \sqrt{(x-3)^{8}} \\  & =({x}^{2}+1)^{3/2}(x-3)^{8/2} \\  & =({x}^{2}+1)^{3/2}(x-3)^{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

First, we take the natural logarithm of both sides and use the product and power rules for logarithms:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(({x}^{2}+1)^{3/2}(x-3)^{4}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(({x}^{2}+1)^{3/2})+\operatorname{ln}⁡((x-3)^{4}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\frac{3}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+1)+4\operatorname{ln}⁡(x-3)\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we differentiate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{3}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+1)+4\operatorname{ln}⁡(x-3)) \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot {y}^{′} & =\frac{3}{2}\cdot \frac{1}{{x}^{2}+1}\cdot 2x+4\cdot \frac{1}{x-3} \\ \frac{{y}^{′}}{y} & =\frac{3x}{{x}^{2}+1}+\frac{4}{x-3}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve for ${y}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =y(\frac{3x}{{x}^{2}+1}+\frac{4}{x-3})\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute $y=\sqrt{({x}^{2}+1)^{3}(x-3)^{8}}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =\sqrt{({x}^{2}+1)^{3}(x-3)^{8}}(\frac{3x}{{x}^{2}+1}+\frac{4}{x-3}) \\  & =\sqrt{({x}^{2}+1)^{3}(x-3)^{8}}\left(\frac{3x(x-3)+4({x}^{2}+1)}{({x}^{2}+1)(x-3)}\right) \\  & =\sqrt{({x}^{2}+1)^{3}(x-3)^{8}}\left(\frac{7{x}^{2}-9x+4}{({x}^{2}+1)(x-3)}\right) \\  & =({x}^{2}+1)^{3/2}(x-3)^{4}\left(\frac{7{x}^{2}-9x+4}{({x}^{2}+1)(x-3)}\right) \\  & =({x}^{2}+1)^{1/2}(x-3)^{3}(7{x}^{2}-9x+4) \\  & =\sqrt{{x}^{2}+1}(x-3)^{3}(7{x}^{2}-9x+4)\end{aligned}
$$

  

Therefore,

$$
a+b+c=7+(-9)+4=2.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186506564 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "102790ff-7839-5d1c-a7c1-c89c090c0d2a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "18" :db/id 17592186505942}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186505942} :answer-field/id #uuid "274547bb-be34-5b65-bb9d-f32876fabd37" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186506398} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "f4323142-e936-5cd3-b6de-3092378faa67" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "16" :db/id 17592186506359}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186506359} :answer-field/id #uuid "94665d5f-2175-540b-accc-e742e344e1b0" :answer-field/key "field-3" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186506448} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "5274db64-5e9a-58d1-a778-b4f7735c7525" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186506050}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186506050} :answer-field/id #uuid "b03d9a12-bbbf-5ee1-a420-92022427414d" :answer-field/key "field-2" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186506461}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "8a442047-ed6e-5bb4-89b9-beaee4b1e553" :question/math-academy-id "q-338291" :question/problem "Consider the function $y=\frac{(x+2)^{4}}{{({x}^{3}+2x-1)}^{3}}.$  Find the derivative of $y.$

$$

$$

Find the value of $a+b+c.$" :question/worked-solution "Our function can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =\sqrt{\frac{{x}^{4}+2x}{{x}^{2}+2x+2}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{{x}^{4}+2x}}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+2x+2}} \\  & =\frac{({x}^{4}+2x)^{1/2}}{({x}^{2}+2x+2)^{1/2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

First, we take the natural logarithm of both sides and use the quotient and power rules for logarithms:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡\left(\frac{({x}^{4}+2x)^{1/2}}{({x}^{2}+2x+2)^{1/2}}\right) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(({x}^{4}+2x)^{1/2})-\operatorname{ln}⁡(({x}^{2}+2x+2)^{1/2}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{4}+2x)-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+2x+2)\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we differentiate both sides with respect to $x:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{4}+2x)-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+2x+2)) \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot {y}^{′} & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{1}{{x}^{4}+2x}\cdot (4{x}^{3}+2)-\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{1}{{x}^{2}+2x+2}\cdot (2x+2) \\ \frac{{y}^{′}}{y} & =\frac{2{x}^{3}+1}{{x}^{4}+2x}-\frac{x+1}{{x}^{2}+2x+2}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we solve for ${y}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =y(\frac{2{x}^{3}+1}{{x}^{4}+2x}-\frac{x+1}{{x}^{2}+2x+2})\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute $y=\sqrt{\frac{{x}^{4}+2x}{{x}^{2}+2x+2}}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =\sqrt{\frac{{x}^{4}+2x}{{x}^{2}+2x+2}}(\frac{2{x}^{3}+1}{{x}^{4}+2x}-\frac{x+1}{{x}^{2}+2x+2}) \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{{x}^{4}+2x}{{x}^{2}+2x+2}}\left(\frac{(2{x}^{3}+1)({x}^{2}+2x+2)-(x+1)({x}^{4}+2x)}{({x}^{4}+2x)({x}^{2}+2x+2)}\right) \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{{x}^{4}+2x}{{x}^{2}+2x+2}}\left(\frac{2{x}^{5}+4{x}^{4}+4{x}^{3}+{x}^{2}+2x+2-({x}^{5}+{x}^{4}+2{x}^{2}+2x)}{({x}^{4}+2x)({x}^{2}+2x+2)}\right) \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{{x}^{4}+2x}{{x}^{2}+2x+2}}\left(\frac{{x}^{5}+3{x}^{4}+4{x}^{3}-{x}^{2}+2}{({x}^{4}+2x)({x}^{2}+2x+2)}\right) \\  & =\frac{1{x}^{5}+3{x}^{4}+4{x}^{3}-{x}^{2}+2}{({x}^{2}+2x+2)^{3/2}\sqrt{{x}^{4}+2x}}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
a+b+c=1+4+2=7.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186506591 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0f59a9ba-364e-508e-a41a-55a558b2bb49" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2x(x+1)\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1)" :db/id 17592186505941} {:answer/id #uuid "478822c2-e030-5e90-884b-19998c062866" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x(x+2)\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)" :db/id 17592186506029} {:answer/id #uuid "75b16ee9-4f9f-5d41-b9b6-01fc0fada42c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x(x+1)\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1)" :db/id 17592186506121} {:answer/id #uuid "9e556be2-fc3f-5682-8727-573dea82908b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2x(x+1)\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)" :db/id 17592186506192} {:answer/id #uuid "cb83d552-a42d-5c11-aa25-bd36f59bc3ed" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x(x+2)\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1)" :db/id 17592186506272}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186505941} :answer-field/id #uuid "63b209a8-1c66-5330-a9ec-0e55e08cba8c" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186506421}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "dbe4c4ed-7bf7-5234-8564-800989eb5aa4" :question/math-academy-id "q-138839" :question/problem "Consider the function $y=\frac{(x+1)^{{x}^{2}}}{{e}^{2-4x}}.$ The derivative of this function is given by
