Given a population in which a proportion $p$ of the population has a particular characteristic, the sampling distribution of the sample proportion $\widehat{\,p}$ can be approximated as

$$
\widehat{\,p}∼N(p,\frac{p(1-p)}{n}),
$$

where the sample size $n$ is much smaller than the population size, $np>5,$ and $n(1-p)>5.$

In our case

- the sample size is $n=350,$ and

- the population proportion is $p=0.7.$

Now, since

$$
np=350(0.7)=245>5
$$

and

$$
n(1-p)=350(1-0.7)=105>5,
$$

and $n=350$ is much smaller than the population size, we can apply the above approximation.

The sampling distribution of the sample proportion, in this case, can be approximated as

$$
\begin{aligned}\widehat{\,p} & ∼N(p,\frac{p(1-p)}{n}) \\  & ∼N(0.7,\frac{0.7(1-0.7)}{350}) \\  & ∼N(0.7,0.0006).\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we determine the probability we wish to find. If fewer than $224$ apricots in the sample weigh more than $40$ g, then 

$$
\widehat{\,p}<\frac{224}{350}=0.64.
$$

Hence, the probability we wish to find is
$P(\widehat{\,p}<0.64).$
So, we convert $\widehat{\,p}$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(\widehat{\,p}<0.64) & =P(Z<\frac{0.64-0.7}{\sqrt{0.0006}}) \\  & ≈P(Z<-2.45) \\  & =Φ(-2.45).\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\operatorname{sinh}⁡x=\frac{1}{2}({e}^{x}-{e}^{-x}).
$$

Substituting the above definition into the equation $4\operatorname{sinh}⁡x=-3,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}4\cdot (\frac{1}{2}({e}^{x}-{e}^{-x})) & =-3 \\ 2({e}^{x}-{e}^{-x}) & =-3 \\ 2{e}^{x}-2{e}^{-x} & =-3.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we multiply both sides of the equation by ${e}^{x},$ and simplify:

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{x}\cdot (2{e}^{x}-2{e}^{-x}) & ={e}^{x}\cdot (-3) \\ 2{e}^{2x}-2 & =-3{e}^{x} \\ 2{e}^{2x}+3{e}^{x}-2 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

This is a quadratic equation in ${e}^{x}$ that we can factor as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}(2{e}^{x}-1)({e}^{x}+2) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

By the zero-product property, we have to solve two equations:

$$
2{e}^{x}-1=0,\,{e}^{x}+2=0
$$

Solving the two equations above for $x,$ we get:

$$
\begin{aligned}2{e}^{x}-1 & =0 &  & \, & {e}^{x}+2 & =0 \\ {e}^{x} & =\frac{1}{2} &  & \, & {e}^{x} & =-2 \\ x & =\operatorname{ln}⁡\left(\frac{1}{2}\right) &  & \, & \end{aligned}
$$

There are no real values of $x$ for which ${e}^{x}=-2.$ Therefore, $x=\operatorname{ln}⁡\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)$ is the only real solution to the equation.

$$

Instead, let's recall the following special limit:

$$
\lim_{n\to \infty }{(1+\frac{1}{n})}^{n}=e
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\lim_{x\to \infty }{\left(\frac{x}{x-1}\right)}^{3x-3} & =\lim_{x\to \infty }{\left(\frac{(x-1)+1}{x-1}\right)}^{3x-3} \\  & =\lim_{x\to \infty }{(1+\frac{1}{x-1})}^{3(x-1)}\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

$$

The Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the surface $z=f(x,y)$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ on the surface can be written as

$$
z-{z}_{0}=(x-{x}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0})+(y-{y}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),
$$

where $$
\displaystyle ⟨\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),-1⟩
$$ represents a normal vector to the tangent plane.

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(xy-3x+2y-5)=y-3 \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(xy-3x+2y-5)=x+2\end{aligned}
$$

 

Hence, the normal vector to the tangent plane is 

$$
⟨y-3,\,x+2,\,-1⟩.
$$

Note that the tangent plane is horizontal if and only if the normal vector is vertical. This means that the $x$- and $y$-components of the vector must be $0:$

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} &=0 \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} &=0\end{aligned}\right.\,⟹\,\left\{\begin{aligned}y-3 &=0 \\ x+2 &=0\end{aligned}\right.
$$

 

From the second equation we get $x=-2,$ while the first equation gives $y=3.$ 

Finally, substituting $x=-2$ and $y=3$ into our function, we get

$$
z=(-2)(3)-3(-2)+2(3)-5=1.
$$

Therefore, the point where the tangent plane is horizontal is $(-2,3,1).$

The Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the surface $z=f(x,y)$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ on the surface can be written as

$$
z-{z}_{0}=(x-{x}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0})+(y-{y}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),
$$

where $$
\displaystyle ⟨\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),-1⟩
$$ represents a normal vector to the tangent plane.

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({e}^{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}) \\  & ={e}^{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\cdot 2x \\  & =2x{e}^{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({e}^{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}) \\  & ={e}^{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\cdot 2y \\  & =2y{e}^{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Hence, the normal vector to the tangent plane is 

$$
⟨2x{e}^{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}},\,2y{e}^{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}},\,-1⟩.
$$

Note that the tangent plane is horizontal if and only if the normal vector is vertical. This means that the $x$- and $y$-components of the vector must be $0:$

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} &=0 \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} &=0\end{aligned}\right.\,⟹\,\left\{\begin{aligned}2x{e}^{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}} &=0 \\ 2y{e}^{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}} &=0\end{aligned}\right.
$$

 

From the first equation, we get $x=0$ while the second equation gives $y=0.$ 

Finally, substituting $x=0$ and $y=0$ into our function, we get

$$
z={e}^{{0}^{2}+{0}^{2}}=1.
$$

Therefore, the point where the tangent plane is horizontal is $(0,0,1).$

A definite integral can be defined as the limit of a left Riemann sum as follows:

$$
{\int }_{a}^{b}f(x)\,\text{d}x=\lim_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=0}^{n-1}f({x}_{k})\cdot Δx
$$

where $Δx=\frac{b-a}{n}$ and ${x}_{k}=a+kΔx.$

Notice that we're given that the lower limit $a=1.$ 

Comparing the given summation with the general expression above, we see that $Δx=\frac{4}{n}.$ Therefore, 

$$
\frac{4}{n}=\frac{b-1}{n}\,⟹\,b=5.
$$

Consequently, ${x}_{k}=1+\frac{4k}{n}$ and $f({x}_{k})=\sqrt{{x}_{k}+1}.$

Hence,

$$
{\int }_{1}^{5}\sqrt{x+1}\,\text{d}x=\lim_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=0}^{n-1}[\sqrt{(1+\frac{4k}{n})+1}\cdot \frac{4}{n}].
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is 

$$
f(x)=\sqrt{x+1}\,\text{and}\,b=5.
$$

The Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the surface $z=f(x,y)$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ on the surface can be written as

$$
z-{z}_{0}=(x-{x}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0})+(y-{y}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),
$$

where $$
\displaystyle ⟨\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),-1⟩
$$ represents a normal vector to the tangent plane.

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(x\operatorname{ln}⁡y)=\operatorname{ln}⁡y \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(x\operatorname{ln}⁡y)=\frac{x}{y}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Hence, the normal vector to the tangent plane is 

$$
⟨\operatorname{ln}⁡y,\,\frac{x}{y},\,-1⟩.
$$

Note that the tangent plane is horizontal if and only if the normal vector is vertical. This means that the $x$- and $y$-components of the vector must be $0:$

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} &=0 \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} &=0\end{aligned}\right.\,⟹\,\left\{\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡y &=0 \\ \frac{x}{y} &=0\end{aligned}\right.
$$

 

From the first equation we get $y=1,$ while the second equation gives $x=0.$ 

Finally, substituting $x=0$ and $y=1$ into our function, we get

$$
z=0\operatorname{ln}⁡1=0.
$$

Therefore, the point where the tangent plane is horizontal is $(0,1,0).$

The painter had $(8\,\frac{5}{6}-7\,\frac{2}{3})$ liters of thinner left over.

Writing $8\,\frac{5}{6}$ as an improper fraction, we have

$$
8\,\frac{5}{6}=\frac{8\times 6+5}{6}=\frac{53}{6}.
$$

Writing $7\,\frac{2}{3}$ as an improper fraction, we have

$$
7\,\frac{2}{3}=\frac{7\times 3+2}{3}=\frac{23}{3}.
$$

Therefore, our problem now is to work out the following:

$$
\frac{53}{6}-\frac{23}{3}
$$

To subtract two fractions with unlike denominators, we need to express each fraction as an equivalent fraction with a common denominator.

In this question, we can make a common denominator of $6.$

To put $\frac{23}{3}$ over a denominator of $6,$ we multiply the numerator and denominator by $2:$

$$
\frac{23}{3}=\frac{23\times 2}{3\times 2}=\frac{46}{6}
$$

We can now subtract the fractions. We keep the denominator the same, and we subtract the numerators:

$$
\frac{53}{6}-\frac{46}{6}=\frac{7}{6}
$$

Finally, we convert back to a mixed number:

$$
\frac{7}{6}=1\,\text{R}\,1=1\,\frac{1}{6}
$$

Therefore, the painter had $1\,\frac{1}{6}$ liters of thinner left over.

So, $X$ follows a binomial distribution, where $X∼B(21,\frac{1}{3}).$

For a binomial random variable $X,$ the variance is given by

$$
\text{Var}[X]=np(1-p),
$$

where $n$ is the number of experiments and $p$ is the probability of success on each experiment.

Remember, when multiplying or dividing an inequality by a negative number, we need to flip the inequality sign:

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{a}{4}\,\, & >\,\,-2 \\ (-4)\cdot \left(-\frac{a}{4}\right)\,\, & <\,\,(-4)\cdot (-2) \\ (-4)\cdot \left(-\frac{a}{4}\right)\,\, & <\,\,8\end{aligned}
$$

Since two negative numbers multiply to give a positive number, we first cancel the negatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}(-4)\cdot \left(-\frac{a}{4}\right) & <8 \\ (\cancel{-}4)\cdot (\cancel{-}\frac{a}{4}) & <8 \\ 4\cdot \frac{a}{4} & <8\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can cancel a common factor of $4$ from both the numerator and denominator.

$$
\begin{aligned}4\cdot \frac{a}{4} & <8 \\ \frac{4a}{4} & <8 \\ \frac{\cancel{4}a}{\cancel{4}} & <8 \\ a & <8\end{aligned}
$$

\begin{aligned}L\{{\int }_{0}^{t}f(τ)\,\text{d}τ\} & =L\{A(t)\}={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}A(t)\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's use integration by parts:

$$
\begin{aligned}u=A(t) & \,⇒\, & du={A}^{′}(t)\,dt \\ dv={e}^{-st}\,dt & ⇒ & v=-\frac{1}{s}{e}^{-st}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting into the integration by parts formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}A(t)\,dt & =A(t)\left(-\frac{1}{s}{e}^{-st}\right)\,{|}_{0}^{\infty }-{\int }_{0}^{\infty }\left(-\frac{1}{s}{e}^{-st}\right){A}^{′}(t)\,dt.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $A(0)=0$ and $\frac{1}{s}{e}^{-st}\to 0$ as $t\to \infty ,$ we have $-\frac{1}{s}A(t){e}^{-st}{|}_{0}^{\infty }=0$ and

$$
{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}A(t)\,dt=\frac{1}{s}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}{A}^{′}(t)\,dt.
$$

Finally, using that ${A}^{′}(t)=f(t),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{s}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}{A}^{′}(t)\,dt & =\frac{1}{s}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}f(t)\,dt \\  & =\frac{1}{s}\cdot F(s) \\  & =\frac{F(s)}{s}.\end{aligned}
$$

The "square of a difference" formula states that

$$
{x}^{2}-2ax+{a}^{2}=(x-a)^{2}.
$$

We will use this formula to factor the given trinomial. Our trinomial is

$$
{x}^{2}-x+\frac{1}{4}.

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-x+{\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)}^{2}\end{aligned}

$$

The definitions of $\operatorname{cosh}⁡x$ and $\operatorname{sinh}⁡x$ are

$$
\operatorname{cosh}⁡x=\frac{1}{2}({e}^{x}+{e}^{-x}),\,\operatorname{sinh}⁡x=\frac{1}{2}({e}^{x}-{e}^{-x}).
$$

Substituting the above definitions into the equation $\operatorname{cosh}⁡x+5\operatorname{sinh}⁡x=5,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}({e}^{x}+{e}^{-x})+5\cdot (\frac{1}{2}({e}^{x}-{e}^{-x})) & =5 \\ \frac{1}{2}({e}^{x}+{e}^{-x})+\frac{5}{2}({e}^{x}-{e}^{-x}) & =5 \\ \frac{1}{2}{e}^{x}+\frac{1}{2}{e}^{-x}+\frac{5}{2}{e}^{x}-\frac{5}{2}{e}^{-x} & =5 \\ 3{e}^{x}-2{e}^{-x} & =5.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we multiply both sides of the equation by ${e}^{x},$ and simplify:

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{x}\cdot (3{e}^{x}-2{e}^{-x}) & ={e}^{x}\cdot 5 \\ 3{e}^{2x}-2 & =5{e}^{x} \\ 3{e}^{2x}-5{e}^{x}-2 & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

This is a quadratic equation in ${e}^{x}$ that we can factor as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}(3{e}^{x}+1)({e}^{x}-2) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

By the zero-product property, we have to solve two equations:

$$
3{e}^{x}+1=0,\,{e}^{x}-2=0.
$$

Solving the two equations above for $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}3{e}^{x}+1 & =0 &  & \, & {e}^{x}-2 & =0 \\ 3{e}^{x} & =-1 &  & \, & {e}^{x} & =2 \\ {e}^{x} & =-\frac{1}{3} &  & \, & x & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(2).\end{aligned}
$$

There are no real values of $x$ for which ${e}^{x}=-\frac{1}{3}.$ Therefore, the only real solution to the equation is

$$
x=\operatorname{ln}⁡(2).
$$

Given a binomial random variable $X∼B(n,p),$ if 

- $np>5,$ and

- $n(1-p)>5,$

we can approximate $X$ as a normal random variable $Y$ with mean $\mu =np$ and variance ${\sigma }^{2}=np(1-p),$ that is, 

$$
Y∼N(np,np(1-p)).
$$

Here, we have $n=180$ and $p=0.45.$ Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}np & =180\cdot 0.45 \\  & =81 \\  & >5\,✓ \\ n(1-p) & =180\cdot (1-0.45) \\  & =99 \\  & >5.\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

So, we can approximate our binomial random variable $X$ with a normal random variable $Y$ with mean

$$
\mu =np=(180)(0.45)=81
$$

and variance

$$
{\sigma }^{2}=np(1-p)=(180)(0.45)(1-0.45)=44.55.
$$

That is, we can approximate $X$ by $Y∼N(81,44.55).$

Now, we can approximate the desired probability $P(X=85).$ Using a continuity correction, we have

$$
P(X=85)≈P(84.5\le Y\le 85.5).
$$

To compute this probability, we transform to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(84.5\le Y\le 85.5) & =P(\frac{84.5-81}{\sqrt{44.55}}\le Z\le \frac{85.5-81}{\sqrt{44.55}}) \\  & ≈P(0.52\le Z\le 0.67) \\  & =P(Z\le 0.67)-P(Z<0.52) \\  & =P(Z\le 0.67)-P(Z\le 0.52) \\  & =Φ(0.67)-Φ(0.52) \\  & =0.7486-0.6985 \\  & =0.0501\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
P(X=85)≈0.050.
$$

Note: Using a software package for the approximation gives a probability of $0.0499.$

Suppose that ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{n}$ is a random sample of size $n$ from a population with population mean $\mu $ and population standard deviation $\sigma .$ The central limit theorem (or CLT) states that for sufficiently large $n,$ the distribution of the sample mean $\overset{―}{X}$ can be approximated as 

$$
\overset{―}{X}∼N\,(\mu ,\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n}).
$$

In our case:

- the sample size is 

$$
n=80,
$$

- the population mean is

$$
\begin{aligned}\mu  & =\text{E}[X] \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}f({x}_{i}) \\  & =-1\cdot 0.3+0\cdot 0.5+1\cdot 0.1+2\cdot 0.1 \\  & =-0.3+0+0.1+0.3 \\  & =0,\end{aligned}
$$

- the population variance is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sigma }^{2} & =\text{Var}[X] \\  & =\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2} \\  & =((-1)^{2}\cdot 0.3+{0}^{2}\cdot 0.5+{1}^{2}\cdot 0.1+{2}^{2}\cdot 0.1)-{0}^{2} \\  & =(0.3+0+0.1+0.4)-0 \\  & =0.8.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, by the CLT, we have that the distribution of the sample mean can be approximated as

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{―}{X} & ∼N\,(\mu ,\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n}) \\  & ∼N\,(0,\frac{0.8}{80}) \\  & ∼N(0,0.01).\end{aligned}
$$

We want to find $P(\overset{―}{X}>0.1).$ So, we convert $\overset{―}{X}$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(\overset{―}{X}>0.1) & ≈P(Z>\frac{0.1-0}{\sqrt{0.01}}) \\  & =P(Z>1) \\  & =1-Φ(1).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
P(\overset{―}{X}>0.1)=1-Φ(1).

$$
\overset{―}{X}∼N\,\left(\mu ,\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n}\right).
$$

In our case:

- the sample size is 

$$
n=80,
$$

- the population mean is

$$
\begin{aligned}\mu  & =\text{E}[X] \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}f({x}_{i}) \\  & =-1\cdot 0.3+0\cdot 0.5+1\cdot 0.1+2\cdot 0.1 \\  & =-0.3+0+0.1+0.3 \\  & =0,\end{aligned}
$$

- the population variance is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sigma }^{2} & =\text{Var}[X] \\  & =\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2} \\  & =((-1)^{2}\cdot 0.3+{0}^{2}\cdot 0.5+{1}^{2}\cdot 0.1+{2}^{2}\cdot 0.1)-{0}^{2} \\  & =(0.3+0+0.1+0.4)-0 \\  & =0.8.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, by the CLT, we have that the distribution of the sample mean can be approximated as

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{―}{X} & ∼N\,\left(\mu ,\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n}\right) \\  & ∼N\,\left(0,\frac{0.8}{80}\right) \\  & ∼N(0,0.01).\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

$$

- $np>5,$ and

- $n(1-p)>5,$

we can approximate $X$ as a normal random variable $Y$ with mean $\mu =np$ and variance ${\sigma }^{2}=np(1-p),$ that is, 

$$
Y∼N(np,np(1-p)).
$$

Here, we have $n=80$ and $p=0.4.$ Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}np & =80\cdot 0.4 \\  & =32 \\  & >5\,✓ \\ n(1-p) & =80\cdot (1-0.4) \\  & =48 \\  & >5.\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\mu =np=(80)(0.4)=32
$$

and variance

$$
{\sigma }^{2}=np(1-p)=(80)(0.4)(1-0.4)=19.2.
$$

$$

$$

$$

$$

$$

$$

The "square of a sum" formula states that

$$
{x}^{2}+2ax+{a}^{2}=(x+a)^{2}.
$$

We will use this formula to factor the given trinomial. Our trinomial is

$$
{x}^{2}+\frac{3}{2}x+\frac{9}{16}.
$$

First, we write the constant term as a perfect square:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+\frac{3}{2}x+{\left(\frac{3}{4}\right)}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we factor a $2$ out of the linear term:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+2\cdot \frac{3}{4}x+{\left(\frac{3}{4}\right)}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we factor the trinomial using the square of sum formula with $a=\frac{3}{4}.$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{(x+\frac{3}{4})}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Let $X$ represent a sandwich price. Then we have $X∼N(\mu ,{1.10}^{2}),$ and we want to find the mean $\mu .$ 

We know that $P(0.80\mu <X<1.20\mu )=0.90.$ First, we convert this to a cumulative probability:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(0.80\mu <X<1.20\mu ) & =0.90 \\ 2P(\mu <X<1.20\mu ) & =0.90 \\ P(\mu <X<1.20\mu ) & =0.45 \\ P(X<\mu )+P(\mu <X<1.20\mu ) & =0.5+0.45 \\ P(X<1.20\mu ) & =0.95.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we convert $X$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X<1.20\mu ) & =0.95 \\ P(Z<\frac{0.20\mu }{1.10}) & =0.95 \\ Φ\left(\frac{0.20\mu }{1.10}\right) & =0.95 \\ \frac{0.20\mu }{1.10} & ={Φ}^{-1}(0.95).\end{aligned}
$$

From the table, 

$$
{Φ}^{-1}(0.95)=1.6449.
$$

Finally then,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{0.20\mu }{1.10} & =1.6449 \\ 0.20\mu  & =1.809\,39 \\ \mu  & =\frac{1.809\,39}{0.20} \\  & ≈9.05\,\text{dollars}.\end{aligned}

If $X$ and $Y$ are two continuous random variables with joint probability density function $f(x,y),$ then the marginal density functions for $X$ and $Y$ are

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{X}(x)={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }f(x,y)\,\text{d}y,\,{f}_{Y}(y)={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }f(x,y)\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

First, let's sketch the region $D=\{(x,y)\,:\,x\ge 0,\,y\ge 0,\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\le 1\}.$

![](images/df/dfa15482cfa0e8fdc9e98b05a71d2b64a89b3886da44f6966fee9f1b5e096eef.png)

In our case, the marginal density function of $X$ for $0\le x\le 1$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{X}(x) & ={\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}}}15{x}^{2}y\,\text{d}y \\  & =15{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}}}{x}^{2}y\,\text{d}y \\  & =15{[\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}{y}^{2}]}_{y=0}^{y=\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{15}{2}[{x}^{2}{y}^{2}]_{y=0}^{y=\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{15}{2}[{x}^{2}\cdot {(\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}})}^{2}-{x}^{2}\cdot {0}^{2}] \\  & =\frac{15}{2}[{x}^{2}\cdot (1-{x}^{2})-0] \\  & =\frac{15({x}^{2}-{x}^{4})}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the full expression for ${f}_{X}(x)$ is given by

$$
{f}_{X}(x)=\left\{\begin{aligned}\frac{15({x}^{2}-{x}^{4})}{2}, & 0\le x\le 1, \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

The variable $z$ is being *divided* by $6.$ To isolate $z$ and remove the negative sign, we *multiply* by $-6$ 

Remember, when multiplying or dividing an inequality by a negative number, we need to flip the inequality sign:

$$
\begin{aligned}4\,\, & <\,\,-\frac{z}{6} \\ (-6)\cdot 4\,\, & >\,\,(-6)\cdot \left(-\frac{z}{6}\right) \\ -24\,\, & >\,\,(-6)\cdot \left(-\frac{z}{6}\right)\end{aligned}
$$

Since two negative numbers multiply to give a positive number, we first cancel the negatives:

$$

has a natural frequency of 

$$
\omega =\sqrt{\frac{4{\pi }^{2}}{9}}=\frac{2\pi }{3}.
$$

The frequencies of the forcing harmonics for a $6$-periodic function $(L=3)$ are 

$$
{\omega }_{n}=\frac{n\pi }{3}.
$$

For $n=2$, we have ${\omega }_{2}=\frac{2\pi }{3}.$ Since ${\omega }_{2}=\omega ,$ the $n=2$ harmonic of the forcing function causes resonance.

For the $n=2$ harmonic, the forcing term is 

$$
{f}_{2}(x)=-\frac{3}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{2\pi x}{3}\right).
$$

$$
{y}_{{p}_{2}}=x(A\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{2\pi x}{3}\right)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{2\pi x}{3}\right)).
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,{y}_{{p}_{2}}^{′} & =(A\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{2\pi x}{3}\right)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{2\pi x}{3}\right))+x(-\frac{2\pi }{3}A\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{2\pi x}{3}\right)+\frac{2\pi }{3}B\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{2\pi x}{3}\right)) \\ \,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,{y}_{{p}_{2}}^{″} & =-\frac{4\pi }{3}A\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{2\pi x}{3}\right)+\frac{4\pi }{3}B\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{2\pi x}{3}\right)-\frac{4{\pi }^{2}}{9}x(A\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{2\pi x}{3}\right)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{2\pi x}{3}\right))\end{aligned}
$$

\displaystyle {y}^{″}+\frac{4{\pi }^{2}}{9}y=-\frac{3}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{2\pi x}{3}\right):
$$

$$

The definitions of $\operatorname{cosh}⁡x$ and $\operatorname{sinh}⁡x$ are

$$
\operatorname{cosh}⁡x=\frac{1}{2}({e}^{x}+{e}^{-x}),\,\operatorname{sinh}⁡x=\frac{1}{2}({e}^{x}-{e}^{-x}).
$$

Substituting the above definitions into the equation  $5\operatorname{cosh}⁡x-\operatorname{sinh}⁡x=5,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}5\cdot (\frac{1}{2}({e}^{x}+{e}^{-x}))-\frac{1}{2}({e}^{x}-{e}^{-x}) & =5 \\ \frac{5}{2}{e}^{x}+\frac{5}{2}{e}^{-x}-\frac{1}{2}{e}^{x}+\frac{1}{2}{e}^{-x} & =5 \\ 2{e}^{x}+3{e}^{-x} & =5.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we multiply both sides of the equation by ${e}^{x},$ and simplify:

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{x}\cdot (2{e}^{x}+3{e}^{-x}) & ={e}^{x}\cdot 5 \\ 2{e}^{2x}+3 & =5{e}^{x} \\ 2{e}^{2x}-5{e}^{x}+3 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

This is a quadratic equation in ${e}^{x}$ that we can factor as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}(2{e}^{x}-3)({e}^{x}-1) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

By the zero-product property, we have to solve two equations:

$$
2{e}^{x}-3=0,\,{e}^{x}-1=0
$$

Solving the two equations above for $x,$ we get:

$$
\begin{aligned}2{e}^{x}-3 & =0 &  & \, & {e}^{x}-1 & =0 \\ {e}^{x} & =\frac{3}{2} &  & \, & {e}^{x} & =1 \\ {e}^{x} & =\operatorname{ln}⁡\left(\frac{3}{2}\right) &  & \, & x & =\operatorname{ln}⁡1=0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $x=0$ and $x=\operatorname{ln}⁡\left(\frac{3}{2}\right)$ are the real solutions to the equation.

Given a binomial random variable $X∼B(n,p),$ if 

- $np>5,$ and

- $n(1-p)>5,$

we can approximate $X$ as a normal random variable $Y$ with mean $\mu =np$ and variance ${\sigma }^{2}=np(1-p),$ that is, 

$$
Y∼N(np,np(1-p)).
$$

Here, we have $n=100$ and $p=0.5.$ Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}np & =100\cdot 0.5 \\  & =50 \\  & >5\,✓ \\ n(1-p) & =100\cdot (1-0.5) \\  & =50 \\  & >5.\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

So, we can approximate our binomial random variable $X$ with a normal random variable $Y$ with mean

$$
\mu =np=(100)(0.5)=50
$$

and variance

$$
{\sigma }^{2}=np(1-p)=(100)(0.5)(1-0.5)=25.
$$

That is, we can approximate $X$ by $Y∼N(50,25).$

Now, we can approximate the desired probability $P(X=58).$ Using a continuity correction, we have

$$
P(X=58)≈P(57.5\le Y\le 58.5).
$$

To compute this probability, we transform to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(57.5\le Y\le 58.5) & =P(\frac{57.5-50}{\sqrt{25}}\le Z\le \frac{58.5-50}{\sqrt{25}}) \\  & ≈P(1.5\le Z\le 1.7) \\  & =P(Z\le 1.7)-P(Z<1.5) \\  & =P(Z\le 1.7)-P(Z\le 1.5) \\  & =Φ(1.7)-Φ(1.5) \\  & =0.9554-0.9332 \\  & =0.022\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
P(X=58)≈0.022.
$$

Note: Using a software package for the approximation gives a probability of $0.0223.$

Recall that the general solution of a linear differential equation of the form ${y}^{′}+P(x)y=f(x)$ is given by

$$
y={y}_{c}+{y}_{p},
$$

where ${y}_{c}$ is the general solution of the corresponding homogeneous equation, and ${y}_{p}$ is a particular solution.

First, we find the homogeneous solution. The general solution of ${y}^{′}+2y=0$ is 

$$
{y}_{c}=A{e}^{-2x},
$$

where $A$ is an arbitrary constant.

Next, we identify the form of the general solution. Because the operator ${y}^{′}+2y$ involves a first derivative, a periodic forcing function $f(x)$ results in a particular solution containing both sine and cosine terms:

$$
y(x)∼A{e}^{-2x}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }({a}_{n}\cos \,(\frac{\pi n}{2}x)+{b}_{n}\sin \,(\frac{\pi n}{2}x))
$$

Now, we apply the initial condition $y(4)=3.$ Using the hint that the particular solution part evaluates to zero at $x=4,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}y(4) & =A{e}^{-2(4)}+{y}_{p}(4) \\ 3 & =A{e}^{-8}+0 \\ A & =3{e}^{8}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute $A$ back into the homogeneous part:

$$
{y}_{c}=(3{e}^{8}){e}^{-2x}=3{e}^{8-2x}
$$

Therefore, the solution is

$$
y(x)∼3{e}^{8-2x}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }({a}_{n}\cos \,(\frac{\pi n}{2}x)+{b}_{n}\sin \,(\frac{\pi n}{2}x)).

$$

Notice that as $x\to \infty ,$ 

- the expression inside the parentheses approaches $1,$ while

- the exponent approaches $\infty .$

So, if we attempt to evaluate the limit directly, we get

$$
\lim_{x\to \infty }{\left(\frac{x+2}{x+1}\right)}^{2x+2}={1}^{\infty },
$$

which is an indeterminate form.

Instead, let's recall the following special limit:

$$
\lim_{n\to \infty }{(1+\frac{1}{n})}^{n}=e
$$

We rewrite the given limit as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\lim_{x\to \infty }{\left(\frac{x+2}{x+1}\right)}^{2x+2} & =\lim_{x\to \infty }{\left(\frac{(x+1)+1}{x+1}\right)}^{2x+2} \\  & =\lim_{x\to \infty }{(1+\frac{1}{x+1})}^{2(x+1)}\end{aligned}
$$

Let $x+1=n.$ Therefore, since $n\to \infty $ as $x\to \infty ,$ we rewrite the limit using the algebra of limits, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\lim_{x\to \infty }{\left(\frac{x+2}{x+1}\right)}^{2x+2} & =\lim_{x\to \infty }{(1+\frac{1}{x+1})}^{2(x+1)} \\  & =\lim_{n\to \infty }{(1+\frac{1}{n})}^{2n} \\  & =\lim_{n\to \infty }{[{(1+\frac{1}{n})}^{n}]}^{2} \\  & ={[\lim_{n\to \infty }{(1+\frac{1}{n})}^{n}]}^{2} \\  & ={e}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

Now, using the fact that $z=2y,$ we get the constraint equation

$$
\begin{aligned}432 & =2xy+2x(2y)+2y(2y) \\ 432 & =2xy+4xy+4{y}^{2} \\ 432 & =6xy+4{y}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: We make one of the variables the subject in the constraint equation:

$$
x=\frac{72}{y}-\frac{2}{3}y
$$

Then, we substitute the above into the expression $V=2x{y}^{2}$, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}V(y) & =2{y}^{2}(\frac{72}{y}-\frac{2}{3}y) \\  & =144y-\frac{4}{3}{y}^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 4**: We solve the equation ${V}^{′}(y)=0.$ Taking the derivative, we have

$$
{V}^{′}(y)=144-4{y}^{2},
$$

and solving for the stationary points, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{V}^{′}(y) & =0 \\ 144-4{y}^{2} & =0 \\ {y}^{2} & =36 \\ y & =6.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that in the last step, we only considered the positive root because the side length $y$ must be positive.

$$
{V}^{″}(y)=-8y\,⟹\,{V}^{″}(6)=-48<0,
$$

Since ${V}^{″}(6)$ is negative, we conclude that this is indeed a maximum of $V(y).$

$$
A=\frac{1}{2}{r}^{2}\theta .
$$

We know that the perimeter is fixed at $180$ units, so we also have the constraint condition

$$
180=2r+r\theta .
$$

Now, by making $\theta $ the subject of the constraint equation, we find that 

$$
\theta =\frac{180-2r}{r}=\frac{180}{r}-2.
$$

Plugging the above into our expression for $A,$ we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}A(r) & =\frac{1}{2}{r}^{2}(\frac{180}{r}-2) \\  & =90r-{r}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

We want to maximize $A,$ so we need to differentiate $A$ and set the derivative equal to zero. The derivative is 

$$
{A}^{′}(r)=90-2r.
$$

Setting ${A}^{′}(r)=0$ and solving for $r$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{′}(r) & =0 \\ 90-2r & =0 \\ r & =45.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we confirm that $r=45$ is a maximum using the second derivative test. The second derivative gives

$$
{A}^{″}(r)=-2\,⟹\,{A}^{″}(45)=-2<0.
$$

Since ${A}^{″}(45)$ is negative, we conclude that $r=45$ is indeed a maximum of $A(r).$

Notice that as $t\to \infty ,$

$$

$$
\lim_{n\to \infty }{(1+\frac{1}{n})}^{n}=e
$$

In the given limit, we let $3t-6=n.$ Thus, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}3t-6 & =n \\ 3(t-2) & =n \\ t-2 & =\frac{n}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, since $n\to \infty $ as $t\to \infty ,$ we rewrite the given limit using the algebra of limits, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\lim_{t\to \infty }{(1+\frac{1}{3t-6})}^{t-2} & =\lim_{n\to \infty }{(1+\frac{1}{n})}^{n/3} \\  & =\lim_{n\to \infty }{[{(1+\frac{1}{n})}^{n}]}^{1/3} \\  & ={[\lim_{n\to \infty }{(1+\frac{1}{n})}^{n}]}^{1/3} \\  & ={e}^{1/3} \\  & =\sqrt[3]{e}\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{25}{9} & =2rx+\frac{\pi {r}^{2}}{2} \\ 2rx & =\frac{25}{9}-\frac{\pi {r}^{2}}{2} \\ x & =\frac{25}{18r}-\frac{\pi r}{4}.\end{aligned}

$$

- the expression inside the parentheses approaches $1,$ while

- the exponent approaches $\infty .$

So, if we attempt to evaluate the limit directly, we get

$$
\lim_{x\to \infty }{\left(\frac{2x-1}{2x-2}\right)}^{x-1}={1}^{\infty },
$$

which is an indeterminate form.

Instead, let's recall the following special limit:

$$
\lim_{n\to \infty }{(1+\frac{1}{n})}^{n}=e
$$

We rewrite the given limit as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\lim_{x\to \infty }{\left(\frac{2x-1}{2x-2}\right)}^{x-1} & =\lim_{x\to \infty }{\left(\frac{(2x-2)+1}{2x-2}\right)}^{x-1} \\  & =\lim_{x\to \infty }{(1+\frac{1}{2x-2})}^{x-1} \\  & =\lim_{x\to \infty }{(1+\frac{1}{2(x-1)})}^{x-1}\end{aligned}
$$

Let $2(x-1)=n$ Then, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}2(x-1) & =n \\ x-1 & =\frac{n}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, since $n\to \infty $ as $x\to \infty ,$ we rewrite the limit using the algebra of limits, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\lim_{x\to \infty }{\left(\frac{2x-1}{2x-2}\right)}^{x-1} & =\lim_{x\to \infty }{(1+\frac{1}{2(x-1)})}^{x-1} \\  & =\lim_{n\to \infty }{(1+\frac{1}{n})}^{n/2} \\  & =\lim_{n\to \infty }{[{(1+\frac{1}{n})}^{n}]}^{1/2} \\  & ={[\lim_{n\to \infty }{(1+\frac{1}{n})}^{n}]}^{1/2} \\  & ={e}^{1/2} \\  & =\sqrt{e}\end{aligned}
$$

First,  let $r$ the radius of the upper semicircle (top) and $x$ the radius of the lateral semicircle (right), hence the dimensions of the rectangle are $2r$ and $2x.$ We want to maximize the area

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =(2r)(2x)+\frac{\pi {r}^{2}}{2}+\frac{\pi {x}^{2}}{2} \\  & =4rx+\frac{\pi {r}^{2}}{2}+\frac{\pi {x}^{2}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

We know that the perimeter is fixed at $200$ units, so we also have the constraint condition

$$
200=\pi r+\pi x+2x+2r\,.
$$

Now, by making $x$ the subject of the constraint equation, we find that 

$$
\begin{aligned}200 & =\pi r+\pi x+2x+2r \\ x(\pi +2) & =200-r(\pi +2) \\ x & =\frac{200}{\pi +2}-r\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Plugging the above into our expression for $A,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =4rx+\frac{\pi {r}^{2}}{2}+\frac{\pi {x}^{2}}{2} \\  & =4r(\frac{200}{\pi +2}-r)+\frac{\pi {r}^{2}}{2}+\frac{\pi }{2}{(\frac{200}{\pi +2}-r)}^{2}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

We want to maximize $A,$ so we need to differentiate $A$ and set the derivative equal to zero. The derivative is

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{′}(r) & =4(\frac{200}{\pi +2}-r)+4r(-1)+\pi r+\pi (\frac{200}{\pi +2}-r)(-1) \\  & =\frac{800}{\pi +2}-4r-4r+\pi r-\frac{200\pi }{\pi +2}+\pi r \\  & =-8r+2\pi r+\frac{800-200\pi }{\pi +2}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Setting ${A}^{′}(r)=0$ and solving for $r$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{′}(r) & =0 \\ -8r+2\pi r+\frac{800-200\pi }{\pi +2} & =0 \\ 2r(\pi -4) & =-\frac{800-200\pi }{\pi +2} \\ 2r(\pi -4) & =\frac{200\pi -800}{\pi +2} \\ r & =\frac{100\pi -400}{(\pi +2)(\pi -4)} \\ r & =\frac{100(\pi -4)}{(\pi +2)(\pi -4)} \\ r & =\frac{100}{\pi +2}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we confirm that $r=\frac{100}{\pi +2}$ is a maximum using the second derivative test. The second derivative gives

$$
{A}^{″}(r)=-8+2\pi \,⟹\,{A}^{″}\left(\frac{100}{\pi +2}\right)=-8+2\pi <0.
$$

Since ${A}^{″}\left(\frac{100}{\pi +2}\right)$ is negative, we conclude that $r=\frac{100}{\pi +2}$ is indeed a maximum of $A(r).$

Finally, when $r=\frac{100}{\pi +2}$, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =\frac{200}{\pi +2}-\frac{100}{\pi +2} \\  & =\frac{100}{\pi +2}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the length of the side of the field with the largest area is $2x=\frac{200}{\pi +2}.$

is the smallest possible value.

$$
\begin{aligned}V & =x\cdot z\cdot y \\ 50 & =3{z}^{2}y.\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}3{z}^{2}y & =50 \\ y & =\frac{50}{3{z}^{2}}\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}C & =10xz+4xy+4yz \\ C & =10(3z)z+4(3z)\left(\frac{50}{3{z}^{2}}\right)+4\left(\frac{50}{3{z}^{2}}\right)z \\ C & =30{z}^{2}+\frac{200}{z}+\frac{200}{3z} \\ C & =30{z}^{2}+\frac{800}{3z}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
{C}^{′}(z)=60z-\frac{800}{3{z}^{2}},

$$
\begin{aligned}{C}^{′}(z) & =0 \\ 60z-\frac{800}{3{z}^{2}} & =0 \\ 180{z}^{3} & =800 \\ {z}^{3} & =\frac{800}{180} \\ z & =\sqrt[3]{\frac{40}{9}}.\end{aligned}

The initial investment was $\$11\,280$, and this decreased by $\frac{1}{8}$ every month.

If the investment value is reduced by $\frac{1}{8},$ then $\frac{7}{8}$ of its value remained every month. So the decay factor is $\frac{7}{8}.$

The formula for exponential decay (in terms of a decay factor $b$) is

$$
p=a{b}^{t}.
$$

In our case, we have the following:

- $a=11\,280$ is the initial investment.

- $b=\frac{7}{8}$ is the decay factor.

- $t=$ the time, in months.

Therefore, the correct expression for $p(t)$ is

$$
p(t)=11\,280\cdot {(\frac{7}{8})}^{t}.
$$

So the missing number is $\frac{7}{8}.$

Recall that if ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{n}$ are independent and identically distributed continuous random variables with probability density function $f(x;\theta ),$ where $\theta $ is an unknown parameter, then the likelihood function of a random sample ${x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}$ is

$$
L(\theta )=P({X}_{1}={x}_{1},{X}_{2}={x}_{2},…,{X}_{n}={x}_{n})={\prod }_{i=1}^{n}f({x}_{i};\,\theta ).
$$

In our case, we are given a sample of $n=4$ independent normal random variables with unknown mean $\theta $ and variance ${\sigma }^{2}=1,$ for which the probability density function is

$$
f(x;\theta )=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi }}{e}^{-(x-\theta )^{2}/2},\,x\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$

We can calculate the likelihood function as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}L(\theta ) & ={\prod }_{i=1}^{n}(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi }}{e}^{-({x}_{i}-\theta )^{2}/2}) \\  & =(2\pi )^{-n/2}\,{e}^{-\sum ({x}_{i}-\theta )^{2}/2} \\  & =(2\pi )^{-n/2}\,{e}^{-(\sum {x}_{i}^{2}-2\theta \sum {x}_{i}+n{\theta }^{2})/2} \\  & =(2\pi )^{-n/2}\,{e}^{-(C-2S\theta +n{\theta }^{2})/2}\end{aligned}
$$

where $$
\displaystyle S={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}
$$ and $$
\displaystyle C={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}^{2}.
$$

We are told that $$
\displaystyle S={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}=8.98,
$$ $$
\displaystyle C={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}^{2}=29.4,
$$ and $n=4.$ Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}L(\theta ) & =(2\pi )^{-4/2}\,{e}^{-(29.4-2(8.98)\theta +4{\theta }^{2})/2} \\  & =\frac{1}{4{\pi }^{2}}\,{e}^{\,-14.7\,+\,8.98\theta \,-\,2{\theta }^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
g(\theta )=-14.7+8.98\theta -2{\theta }^{2}.
$$

First, let's make a diagram of the situation:

![](images/51/513739a7ddcd73dab6cdf5374d24da54cf062e45ddf1b5b3985890e04a7cacdd.png)

Let $x$ and $y$ be the width and height of the rectangle, respectively. Given a width $x,$ the height $y$ of the rectangle rises up to the curve $y=32-\frac{4}{7}{x}^{6}.$

We want to maximize the area of the rectangle, which is given by

$$
A=xy=x(32-\frac{4}{7}{x}^{6})=32x-\frac{4}{7}{x}^{7}.
$$

Let's compute the critical points. Taking the derivative of the area, we get

$$
{A}^{′}(x)=32-4{x}^{6},
$$

and solving ${A}^{′}(x)=0$ gives the following critical point:

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{′}(x) & =0 \\ 32-4{x}^{6} & =0 \\ 4{x}^{6} & =32 \\ {x}^{6} & =8 \\ x & =\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

All that's left now is to confirm that $x=\sqrt{2}$ does indeed give a maximum value of $A(x).$ To do this, we use the first derivative test. We write up a table of values:

| Interval | $(0,\sqrt{2})$ | $\sqrt{2}$ | $(\sqrt{2},\sqrt{2}\sqrt[6]{7})$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Test Point | $1$ |  | $1.5$ |
| ${A}^{′}$ | $+$ | $0$ | $-$ |
| $A$ | $↗$ | $\text{max}$ | $↘$ |

So $x=\sqrt{2}$ does indeed give a maximum, and the area of the resulting rectangle will be the largest possible.

Therefore, the greatest area that a rectangle can have is

$$
\begin{aligned}A(\sqrt{2}) & =32(\sqrt{2})-\frac{4}{7}(\sqrt{2})^{7} \\  & =32\sqrt{2}-\frac{32\sqrt{2}}{7} \\  & =\frac{192\sqrt{2}}{7}.\end{aligned}
$$

Let's call $l$ the length of one leg. By the Pythagorean theorem, the length of the other leg is $\sqrt{\frac{1}{2}-{l}^{2}}.$

Therefore, the area of the triangle is given by

$$
A(l)=\frac{1}{2}l\sqrt{\frac{1}{2}-{l}^{2}}\,.
$$

Since $l$ is the length of a leg of a right triangle whose hypotenuse is $\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}$, the permitted range of $l$ is $0<l<\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}.$

We want to maximize $A(l),$ so we need to compute the critical points. Taking the derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{′}(l) & =\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{\frac{1}{2}-{l}^{2}}-\frac{{l}^{2}}{2\sqrt{\frac{1}{2}-{l}^{2}}},\end{aligned}
$$

and solving ${A}^{′}(l)=0$ gives the following critical point:

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{′}(l) & =0 \\ \frac{1}{2}\sqrt{\frac{1}{2}-{l}^{2}}-\frac{{l}^{2}}{2\sqrt{\frac{1}{2}-{l}^{2}}} & =0 \\ \frac{1}{2}-{l}^{2}-{l}^{2} & =0 \\ {l}^{2} & =\frac{1}{4} \\ l & =\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

All that's left now is to confirm that $l=\frac{1}{2}$ does indeed give a maximum value of $A(l).$ To do this, we use the first derivative test. We write up a table of values:

| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Test Point | $\frac{1}{3}$ |  | $\frac{3}{5}$ |
| ${A}^{′}$ | $+$ | $0$ | $-$ |
| $A$ | $↗$ | $\text{max}$ | $↘$ |

$$

In order to find ${f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,x),$ let's first find the marginal distribution for $X,$ corresponding to the row totals:

The critical points of a multivariable function $f$ are the points $a$ in the domain of $f$ such that ${f}^{′}(a)={0}^{T}$ or ${f}^{′}(a)$ does not exist, where

$$
{f}^{′}(a)={\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{n}}\end{bmatrix}|}_{x=a}.
$$

In this case, the domain of $f$ is ${R}^{2},$ and the first partial derivatives of $f$ are

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =(1-2{x}^{2}){e}^{-({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =-2xy{e}^{-({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})}.\end{aligned}
$$

 

So, the first derivative of $f$ is

$$
{f}^{′}(x,y)=\begin{bmatrix}(1-2{x}^{2}){e}^{-({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})} & -2xy{e}^{-({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

To find the critical points, we need to find the points $(x,y)\in {R}^{2}$ such that ${f}^{′}(x,y)={0}^{T}$ or ${f}^{′}(x,y)$ does not exist. Note that, in our case, ${f}^{′}(x,y)$ exists everywhere, so we just need to find the points where ${f}^{′}(x,y)={0}^{T}.$

Setting ${f}^{′}(x,y)={0}^{T},$ we have the following system:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}(1-2{x}^{2}){e}^{-({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})} &=0 \\ -2xy{e}^{-({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})} &=0\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Since ${e}^{-({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})}\ne 0$ for any point $(x,y)\in {R}^{2},$ we must have 

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}1-2{x}^{2} &=0 \\ -2xy &=0\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Solving for $x$ in the first equation, we get

$$
1-2{x}^{2}=0\,⟹\,x=\pm \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}.
$$

 

Substituting these values into the second equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}-(\pm \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2})y=0\,⟹\,y=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our system has two solutions, $(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2},0)$ and $(-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2},0).$

In conclusion, $f$ has two critical points, $(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2},0)$ and $(-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2},0).$ Note that since ${f}^{′}(x)={0}^{T}$ at these two points, they are also both stationary points.

$$

$$
{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s=L.

In polar coordinates, the arc length element $\text{d}s$ is given by

$$

$$

$$

$$

$$

$$

The Newton-Raphson process for optimization is

$$
{x}_{n+1}={x}_{n}-\frac{{f}^{′}({x}_{n})}{{f}^{″}({x}_{n})},
$$

where ${f}^{′}({x}_{n})$ and ${f}^{″}({x}_{n})$ are the first and second derivatives of $f(x)$ evaluated at ${x}_{n},$ respectively.

In our case, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =(\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2})-4x)^{′}=\frac{2}{x}-4, \\ {f}^{″}(x) & ={(\frac{2}{x}-4)}^{′}=-\frac{2}{{x}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our Newton-Raphson formula is

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{n+1} & ={x}_{n}-\frac{\frac{2}{{x}_{n}}-4}{-\frac{2}{{x}_{n}^{2}}} \\  & ={x}_{n}+{x}_{n}(1-2{x}_{n}) \\  & =2{x}_{n}(1-{x}_{n}).\end{aligned}
$$

Starting with ${x}_{0}=0.2,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =2{x}_{0}(1-{x}_{0}) \\  & =2(0.2)(1-0.2) \\  & =0.32\end{aligned}
$$

For the second iteration, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{2} & =2{x}_{1}(1-{x}_{1}) \\  & =2(0.32)(1-0.32) \\  & =0.4352\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, ${x}_{1}=0.32$ and ${x}_{2}≈0.435,$ rounded to three decimal places.

Given a population in which a proportion $p$ of the population has a particular characteristic, the sampling distribution of the sample proportion $\widehat{\,p}$ can be approximated as

$$
\widehat{\,p}∼N(p,\frac{p(1-p)}{n}),
$$

where the sample size $n$ is much smaller than the population size, $np>5,$ and $n(1-p)>5.$

In our case

- the sample size is $n=96,$ and

- the population proportion is $p=0.72.$

Now, since

$$
np=96(0.72)=69.12>5
$$

and

$$
n(1-p)=96(1-0.72)=26.88>5,
$$

and $n=96$ is much smaller than the population size, we can apply the above approximation.

The sampling distribution of the sample proportion, in this case, can be approximated as

$$
\begin{aligned}\widehat{\,p} & ∼N(p,\frac{p(1-p)}{n}) \\  & ∼N(0.72,\frac{0.72(1-0.72)}{96}) \\  & ∼N(0.72,0.0021).\end{aligned}
$$

The probability we wish to find is
$P(0.7<\widehat{\,p}\le 0.8).$
So, we convert $\widehat{\,p}$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(0.7<\widehat{\,p}<0.8) & =P(\frac{0.7-0.72}{\sqrt{0.0021}}<Z\le \frac{0.8-0.72}{\sqrt{0.0021}}) \\  & ≈P(-0.44<Z\le 1.75) \\  & =P(Z\le 1.75)-P(Z\le -0.44) \\  & =Φ(1.75)-Φ(-0.44)\end{aligned}
$$

From the table, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Φ(1.75) & =0.9599 \\ Φ(-0.44) & =0.3300.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(0.7<\widehat{\,p}<0.8) & =Φ(1.75)-Φ(-0.44) \\  & =0.9599-0.3300 \\  & =0.6299.\end{aligned}
$$

The covariance of $X$ and $Y$ can be calculated using the formula

$$
\text{Cov}[X,Y]=\text{E}[XY]-\text{E}[X]\cdot \text{E}[Y].
$$

To find $\text{E}[XY],$ we use the rule of the lazy statistician:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[XY] & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}xyf(x,y)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}xy\cdot \frac{2}{5}({x}^{3}+y)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{2}{5}y{\int }_{0}^{1}({x}^{4}+xy)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{2}{5}y{[\frac{1}{5}{x}^{5}+\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}y]}_{x=0}^{x=1}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{2}{5}y[\frac{1}{5}+\frac{1}{2}y]\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}(\frac{2}{25}y+\frac{1}{5}{y}^{2})\,\text{d}y \\  & ={[\frac{1}{25}{y}^{2}+\frac{1}{15}{y}^{3}]}_{y=0}^{y=1} \\  & =\frac{52}{75}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, using the covariance formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Cov}[X,Y] & =\text{E}[XY]-\text{E}[X]\cdot \text{E}[Y] \\  & =\frac{52}{75}-\left(\frac{14}{25}\right)\left(\frac{19}{15}\right) \\  & =-\frac{2}{125}.\end{aligned}
$$

Let ${X}_{i}$ denote the length of cable in the $i$th coil. Then, we have

$$
{X}_{i}∼N(50,{0.7}^{2}),\,1\le i\le 5.
$$

Let the random variable $L$ denote the total length of the cables in $5$ randomly selected coils. Then, since

$$
L={X}_{1}+{X}_{2}+⋯+{X}_{5},
$$

we have that $L$ is normally distributed, where

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[L] & =5\cdot 50 \\  & =250, \\ \text{Var}[L] & =5\cdot {0.7}^{2} \\  & =2.45.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
L∼N(250,2.45).
$$

In order to find $P(250<L<253),$ we convert $L$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(250<L<253) & =P(\frac{250-250}{\sqrt{2.45}}<Z<\frac{253-250}{\sqrt{2.45}}) \\  & ≈P(0<Z<1.92) \\  & =Φ(1.92)-Φ(0) \\  & =Φ(1.92)-0.5\end{aligned}
$$

Using the $z$-table, we see that

$$
Φ(1.92)≈0.9726.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(250<L<253) & ≈Φ(0.95)-0.5 \\  & ≈0.4726.\end{aligned}
$$

The Newton-Raphson process for optimization is

$$
{x}_{n+1}={x}_{n}-\frac{{f}^{′}({x}_{n})}{{f}^{″}({x}_{n})},
$$

where ${f}^{′}({x}_{n})$ and ${f}^{″}({x}_{n})$ are the first and second derivatives of $f(x)$ evaluated at ${x}_{n},$ respectively.

In our case, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & ={(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+2)+\frac{1}{x+1})}^{′} \\  & =\frac{1}{x+2}-\frac{1}{(x+1)^{2}}, \\ {f}^{″}(x) & ={(\frac{1}{x+2}-\frac{1}{(x+1)^{2}})}^{′} \\  & =-\frac{1}{(x+2)^{2}}+\frac{2}{(x+1)^{3}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our Newton-Raphson formula is

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{n+1}={x}_{n}-\frac{(\frac{1}{{x}_{n}+2}-\frac{1}{({x}_{n}+1)^{2}})}{(-\frac{1}{({x}_{n}+2)^{2}}+\frac{2}{({x}_{n}+1)^{3}})}.\end{aligned}
$$

Starting with ${x}_{0}=0.8,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & ={x}_{0}-\frac{(\frac{1}{{x}_{0}+2}-\frac{1}{({x}_{0}+1)^{2}})}{(-\frac{1}{({x}_{0}+2)^{2}}+\frac{2}{({x}_{0}+1)^{3}})} \\  & =0.8-\frac{(\frac{1}{0.8+2}-\frac{1}{(0.8+1)^{2}})}{(-\frac{1}{(0.8+2)^{2}}+\frac{2}{(0.8+1)^{3}})} \\  & ≈0.575,\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to three decimal places.

Given a population in which a proportion $p$ of the population has a particular characteristic, the sampling distribution of the sample proportion $\widehat{\,p}$ can be approximated as

$$
\widehat{\,p}∼N(p,\frac{p(1-p)}{n}),
$$

where the sample size $n$ is much smaller than the population size, $np>5,$ and $n(1-p)>5.$

In our case

- the sample size is $n=60,$ and

- the population proportion is $p=\frac{480}{1600}=0.3.$

Now, since

$$
np=60(0.3)=18>5
$$

and

$$
n(1-p)=60(1-0.3)=42>5,
$$

and the $n=60$ is much smaller than the population size, we can apply the above approximation.

The sampling distribution of the sample proportion, in this case, can be approximated as

$$
\begin{aligned}\widehat{\,p} & ∼N(p,\frac{p(1-p)}{n}) \\  & ∼N(0.3,\frac{0.3(1-0.3)}{60}) \\  & ∼N(0.3,0.0035).\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we determine the probability we wish to find. If more than $24$ members in the sample play tennis, then

$$
\begin{aligned}\widehat{\,p} & >\frac{24}{60}=0.4\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the probability we wish to find is
$P(\widehat{\,p}>0.4).$
So, we convert $\widehat{\,p}$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(\widehat{\,p}>0.4) & =P(Z>\frac{0.4-0.3}{\sqrt{0.0035}}) \\  & ≈P(Z>1.69) \\  & =1-P(Z\le 1.69) \\  & =1-Φ(1.69)\end{aligned}
$$

From the table, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Φ(1.69)=0.9545.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(0.4\le \widehat{\,p}) & =1-Φ(1.69) \\  & =0.0455.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, $\frac{a}{b}=\frac{\pi }{-\pi }=-1.$"] [:db/cas 17592186475984 :question/worked-solution "If $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $n,$ and $F$ is continuous vector field, then the flux of $F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $n$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S.
$$

Notice that only the $y$-component of $F=⟨0,\,xy-z,\,0⟩$ is non-zero. Since the lateral sides of $S$ are parallel to the $y$-axis, the flux of $F$ through $S$ will be non-zero only at the right and left sides. 

![](images/de/de9eb8381df05d2d5e6222a51b0ccbc5729e522df94a4aace570881d1226a1ca.png)

 

Let's consider the flux of $F$ through these two sides.

- Let ${S}_{1}$ denote the right surface. On this surface, we have $y=1$ for $0\le x\le 1$ and $0\le z\le 2.$ The outward-pointing unit normal vector to ${S}_{1}$ is

$$
{n}_{1}=⟨0,\,1,\,0⟩.
$$

Using the fact that $y=1$ on ${S}_{1},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot {n}_{1} & =⟨0,\,xy-z,\,0⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,1,\,0⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,x-z,\,0⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,1,\,0⟩ \\  & =x-z.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v \\ w\end{bmatrix}⟶\begin{bmatrix}x(u,v,w) \\ y(u,v,w) \\ z(u,v,w)\end{bmatrix}
$$

This transformation maps some region $Δ$ in the $uvw$-space to our region $R$ in the $xyz$-space.

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\text{ }dV={∭}_{Δ}\text{ }f(x(u,v,w),y(u,v,w),z(u,v,w))\,|\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v\text{d}w
$$

where $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T.$

Note that the change of variables

$$
u=x,\,v=xy,\,w=3z,
$$

 

gives us the *inverse* function ${T}^{-1},$ that is

$$
{T}^{-1}:\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y \\ z\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}u(x,y,z) \\ v(x,y,z) \\ w(x,y,z)\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Our domain in the $uvw$-space is

$$
\begin{aligned}Δ & =\{(u,v,w)\,:\,1\le u\le 2,\,0\le v\le 2,\,0\le w\le 3\}.\end{aligned}
$$

 

**Step 2**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} & \frac{∂u}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y} & \frac{∂v}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & \frac{∂w}{∂y} & \frac{∂w}{∂z}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ y & x & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 3\end{vmatrix} \\  & =3\begin{vmatrix}1 & 0 \\ y & x\end{vmatrix} \\  & =3(x-0) \\  & =3x \\  & =3u.\end{aligned}

$$

$$

In our case, we have

$$
r(x,y)=\frac{1}{xy}.

$$

Writing $3\,\frac{3}{4}$ as an improper fraction, we have

$$

Therefore, our problem now is to work out the following:

$$
\frac{41}{8}-\frac{15}{4}

To subtract two fractions with unlike denominators, we need to express each fraction as an equivalent fraction with a common denominator.

In this question, we can make a common denominator of $8.$

To put $\frac{15}{4}$ over a denominator of $8,$ we multiply the numerator and denominator by $2:$

$$

Let's define a transformation $T$ as follows: 

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{bmatrix}
$$

This transformation maps some region $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane to our region $D$ in the $xy$-plane.

To compute the required area, we will use the change of variables formula

$$
{∬}_{D}dxdy={∬}_{Δ}|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\text{ }dudv
$$

where $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T.$  

Note that the changes of variables

$$
u=x-y,\,v=y
$$

 

gives us the *inverse* function ${T}^{-1},$ that is

$$
{T}^{-1}:\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}u(x,y) \\ v(x,y)\end{bmatrix}.
$$

To compute the required area, we proceed in four steps:

**Step 1**: Find $Δ,$ which is the image of $D$ under the action of ${T}^{-1}.$ 

Substituting $x-y=u$ and $y=v$ into the equation of the first curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y+(x-y)^{4}=3\,⟹\,v+{u}^{4}=3\,⟹\,v=3-{u}^{4},\end{aligned}
$$

while substituting $y=v$ into the equation of the second curve, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}y=2\,⟹\,v=2.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the intersections of the curves in the $uv$-plane, we solve the following system:

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}v &=3-{u}^{4} \\ v &=2\end{aligned}\right.\,⟹\,\left\{\begin{aligned}u &=\pm 1 \\ v &=2.\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the intersection points are $(\pm 1,2).$

Therefore, our domain in the $uv$-plane has the type I representation

$$
Δ=\{(u,v)\,:\,-1\le u\le 1,\,2\le v\le 3-{u}^{4}\}.
$$

![](images/81/81ff220903cbe53cebf5e8f8b704e2a316be6092e1f14e527a7321e8f61bffb8.png)

**Step 2**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}1 & -1 \\ 0 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T$ is

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}={\left(\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)}\right)}^{-1}=(1)^{-1}=1.
$$

Note that $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}\ne 0$ everywhere inside $Δ.$  In other words, $T$ has no critical points inside $Δ.$

We calculate the required area by performing the change of variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\text{d}x\text{d}y & ={∬}_{Δ}|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}|1|\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}[{\int }_{2}^{3-{u}^{4}}\,dv]du \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}[v]_{2}^{3-{u}^{4}}\,du \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}((3-{u}^{4})-2)\,du \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}(1-{u}^{4}))\,du \\  & ={[u-\frac{{u}^{5}}{5}]}_{-1}^{1} \\  & =2-\frac{2}{5} \\  & =\frac{8}{5}\end{aligned}
$$" "The area of the required region is given by

$$

To compute the required integral, we can use the change of variables formula

$$

where $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T.$

To compute the required integral, we proceed as follows:

**Step 1**: Find a suitable change of variables.

The inequalities that define the region $D,$

$$
0\le y-2x\le 2,\,2\le y+2x\le 6,
$$

$$
u=y-2x\,\text{and}\,v=y+2x.
$$

This change of variables gives us the *inverse* function ${T}^{-1},$ that is

$$

$$

The current $I,$ measured in amperes, is defined as the rate of flow of charge $q,$ measured in coulombs.

$$

$$

Kirchhoff's voltage law states that in a series circuit, the source voltage (EMF) equals the sum of the voltage drops.

In an RCL circuit, there are three voltage drops:

- The voltage drop across the resistor is proportional to the current, with a constant of proportionality $R=18\,Ω.$ So,

$$
{V}_{R}=18I.
$$

- The voltage drop across the capacitor is related to its charge by $q=C{V}_{C}.$ Therefore,

$$
{V}_{C}=\frac{q}{C}=\frac{q}{0.002}=500q.
$$

- The voltage drop across the inductor is proportional to the rate of change of current, with a constant of proportionality $L=9\,\text{H}.$ Hence,

$$
{V}_{L}=9\,\frac{dI}{dt}.
$$

Therefore, by Kirchhoff's voltage law, these values are related by the equation

$$
9\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)=18I+500q+9\,\frac{dI}{dt}.
$$

Differentiating with respect to $t,$ the differential equation governing the current in the circuit is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{d}{dt}(9\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)) & =\frac{d}{dt}(18I+500q+9\,\frac{dI}{dt}) \\ 27\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t) & =18\,\frac{dI}{dt}+500\,\frac{dq}{dt}+9\,\frac{{d}^{2}I}{d{t}^{2}},\end{aligned}
$$

which, when substituting in $I=\frac{dq}{dt},$ gives

$$
\frac{{d}^{2}I}{d{t}^{2}}+2\,\frac{dI}{dt}+\frac{500}{9}I=3\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t).

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v \\ w\end{bmatrix}⟶\begin{bmatrix}x(u,v,w) \\ y(u,v,w) \\ z(u,v,w)\end{bmatrix}
$$

This transformation maps some region $Δ$ in the $uvw$-space to our region $R$ in the $xyz$-space.

To find the required integral, we can use the change of variables formula

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\text{ }dV={∭}_{Δ}\text{ }f(x(u,v,w),y(u,v,w),z(u,v,w))\,|\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v\text{d}w
$$

where $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T.$

Note that the change of variables

$$
u=\frac{2x-y}{2},\,v=\frac{y}{2},\,w=\frac{z}{3},
$$

gives us the *inverse* function ${T}^{-1},$ that is

$$
{T}^{-1}:\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y \\ z\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}u(x,y,z) \\ v(x,y,z) \\ w(x,y,z)\end{bmatrix}.
$$

To find the required integral, we proceed in four steps:

**Step 1**: Find $Δ,$ which is the image of $R$ under the action of ${T}^{-1}.$ 

Our domain in the $uvw$-space is

$$
\begin{aligned}Δ & =\{(u,v,w)\,:\,0\le u\le 1,\,0\le v\le 2,\,0\le w\le 1\}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} & \frac{∂u}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y} & \frac{∂v}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & \frac{∂w}{∂y} & \frac{∂w}{∂z}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}1 & -\frac{1}{2} & 0 \\ 0 & \,\,\,\frac{1}{2} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & \frac{1}{3}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\begin{vmatrix}1 & -\frac{1}{2} \\ 0 & \,\,\,\frac{1}{2}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}(\frac{1}{2}-0) \\  & =\frac{1}{6}.\end{aligned}

$$

$$

$$

Therefore, by Kirchhoff's voltage law, these values are related by the equation

$$

$$

Differentiating with respect to $t,$ the differential equation governing the current in the circuit is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{d}{dt}(9) & =\frac{d}{dt}(12I+16q+2\,\frac{dI}{dt}) \\ 0 & =12\,\frac{dI}{dt}+16\,\frac{dq}{dt}+2\,\frac{{d}^{2}I}{d{t}^{2}},\end{aligned}
$$

which, when substituting in $I=\frac{dq}{dt},$ gives

$$
\frac{{d}^{2}I}{d{t}^{2}}+6\,\frac{dI}{dt}+8I=0.
$$

The given equation is a second-order linear homogeneous equation with constant coefficients. To find the general solution, we must take a linear combination of two linearly independent solutions.

Assuming the solutions take the form $I={e}^{\lambda t},$ we obtain two solutions, namely, $I={e}^{-4t}$ and $I={e}^{-2t}.$
So, the general solution in our case is

$$

$$

$$
{∬}_{D}dxdy.
$$

Let's define a transformation $T$ as follows: 

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{bmatrix}
$$

This transformation maps some region $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane to our region $D$ in the $xy$-plane.

To compute the required area, we will use the change of variables formula

$$
{∬}_{D}dxdy={∬}_{Δ}|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\text{ }dudv
$$

where $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T.$  

Note that the changes of variables

$$
u=x+y,\,v=y
$$

 

gives us the *inverse* function ${T}^{-1},$ that is

$$
{T}^{-1}:\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}u(x,y) \\ v(x,y)\end{bmatrix}.
$$

To compute the required area, we proceed in four steps:

**Step 1**: Find $Δ,$ which is the image of $D$ under the action of ${T}^{-1}.$ 

Substituting $x+y=u$ and $y=v$ into the equation of the first curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}(x+y)^{3}-y=0\,⟹\,{u}^{3}-v=0\,⟹\,v={u}^{3},\end{aligned}
$$

while substituting $x+y=u$ and $y=v$ into the equation of the second curve, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}(x+y)^{2}-y=0\,⟹\,{u}^{2}-v=0\,⟹\,v={u}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the intersections of the curves in the $uv$-plane, we solve the following system:

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}v &={u}^{3} \\ v &={u}^{2}\end{aligned}\right.\,⟹\,\left\{\begin{aligned}{u}^{2}(u-1) &=0 \\ v &=u.\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the intersection points are $(0,0)$ and $(1,1).$

Therefore, our domain in the $uv$-plane has the type I representation 

$$
Δ=\{(u,v)\,:\,0\le u\le 1,\,{u}^{3}\le v\le {u}^{2}\}.
$$

![](images/a8/a8d2549c665a918cc8d69c69136fcb49e654ebb9aa5e53611155798e791b36a9.png)

   

**Step 2**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T$ is

$$

The current $I,$ measured in amperes, is defined as the rate of flow of charge $q,$ measured in coulombs.

$$
I=\frac{dq}{dt}
$$

Kirchhoff's voltage law states that in a series circuit, the source voltage (EMF) equals the sum of the voltage drops.

In an RCL circuit, there are three voltage drops:

- The voltage drop across the resistor is proportional to the current, with a constant of proportionality $R=90\,Ω.$ So,

$$
{V}_{R}=90I=90\,\frac{dq}{dt}.
$$

- The voltage drop across the capacitor is related to its charge by $q=C{V}_{C}.$ Therefore,

$$
{V}_{C}=\frac{q}{C}=\frac{q}{(1/200)}=200q.
$$

- The voltage drop across the inductor is proportional to the rate of change of current, with a constant of proportionality $L=10\,\text{H}.$ Hence,

$$
{V}_{L}=10\,\frac{dI}{dt}=10\,\frac{d}{dt}\left(\frac{dq}{dt}\right)=10\,\frac{{d}^{2}q}{d{t}^{2}}.
$$

Therefore, by Kirchhoff's voltage law, the differential equation governing the amount of charge $q$ on the capacitor is

$$
40\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)=90\,\frac{dq}{dt}+200q+10\,\frac{{d}^{2}q}{d{t}^{2}},
$$

which gives

$$
\frac{{d}^{2}q}{d{t}^{2}}+9\cdot \frac{dq}{dt}+20q=4\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t).
$$

The given equation is a second-order linear equation with constant coefficients. To find the general solution, we must sum the complementary and particular solutions.

- To find the complementary solution ${q}_{c},$ we solve the corresponding homogeneous equation, given by

$$
\frac{{d}^{2}{q}_{c}}{d{t}^{2}}+9\cdot \frac{d{q}_{c}}{dt}+20{q}_{c}=0.
$$

Solving using an integration technique, such as a trial solution, we obtain the complementary solution

$$
{q}_{c}(t)=A{e}^{-4t}+B{e}^{-5t},
$$

where $A$ and $B$ are constants.

- Next, we find the particular solution. Note that the right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is sinusoidal with argument $2t.$ So, we assume that the particular solution is also a sinusoidal with argument $2t,$ i.e.,

$$
{q}_{p}(t)=\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t).
$$

To find the values of $\alpha $ and $\beta ,$ we substitute

$$
\begin{aligned}{q}_{p} & =\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t), \\ \frac{d{q}_{p}}{dt} & =-2\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+2\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t), \\ \frac{{d}^{2}{q}_{p}}{d{t}^{2}} & =-4\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)-4\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t),\end{aligned}
$$

into the inhomogeneous equation and group like terms on the left-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,(-4\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)-4\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t))+9(-2\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+2\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t))\,\, &  \\ +20(\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)) & =4\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\ (16\alpha +18\beta )\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+(-18\alpha +16\beta )\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) & =4\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the coefficients, we get the following system of equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}16\alpha +18\beta &=0\, && (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)) \\ -18\alpha +16\beta &=4\, && (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t))\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Solving this system gives $\alpha =-\frac{18}{145},$ $\beta =\frac{16}{145}.$ Therefore, the particular solution is

$$
{q}_{p}(t)=-\frac{18}{145}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\frac{16}{145}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t).
$$

Now, since the general solution is given by the sum of the complementary solution and the particular solution, the general solution in our case is

$$
q(t)={q}_{c}(t)+{q}_{p}(t)=A{e}^{-4t}+B{e}^{-5t}-\frac{18}{145}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\frac{16}{145}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t).
$$

Differentiating this expression for $q(t),$ we obtain the following expression for $I$ in amperes:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(t) & =\frac{d}{dt}(A{e}^{-4t}+B{e}^{-5t}-\frac{18}{145}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\frac{16}{145}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)) \\  & =-4A{e}^{-4t}-5B{e}^{-5t}+\frac{36}{145}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+\frac{32}{145}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t).\end{aligned}
$$

Note the following:

- The quantity ${I}_{c}(t)=-4A{e}^{-4t}-5B{e}^{-5t}$ is the *transient current*, since it goes to zero as $t\to \infty .$

- The function $$
\displaystyle {I}_{p}(t)=\frac{36}{145}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+\frac{32}{145}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)
$$ is the *steady-state current*. It governs the current's long-term behavior.

Therefore, as $t\to \infty ,$ we have

$$
I(t)≈{I}_{p}(t)=\frac{36}{145}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+\frac{32}{145}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t).
$$

Finally, the amplitude of the steady-state current, in amperes, is given by

$$
\sqrt{{\left(\frac{36}{145}\right)}^{2}+{\left(\frac{32}{145}\right)}^{2}}≈0.33,
$$

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}⟶\begin{bmatrix}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{bmatrix}

This transformation maps some region $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane to our region $D$ in the $xy$-plane.

To compute the required integral, we can use the change of variables formula

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dxdy={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(x(u,v),y(u,v))\,|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\text{ }dudv
$$

where $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T.$

To compute the required integral, we proceed as follows:

**Step 1**: Find a suitable change of variables.

The integrand

$$
f(x,y)=(x-y){e}^{x+y}
$$

suggests that we use the change of variables 

$$
u=x-y,\,v=x+y.
$$

This change of variables gives us the *inverse* function ${T}^{-1},$ that is

$$
{T}^{-1}:\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}u(x,y) \\ v(x,y)\end{bmatrix}.
$$

**Step 2**: Find $Δ,$ which is the image of $D$ under the action of ${T}^{-1}.$ 

The vertices of our domain $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane are as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{T}^{-1}(0,0) & =(0-0,0+0) \\  & =(0,0) \\ {T}^{-1}(2,-2) & =(2-(-2),2+(-2)) \\  & =(4,0) \\ {T}^{-1}(3,-1) & =(3-(-1),3+(-1)) \\  & =(4,2) \\ {T}^{-1}(1,1) & =(1-1,1+1) \\  & =(0,2)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our domain in the $uv$-plane is the following rectangle:

$$
Δ=\{(u,v)\,:\,0\le u\le 4,\,0\le v\le 2\}
$$

![](images/0b/0b23c6463447aa1fb64bdeeca689a40711f8dad59b348bb7943c2b9d2de7e8fc.png)

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}:$

$$"] [:db/cas 17592186502072 :question/worked-solution "Since $Q$ is the amount of ink dye in the reservoir at time $t,$ the derivative 

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}
$$

describes how this amount changes with respect to time $t,$ in minutes. This is equal to the rate at which ink dye enters the reservoir minus the rate at which ink dye leaves the reservoir.

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}
$$

Note that the units of $\frac{dQ}{dt},{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}$ and ${Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}$ are $\text{lb}/\text{min}.$ Now, let's compute the required rates of change in steps.

**Step 1**: Calculating the rate at which ink dye enters the reservoir.

First, note that a solution containing $\frac{4}{3}\,\text{lb/gal}$ of ink dye enters the reservoir at a rate of $9\,\text{gal/min}.$ So, the rate at which the *ink dye* enters the reservoir is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′} & =(\frac{4}{3}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{gal}})\cdot (9\,\frac{\text{gal}}{\text{min}}) \\  & =(\frac{4}{3}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\cancel{\text{gal}}})\cdot (9\,\frac{\cancel{\text{gal}}}{\text{min}}) \\  & =12\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Calculating the rate at which ink dye exits the reservoir.

To find the rate at which ink dye leaves the reservoir, we must first determine the volume of solution in the reservoir at time $t.$

The reservoir initially contains $60\,\text{gal}$ of solution; solution enters at $9\,\text{gal/min}$ and mixed solution leaves at $6\,\text{gal/min}.$
As a result, the amount of solution in the reservoir after $t$ minutes is 

$$
V(t)=60+9t-6t=3(20+t)\,\text{gal}.
$$

Note that $V(t)$ is an increasing function, so the reservoir is filling.

Since $Q$ is the amount of ink dye in the reservoir, the concentration of the solution at time $t$ is

$$
\frac{Q}{3(20+t)}\,\text{lb/gal}.
$$

Therefore, as the completely mixed solution leaves at a rate of $6\,\text{gal/min},$ *ink dye* leaves at a rate of

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} & =(6\,\frac{\text{gal}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{3(20+t)}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{gal}}) \\  & =(6\,\frac{\cancel{\text{gal}}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{3(20+t)}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\cancel{\text{gal}}}) \\  & =\frac{6Q}{3(20+t)}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{min}} \\  & =\frac{2Q}{20+t}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Calculate the overall rate of change.

The rate of change equals the rate of entry minus the rate of exit. Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dQ}{dt} & ={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} \\  & =12-\frac{2Q}{20+t}\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the equation

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}+\frac{2}{20+t}\,Q=12.
$$

**Step 4**: Integrate the equation.

This is a first-order linear equation with variable coefficients. So we find the general solution using an integrating factor:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(t) & ={e}^{\int 2/(20+t)\,dt} \\  & ={e}^{2\operatorname{ln}⁡|20+t|} \\  & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(20+t)^{2}} \\  & =(20+t)^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying both sides of the differential equation by $I(t)=(20+t)^{2}$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}(20+t)^{2}\cdot (\frac{dQ}{dt}+\frac{2}{20+t}\,Q) & =(20+t)^{2}\cdot 12 \\ (20+t)^{2}\frac{dQ}{dt}+2(20+t)Q & =12(20+t)^{2} \\ \frac{d}{dt}(Q(20+t)^{2}) & =12(20+t)^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate with respect to $t:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{d}{dt}(Q(20+t)^{2})\,dt & =\int 12(20+t)^{2}\,dt \\ Q(20+t)^{2} & =12\cdot \frac{1}{3}(20+t)^{3}+C \\ Q(t) & =4(20+t)+\frac{C}{(20+t)^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

We're told that the reservoir initially contains $18\,\text{lb}$ of ink dye. So, we can apply the initial condition $Q(0)=18,$ and solve for $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(0) & =18 \\ 4(20+0)+\frac{C}{(20+0)^{2}} & =18 \\ 80+\frac{C}{(20)^{2}} & =18 \\ \frac{C}{{20}^{2}} & =-62 \\ C & =-62(20)^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we obtain the following expression for $Q(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(t) & =4(20+t)-\frac{62(20)^{2}}{(20+t)^{2}} \\  & =4(20+t)-62{\left(\frac{20}{20+t}\right)}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let ${t}_{o}$ be the time when the reservoir begins to overflow. The reservoir has a capacity of $150\,\text{gal},$ so we can use the condition $V({t}_{o})=150$ to solve for ${t}_{o}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}V({t}_{o}) & =150 \\ 60+9{t}_{o}-6{t}_{o} & =150 \\ 60+3{t}_{o} & =150 \\ 3{t}_{o} & =90 \\ {t}_{o} & =30\,\text{min}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, rounded to one decimal place, the amount of ink dye in the reservoir at the moment it begins to overflow is

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(30) & =4(20+30)-62{\left(\frac{20}{20+30}\right)}^{2} \\  & =200-62{\left(\frac{20}{50}\right)}^{2} \\  & ≈190.1\,\text{lb}.\end{aligned}

$$
\widehat{\,p}∼N(p,\frac{p(1-p)}{n}),
$$

where the sample size $n$ is much smaller than the population size, $np>5,$ and $n(1-p)>5.$

In our case

- the sample size is $n=65,$ and

- the population proportion is $p=0.35.$

Now, since

$$
np=65(0.35)=22.75>5
$$

and

$$
n(1-p)=65(1-0.35)=42.25>5,
$$

and $n=65$ is much smaller than the population size, we can apply the above approximation.

The sampling distribution of the sample proportion, in this case, can be approximated as

$$
\begin{aligned}\widehat{\,p} & ∼N(p,\frac{p(1-p)}{n}) \\  & ∼N(0.35,\frac{0.35(1-0.35)}{65}) \\  & ∼N(0.35,0.0035).\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we determine the probability we wish to find. If more than $13$ but fewer than $26$ people bought something, then 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{13}{65}<\widehat{\,p} & <\frac{26}{65} \\ 0.2<\widehat{\,p} & <0.4.\end{aligned}
$$

$P(0.2\le \widehat{\,p}\le 0.4).$

$$

$$

Therefore,

$$

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}
$$

describes how this amount changes with respect to time $t,$ in minutes. This is equal to the rate at which salt enters the tank minus the rate at which salt leaves the tank.

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}
$$

Note that the units of $\frac{dQ}{dt},{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}$ and ${Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}$ are $\text{lb}/\text{min}.$ Now, let's compute the required rates of change in steps.

**Step 1**: Calculating the rate at which salt enters the tank.

Note that fresh water (i.e., water containing $0\,\text{lb/gal}$ of salt) enters the tank at a rate of $12\,\text{gal/min}.$ So, the rate at which the *salt* enters the tank is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′} & =(0\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{gal}})\cdot (12\,\frac{\text{gal}}{\text{min}}) \\  & =(0\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\cancel{\text{gal}}})\cdot (12\,\frac{\cancel{\text{gal}}}{\text{min}}) \\  & =0\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Calculating the rate at which salt exits the tank.

To find the rate at which salt leaves the tank, we first determine the volume of brine in the tank at time $t.$

The tank initially contains $420\,\text{gal}$ of brine; water enters at $12\,\text{gal/min}$ and drains out at $12\,\text{gal/min}.$
As a result, the amount of brine in the tank after $t$ minutes is 

$$
420+12t-12t=420\,\text{gal}.
$$

Since $Q$ is the amount of salt in the tank, the *concentration* of the brine at time $t$ is

$$
\frac{Q}{420}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{gal}}.
$$

Therefore, as the completely mixed brine leaves at a rate of $12\,\text{gal/min},$ *salt* leaves at a rate of

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} & =(12\,\frac{\text{gal}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{420}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{gal}}) \\  & =(12\,\frac{\cancel{\text{gal}}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{420}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\cancel{\text{gal}}}) \\  & =\frac{12Q}{420}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{min}} \\  & =\frac{Q}{35}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Calculate the overall rate of change.

The rate of change equals the rate of entry minus the rate of exit. Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dQ}{dt} & ={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} \\  & =0-\frac{Q}{35}\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the equation

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}=-\frac{1}{35}\,Q.
$$

**Step 4**: Integrate the equation.

Separating variables and integrating both sides with respect to $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{Q}\cdot \frac{dQ}{dt} & =-\frac{1}{35} \\ \int \frac{1}{Q}\cdot \frac{dQ}{dt}dt & =\int \left(-\frac{1}{35}\right)\,dt \\ \int \frac{1}{Q}\cdot \,dQ & =-\frac{1}{35}\int 1\,dt \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|Q| & =-\frac{t}{35}+C \\ |Q| & ={e}^{-\frac{t}{35}+C} \\ Q(t) & =A{e}^{-t/35},\end{aligned}
$$

where $A=\pm {e}^{C}$ is a constant of integration.

We're told that the tank initially contains $14\,\text{lb}$ of salt. So, we can apply the initial condition $Q(0)=14,$ and solve for $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(0) & =14 \\ A{e}^{-0/35} & =14 \\ A & =14\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we obtain the following expression for $Q(t):$

$$
Q(t)=14{e}^{-t/35}
$$

Finally, the amount of salt in the tank $20$ minutes after the fresh water is first pumped in is

$$
Q(20)=14{e}^{-20/35}≈7.91\,\text{lb},
$$

Note that the units of $\frac{dQ}{dt},{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}$ and ${Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}$ are $\text{lb}/\text{min}.$ Now, let's compute the required rates of change in steps.

**Step 1**: Calculating the rate at which contaminant enters the tank.

First, note that clean water (i.e., water containing $0\,\text{lb/gal}$ of contaminant) enters the tank at a rate of $6\,\text{gal/min}.$ So, the rate at which the *contaminant* enters the tank is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′} & =(0\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{gal}})\cdot (6\,\frac{\text{gal}}{\text{min}}) \\  & =(0\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\cancel{\text{gal}}})\cdot (6\,\frac{\cancel{\text{gal}}}{\text{min}}) \\  & =0\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Calculating the rate at which contaminant exits the tank.

To find the rate at which contaminant leaves the tank, we must first determine the volume of water in the tank at time $t.$

The tank initially contains $180\,\text{gal}$ of water; clean water enters at $6\,\text{gal/min},$ and mixed water leaves at $4\,\text{gal/min}.$
As a result, the amount of water in the tank after $t$ minutes is 

$$
V(t)=180+6t-4t=(180+2t)\,\text{gal}.
$$

Note that $V(t)$ is an increasing function, so the tank is filling.

Since $Q$ is the amount of contaminant in the tank, the concentration of the water at time $t$ is

$$

$$

$$

$$

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}
$$

describes how this amount changes with respect to time $t,$ in minutes. This is equal to the rate at which fertilizer enters the tank minus the rate at which fertilizer leaves the tank.

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}
$$

Note that the units of $\frac{dQ}{dt},{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}$ and ${Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}$ are $\text{lb}/\text{min}.$ Now, let's compute the required rates of change in steps.

**Step 1**: Calculating the rate at which fertilizer enters the tank.

First, note that a solution containing $0.5\,\text{lb/gal}$ of fertilizer enters the tank at a rate of $18\,\text{gal/min}.$ So, the rate at which the *fertilizer* enters the tank is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′} & =(0.5\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{gal}})\cdot (18\,\frac{\text{gal}}{\text{min}}) \\  & =(0.5\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\cancel{\text{gal}}})\cdot (18\,\frac{\cancel{\text{gal}}}{\text{min}}) \\  & =9\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Calculating the rate at which fertilizer exits the tank.

To find the rate at which fertilizer leaves the tank, we must first determine the volume of solution in the tank at time $t.$

The tank initially contains $90\,\text{gal}$ of solution; solution enters at $18\,\text{gal/min}$ and mixed solution leaves at $12\,\text{gal/min}.$
As a result, the amount of solution in the tank after $t$ minutes is 

$$
V(t)=90+18t-12t=6(15+t)\,\text{gal}.
$$

Note that $V(t)$ is an increasing function, so the tank is filling.

Since $Q$ is the amount of fertilizer in the tank, the concentration of the solution at time $t$ is

$$
\frac{Q}{6(15+t)}\,\text{lb/gal}.
$$

Therefore, as the completely mixed solution leaves at a rate of $12\,\text{gal/min},$ *fertilizer* leaves at a rate of

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} & =(12\,\frac{\text{gal}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{6(15+t)}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{gal}}) \\  & =(12\,\frac{\cancel{\text{gal}}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{6(15+t)}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\cancel{\text{gal}}}) \\  & =\frac{12Q}{6(15+t)}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{min}} \\  & =\frac{2Q}{15+t}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Calculate the overall rate of change.

The rate of change equals the rate of entry minus the rate of exit. Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dQ}{dt} & ={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} \\  & =9-\frac{2Q}{15+t}\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the equation

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}+\frac{2}{15+t}\,Q=9.
$$

This is a first-order linear equation with variable coefficients. So we find the general solution using an integrating factor:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(t) & ={e}^{\int 2/(15+t)\,dt} \\  & ={e}^{2\operatorname{ln}⁡|15+t|} \\  & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(15+t)^{2}} \\  & =(15+t)^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying both sides of the differential equation by $I(t)=(15+t)^{2}$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}(15+t)^{2}\cdot (\frac{dQ}{dt}+\frac{2}{15+t}\,Q) & =(15+t)^{2}\cdot 9 \\ (15+t)^{2}\frac{dQ}{dt}+2(15+t)Q & =9(15+t)^{2} \\ \frac{d}{dt}(Q(15+t)^{2}) & =9(15+t)^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate with respect to $t:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{d}{dt}(Q(15+t)^{2})\,dt & =\int 9(15+t)^{2}\,dt \\ Q(15+t)^{2} & =9\cdot \frac{1}{3}(15+t)^{3}+C \\ Q(t) & =3(15+t)+\frac{C}{(15+t)^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

We're told that the tank initially contains $18\,\text{lb}$ of fertilizer. So, we can apply the initial condition $Q(0)=18,$ and solve for $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(0) & =18 \\ 3(15+0)+\frac{C}{(15+0)^{2}} & =18 \\ 45+\frac{C}{(15)^{2}} & =18 \\ \frac{C}{{15}^{2}} & =-27 \\ C & =-27(15)^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we obtain the following expression for $Q(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(t) & =3(15+t)-\frac{27(15)^{2}}{(15+t)^{2}} \\  & =3(15+t)-27{\left(\frac{15}{15+t}\right)}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let ${t}_{o}$ be the time when the tank begins to overflow. The tank has a capacity of $210\,\text{gal},$ so we can use the condition $V({t}_{o})=210$ to solve for ${t}_{o}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}V({t}_{o}) & =210 \\ 90+18{t}_{o}-12{t}_{o} & =210 \\ 90+6{t}_{o} & =210 \\ 6{t}_{o} & =120 \\ {t}_{o} & =20\,\text{min}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, rounded to one decimal place, the amount of fertilizer in the tank at the moment it begins to overflow is

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(20) & =3(15+20)-27{\left(\frac{15}{15+20}\right)}^{2} \\  & =105-27{\left(\frac{15}{35}\right)}^{2} \\  & ≈100.0\,\text{lb}.\end{aligned}
