$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}
$$

describes how this amount changes with respect to time $t,$ in seconds. This is equal to the rate at which contaminant enters the tank minus the rate at which contaminant leaves the tank.

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}
$$

Note that the units of $\frac{dQ}{dt},{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}$ and ${Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}$ are $\text{g}/\text{s}.$ Now, let's compute the required rates of change in steps.

**Step 1**: Calculating the rate at which contaminant enters the tank.

First, note that clean water (i.e., water containing $0\,\text{g/mL}$ of contaminant) enters the tank at a rate of $90\,\text{mL/s}.$ So, the rate at which the *contaminant* enters the tank is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′} & =(0\,\frac{\text{g}}{\text{mL}})\cdot (90\,\frac{\text{mL}}{\text{s}}) \\  & =(0\,\frac{\text{g}}{\cancel{\text{mL}}})\cdot (90\,\frac{\cancel{\text{mL}}}{\text{s}}) \\  & =0\,\frac{\text{g}}{\text{s}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Calculating the rate at which contaminant exits the tank.

To find the rate at which contaminant leaves the tank, we must first determine the volume of water in the tank at time $t.$

The tank initially contains $7\,200\,\text{mL}$ of water; clean water enters at $90\,\text{mL/s},$ and mixed water leaves at $60\,\text{mL/s}.$
As a result, the amount of water in the tank after $t$ seconds is 

$$
V(t)=7\,200+90t-60t=30(240+t)\,\text{mL}.
$$

Note that $V(t)$ is an increasing function, so the tank is filling.

Since $Q$ is the amount of contaminant in the tank, the concentration of the water at time $t$ is

$$
\frac{Q}{30(240+t)}\,\frac{\text{g}}{\text{mL}}.
$$

Therefore, as the completely mixed water leaves at a rate of $60\,\text{mL/s},$ *contaminant* leaves at a rate of

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} & =(60\,\frac{\text{mL}}{\text{s}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{30(240+t)}\,\frac{\text{g}}{\text{mL}}) \\  & =(60\,\frac{\cancel{\text{mL}}}{\text{s}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{30(240+t)}\,\frac{\text{g}}{\cancel{\text{mL}}}) \\  & =\frac{2Q}{240+t}\,\frac{\text{g}}{\text{s}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Calculate the overall rate of change.

The rate of change equals the rate of entry minus the rate of exit. Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dQ}{dt} & ={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} \\  & =0-\frac{2Q}{240+t}\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the equation

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}=-\frac{2}{240+t}\,Q.
$$

**Step 4**: Integrate the equation

Separating variables and integrating both sides with respect to $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{Q}\cdot \frac{dQ}{dt} & =-\frac{2}{240+t} \\ \int \frac{1}{Q}\cdot \frac{dQ}{dt}dt & =\int \left(-\frac{2}{240+t}\right)\,dt \\ \int \frac{1}{Q}\cdot \,dQ & =-2\int \frac{1}{240+t}\,dt \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|Q| & =-2(\operatorname{ln}⁡|240+t|)+C \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|Q| & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|(240+t)^{-2}|+C \\ |Q| & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡|(240+t)^{-2}|+C} \\ Q(t) & =\frac{A}{(240+t)^{2}},\end{aligned}
$$

where $A=\pm {e}^{C}$ is a constant of integration.

We're told that the tank initially contains $210\,\text{g}$ of contaminant. So, we can apply the initial condition $Q(0)=210,$ and solve for $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(0) & =210 \\ \frac{A}{(240+0)^{2}} & =210 \\ A & =210(240)^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we obtain the following expression for $Q(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(t) & =\frac{210(240)^{2}}{(240+t)^{2}} \\  & =210{\left(\frac{240}{240+t}\right)}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let ${t}_{o}$ be the time when the tank begins to overflow. The tank has a capacity of $10\,500\,\text{mL},$ so we can use the condition $V({t}_{o})=10\,500$ to solve for ${t}_{o}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}V({t}_{o}) & =10\,500 \\ 30(240+{t}_{o}) & =10\,500 \\ 240+{t}_{o} & =350 \\ {t}_{o} & =110\,\text{s}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the amount of contaminant in the tank at the moment it begins to overflow is

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(110) & =210{\left(\frac{240}{240+110}\right)}^{2} \\  & =210{\left(\frac{24}{35}\right)}^{2} \\  & ≈98.74\,\text{g},\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

 

Hence, the normal vector to the tangent plane is 

$$
⟨y-3,\,x+2,\,-1⟩.

$$

$$

$$

$$

where $$
\displaystyle ⟨\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),-1⟩
$$ represents a normal vector to the tangent plane.

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({e}^{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}) \\  & ={e}^{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\cdot 2x \\  & =2x{e}^{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({e}^{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}) \\  & ={e}^{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\cdot 2y \\  & =2y{e}^{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Hence, the normal vector to the tangent plane is 

$$
⟨2x{e}^{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}},\,2y{e}^{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}},\,-1⟩.
$$

Note that the tangent plane is horizontal if and only if the normal vector is vertical. This means that the $x$- and $y$-components of the vector must be $0:$

$$

where $$

$$ represents a normal vector to the tangent plane.

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(x\operatorname{ln}⁡y)=\operatorname{ln}⁡y \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(x\operatorname{ln}⁡y)=\frac{x}{y}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Hence, the normal vector to the tangent plane is 

$$
⟨\operatorname{ln}⁡y,\,\frac{x}{y},\,-1⟩.
$$

Note that the tangent plane is horizontal if and only if the normal vector is vertical. This means that the $x$- and $y$-components of the vector must be $0:$

$$

$$

 

From the first equation we get $y=1,$ while the second equation gives $x=0.$ 

Finally, substituting $x=0$ and $y=1$ into our function, we get

$$
z=0\operatorname{ln}⁡1=0.
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{a}{4}\,\, & >\,\,-2 \\ (-4)\cdot \left(-\frac{a}{4}\right)\,\, & <\,\,(-4)\cdot (-2) \\ (-4)\cdot \left(-\frac{a}{4}\right)\,\, & <\,\,8\end{aligned}
$$

Since two negative numbers multiply to give a positive number, we first cancel the negatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}(-4)\cdot \left(-\frac{a}{4}\right) & <8 \\ (\cancel{-}4)\cdot (\cancel{-}\frac{a}{4}) & <8 \\ 4\cdot \frac{a}{4} & <8\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can cancel a common factor of $4$ from both the numerator and denominator.

$$

$$

$$

$$

For a continuous random variable $X$ with probability density function $f(x)$ defined over a set $S,$ the $n$th raw moment of $X$ is given by

$$
\text{E}[{X}^{n}]={\int }_{S}{x}^{n}\cdot f(x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

We already know $\text{E}[X].$ So, we compute the second raw moment of $X$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{X}^{2}] & ={\int }_{S}{x}^{2}\cdot f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{\infty }{x}^{2}\cdot \frac{3}{{x}^{4}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{\infty }\frac{3}{{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\lim_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{1}^{a}\frac{3}{{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\lim_{a\to \infty }{\left(-\frac{3}{x}\right)|}_{1}^{a} \\  & =\lim_{a\to \infty }(3-\frac{3}{a}) \\  & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $\text{E}[X]=\frac{3}{2}$ and $\text{E}[{X}^{2}]=3$ into the simplified expression, we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{X}^{2}+2X-1] & =\text{E}[{X}^{2}]+2\text{E}[X]-1 \\  & =3+2\cdot \frac{3}{2}-1 \\  & =3+3-1 \\  & =5.\end{aligned}

\begin{aligned}A & =(2r)(2x)+\frac{\pi {r}^{2}}{2}+\frac{\pi {x}^{2}}{2} \\  & =4rx+\frac{\pi {r}^{2}}{2}+\frac{\pi {x}^{2}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

We know that the perimeter is fixed at $200$ units, so we also have the constraint condition

$$
200=\pi r+\pi x+2x+2r\,.
$$

Now, by making $x$ the subject of the constraint equation, we find that 

$$
\begin{aligned}200 & =\pi r+\pi x+2x+2r \\ x(\pi +2) & =200-r(\pi +2) \\ x & =\frac{200}{\pi +2}-r\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Plugging the above into our expression for $A,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =4rx+\frac{\pi {r}^{2}}{2}+\frac{\pi {x}^{2}}{2} \\  & =4r(\frac{200}{\pi +2}-r)+\frac{\pi {r}^{2}}{2}+\frac{\pi }{2}{(\frac{200}{\pi +2}-r)}^{2}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

We want to maximize $A,$ so we need to differentiate $A$ and set the derivative equal to zero. The derivative is

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{′}(r) & =4(\frac{200}{\pi +2}-r)+4r(-1)+\pi r+\pi (\frac{200}{\pi +2}-r)(-1) \\  & =\frac{800}{\pi +2}-4r-4r+\pi r-\frac{200\pi }{\pi +2}+\pi r \\  & =-8r+2\pi r+\frac{800-200\pi }{\pi +2}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Setting ${A}^{′}(r)=0$ and solving for $r$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{′}(r) & =0 \\ -8r+2\pi r+\frac{800-200\pi }{\pi +2} & =0 \\ 2r(\pi -4) & =-\frac{800-200\pi }{\pi +2} \\ 2r(\pi -4) & =\frac{200\pi -800}{\pi +2} \\ r & =\frac{100\pi -400}{(\pi +2)(\pi -4)} \\ r & =\frac{100(\pi -4)}{(\pi +2)(\pi -4)} \\ r & =\frac{100}{\pi +2}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we confirm that $r=\frac{100}{\pi +2}$ is a maximum using the second derivative test. The second derivative gives

$$
{A}^{″}(r)=-8+2\pi \,⟹\,{A}^{″}\left(\frac{100}{\pi +2}\right)=-8+2\pi <0.

Since ${A}^{″}\left(\frac{100}{\pi +2}\right)$ is negative, we conclude that $r=\frac{100}{\pi +2}$ is indeed a maximum of $A(r).$

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =\frac{200}{\pi +2}-\frac{100}{\pi +2} \\  & =\frac{100}{\pi +2}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the length of the side of the field with the largest area is $2x=\frac{200}{\pi +2}.$" "First,  let $r$ the radius of the upper semicircle (top) and $x$ the radius of the lateral semicircle (right), hence the dimensions of the rectangle are $2r$ and $2x.$ We want to maximize the area

$$
{f}^{′}(a)={\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{n}}\end{bmatrix}|}_{x=a}.
$$

In this case, the domain of $f$ is ${R}^{2},$ and the first partial derivatives of $f$ are

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =(1-2{x}^{2}){e}^{-({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =-2xy{e}^{-({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})}.\end{aligned}
$$

 

So, the first derivative of $f$ is

$$
{f}^{′}(x,y)=\begin{bmatrix}(1-2{x}^{2}){e}^{-({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})} & -2xy{e}^{-({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

To find the critical points, we need to find the points $(x,y)\in {R}^{2}$ such that ${f}^{′}(x,y)={0}^{T}$ or ${f}^{′}(x,y)$ does not exist. Note that, in our case, ${f}^{′}(x,y)$ exists everywhere, so we just need to find the points where ${f}^{′}(x,y)={0}^{T}.$

Setting ${f}^{′}(x,y)={0}^{T},$ we have the following system:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}(1-2{x}^{2}){e}^{-({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})} &=0 \\ -2xy{e}^{-({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})} &=0\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Since ${e}^{-({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})}\ne 0$ for any point $(x,y)\in {R}^{2},$ we must have 

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}1-2{x}^{2} &=0 \\ -2xy &=0\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Solving for $x$ in the first equation, we get

$$
1-2{x}^{2}=0\,⟹\,x=\pm \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}.
$$

 

Substituting these values into the second equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}-(\pm \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2})y=0\,⟹\,y=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our system has two solutions, $(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2},0)$ and $(-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2},0).$

In conclusion, $f$ has two critical points, $(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2},0)$ and $(-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2},0).$ Note that since ${f}^{′}(x)={0}^{T}$ at these two points, they are also both stationary points." The Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$

$$

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T:$

$$"] [17592186482535 :question/worked-solution "We will use the change of variables formula in the form

If $(\rho ,\theta ,ϕ)$ are the spherical coordinates of a point, then its Cartesian coordinates $(x,y,z)$ can be found by using the following formulas:

$$

$$

Notice that the region $R$ represents the sphere of radius $2$ centered at $(0,0,2).$

$$

As a result, we obtain that in spherical polar coordinates, our region can be expressed as

$$"] [17592186482547 :question/worked-solution "Recall that the volume of $R$ can be found as

$$"] [17592186482578 :question/problem "${\left(\frac{p}{2}+\frac{3}{2}\right)}^{2}=$"] [17592186482578 :question/worked-solution "We will use the following formula:

Therefore, the function reaches a minimum value at $\left(-\frac{1}{2},\frac{\sqrt{15}}{2}\right),$ and its minimum value is $-20.$"] [17592186483373 :question/worked-solution "The line integral of unity with respect to arc length over $C$ is equal to the arc length $L$ of $C,$ i.e.,

$$"] [17592186483374 :question/worked-solution "Recall that if ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{n}$ are independent and identically distributed discrete random variables with probability mass function $f(x;\theta ),$ where $\theta $ is an unknown parameter, then the log-likelihood function of a random sample ${x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}$ is

$$"] [17592186483382 :question/worked-solution "Recall that the general solution of an inhomogeneous system can be written as 

$$
x(t)={x}_{c}(t)+{x}_{p}(t)

$$

$$"] [17592186485562 :question/worked-solution "Let $S$ be the event that the second bin is selected, and let $G$ be the event that a randomly selected chip is green. Then, we require $P(S|G),$ which we can compute using Bayes' theorem.

The extrema of the velocity occur at the critical points of $v.$ Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ is $(7-x)\,{m/s}^{2},$ we have

$$

To find the moments where $v$ is a maximum, we need to solve $\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=0$ and test each solution using the first or second derivative test.

Solving $\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=0$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}7-x & =0 \\ x & =7.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the extremum of the velocity function occurs when $x=7\,m.$

We now test the extreme value using the first derivative test. We summarize the necessary information in a table, shown below.

| $x$ | $(0,7)$ | $7$ | $(7,\infty )$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Test Point | $6$ |  | $8$ |
| $\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}$ | $1>0$ | $0$ | $-1<0$ |
| $v$ | $↗$ | max | $↘$ |

We conclude that the velocity is maximized when $x=7\,m.$

Next, using the fact that

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}\left(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}\right),
$$

we can rewrite our initial equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}\left(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}\right)=7-x.
$$

$$
\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}\left(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}\right)\text{d}x=\int (7-x)\,\text{d}x

which gives the general solution

$$

$$

$$

Since the particle is moving in the direction of increasing $x,$ we have that $v(x)>0,$ so we can disregard the negative square root. Therefore,

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}⟶\begin{bmatrix}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{bmatrix}

This transformation maps some region $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane to our region $D$ in the $xy$-plane.

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,dx\,dy={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(x(u,v),y(u,v))|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|du\,dv
$$

where $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T.$

Note that the change of variables

$$
u=\frac{y}{x},\,v=xy
$$

 
gives us the *inverse* function ${T}^{-1},$ that is

$$

$$

To compute the required integral, we proceed as follows:

**Step 1**: Find $Δ,$ which is the image of $D$ under the action of ${T}^{-1}.$ 

Our domain in the $uv$-plane is

$$
\begin{aligned}Δ & =\{(u,v)\,:\,\frac{1}{4}\le u\le 2,\,1\le v\le 4\}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}-\frac{y}{{x}^{2}} & \frac{1}{x} \\ y & \text{ }\text{ }x\end{vmatrix} \\  & =-\frac{2y}{x}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T$ is

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}={\left(\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)}\right)}^{-1}=\frac{1}{\left(-\frac{2y}{x}\right)}=-\frac{1}{2u}.
$$

Note that $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}\ne 0$ everywhere inside $Δ.$ In other words, $T$ has no critical points inside $Δ.$

**Step 4**: Perform the change of variables:

Performing the change of variables, we obtain

$$

$$

To compute the required integral, we proceed as follows:

**Step 1**: Find a suitable change of variables.

The inequalities that define the region $D,$

$$

$$

suggest that we use the change of variables 

$$

$$

$$

$$

**Step 2**: Find $Δ,$ which is the image of $D$ under the action of ${T}^{-1}.$ 

Our domain in the $uv$-plane is

$$
\begin{aligned}Δ & =\{(u,v)\,:\,1\le u\le 4,\,1\le v\le 5\}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}\text{ }\text{ }\text{ }y & x \\ -\frac{y}{{x}^{2}} & \frac{1}{x}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\frac{2y}{x}.\end{aligned}

$$

This is known as differentiating under the integral sign.

We wish to compute ${K}^{′}(t),$ where

$$

Differentiating under the integral sign, we get

$$

$$

Next, let's compute the partial derivative with respect to $t$:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂t}[(x+\operatorname{cos}⁡(t))^{3}] & =3(x+\operatorname{cos}⁡(t))^{2}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂t}(x+\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)) \\  & =3(x+\operatorname{cos}⁡(t))^{2}\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)) \\  & =-3(x+\operatorname{cos}⁡(t))^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this back into our integral, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{K}^{′}(t) & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}-3(x+\operatorname{cos}⁡(t))^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)\,\text{d}x \\  & =-3\operatorname{sin}⁡(t){\int }_{-1}^{1}(x+\operatorname{cos}⁡(t))^{2}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}

Finally, let's evaluate the remaining integral. We first expand the squared term:

$$

$$

Therefore,

$$

$$

Using the $z$-table, we see that

$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(5<Y<10) & =Φ(0.18)-Φ(-0.27) \\  & ≈0.5714-0.3936 \\  & =0.1778.\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186499442 :question/worked-solution "The diagram for our circuit is shown below.

![](images/a3/a3bbe131778b11fe61a7e436d3d4729958bb207961ca9faaac91250cf4f2dde0.png)

The current $I,$ measured in amperes, is defined as the rate of flow of charge $q,$ measured in coulombs.

$$
I=\frac{dq}{dt}
$$

Kirchhoff's voltage law states that in a series circuit, the source voltage (EMF) equals the sum of the voltage drops.

In an RCL circuit, there are three voltage drops:

- The voltage drop across the resistor is proportional to the current, with a constant of proportionality $R=18\,Ω.$ So,

$$
{V}_{R}=18I.
$$

- The voltage drop across the capacitor is related to its charge by $q=C{V}_{C}.$ Therefore,

$$
{V}_{C}=\frac{q}{C}=\frac{q}{0.002}=500q.
$$

- The voltage drop across the inductor is proportional to the rate of change of current, with a constant of proportionality $L=9\,\text{H}.$ Hence,

$$
{V}_{L}=9\,\frac{dI}{dt}.
$$

Therefore, by Kirchhoff's voltage law, these values are related by the equation

$$
9\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)=18I+500q+9\,\frac{dI}{dt}.
$$

Differentiating with respect to $t,$ the differential equation governing the current in the circuit is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{d}{dt}(9\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)) & =\frac{d}{dt}\left(18I+500q+9\,\frac{dI}{dt}\right) \\ 27\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t) & =18\,\frac{dI}{dt}+500\,\frac{dq}{dt}+9\,\frac{{d}^{2}I}{d{t}^{2}},\end{aligned}
$$

which, when substituting in $I=\frac{dq}{dt},$ gives

$$
\frac{{d}^{2}I}{d{t}^{2}}+2\,\frac{dI}{dt}+\frac{500}{9}I=3\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t).
$$"] [17592186499449 :question/problem "Consider the finite region $R$ in the $xyz$-space, given by

$$
R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,0\le \frac{2x-y}{2}\le 1,\,0\le \frac{y}{2}\le 2,\,0\le z\le 3\}.
$$

Given the change of variables

$$
u=\frac{2x-y}{2},\,v=\frac{y}{2},\,w=\frac{z}{3},
$$

which of the following could be the missing part of the expression below?

$$
{∭}_{R}\left(\frac{2x-y}{2}+\frac{z}{3}\right)\,dV={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}\bbox[3pt,border:1pt solid black]{\phantom{AAAAAA}}\,dw\,dv\,du
$$"] [17592186499449 :question/worked-solution "Let's define a transformation $T$ as follows:

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v \\ w\end{bmatrix}⟶\begin{bmatrix}x(u,v,w) \\ y(u,v,w) \\ z(u,v,w)\end{bmatrix}
$$

This transformation maps some region $Δ$ in the $uvw$-space to our region $R$ in the $xyz$-space.

To find the required integral, we can use the change of variables formula

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\text{ }dV={∭}_{Δ}\text{ }f(x(u,v,w),y(u,v,w),z(u,v,w))\,|\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v\text{d}w
$$

where $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T.$

Note that the change of variables

$$
u=\frac{2x-y}{2},\,v=\frac{y}{2},\,w=\frac{z}{3},
$$

gives us the *inverse* function ${T}^{-1},$ that is

$$
{T}^{-1}:\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y \\ z\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}u(x,y,z) \\ v(x,y,z) \\ w(x,y,z)\end{bmatrix}.
$$

To find the required integral, we proceed in four steps:

**Step 1**: Find $Δ,$ which is the image of $R$ under the action of ${T}^{-1}.$ 

Our domain in the $uvw$-space is

$$
\begin{aligned}Δ & =\{(u,v,w)\,:\,0\le u\le 1,\,0\le v\le 2,\,0\le w\le 1\}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} & \frac{∂u}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y} & \frac{∂v}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & \frac{∂w}{∂y} & \frac{∂w}{∂z}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}1 & -\frac{1}{2} & 0 \\ 0 & \,\,\,\frac{1}{2} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & \frac{1}{3}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\begin{vmatrix}1 & -\frac{1}{2} \\ 0 & \,\,\,\frac{1}{2}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\left(\frac{1}{2}-0\right) \\  & =\frac{1}{6}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T$ is

$$
\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}={\left(\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)}\right)}^{-1}=6.
$$

Note that $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}\ne 0$ everywhere inside $Δ.$ In other words, $T$ has no critical points inside $Δ.$

**Step 4**: Perform the change of variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∭}_{R}\left(\frac{2x-y}{2}+\frac{z}{3}\right)\,dV & ={∭}_{Δ}(u+w)\cdot |\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v\text{d}w \\  & ={∭}_{Δ}(u+w)\cdot |6|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v\text{d}w \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}\,6(u+w)\,dw\,dv\,du\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186499451 :question/worked-solution "Suppose that ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{n}$ is a random sample of size $n$ from a population with population mean $\mu $ and population standard deviation $\sigma .$ The central limit theorem (or CLT) states that for sufficiently large $n,$ the distribution of the sample mean $\overset{―}{X}$ can be approximated as 

$$
\overset{―}{X}∼N\,\left(\mu ,\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n}\right).
$$

In our case:

- the sample size is

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =40,\end{aligned}
$$

- the population mean is

$$
\begin{aligned}\mu  & =\text{E}[X] \\  & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }x\,f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}x\cdot 1\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}\,{|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{2} \\  & =0.5,\end{aligned}
$$

- the population variance is ${\sigma }^{2}=0.08.$

Therefore, by the CLT, we have that the distribution of the sample mean can be approximated as

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{―}{X} & ∼N\,\left(\mu ,\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n}\right) \\  & ∼N\,\left(0.5,\frac{0.08}{40}\right) \\  & ∼N(0.5,0.002).\end{aligned}
$$

We want to find $P(0.51<\overset{―}{X}<0.55).$ So, we convert $\overset{―}{X}$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(0.51<\overset{―}{X}<0.55) & =P\left(\frac{0.51-0.5}{\sqrt{0.002}}<Z<\frac{0.55-0.5}{\sqrt{0.002}}\right) \\  & ≈P(0.22<Z<1.12) \\  & =P(Z<1.12)-P(Z<0.22) \\  & =Φ(1.12)-Φ(0.22)\end{aligned}
$$

From the tables, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Φ(0.22)=0.5871, \\ Φ(1.12)=0.8686.\end{aligned}
$$

which, when substituting in $I=\frac{dq}{dt},$ gives

$$"] [17592186499479 :question/worked-solution "The area of the required region is given by

$$
{∬}_{D}dxdy.
$$

Let's define a transformation $T$ as follows: 

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{bmatrix}
$$

This transformation maps some region $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane to our region $D$ in the $xy$-plane.

To compute the required area, we will use the change of variables formula

$$
{∬}_{D}dxdy={∬}_{Δ}|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\text{ }dudv
$$

where $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T.$  

Note that the changes of variables

$$
u=x+y,\,v=y
$$

 

gives us the *inverse* function ${T}^{-1},$ that is

$$
{T}^{-1}:\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}u(x,y) \\ v(x,y)\end{bmatrix}.
$$

To compute the required area, we proceed in four steps:

**Step 1**: Find $Δ,$ which is the image of $D$ under the action of ${T}^{-1}.$ 

Substituting $x+y=u$ and $y=v$ into the equation of the first curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}(x+y)^{3}-y=0\,⟹\,{u}^{3}-v=0\,⟹\,v={u}^{3},\end{aligned}
$$

while substituting $x+y=u$ and $y=v$ into the equation of the second curve, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}(x+y)^{2}-y=0\,⟹\,{u}^{2}-v=0\,⟹\,v={u}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the intersections of the curves in the $uv$-plane, we solve the following system:

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}v &={u}^{3} \\ v &={u}^{2}\end{aligned}\right.\,⟹\,\left\{\begin{aligned}{u}^{2}(u-1) &=0 \\ v &=u.\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the intersection points are $(0,0)$ and $(1,1).$

Therefore, our domain in the $uv$-plane has the type I representation 

$$
Δ=\{(u,v)\,:\,0\le u\le 1,\,{u}^{3}\le v\le {u}^{2}\}.
$$

![](images/a8/a8d2549c665a918cc8d69c69136fcb49e654ebb9aa5e53611155798e791b36a9.png)

   

**Step 2**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T$ is

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}={\left(\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)}\right)}^{-1}=(1)^{-1}=1.
$$

Note that $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}\ne 0$ everywhere inside $Δ.$  In other words, $T$ has no critical points inside $Δ.$

**Step 4**: Compute the required area.

We calculate the required area by performing the change of variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\text{d}x\text{d}y & ={∬}_{Δ}|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}|1|\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[{\int }_{{u}^{3}}^{{u}^{2}}\,dv]du \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}v{|}_{{u}^{3}}^{{u}^{2}}\,du \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}({u}^{2}-{u}^{3})du \\  & ={\left[\frac{{u}^{3}}{3}-\frac{{u}^{4}}{4}\right]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}-\frac{1}{4} \\  & =\frac{1}{12}.\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186499482 :question/worked-solution "The current $I,$ measured in amperes, is defined as the rate of flow of charge $q,$ measured in coulombs.

**Step 2**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} & \frac{∂u}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y} & \frac{∂v}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & \frac{∂w}{∂y} & \frac{∂w}{∂z}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}1 & 1 & 0 \\ -1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =1(-1)^{3+3}\begin{vmatrix}1 & 1 \\ -1 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =1-(-1) \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T:$

$$

The current $I,$ measured in amperes, is defined as the rate of flow of charge $q,$ measured in coulombs.

$$
I=\frac{dq}{dt}
$$

Kirchhoff's voltage law states that in a series circuit, the source voltage (EMF) equals the sum of the voltage drops.

In an RCL circuit, there are three voltage drops:

- The voltage drop across the resistor is proportional to the current, with a constant of proportionality $R=90\,Ω.$ So,

$$
{V}_{R}=90I=90\,\frac{dq}{dt}.
$$

- The voltage drop across the capacitor is related to its charge by $q=C{V}_{C}.$ Therefore,

$$
{V}_{C}=\frac{q}{C}=\frac{q}{(1/200)}=200q.
$$

- The voltage drop across the inductor is proportional to the rate of change of current, with a constant of proportionality $L=10\,\text{H}.$ Hence,

$$
{V}_{L}=10\,\frac{dI}{dt}=10\,\frac{d}{dt}\left(\frac{dq}{dt}\right)=10\,\frac{{d}^{2}q}{d{t}^{2}}.
$$

Therefore, by Kirchhoff's voltage law, the differential equation governing the amount of charge $q$ on the capacitor is

$$
40\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)=90\,\frac{dq}{dt}+200q+10\,\frac{{d}^{2}q}{d{t}^{2}},
$$

which gives

$$
\frac{{d}^{2}q}{d{t}^{2}}+9\cdot \frac{dq}{dt}+20q=4\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t).
$$

The given equation is a second-order linear equation with constant coefficients. To find the general solution, we must sum the complementary and particular solutions.

- To find the complementary solution ${q}_{c},$ we solve the corresponding homogeneous equation, given by

$$
\frac{{d}^{2}{q}_{c}}{d{t}^{2}}+9\cdot \frac{d{q}_{c}}{dt}+20{q}_{c}=0.
$$

Solving using an integration technique, such as a trial solution, we obtain the complementary solution

$$
{q}_{c}(t)=A{e}^{-4t}+B{e}^{-5t},
$$

where $A$ and $B$ are constants.

- Next, we find the particular solution. Note that the right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is sinusoidal with argument $2t.$ So, we assume that the particular solution is also a sinusoidal with argument $2t,$ i.e.,

$$
{q}_{p}(t)=\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t).
$$

To find the values of $\alpha $ and $\beta ,$ we substitute

$$
\begin{aligned}{q}_{p} & =\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t), \\ \frac{d{q}_{p}}{dt} & =-2\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+2\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t), \\ \frac{{d}^{2}{q}_{p}}{d{t}^{2}} & =-4\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)-4\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t),\end{aligned}
$$

into the inhomogeneous equation and group like terms on the left-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,(-4\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)-4\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t))+9(-2\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+2\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t))\,\, &  \\ +20(\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)) & =4\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\ (16\alpha +18\beta )\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+(-18\alpha +16\beta )\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) & =4\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the coefficients, we get the following system of equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}16\alpha +18\beta &=0\, && (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)) \\ -18\alpha +16\beta &=4\, && (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t))\end{aligned}\right.

Now, since the general solution is given by the sum of the complementary solution and the particular solution, the general solution in our case is

Differentiating this expression for $q(t),$ we obtain the following expression for $I$ in amperes:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(t) & =\frac{d}{dt}\left(A{e}^{-4t}+B{e}^{-5t}-\frac{18}{145}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\frac{16}{145}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\right) \\  & =-4A{e}^{-4t}-5B{e}^{-5t}+\frac{36}{145}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+\frac{32}{145}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t).\end{aligned}
$$

- The quantity ${I}_{c}(t)=-4A{e}^{-4t}-5B{e}^{-5t}$ is the *transient current*, since it goes to zero as $t\to \infty .$

\displaystyle {I}_{p}(t)=\frac{36}{145}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+\frac{32}{145}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)
$$ is the *steady-state current*. It governs the current's long-term behavior.

Therefore, as $t\to \infty ,$ we have

$$
I(t)≈{I}_{p}(t)=\frac{36}{145}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+\frac{32}{145}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t).
$$

Finally, the amplitude of the steady-state current, in amperes, is given by

$$
\sqrt{{\left(\frac{36}{145}\right)}^{2}+{\left(\frac{32}{145}\right)}^{2}}≈0.33,
$$

In an RCL circuit, there are three voltage drops:

- The voltage drop across the resistor is proportional to the current, with a constant of proportionality $R=32\,Ω.$ So,

$$
{V}_{R}=32I.
$$

- The voltage drop across the capacitor is related to its charge by $q=C{V}_{C}.$ Therefore,

$$
{V}_{C}=\frac{q}{C}=\frac{q}{0.005}=200q.
$$

- The voltage drop across the inductor is proportional to the rate of change of current, with a constant of proportionality $L=8\,\text{H}.$ Hence,

$$
{V}_{L}=8\,\frac{dI}{dt}.
$$

Therefore, by Kirchhoff's voltage law, these values are related by the equation

$$
10=32I+200q+8\,\frac{dI}{dt}.
$$

Differentiating with respect to $t,$ the differential equation governing the current in the circuit is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{d}{dt}(10) & =\frac{d}{dt}\left(32I+200q+8\,\frac{dI}{dt}\right) \\ 0 & =32\,\frac{dI}{dt}+200\,\frac{dq}{dt}+8\,\frac{{d}^{2}I}{d{t}^{2}},\end{aligned}
$$

which, when substituting in $I=\frac{dq}{dt},$ gives

$$
\frac{{d}^{2}I}{d{t}^{2}}+4\,\frac{dI}{dt}+25I=0.
$$"] [17592186499566 :question/worked-solution "Suppose that ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{n}$ is a random sample of size $n$ from a population with population mean $\mu $ and population standard deviation $\sigma .$ The central limit theorem (or CLT) states that for sufficiently large $n,$ the distribution of the sample mean $\overset{―}{X}$ can be approximated as 

$$
\overset{―}{X}∼N\,\left(\mu ,\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n}\right).
$$

In our case:

- the sample size is

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =50,\end{aligned}
$$

- the population mean is

$$
\begin{aligned}\mu  & =\text{E}[X] \\  & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }x\,f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{\infty }x\cdot \frac{5}{{x}^{6}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{\infty }\frac{5}{{x}^{5}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\lim_{b\to \infty }{\int }_{1}^{b}\frac{5}{{x}^{5}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\lim_{b\to \infty }{\left[-\frac{5}{4{x}^{4}}\right]}_{1}^{b} \\  & =\frac{5}{4} \\  & =1.25,\end{aligned}
$$

- the population variance is ${\sigma }^{2}=0.1.$

Therefore, by the CLT, we have that the distribution of the sample mean can be approximated as

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{―}{X} & ∼N\,\left(\mu ,\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n}\right) \\  & ∼N\,\left(1.25,\frac{0.1}{50}\right) \\  & ∼N(1.25,0.002).\end{aligned}
$$

We want to find $P(\overset{―}{X}<1.2).$ So, we convert $\overset{―}{X}$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(\overset{―}{X}<1.2) & =P\left(Z<\frac{1.2-1.25}{\sqrt{0.002}}\right) \\  & ≈P(Z<-1.12) \\  & =Φ(-1.12)\end{aligned}
$$

From the table, we have that

$$
Φ(-1.12)=0.1314.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(\overset{―}{X}<1.2) & =Φ(-1.12) \\  & =0.1314.\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186500281 :multistep/context "Mike needs to paint some walls. Each wall has an area of ${\left(\frac{17}{4}\right)}^{2}$ square meters."] [17592186500288 :question/worked-solution "After finishing, Mike had $\left(4\,\frac{4}{5}-3\,\frac{3}{10}\right)$ liters of paint left.

Writing $4\,\frac{4}{5}$ as an improper fraction, we have

$$
4\,\frac{4}{5}=\frac{4\times 5+4}{5}=\frac{24}{5}.
$$

Writing $3\,\frac{3}{10}$ as an improper fraction, we have

$$
3\,\frac{3}{10}=\frac{3\times 10+3}{10}=\frac{33}{10}.
$$

Therefore, our problem now is to work out the following:

$$
\frac{24}{5}-\frac{33}{10}
$$

To subtract two fractions with unlike denominators, we need to express each fraction as an equivalent fraction with a common denominator.

In this question, we can make a common denominator of $10.$

To put $\frac{24}{5}$ over a denominator of $10,$ we multiply the numerator and denominator by $2:$

$$
\frac{24}{5}=\frac{24\times 2}{5\times 2}=\frac{48}{10}
$$

We can now subtract the fractions. We keep the denominator the same, and we subtract the numerators:

$$
\frac{48}{10}-\frac{33}{10}=\frac{15}{10}
$$

Simplifying, we have

$$
\frac{15}{10}=\frac{15÷5}{10÷5}=\frac{3}{2}.
$$

Finally, we convert back to a mixed number:

$$
\frac{3}{2}=1\,\text{R}\,1=1\,\frac{1}{2}
$$

Therefore, Mike had $1\,\frac{1}{2}$ liters of paint left."] [17592186500293 :question/worked-solution "We can perform this computation as follows:

$$"] [17592186500307 :question/problem "Consider the finite region $D$ enclosed in the first quadrant of the $xy$-plane between the lines and curves

what could be the missing expression?"] [17592186500307 :question/worked-solution "We would like to find a rectangular region of the form

$$
\begin{aligned}Δ & =\{(u,v)\,:\,a\le u\le b,\,\,c\le v\le d\} \\  & =\{(u,v)\,:\,a\le u(x,y)\le b,\,\,c\le v(x,y)\le d\},\end{aligned}

where the equations of the left, right, bottom, and top sides are

With that in mind, let's analyze the boundary of our region $D.$

by moving both variables $x$ and $y$ to the left-hand side, we obtain

Therefore, if we put $u(x,y)=\frac{x}{y}$ and $v(x,y)={e}^{x+y},$ we can define the transformation ${T}^{-1}$ as

To find $T,$ we should express $x$ and $y$ in terms of $u$ and $v.$ Recall that we have

$$

$$

$$"] [17592186500327 :question/worked-solution "For a plane lamina of mass $M$ and a line ${l}_{M}$ perpendicular to the lamina passing through its center of mass, the parallel axis theorem states that the moment of inertia of the lamina about a line $l$ parallel to ${l}_{M}$ is given by

where $d$ is the distance between the lines, and ${I}_{M}$ and ${I}_{l}$ are the moments of inertia about the lines ${l}_{M}$ and $l,$ respectively.

First, we find the mass of the plate as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ={∬}_{D}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{3}\frac{1}{9}xy\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{9}{\int }_{0}^{3}x\,\text{d}x{\int }_{0}^{3}y\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{9}\cdot \frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}{|}_{0}^{3}\cdot \frac{1}{2}{y}^{2}{|}_{0}^{3} \\  & =\frac{1}{9}\cdot \frac{9}{2}\cdot \frac{9}{2} \\  & =\frac{9}{4}\,\text{kg}\end{aligned}

Next, the moment of inertia about the perpendicular line through the center of mass $(2,2)$ is

\begin{aligned}{I}_{M} & ={∬}_{D}((x-\overset{―}{x})^{2}+(y-\overset{―}{y})^{2})\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}((x-2)^{2}+(y-2)^{2})\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{3}((x-2)^{2}+(y-2)^{2})\cdot \frac{1}{9}xy\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{9}{\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{3}x(x-2)^{2}y+x{y}^{3}-4x{y}^{2}+4xy\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{9}{\int }_{0}^{3}{\left[\frac{1}{2}x(x-2)^{2}{y}^{2}+\frac{1}{4}x{y}^{4}-\frac{4}{3}x{y}^{3}+2x{y}^{2}\right]}_{y=0}^{y=3}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}\frac{1}{2}{x}^{3}-2{x}^{2}+\frac{9}{4}x\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\left[\frac{1}{8}{x}^{4}-\frac{2}{3}{x}^{3}+\frac{9}{8}{x}^{2}\right]}_{0}^{3} \\  & =\frac{81}{8}-18+\frac{81}{8} \\  & =\frac{9}{4}\,\text{kg}\cdot {\text{m}}^{2}.\end{aligned}

$$"] [17592186500341 :question/problem "The curve $C$ is the intersection of a surface $S,$ defined by $z=f(x,y),$ with the plane $y=0.$ Given that the point $P\left(\frac{1}{2},0,1\right)$ lies on $C$, and that ${f}_{x}=(y+1)\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi x)+2x\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi y)\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x)$, find the equations of the tangent line to $C$ at $P.$"] [17592186500341 :question/worked-solution "The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface $z=f(x,y)$ with the plane $y=0.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve at the point $P\left(\frac{1}{2},0,1\right)$ will be given by the partial derivative $\frac{∂z}{∂x}{|}_{\left(\frac{1}{2},0\right)}.$

Hence, the $y$-intercept is $-\frac{7}{3}.$ Thus, the line intersects the $y$-axis at $\left(0,-\frac{7}{3}\right).$"] [17592186501163 :question/worked-solution "Notice that the leading coefficient is $-1$. So, we take out a factor of $-1$ from the entire expression:

$$
-\left({y}^{2}-9y-\frac{1}{4}\right)
$$

Let's now complete the square for the expression inside the parentheses:

$$
{y}^{2}-9y-\frac{1}{4}

$$

$$"] [17592186501166 :question/worked-solution "Notice that the leading coefficient is $-5$. So, we take out a factor of $-5$ from the entire expression:

$$"] [17592186501199 :question/worked-solution "Let's highlight the important words in the given statement:

*The **volume** of a sphere **increases** at a rate **proportional** to the **square of its radius**.* 

We note the following:

- The question describes the *rate* at which the *volume $V$ of a sphere* varies. Therefore, this is a statement about the quantity 

$$
\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t}.
$$

- We're told that $\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t}$ *increases* at a rate *proportional to the square of its radius.* Therefore,

$$
\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t}=k{r}^{2},
$$

where $k>0.$

We wish to use this information to find an expression for $\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}.$

The volume $V$ of a sphere is given by

$$
V=\frac{4}{3}\pi {r}^{3}.
$$

Differentiating this equation with respect to $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}\left(\frac{4}{3}\pi {r}^{3}\right) \\ \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =4\pi {r}^{2}\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =k{r}^{2} \\ 4\pi {r}^{2}\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} & =k{r}^{2} \\ \frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{k{r}^{2}}{4\pi {r}^{2}} \\ \frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{k}{4\pi }.\end{aligned}
$$

We now introduce a new constant:

$$
K=\frac{k}{4\pi }>0
$$

 

Therefore, our equation becomes

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}=K.
$$"] [17592186501201 :question/worked-solution "The rate of change of $g(x,y)$ at the point $(1,1)$ in the direction of $v$ is equal to the directional derivative ${g}_{u}^{′}(1,1).$ 

First, we find the unit vector $u$ in the direction of $v:$

$$
\begin{aligned}‖v‖ & =\sqrt{{2}^{2}+{4}^{2}}=\sqrt{20}=2\sqrt{5} \\ u & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{5}}⟨2,4⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}⟨1,2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we find the gradient $∇g(x,y)$ and evaluate it at the point $(1,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇g(x,y) & =\left\langle \frac{∂}{∂x}\left(\frac{{e}^{y}}{yx}\right),\,\frac{∂}{∂y}\left(\frac{{e}^{y}}{yx}\right)\right\rangle  \\  & =\left\langle -\frac{{e}^{y}}{{x}^{2}y},\,\frac{{e}^{y}(y-1)}{x{y}^{2}}\right\rangle  \\ ∇g(1,1) & =\left\langle -\frac{{e}^{1}}{{1}^{2}\cdot 1},\,\frac{{e}^{1}\cdot (1-1)}{1\cdot {1}^{2}}\right\rangle  \\  & =⟨-e,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the directional derivative ${g}_{u}^{′}(1,1)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{g}_{u}^{′}(1,1) & =∇g(1,1)\cdot u \\  & =⟨-e,0⟩\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}⟨1,2⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}(-e\cdot 1+0\cdot 2) \\  & =-\frac{e}{\sqrt{5}} \\  & =-\frac{e\sqrt{5}}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186501204 :question/worked-solution "Let's highlight the important words in the given statement:

*The **volume** of the ball **decreases** at a **rate** that's **proportional** to its **volume**.* 

We note the following:

- The question describes the *rate* at which the *volume $V$ of a sphere* varies. Therefore, this is a statement about the quantity 

$$
\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t}.
$$

- We're told that $\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t}$ *decreases* at a rate that's *proportional to its volume.* Therefore,

$$
\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t}=-kV,
$$

where $k>0.$

We wish to use this information to find an expression for $\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}.$

The volume $V$ of a sphere is given by

$$
V=\frac{4}{3}\pi {r}^{3}.
$$

Differentiating this equation with respect to $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}\left(\frac{4}{3}\pi {r}^{3}\right) \\ \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =4\pi {r}^{2}\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =-kV \\ 4\pi {r}^{2}\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} & =-k\cdot \frac{4}{3}\pi {r}^{3} \\ 4\pi {r}^{2}\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} & =-\frac{4\pi k{r}^{3}}{3} \\ \frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} & =-\frac{\left(\frac{4\pi k{r}^{3}}{3}\right)}{4\pi {r}^{2}} \\ \frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} & =-\frac{4\pi k{r}^{3}}{12\pi {r}^{2}} \\ \frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} & =-\frac{kr}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

We now introduce a new constant:

$$
K=\frac{k}{3}>0
$$

 

Therefore, our equation becomes

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}=-Kr.
$$"] [17592186501206 :question/worked-solution "We begin by completing the square for the expression inside the parentheses:

$$
{x}^{2}-3x+1

First, we rewrite the coefficient of the linear term as a product with $2$ as a factor:

Then, we *add* and *then subtract* ${\left(\frac{3}{2}\right)}^{2}$, writing the constant term $1$ last:

Finally, we substitute this result back into our original expression:

$$"] [17592186501218 :question/worked-solution "Notice that the leading coefficient is $-3$. So, we take out a factor of $-3$ from the entire expression:

$$"] [17592186501225 :question/worked-solution "Since our random variable $X$ has a probability distribution function $f(x)$ that involves an absolute value, the cumulative distribution function takes the following form:

$$
F(x)=P(X\le x)=\left\{\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{x}\frac{{e}^{t}}{2}\,\text{d}t, & x<0 \\ {\int }_{-\infty }^{0}\frac{{e}^{t}}{2}\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{0}^{x}\frac{{e}^{-t}}{2}\,\text{d}t, & x\ge 0\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Let's compute the integrals.

- If $x\le 0,$ we have

$$

$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{0}\frac{{e}^{t}}{2}\,\text{d}t & ={\frac{{e}^{x}}{2}|}_{x=0} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

- If $x>0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{x}\frac{{e}^{-t}}{2}\,\text{d}t & =-{\frac{{e}^{-t}}{2}|}_{0}^{x} \\  & =-\frac{{e}^{-x}}{2}+\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

As a result, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{0}\frac{{e}^{t}}{2}\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{0}^{x}\frac{{e}^{-t}}{2}\,\text{d}t & =\frac{1}{2}+\left(-\frac{{e}^{-x}}{2}+\frac{1}{2}\right) \\  & =1-\frac{{e}^{-x}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the cumulative distribution function is given by

$$
F(x)=\left\{\begin{aligned}\frac{{e}^{x}}{2},\, & x\le 0 \\ 1-\frac{{e}^{-x}}{2},\, & x>0.\end{aligned}\right.
$$"] [17592186501235 :question/worked-solution "Let's define a transformation $T$ as follows:

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}⟶\begin{bmatrix}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{bmatrix}
$$

This transformation maps some region $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane to our region $D$ in the $xy$-plane.

To compute the required integral, we can use the change of variables formula

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dxdy={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(x(u,v),y(u,v))\,|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\text{ }dudv
$$

where $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T.$

To compute the required integral, we proceed as follows:

**Step 1**: Find a suitable change of variables.

The integrand

$$
f(x,y)=(x-y){e}^{x+y}
$$

suggests that we use the change of variables 

$$
u=x-y,\,v=x+y.
$$

This change of variables gives us the *inverse* function ${T}^{-1},$ that is

$$
{T}^{-1}:\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}u(x,y) \\ v(x,y)\end{bmatrix}.
$$

**Step 2**: Find $Δ,$ which is the image of $D$ under the action of ${T}^{-1}.$ 

The vertices of our domain $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane are as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{T}^{-1}(0,0) & =(0-0,0+0) \\  & =(0,0) \\ {T}^{-1}(2,-2) & =(2-(-2),2+(-2)) \\  & =(4,0) \\ {T}^{-1}(3,-1) & =(3-(-1),3+(-1)) \\  & =(4,2) \\ {T}^{-1}(1,1) & =(1-1,1+1) \\  & =(0,2)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our domain in the $uv$-plane is the following rectangle:

$$
Δ=\{(u,v)\,:\,0\le u\le 4,\,0\le v\le 2\}
$$

![](images/0b/0b23c6463447aa1fb64bdeeca689a40711f8dad59b348bb7943c2b9d2de7e8fc.png)

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}1 & -1 \\ 1 & \text{ }\text{ }1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 4**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T:$

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}={\left(\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)}\right)}^{-1}=\frac{1}{2}
$$

Note that $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}\ne 0$ everywhere inside $Δ.$ In other words, $T$ has no critical points inside $Δ.$

**Step 5**: Perform the change of variables, and evaluate the integral:

Performing the change of variables, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}(x-y){e}^{x+y}\,\text{d}x\text{d}y & ={∬}_{Δ}u{e}^{v}\,|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}u{e}^{v}\,|\frac{1}{2}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{4}u{e}^{v}\,\text{d}u\,\text{d}v \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}{e}^{v}\,\text{d}v{\int }_{0}^{4}u\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot [{e}^{v}]_{0}^{2}\cdot {\left[\frac{1}{2}{u}^{2}\right]}_{0}^{4}\,\text{d}v \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot ({e}^{2}-1)\cdot 8 \\  & =4({e}^{2}-1).\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186501236 :question/worked-solution "Notice that the leading coefficient is $-1$. So, we take out a factor of $-1$ from the entire expression:

$$
-({x}^{2}+7x+11)
$$

Let's now complete the square for the expression inside the parentheses:

$$
{x}^{2}+7x+11
$$

First, we rewrite the coefficient of the linear term as a product with $2$ as a factor:

$$
{x}^{2}+2\cdot \frac{7}{2}x+11
$$

Then, we *add* and *then subtract* ${\left(\frac{7}{2}\right)}^{2}$, writing the constant term $11$ last:

$$
\underbrace{{x}^{2}+2\cdot \frac{7}{2}x+{\left(\frac{7}{2}\right)}^{2}}-{\left(\frac{7}{2}\right)}^{2}+11
$$

The first three terms form a perfect square, which we factor as follows:

$$
{\left(x+\frac{7}{2}\right)}^{2}-{\left(\frac{7}{2}\right)}^{2}+11
$$

Evaluating the last two terms, we get

$$
{\left(x+\frac{7}{2}\right)}^{2}-\frac{5}{4}.
$$

Finally, we substitute this result back into our original expression:

$$
\begin{aligned}-{x}^{2}-7x-11 & =-\left({\left(x+\frac{7}{2}\right)}^{2}-\frac{5}{4}\right) \\  & =\frac{5}{4}-{\left(x+\frac{7}{2}\right)}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186501243 :question/worked-solution "Notice that the leading coefficient is $-8$. So, we take out a factor of $-8$ from the entire expression:

$$
-8\left({x}^{2}+\frac{1}{2}x\right)
$$

Let's now complete the square for the expression inside the parentheses:

$$
{x}^{2}+\frac{1}{2}x
$$

First, we rewrite the coefficient of the linear term as a product with $2$ as a factor:

$$
{x}^{2}+2\cdot \frac{1}{4}x
$$

Then, we *add* and *then subtract* ${\left(\frac{1}{4}\right)}^{2}$: 

$$
\underbrace{{x}^{2}+2\cdot \frac{1}{4}x+{\left(\frac{1}{4}\right)}^{2}}-{\left(\frac{1}{4}\right)}^{2}
$$

The first three terms form a perfect square, which we factor as follows:

$$
{\left(x+\frac{1}{4}\right)}^{2}-{\left(\frac{1}{4}\right)}^{2}
$$

Evaluating the last term, we get

$$
{\left(x+\frac{1}{4}\right)}^{2}-\frac{1}{16}
$$

Finally, we substitute this result back into our original expression:

$$
\begin{aligned}-8\left({x}^{2}+\frac{1}{2}x\right) & =-8\left({\left(x+\frac{1}{4}\right)}^{2}-\frac{1}{16}\right) \\  & =-8{\left(x+\frac{1}{4}\right)}^{2}+(-8)\cdot \left(-\frac{1}{16}\right) \\  & =-8{\left(x+\frac{1}{4}\right)}^{2}+\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186502072 :question/worked-solution "Since $Q$ is the amount of ink dye in the reservoir at time $t,$ the derivative 

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}
$$

describes how this amount changes with respect to time $t,$ in minutes. This is equal to the rate at which ink dye enters the reservoir minus the rate at which ink dye leaves the reservoir.

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}
$$

Note that the units of $\frac{dQ}{dt},{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}$ and ${Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}$ are $\text{lb}/\text{min}.$ Now, let's compute the required rates of change in steps.

**Step 1**: Calculating the rate at which ink dye enters the reservoir.

First, note that a solution containing $\frac{4}{3}\,\text{lb/gal}$ of ink dye enters the reservoir at a rate of $9\,\text{gal/min}.$ So, the rate at which the *ink dye* enters the reservoir is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′} & =\left(\frac{4}{3}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{gal}}\right)\cdot \left(9\,\frac{\text{gal}}{\text{min}}\right) \\  & =\left(\frac{4}{3}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\cancel{\text{gal}}}\right)\cdot \left(9\,\frac{\cancel{\text{gal}}}{\text{min}}\right) \\  & =12\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Calculating the rate at which ink dye exits the reservoir.

To find the rate at which ink dye leaves the reservoir, we must first determine the volume of solution in the reservoir at time $t.$

The reservoir initially contains $60\,\text{gal}$ of solution; solution enters at $9\,\text{gal/min}$ and mixed solution leaves at $6\,\text{gal/min}.$
As a result, the amount of solution in the reservoir after $t$ minutes is 

$$
V(t)=60+9t-6t=3(20+t)\,\text{gal}.
$$

Note that $V(t)$ is an increasing function, so the reservoir is filling.

Since $Q$ is the amount of ink dye in the reservoir, the concentration of the solution at time $t$ is

$$
\frac{Q}{3(20+t)}\,\text{lb/gal}.
$$

Therefore, as the completely mixed solution leaves at a rate of $6\,\text{gal/min},$ *ink dye* leaves at a rate of

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} & =\left(6\,\frac{\text{gal}}{\text{min}}\right)\cdot \left(\frac{Q}{3(20+t)}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{gal}}\right) \\  & =\left(6\,\frac{\cancel{\text{gal}}}{\text{min}}\right)\cdot \left(\frac{Q}{3(20+t)}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\cancel{\text{gal}}}\right) \\  & =\frac{6Q}{3(20+t)}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{min}} \\  & =\frac{2Q}{20+t}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Calculate the overall rate of change.

The rate of change equals the rate of entry minus the rate of exit. Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dQ}{dt} & ={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} \\  & =12-\frac{2Q}{20+t}\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the equation

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}+\frac{2}{20+t}\,Q=12.
$$

**Step 4**: Integrate the equation.

This is a first-order linear equation with variable coefficients. So we find the general solution using an integrating factor:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(t) & ={e}^{\int 2/(20+t)\,dt} \\  & ={e}^{2\operatorname{ln}⁡|20+t|} \\  & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(20+t)^{2}} \\  & =(20+t)^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying both sides of the differential equation by $I(t)=(20+t)^{2}$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}(20+t)^{2}\cdot \left(\frac{dQ}{dt}+\frac{2}{20+t}\,Q\right) & =(20+t)^{2}\cdot 12 \\ (20+t)^{2}\frac{dQ}{dt}+2(20+t)Q & =12(20+t)^{2} \\ \frac{d}{dt}(Q(20+t)^{2}) & =12(20+t)^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate with respect to $t:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{d}{dt}(Q(20+t)^{2})\,dt & =\int 12(20+t)^{2}\,dt \\ Q(20+t)^{2} & =12\cdot \frac{1}{3}(20+t)^{3}+C \\ Q(t) & =4(20+t)+\frac{C}{(20+t)^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

We're told that the reservoir initially contains $18\,\text{lb}$ of ink dye. So, we can apply the initial condition $Q(0)=18,$ and solve for $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(0) & =18 \\ 4(20+0)+\frac{C}{(20+0)^{2}} & =18 \\ 80+\frac{C}{(20)^{2}} & =18 \\ \frac{C}{{20}^{2}} & =-62 \\ C & =-62(20)^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we obtain the following expression for $Q(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(t) & =4(20+t)-\frac{62(20)^{2}}{(20+t)^{2}} \\  & =4(20+t)-62{\left(\frac{20}{20+t}\right)}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let ${t}_{o}$ be the time when the reservoir begins to overflow. The reservoir has a capacity of $150\,\text{gal},$ so we can use the condition $V({t}_{o})=150$ to solve for ${t}_{o}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}V({t}_{o}) & =150 \\ 60+9{t}_{o}-6{t}_{o} & =150 \\ 60+3{t}_{o} & =150 \\ 3{t}_{o} & =90 \\ {t}_{o} & =30\,\text{min}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, rounded to one decimal place, the amount of ink dye in the reservoir at the moment it begins to overflow is

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(30) & =4(20+30)-62{\left(\frac{20}{20+30}\right)}^{2} \\  & =200-62{\left(\frac{20}{50}\right)}^{2} \\  & ≈190.1\,\text{lb}.\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186502074 :question/problem "A rinse tank initially holds $240\,\text{L}$ of water containing $9\,\text{kg}$ of dissolved dye.
A solution containing $0.025\,\text{kg/L}$ of dissolved dye is pumped into the tank at a rate of $16\,\text{L/min},$ while the completely mixed water is drained out at a rate of $24\,\text{L/min}.$ If the amount of dye $Q(t),$ in kilograms, in the tank $t$ minutes after pumping begins is given by

$$
Q(t)=\alpha \,\left(1-\frac{t}{30}\right)+\beta {\left(1-\frac{t}{30}\right)}^{3}
$$

where $\alpha $ and $\beta $ are constants, what is the value of $\alpha -\beta ?$"] [17592186502074 :question/worked-solution "Since $Q$ is the amount of dye in the tank at time $t,$ the derivative 

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}
$$

describes how this amount changes with respect to time $t,$ in minutes. This is equal to the rate at which dye enters the tank minus the rate at which dye leaves the tank.

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}
$$

Note that the units of $\frac{dQ}{dt},{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}$ and ${Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}$ are $\text{kg}/\text{min}.$ Now, let's compute the required rates of change in steps.

**Step 1**: Calculating the rate at which dye enters the tank.

First, note that a water solution containing $0.025\,\text{kg/L}$ of dye enters the tank at a rate of $16\,\text{L/min}.$ So, the rate at which the *dye* enters the tank is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′} & =\left(0.025\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{L}}\right)\cdot \left(16\,\frac{\text{L}}{\text{min}}\right) \\  & =\left(0.025\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\cancel{\text{L}}}\right)\cdot \left(16\,\frac{\cancel{\text{L}}}{\text{min}}\right) \\  & =0.4\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Calculating the rate at which dye exits the tank.

To find the rate at which dye leaves the tank, we must first determine the volume of water in the tank at time $t.$

The tank initially contains $240\,\text{L}$ of water; a solution enters at $16\,\text{L/min}$ and leaves at $24\,\text{L/min}.$
As a result, the amount of water in the tank after $t$ minutes is 

$$
240+16t-24t=(240-8t)\,\text{L}.
$$

Since $Q$ is the amount of dye in the tank, the *concentration* of the mixed solution at time $t$ is

$$
\frac{Q}{240-8t}\,\text{kg/L}.
$$

Therefore, as the completely mixed water leaves at a rate of $24\,\text{L/min},$ *dye* leaves at a rate of

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} & =\left(24\,\frac{\text{L}}{\text{min}}\right)\cdot \left(\frac{Q}{240-8t}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{L}}\right) \\  & =\left(24\,\frac{\cancel{\text{L}}}{\text{min}}\right)\cdot \left(\frac{Q}{240-8t}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\cancel{\text{L}}}\right) \\  & =\frac{24Q}{240-8t}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{min}} \\  & =\frac{3Q}{30-t}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Calculate the overall rate of change.

The rate of change equals the rate of entry minus the rate of exit. Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dQ}{dt} & ={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} \\  & =0.4-\frac{3Q}{30-t}\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the equation

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dQ}{dt}+\frac{3}{30-t}Q=0.4.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 4**: Integrate the equation.

This is a first-order linear equation with variable coefficients. So we find the general solution using an integrating factor:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(t) & ={e}^{\int 3/(30-t)\,dt} \\  & ={e}^{-3\operatorname{ln}⁡|30-t|} \\  & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(30-t)^{-3}} \\  & =(30-t)^{-3}\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying both sides of the differential equation by $I(t)=(30-t)^{-3}$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}(30-t)^{-3}\cdot \left(\frac{dQ}{dt}+\frac{3}{30-t}Q\right) & =(30-t)^{-3}\cdot 0.4 \\ (30-t)^{-3}\frac{dQ}{dt}+3(30-t)^{-4}Q & =0.4(30-t)^{-3} \\ \frac{d}{dt}(Q(30-t)^{-3}) & =0.4(30-t)^{-3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate with respect to $t:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{d}{dt}(Q(30-t)^{-3})\,dt & =\int 0.4(30-t)^{-3}\,dt \\ Q(30-t)^{-3} & =0.4\cdot \frac{1}{2}(30-t)^{-2}+C \\ Q(t) & =0.2(30-t)+C(30-t)^{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $C$ is a constant of integration.

We're told that the tank initially contains $9\,\text{kg}$ of dye. So, we can apply the initial condition $Q(0)=9,$ and solve for $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(0) & =9 \\ C(30-0)^{3}+0.2(30-0) & =9 \\ C(30)^{3}+6 & =9 \\ C & =\frac{3}{{30}^{3}}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we obtain the following expression for $Q(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(t) & =0.2(30-t)+\frac{3}{{30}^{3}}(30-t)^{3} \\  & =0.2\cdot 30\,\left(\frac{30-t}{30}\right)+3{\left(\frac{30-t}{30}\right)}^{3} \\  & =6\,\left(1-\frac{t}{30}\right)+3{\left(1-\frac{t}{30}\right)}^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we have $\alpha =6,\beta =3,$ and

$$
\alpha -\beta =6-3=3.
$$"] [17592186502075 :question/worked-solution "Given a population in which a proportion $p$ of the population has a particular characteristic, the sampling distribution of the sample proportion $\widehat{\,p}$ can be approximated as

$$
\widehat{\,p}∼N\left(p,\frac{p(1-p)}{n}\right),
$$

where the sample size $n$ is much smaller than the population size, $np>5,$ and $n(1-p)>5.$

In our case

- the sample size is $n=99,$ and

- the population proportion is $p=0.45.$

Now, since

$$
np=99(0.45)=44.55>5
$$

and

$$
n(1-p)=99(1-0.45)=54.45>5,
$$

and $n=99$ is much smaller than the population size, we can apply the above approximation.

The sampling distribution of the sample proportion, in this case, can be approximated as

$$

describes how this amount changes with respect to time $t.$ This is equal to the rate at which cleanser enters the tank minus the rate at which cleanser leaves the tank.

$$

$$

Note that the units of $\frac{dQ}{dt},{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}$ and ${Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}$ are $\text{kg}/\text{min}.$ Now, let's compute the required rates of change in steps.

**Step 1**: Calculating the rate at which additives enter the tank.

Note that a feed solution containing $0.04\,\text{kg/L}$ of the cleanser enters the tank at a rate of $15\,\text{L/min}.$ So, the rate at which the *cleanser* enters the tank is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′} & =\left(0.04\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{L}}\right)\cdot \left(15\,\frac{\text{L}}{\text{min}}\right) \\  & =\left(0.04\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\cancel{\text{L}}}\right)\cdot \left(15\,\frac{\cancel{\text{L}}}{\text{min}}\right) \\  & =0.6\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Calculating the rate at which additives exit the tank.

Next, note that the rate of flow in equals the rate of flow out, so the volume in the tank remains $600\,\text{L}.$ Then, since $Q$ is the amount of cleanser in the tank, the *concentration* of the solution at time $t$ is

$$
\frac{Q}{600}\,\text{kg/L}.
$$

Therefore, as the completely mixed liquid leaves at a rate of $15\,\text{L/min},$ *cleanser* leaves at a rate of

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} & =\left(15\,\frac{\text{L}}{\text{min}}\right)\cdot \left(\frac{Q}{600}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{L}}\right) \\  & =\left(15\,\frac{\cancel{\text{L}}}{\text{min}}\right)\cdot \left(\frac{Q}{600}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\cancel{\text{L}}}\right) \\  & =\frac{15Q}{600}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{min}} \\  & =\frac{Q}{40}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Calculate the overall rate of change.

The rate of change equals the rate of entry minus the rate of exit. Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dQ}{dt} & ={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} \\  & =0.6-\frac{Q}{40}\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the equation

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}+\frac{1}{40}Q=0.6.
$$

**Step 4**: Integrate the equation.

This is a first-order linear equation with constant coefficients. To find the general solution, we must sum the complementary and particular solutions.

- To find the complementary solution ${Q}_{c},$ we solve the corresponding homogeneous equation, given by

$$
\frac{d{Q}_{c}}{dt}+\frac{1}{40}{Q}_{c}=0.
$$

Solving using an integration technique, such as separation of variables, we obtain the complementary solution

$$
{Q}_{c}(t)=A{e}^{-t/40},
$$

where $A$ is a constant of integration.

- Next, we find the particular solution. Note that the right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is a polynomial of degree $0.$ So, we assume that the particular solution is also a polynomial of degree $0,$ i.e.,

$$
{Q}_{p}(t)=\alpha .
$$

To find the value of $\alpha ,$ we substitute ${Q}_{p}=\alpha $ and $\frac{d{Q}_{p}}{dt}=(\alpha )^{′}=0$ into the inhomogeneous equation:

$$
0+\frac{1}{40}\alpha =0.6\,⟹\,\alpha =24.
$$

Therefore, the particular solution is ${Q}_{p}(t)=24.$

Now, since the general solution is given by the sum of the complementary solution and the particular solution, the general solution in our case is

$$
Q(t)={Q}_{c}(t)+{Q}_{p}(t)=A{e}^{-t/40}+24.
$$

We're told that the tank initially contains $10\,\text{kg}$ of dissolved cleanser. So, we can apply the initial condition $Q(0)=10,$ and solve for $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(0) & =10 \\ A{e}^{-0/40}+24 & =10 \\ A & =-14\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$"] [17592186502085 :question/worked-solution "Given a population in which a proportion $p$ of the population has a particular characteristic, the sampling distribution of the sample proportion $\widehat{\,p}$ can be approximated as

$$

and

and $n=65$ is much smaller than the population size, we can apply the above approximation.

The sampling distribution of the sample proportion, in this case, can be approximated as

$$

$$

Next, we determine the probability we wish to find. If more than $13$ but fewer than $26$ people bought something, then 

$$

$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(0.2\le \widehat{\,p}\le 0.4) & =Φ(0.85)-Φ(-2.54).\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186502100 :question/worked-solution "Let $Q$ be the amount of salt in the tank at time $t.$ Then, the derivative 

$$

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}

Note that the units of $\frac{dQ}{dt},{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}$ and ${Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}$ are $\text{lb}/\text{min}.$ Now, let's compute the required rates of change in steps.

**Step 1**: Calculating the rate at which salt enters the tank.

Note that fresh water (i.e., water containing $0\,\text{lb/gal}$ of salt) enters the tank at a rate of $12\,\text{gal/min}.$ So, the rate at which the *salt* enters the tank is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′} & =\left(0\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{gal}}\right)\cdot \left(12\,\frac{\text{gal}}{\text{min}}\right) \\  & =\left(0\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\cancel{\text{gal}}}\right)\cdot \left(12\,\frac{\cancel{\text{gal}}}{\text{min}}\right) \\  & =0\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Calculating the rate at which salt exits the tank.

To find the rate at which salt leaves the tank, we first determine the volume of brine in the tank at time $t.$

The tank initially contains $420\,\text{gal}$ of brine; water enters at $12\,\text{gal/min}$ and drains out at $12\,\text{gal/min}.$
As a result, the amount of brine in the tank after $t$ minutes is 

$$
420+12t-12t=420\,\text{gal}.
$$

Since $Q$ is the amount of salt in the tank, the *concentration* of the brine at time $t$ is

$$
\frac{Q}{420}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{gal}}.
$$

Therefore, as the completely mixed brine leaves at a rate of $12\,\text{gal/min},$ *salt* leaves at a rate of

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} & =\left(12\,\frac{\text{gal}}{\text{min}}\right)\cdot \left(\frac{Q}{420}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{gal}}\right) \\  & =\left(12\,\frac{\cancel{\text{gal}}}{\text{min}}\right)\cdot \left(\frac{Q}{420}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\cancel{\text{gal}}}\right) \\  & =\frac{12Q}{420}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{min}} \\  & =\frac{Q}{35}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Calculate the overall rate of change.

The rate of change equals the rate of entry minus the rate of exit. Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dQ}{dt} & ={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} \\  & =0-\frac{Q}{35}\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the equation

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}=-\frac{1}{35}\,Q.
$$

**Step 4**: Integrate the equation.

Separating variables and integrating both sides with respect to $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{Q}\cdot \frac{dQ}{dt} & =-\frac{1}{35} \\ \int \frac{1}{Q}\cdot \frac{dQ}{dt}dt & =\int \left(-\frac{1}{35}\right)\,dt \\ \int \frac{1}{Q}\cdot \,dQ & =-\frac{1}{35}\int 1\,dt \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|Q| & =-\frac{t}{35}+C \\ |Q| & ={e}^{-\frac{t}{35}+C} \\ Q(t) & =A{e}^{-t/35},\end{aligned}
$$

where $A=\pm {e}^{C}$ is a constant of integration.

We're told that the tank initially contains $14\,\text{lb}$ of salt. So, we can apply the initial condition $Q(0)=14,$ and solve for $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(0) & =14 \\ A{e}^{-0/35} & =14 \\ A & =14\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we obtain the following expression for $Q(t):$

$$
Q(t)=14{e}^{-t/35}
$$

Finally, the amount of salt in the tank $20$ minutes after the fresh water is first pumped in is

$$
Q(20)=14{e}^{-20/35}≈7.91\,\text{lb},

rounded to two decimal places."] [17592186502104 :question/worked-solution "Let $Q$ be the amount of cleaning agent in the tank at time $t,$ in minutes. Then, the derivative

\begin{aligned}n & =30 \\  & \le 5\%\cdot N \\  & =0.05\cdot 1\,000 \\  & =50\,✓ \\ np & =30(0.7) \\  & =21 \\  & >5\,✓ \\ n(1-p) & =30(1-0.7) \\  & =9 \\  & >5.\,✓\end{aligned}

Therefore, we can approximate the distribution of $\widehat{\,p}$ using the given model.

Therefore, the correct answer is "II and III only.""] [17592186502115 :question/worked-solution "Since $Q$ is the amount of dissolved chemical in the tank at time $t,$ the derivative 

$$

$$

describes how this amount changes with respect to time $t,$ in minutes. This is equal to the rate at which dissolved chemical enters the tank minus the rate at which dissolved chemical leaves the tank.

$$

Note that the units of $\frac{dQ}{dt},{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}$ and ${Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}$ are $\text{kg}/\text{min}.$ Now, let's compute the required rates of change in steps.

**Step 1**: Calculating the rate at which dissolved chemical enters the tank.

First, note that a chemical solution containing $0.20\,\text{kg/L}$ of dissolved chemical enters the tank at a rate of $16\,\text{L/min}.$ So, the rate at which the *dissolved chemical* enters the tank is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′} & =\left(0.20\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{L}}\right)\cdot \left(16\,\frac{\text{L}}{\text{min}}\right) \\  & =\left(0.20\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\cancel{\text{L}}}\right)\cdot \left(16\,\frac{\cancel{\text{L}}}{\text{min}}\right) \\  & =3.2\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Calculating the rate at which dissolved chemical exits the tank.

Now, to find the rate at which dissolved chemical leaves the tank, we must first determine the volume of solution in the tank at time $t.$

- The tank initially contains $280\,\text{L}$ of solution.

- Chemical solution enters the tank at a rate of $16\,\text{L/min}.$ So, after $t$ minutes, $16t\,\text{L}$ have entered the tank.

- The completely mixed solution leaves the tank at a rate of $16\,\text{L/min}.$ So, after $t$ minutes, $16t\,\text{L}$ have left the tank.

As a result, the volume of solution in the tank after $t$ minutes is 

$$
280+16t-16t=280\,\text{L}.
$$

Since $Q$ is the mass of dissolved chemical in the tank, the *concentration* of the solution at time $t$ is

$$
\frac{Q}{280}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{L}}.
$$

Therefore, as the completely mixed solution leaves at a rate of $16\,\text{L/min},$ *dissolved chemical* leaves at a rate of

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} & =\left(16\,\frac{\text{L}}{\text{min}}\right)\cdot \left(\frac{Q}{280}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{L}}\right) \\  & =\left(16\,\frac{\cancel{\text{L}}}{\text{min}}\right)\cdot \left(\frac{Q}{280}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\cancel{\text{L}}}\right) \\  & =\frac{16Q}{280}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{min}} \\  & =\frac{2Q}{35}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Calculate the overall rate of change.

Finally, the rate of change equals the rate of entry minus the rate of exit: 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dQ}{dt} & ={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} \\  & =3.2-\frac{2Q}{35}\end{aligned}
$$

which finally gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dQ}{dt}+\frac{2}{35}Q=3.2.\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186502117 :question/worked-solution "Given a population in which a proportion $p$ of the population has a particular characteristic, the sampling distribution of the sample proportion $\widehat{\,p}$ can be approximated as

where the sample size $n$ is much smaller than the population size, $np>5,$ and $n(1-p)>5.$

In our case

$$

and $n=125$ is much smaller than the population size, we can apply the above approximation.

The sampling distribution of the sample proportion, in this case, can be approximated as

$$

$$

Next, we determine the probability we wish to find. If fewer than $40$ visitors in the sample rode the rollercoaster, then

So, we convert $\widehat{\,p}$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(\widehat{\,p}>0.4) & =P\left(Z<\frac{0.32-0.25}{\sqrt{0.0015}}\right) \\  & ≈P(Z<1.81) \\  & =Φ(1.81).\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186502122 :question/worked-solution "Since $Q$ is the amount of reactant in the reactor at time $t,$ the derivative 

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}
$$

describes how this amount changes with respect to time $t,$ in minutes. This is equal to the rate at which reactant enters the reactor minus the rate at which reactant leaves the reactor.

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}
$$

Note that the units of $\frac{dQ}{dt},{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}$ and ${Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}$ are $\text{kg}/\text{min}.$ Now, let's compute the required rates of change in steps.

**Step 1**: Calculating the rate at which reactant enters the reactor.

First, note that the incoming solvent (i.e., a solution containing $0\,\text{kg/L}$ of reactant) enters the reactor at a rate of $16\,\text{L/min}.$ So, the rate at which the *reactant* enters the reactor is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′} & =\left(0\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{L}}\right)\cdot \left(16\,\frac{\text{L}}{\text{min}}\right) \\  & =\left(0\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\cancel{\text{L}}}\right)\cdot \left(16\,\frac{\cancel{\text{L}}}{\text{min}}\right) \\  & =0\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Calculating the rate at which reactant exits the reactor.

Now, to find the rate at which reactant leaves the reactor, we must first determine the volume of solution in the reactor at time $t.$

- The reactor initially contains $520\,\text{L}$ of solution.

- Solvent enters the reactor at a rate of $16\,\text{L/min}.$ So, after $t$ minutes, $16t\,\text{L}$ have entered the reactor.

- The completely mixed solution leaves the reactor at a rate of $20\,\text{L/min}.$ So, after $t$ minutes, $20t\,\text{L}$ have left the reactor.

As a result, the volume of solution in the reactor after $t$ minutes is 

$$
520+16t-20t=(520-4t)\,\text{L}.
$$

Since $Q$ is the mass of reactant in the reactor, the *concentration* of the solution at time $t$ is

$$
\frac{Q}{520-4t}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{L}}.
$$

Therefore, as the completely mixed solution leaves at a rate of $20\,\text{L/min},$ *reactant* leaves at a rate of

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} & =\left(20\,\frac{\text{L}}{\text{min}}\right)\cdot \left(\frac{Q}{520-4t}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{L}}\right) \\  & =\left(20\,\frac{\cancel{\text{L}}}{\text{min}}\right)\cdot \left(\frac{Q}{520-4t}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\cancel{\text{L}}}\right) \\  & =\frac{20Q}{520-4t}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{min}} \\  & =\frac{5Q}{130-t}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Calculate the overall rate of change.

Finally, the rate of change equals the rate of entry minus the rate of exit: 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dQ}{dt} & ={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} \\  & =0-\frac{5Q}{130-t}\end{aligned}
$$

which finally gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dQ}{dt}+\frac{5}{130-t}Q=0.\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186502123 :question/worked-solution "Given a population in which a proportion $p$ of the population has a particular characteristic, the sampling distribution of the sample proportion $\widehat{\,p}$ can be approximated as

$$

where the sample size $n$ is much smaller than the population size, $np>5,$ and $n(1-p)>5.$

$$
np=50(0.2)=10>5

and

$$

and $n=50$ is much smaller than the population size, we can apply the above approximation.

The sampling distribution of the sample proportion, in this case, can be approximated as

$$
\begin{aligned}\widehat{\,p} & ∼N\left(p,\frac{p(1-p)}{n}\right) \\  & ∼N\left(0.2,\frac{0.2(1-0.2)}{50}\right) \\  & ∼N(0.2,0.0032).\end{aligned}

The probability we wish to find is

So, we convert $\widehat{\,p}$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
